# P r e f a c e .

In the effort to trace the more distant sources of the systems of **Fichte**, **Schelling**, and **Hegel**, I have been led back to the German mysticism of the 14th century. As soon as the figure of **Master Eckhart** <note>Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328) was a German theologian, philosopher, and mystic whose work influenced later German philosophy.</note> first appeared before me, it captivated me with irresistible force. An opportunity to share what I found in his work arose through a request from my friend **Ueberweg**, who included a section I had prepared on German mysticism in the second part of his work: "**Outline of the History of Philosophy**" in its 2nd and 3rd editions. However, precisely during the preparation of this section, it became clear to me that it would be useful to treat the subject more extensively. The more detailed presentations of **Eckhart's** doctrine by **R. Heidrich** (Posen, 1864) and by **Joseph Bach** (Vienna, 1864)—the only ones that had already utilized the material made accessible by **Pfeiffer's** 1857 edition—seemed to me insufficient for the task. Thus, I decided to make **Master Eckhart** the subject of a monograph. This narrowly defined task suited my temperament and my limited leisure; a certain spiritual kinship drew me toward the subject. Unless I overestimate **Eckhart's** significance too greatly, I may hope to have undertaken something useful.

My intention was to provide a contribution to the history of philosophical and religious thought in Germany and to bring the nation closer to one of its greatest sons. **Eckhart** appears to me as a true reflection of German character; his significance for the

<summary>The author explains his motivation for writing a monograph on Master Eckhart, linking medieval German mysticism to the later philosophical systems of Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel.</summary>
<keywords>Master Eckhart, German Mysticism, History of Philosophy, German Idealism, Friedrich Ueberweg, Franz Pfeiffer, 14th Century</keywords>

# Preface

The cultural life of the German people is very great. I would like to assume that, in all silence, the influence of the thoughts first expressed by him <note>Referring to Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328), a German theologian and philosopher.</note> continues to this day. It was therefore not merely a historical interest that guided me; it was a matter of bringing the newest ideas into their natural connection with the old, which lies in the common ground and soil of the German national spirit. Even upon the intellectual circles of the immediate present, a renewed acquaintance with Eckhart might not remain without influence. A form of speculation <note>In this context, "speculation" refers to deep philosophical or theological contemplation.</note> related in many features to the old mysticism, which had displaced the sober view of the intellect, has in its turn been displaced by a trend toward a rigid dogmatism. This dogmatism has finally progressed so far that it is destroying itself in endless and hollow disputes between the Union and Confession <note>Refers to the 19th-century debates between the Prussian Union of churches and traditional Lutheran/Reformed confessions.</note>. Alongside this goes the decomposing work of historical criticism, which seeks to eliminate not only the valid sources of divine revelation but, along with them, the very content of Christian doctrine. How the fundamental ideas of Christianity maintain all their power and significance—even if one were to disregard the strict closure of a dogmatism fixed in intellectual concepts and the sole validity of the source of revelation—is something the example of German mysticism can teach. Above all, however, it is the fundamental ethical outlook of Master Eckhart which seems entitled to claim not merely a historical, but an immediate interest for the generation now living.

The present work is intended essentially only as an incentive for the study of Eckhart. The passages from his writings, shared here in abundance, may serve as a kind of commentary. I have sought to translate these passages completely into our contemporary language; for it was my goal to facilitate understanding and to bring Eckhart’s circle of ideas closer to the present. I believe I have nowhere proceeded without care. That I will have failed in some things is probable; my hope is that many will take the trouble to correct my erroneous interpretations. The systematic form into which I have brought the Master’s thoughts seems

<keywords>Meister Eckhart, German mysticism, dogmatism, historical criticism, Christian doctrine, ethics, theological translation, 19th-century philosophy</keywords>

# Preface

seemed to me to arise simply and naturally from the present circle of ideas; I did not wish to impose them upon it. Others may judge whether I have proceeded with enough impartiality.

In order to guide the reader toward the correct points of view from which a figure like *Eckhart* <note>Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328) was a German theologian, philosopher, and mystic whose work was influential in the development of Western spirituality.</note> should be viewed, I have added a new attempt to define the concept of mysticism to the many existing ones. One still encounters the opinion that mysticism is a sentimental, unclear, and fanatical essence; the uncertain and blurred manner that is almost the rule in the scientific reproduction of mystical teachings must nourish such a prejudice. With *Eckhart* at least, it is the fault of the presenter if a well-constructed whole of firmly defined concepts is not presented, but rather a sum of loosely connected, approximate ideas is passed off as his teaching.

Not long after the reminder to *Franz Pfeiffer* <note>Franz Pfeiffer (1815–1868) was a pioneering scholar of German literature who produced the first major collection of Eckhart's works.</note> on page 62 was printed, news arrived of the death of that highly deserving man. He was no longer able to fulfill his promise to provide a literary-historical introduction to *Eckhart* along with notes and a glossary. For the study of German mysticism, *Pfeiffer’s* death is a very painful loss. *Pfeiffer* himself admitted that the text of *Eckhart* edited by him was not of equal value and correctness throughout; the means for correcting this text will not easily be gathered again by anyone to the extent that *Pfeiffer* was able to do through eighteen years of effort.

In our presentation, we have essentially adhered to the text as *Pfeiffer* established it. No significant objection can be raised against the authenticity of the pieces included by him. *Eckhart’s* spirit, way of looking at things, and expression distinguish him clearly enough even from his closest students and those of similar mind. The danger is rather that one might deny him much that originates from *Eckhart* because it has been made unrecognizable through bold reworking. Only Treatise VII (*Meister Eckhart*, edited by *Franz Pfeiffer*, pp. 475–478) seems not to originate from *Eckhart*; it [corresponds] with the sermon

# Preface

matches Chapter II in the "History of Doctor Tauler" <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous Dominican mystic and disciple of Eckhart</note>. Could a piece by Eckhart have been chosen to exemplify a perverse way of preaching? However, the wearying enumeration of 24 signs of piety deviates too much from Eckhart's usual style. — Sayings 61–65 (p. 622) are fragments of Sermon LXXVII (pp. 249–251); Sayings 3, 12, and 26 are also taken from existing sermons. — Sermon LXXVI, 2 (pp. 243–249) repetitively merges Sermon LXXV (pp. 235–238) and LXXVI, 1 (pp. 238–243). — Treatise III (pp. 394–416) is composed of nothing but individual fragments of Eckhart's work, the majority of which we find again in their proper places within Pfeiffer's collection <note>Franz Pfeiffer's 1857 edition of Eckhart's works was the first major attempt to collect his German writings</note>. — In Greith (*German Mysticism in the Order of Preachers*, Freiburg im Breisgau 1861, pp. 96–202), the writing of a mystic is shared which—discounting a few passages borrowed from Suso <note>Heinrich Suso (1295–1366), another influential student of Eckhart</note> and Tauler—consists almost entirely of fragments from Eckhart; by far the largest part of these, about 100 in number, can still be identified in Pfeiffer's text. — More than 70 times, Eckhart cites statements that he himself has made, and these too are for the most part identifiable in our collection, just as the propositions of Eckhart condemned by the Pope <note>Referring to the papal bull "In Agro Dominico" (1329) which condemned 28 of Eckhart's articles as heretical or dangerous</note> are preserved for us in their correct and natural context. Thus, not only can the material in the Pfeiffer collection be proven authentic almost without exception, but it also seems to encompass the essential core of Eckhart's thoughts in sufficient completeness.

One must, of course, be prepared for the fact that the text has suffered unspeakably in parts through the misunderstanding or carelessness of the scribes. This is particularly easy to see in the pieces that formerly circulated under foreign names, such as many sermons found among those of Tauler (Sermons I–IV, VI, VII, XVII, XL–XLII, XLVII [attributed to Eckhart the Younger], LVII [attributed to Ruusbroec], LXIX, LXXVI, 1, LXXVII), as well as Treatise I, which is found in the *Marrow of the Soul* <note>original: "Medulla animae"</note> attributed to Tauler, Chapter 38, and Treatise XVII, which is found in the same place and as a writing of Ruusbroec *On Certain Principal Virtues* <note>original: "de praecipuis quibusdam virtutibus"</note>. These pieces are undoubtedly Eckhart's property; but especially the

-># Preface<-

both treatises are most grossly distorted in the writings of Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a Dominican mystic</note> and Ruusbroec <note>Jan van Ruusbroec (1293–1381), a Flemish mystic</note>. Where the tradition is faithful, Eckhart’s language is as simple and heartfelt as his thought is clear and transparent; only exceptionally, and where the content makes it unavoidable, does any obscurity of expression occur. Due to the carelessness of the scribes, much has become completely unintelligible. I have endeavored to restore some of the lesser passages, partly with the help of the edition of Tauler's Sermons (Basel, 1521) and the manuscripts of the Royal Library here. I designate these sources as Pfeiffer does (*Meister Eckhart*, Preface, pp. VIII–X) with the letters *d*, *D*, *E*, *c*, *e*. The changes to Pfeiffer’s text <note>Franz Pfeiffer's 1857 edition was the standard at the time, though often criticized for its inaccuracies</note>, which I consider to be somewhat certain, I list here, simply to give an account of my work and to invite others to a thorough study of the text. Some improvements might prove to be evident; most I offer as entirely non-binding suggestions. These improvements were initially undertaken solely for the purpose of making the text readable. No one will be more grateful for further instruction than I.

# Introduction.

## On the Value and Essence of Mysticism.

Mysticism, in the realm of religious life, is the standpoint on which the *immanence* <note>The philosophical and theological concept that the divine is present and active within the physical world and the human soul, rather than being entirely separate or external.</note> of the infinite in the finite and of the finite in the infinite is primarily maintained and emphasized. In this respect, mysticism is not so much a unified, closed worldview as it is a spiritual direction and disposition to adopt religious content in a certain form; this disposition determines the understanding of doctrine through knowledge just as much as it colors religious stirrings of feeling and the expression of what is felt and known in those manifestations of life determined by the will. This one thing is the common element in all the various forms in which mysticism presents itself as a historical phenomenon. It is initially only a kind of mood and inclination, of an immediate nature, and not mediated through scientific <note>original: "wissenschaftlich." In this 19th-century context, this refers to systematic, academic, or rigorous intellectual study rather than just natural sciences.</note> thought; but then the striving to explain and justify itself systematically also follows. The mystic’s gaze clings to the finite only to find in all its life-movements the reflection of the One and Infinite, or to the infinite, in order to see within it the dissolution of all finite and determinate being. In the realm of natural religions, where the divine is primarily grasped as power and only incidentally as holiness, the mystic, with this immediate certainty of the one, all-encompassing being, will primarily revel in the feeling of how all the glory of individual beings

<vocab>Mysticism, Immanence, Infinite, Finite, Natural Religions, Holiness, Manifestations of Life</vocab>

<summary>This introductory page defines mysticism as a spiritual disposition centered on the mutual immanence of the finite and the infinite, serving as a lens through which all religious knowledge and feeling are filtered. It describes mysticism as both an immediate emotional state and a systematic intellectual pursuit.</summary>
<keywords>Mysticism, Immanence, the Infinite, religious philosophy, natural religion, systematic thought</keywords>

In the realm of the Christian religion—for Judaism and mysticism are mutually exclusive opposites <note>The author here reflects a common 19th-century theological view that saw Judaism as a religion of strict distance between God and man, which he considers the opposite of the mystic's "oneness."</note>, while the mysticism of Islam stands on the ground of natural religion—in Christian mysticism, then, the more Christian it is, the more the moral standpoint will prevail. According to this view, God and the human soul are only incidentally <note>original: "zufällig." In this context, it means that their separation is a secondary circumstance or a temporary state, rather than an essential, permanent division.</note> separated, but are rather one in essence; and according to this, this unity *can* and *should* be established through a specific attitude of God toward the soul and of the soul toward God.

An opposing standpoint faces mysticism: that of transcendence, in which the infinite appears at an infinite distance from the finite; here, the separation of the two is their essence, and their unity is only something incidental and occasional that occurs under specific conditions. Thus, neither of the two standpoints absolutely excludes the other; a remnant of transcendence will be present in every doctrine of immanence <term>Immanenzlehre: the belief that the divine is present within the material world</term>, and a remnant of immanence in every doctrine of transcendence. But in almost no individual case will it remain undecided which of the two perspectives is the predominant power that conditions the whole.

Christianity is the doctrine that the entire fullness of the Godhead appeared in the man Jesus—who appeared under specific historical conditions but simultaneously through the direct supersensual workings of God—and that through this, access to reconciliation with God has been opened to all people. Both of the aforementioned ways of looking at things find ample points of connection in Christian doctrine. Man *can* be reconciled with God; yet initially, he is nonetheless separated from God, in a state of sin. God became man, but initially only this one time, in one specific individual, and we others thus remain nonetheless separated from him in our creaturely <note>original: "creatürlichen." Referring to the status of being a created being, as opposed to the Creator.</note> finiteness by an unbridgeable chasm. Thus, within Christianity, there are not so much two different systems of doctrine as two spiritual directions <note>original: "Geistesrichtungen."</note>, each of which has a special inclination toward certain elements of Christian doctrine and prefers them over others; consequently, neither of these directions alone is able to exhaust the entire richness of Christian doctrine, but all in

# On the Value and Essence of Mysticism.

How these two directions develop alongside each other and influence one another is one of the perspectives that must be considered if the development of Christian doctrine and Christian life is to be understood. In general, one can say: wherever reconciliation with God is emphasized above all as the fundamental fact, we have a mystical standpoint; and wherever the emphasis is placed on sin as the cause of a real separation from God, we have the opposite standpoint before us. The actual golden age of religious mysticism within Christianity will therefore lie in that era where the consciousness of sin has not yet come to full dominance—in the pre-Reformation Catholic Church, which moves much more within the opposition of the profane and the sacred, the natural and the spiritual, than in that of sin and salvation.

The name "mysticism," which according to its etymology signifies a secret doctrine into which only chosen individuals are initiated, was assigned to this movement historically and only by chance; it is a commonly used <term>Terminus: technical term</term>, but it cannot claim to express the essence of the matter by virtue of its fundamental etymological meaning. The connection to the Greek <term>Mysterien: mysteries, referring to secret religious rites</term> inherent in the word contributes nothing to the clarification of the subject. In Holy Scripture, the most important doctrines of revelation are designated as <term>Mysterien: mysteries or secrets</term>, partly because they are presented in parables that only become fully understandable through further explanation, and partly because they transcend the power of natural reason and only become accessible to the spirit through divine revelation. The elder teachers of the Church—an Origen and Clement of Alexandria, Gregory the Great and Basil, but above all the so-called Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th or 6th-century author whose writings, falsely attributed to a convert of St. Paul, became the cornerstone of Christian mystical theology.</note>—distinguish within Christianity an esoteric <note>intended for a small, specialized circle</note> and an exoteric <note>intended for the general public</note> doctrine. The former, because it is graspable by only a few and remains a secret to the masses, is called "mystical," with an obvious resonance with the secret teachings of the mysteries that existed alongside Greek folk religion. For while in Scripture Christianity as such is designated as a mystery, these more speculative writers distinguish within Christianity between a popular and a mystical conception, and they separate that which should be taught to everyone from that which only a few are called to know. The masses, they argue, cannot grasp the pure truth in the form of the concept <term>Begriff: a technical philosophical term for a clear, abstract idea or logical definition</term>; for them, the representation of truth in the guise of a parable or figurative expression is the only suitable form. The spiritually mature, however, must press beyond the symbolic expression to the pure concept hidden behind it and strip away everything figurative in favor of pure cognition. Among these thinkers, the knowledge produced in this way essentially carries the color of Platonic and Neo-Platonic philosophy and promises an immediate and perfect contemplation of God—indeed, a becoming-one with God through the mediation of speculating reason and a moral life estranged from the world of the transitory. That distinction between an esoteric <note>intended for or likely to be understood by only a small number of people with specialized knowledge</note> and exoteric <note>intended for or likely to be understood by the general public</note> Christian doctrine did not carry over into later times, but the connection to Platonism certainly did; and it is precisely this Platonic coloring of Christianity that has remained a characteristic feature of all later mysticism.

Mysticism promises a deeper knowledge than the ordinary—indeed, the deepest possible. But it does not have the intention of shutting itself off from the uninitiated in dark riddles. On the contrary, some of its forms strive for the widest popularity. The aristocratic and exclusive character of Dionysian speculation <note>referring to the writings of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, which were highly influential but intellectually dense</note> did not pass into any of the mystical movements that followed Dionysius. German mysticism, for example, explicitly addresses the entire Christian people and seeks to be understandable to everyone in expression and train of thought. Romance mysticism <note>referring to mystical traditions from Latin-influenced cultures such as France, Italy, and Spain</note>, however, is at least a formally developed school of doctrine that claims not only to reveal the essence of Christian science to individuals, but to contain for everyone the deepest sense of revelation and the best guidance for a right and undivided life in Christ <note>original Latin: "in Christo"</note>. Mysticism is therefore far from being, by definition, a secret doctrine.

# On the Value and Essence of Mysticism

more or less clearly and scientifically developed, unfolding predominantly in the form of immediate intuition or conceptual thought, all the peculiarities that lead us to assign a mystical character to a standpoint emerge as natural consequences of the fundamental essence of this direction. First, a **doctrine of immanence** <term>Immanenzlehre: the philosophical belief that the divine or ultimate reality is present within the material world, rather than being separate from it</term> will always carry the character of a speculation that soars above the finite nature of experience and exact intellectual concepts. The intellect separates, establishes differences, and compares; mysticism, however, insists on unity. To the mystic, the infinite is already present within the finite; even in the realm of nature, it is that which possesses true essence; one only needs the eyes to see it. The finite is, in itself, already superseded within the infinite and becomes completely so in the realm of grace; it can therefore claim no true being for itself. Only that which remains eternally the same, the universal, the all-encompassing, is truly real; everything else has only an apparent, non-essential existence. To it belongs only an eternal becoming, which actually signifies a passing away into the infinite. If the senses perceive only the finite, and the intellect only clings to the finite relationships of things, then there is no truth in either. The exact-rational conception of things is unable to penetrate to the essence—the identity of the One and the Many. 

Thus, a higher spiritual faculty is required, which reaches the truth not through a successive rising to the ever-more-general—for in that way it would only slowly approach the goal, never reaching it—but all at once, suddenly, and not from its own intellectual power, but through the immediate influence of the Absolute Being upon the human spirit. All mysticism therefore demands a grasping of the truth by virtue of **intellectual intuition**, and wherever this is required as the organ of knowledge, an essential element of the mystical way of thinking is present.

One can see how much ground was prepared for such a recognition in Plato, Plotinus, and Proclus <note>These Greek philosophers (specifically the Neoplatonists Plotinus and Proclus) were foundational to mystical thought, emphasizing the soul's direct union with "the One"</note>. Philosophy on the ground of Christianity, which set itself the task of bringing the fundamental concepts of Christian doctrine to light according to their inner rational connection, has everywhere connected itself to the existing elements from the thought-circles of the great...

### Introduction

...connected to Greek thinkers. Mysticism could not refrain from referring to Platonic and Neoplatonic <term>Neoplatonism: a philosophical system, originating in the 3rd century AD, which expanded on Plato's ideas to describe how all existence flows from a single source called "the One"</term> teachings, which were so closely related to its own way of thinking. The pagan thinkers themselves appeared to the mystic in a glorified light, as carriers of a kind of revelation. The earliest mystics were essentially Platonists; they sought and found the doctrine of Christ and the Triune God already within the work of the creator of the **Theory of Forms** <term>Theory of Forms: Plato’s belief that the material world is only a shadow of a higher, eternal reality of "Ideas" or "Forms"</term>, and even more so among his later followers. In these followers, they recognized only their agreement with the founder of the Academy, but not the profound modifications of his teachings. Thus, mysticism became almost entirely a Platonism modified by Christian ideas, and we should not be surprised if some mystics venerate figures like Plato and Proclus almost as "Christians before Christ."

This, then, primarily describes the essence of mysticism: the dominance of an **intuition** that—elevated above the finite categories of the intellect—everywhere presses toward a unifying oneness. Skipping over the finite and the individual, it anticipates absolute totality; it then "sees" every individual thing within this Absolute as an integral moment, rather than deriving the individual from it. Just as it strives beyond the limits of empirical thought in general, it specifically reaches out beyond space and time, viewing all things "from the perspective of eternity" <note>original: "sub specie aeterni"</note>. While it rejects the validity of sensory perception, it trusts instead in **speculative reason**. To the mystic, knowledge based on images and symbols is too meager. The Absolute, which serves as the purely spiritual principle and the fundamental prerequisite of their vision, can only be perceived through a purely spiritual understanding.

It is, of course, a contradiction to conceive of God as the immanent essence of all things and yet demand a way of looking at this immanence <term>Immanence: the philosophical idea that the divine is present within every part of the universe</term> that transcends everything finite through a forceful abstraction. But the contradiction between the goal and the method is unavoidable from this standpoint. Pure immanence cannot be thought or expressed at all if one wishes to let the distinctness of things remain. Anyone who wanted to consider every individual thing one after another would never arrive at the most universal truth. Therefore, one does not "consider" the individual; one flies over it. Instead of the things themselves, one retains only the category of "being-a-thing," and says: God is in every thing, and every thing is in God, or God is

# On the Value and Nature of Mysticism

Everything, and everything is God. But in truth, what is meant is this: it is not the physical stone that exists within God, but rather the "idea" of the stone—and strictly speaking, not even the specific idea of the stone, but the idea of "thing-ness" <note>German: *Dingsein*; the philosophical state of being a concrete, individual object</note> in general. This idea, which dwells within God, is also frequently connected to the "Son of God" <term>Son of God: used here in a philosophical sense to represent the "Logos" or Divine Word, the intermediary through which God creates the world</term> in accordance with religious language. 

The doctrine of immanence <term>Immanence: the belief that the divine is fully present and dwells within the material world</term>, when it is immediate and flies over the finite world rather than moving through it step-by-step, can only ever claim or postulate this presence; in reality, it cannot truly master the finite. If the material world is a mere illusion, how can God dwell within it? If it is a true essence, then it is God himself, and everything is merely one single God. How then can anything exist "outside" of God? How can there be a "many" instead of just a "one"? 

And yet, this doctrine of immanence has significance for both religion and science. Those who begin with a doctrine of immanence truly end up standing within transcendence <term>Transcendence: the belief that the divine exists entirely outside of and beyond the physical universe</term>; however, those whose fundamental view is transcendence strive—albeit involuntarily and unconsciously—toward immanence. For the more deeply we look at the world through exact methods, the more everything sensory reveals itself to be pure movement according to eternal laws. These laws are the working forms of a "highest Reason" <note>original: *höchste Vernunft*</note>, which does not drive things from the outside, but constitutes their own inner principle of life. If science is to possess a living conviction and a drive to push its problems further, it is essential to "anticipate" the highest goal, looking beyond everything currently gained through research. This very anticipation is also the necessary expression of religious consciousness, which seeks to clarify its immediate relationship to the Absolute <term>The Absolute: the ultimate, unconditional reality or God, viewed as the source of all being</term> and communicate it understandably. One must accept the doctrine of immanence not as the highest truth itself, but as the closest possible expression of an inner "fullness of life," and use that to determine the rightful boundaries within which it applies.

Every distinct quality is said to be already established and contained within the one absolute essence. By virtue of this fundamental principle, **pantheism** <term>Pantheism: the belief that the universe and God are identical, or that God is everything</term> is never far from any form of mysticism, even when there is a most determined effort to maintain a living, personal interaction with God. Mysticism can only grasp God as the "essence of all essences," and thus as the most abstract and content-less of all beings. For such a being, there is no positive expression; it can only be defined through negations—by stripping away everything that... <note>The author is describing the *via negativa* or "negative theology," where God is described only by what He is not (e.g., infinite, invisible) because He exceeds human language.</note>

### Introduction

it is not. The doctrine of immanence <term>Immanence: the belief that the divine is fully present and dwells within the material world</term> demands a most universal "Being" which is equally present in all creatures; however, for this very reason, it can no longer be anything specific in itself. Thus, it cannot truly be called a "Person" or "Spirit," nor can it possess will or knowledge; it performs no specific activity and possesses no distinguishing characteristics. It is an unconscious deception <note>German: *Erschleichung*; a logical fallacy or a "sneaking in" of a concept without proof</note> when the mystic takes this most abstract point at which he finally arrives—this Being that equals Nothingness <note>original: *Sein = Nichts*</note>—and conceptualizes it as "Spirit" or as "the Good," or even when he describes it as the "Absolute One" that excludes all multiplicity. Mysticism clings to this abstract unity from which it can find no exit, wandering about in its incomprehensible vastness, unable to reach any living, real individual existence. The finite does not exist, and "Being" is instead a contentless nothingness. In a futile effort to speak of this contentless Absolute in human language, the so-called Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Syrian theologian whose mystical writings had a profound influence on medieval thought</note> tosses about; his thinking, stripped of all sensory clarity, generates the hollowest "jingling of phrases" in which all thought is extinguished, and which he is unable to clarify, but only to repeat. His method remained authoritative for the entire Middle Ages, and even a Thomas Aquinas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic philosopher who attempted to synthesize Aristotelian philosophy with Christian principles</note> does not fundamentally rise above this abstract monism <term>Monism: the philosophical view that a variety of existing things can be explained in terms of a single reality or substance</term> when he is tasked with discussing the concept of the Absolute. The denial of a separate existence for finite things leads to acosmism <term>Acosmism: the belief that the world is unreal or illusory, and only the Absolute is real</term> as soon as any consistency in thought is pursued. In the ethical sphere, every relationship to the finite is rejected as the actual source of evil; the dissolution of all individual existence in both thought and desire becomes the true moral demand.

In the doctrine of God and His relationship to the world, the logical consequence of the mystical standpoint may still be veiled by the mood of a prayerful heart. However, it must emerge far more clearly in the conception of the nature and destiny of the human soul. God is immanent in the soul; the life of the soul is, at its root, the divine life itself: this is the most characteristic expression of the mystical perspective. All that is true and divine is innate to the soul from the very beginning; the soul needs only to remember it again. All divine ideas are the soul's inalienable property, and no matter how darkened reason may be, they slumber in its "ground" <note>German: *Grund*; likely referring to the *Seelengrund* or "ground of the soul," a central term in German mysticism (particularly Master Eckhart) denoting the deepest point where the soul and God are one</note>, in

The separation from God is, for the soul, merely something accidental and external; this separation can be absolutely abolished, and thus a full and limitless union with God occurs. Sin is merely <term>Privation: a lack or absence of something that should be present, rather than a positive force of evil in itself</term>; it can certainly obscure the image of God within man, but it cannot abolish it. Sin and hell are nothing "outside" of the divine; nothing can fall out of God. God and the soul are fundamentally one; this relationship, which is always present in itself, fully manifests in the sanctified person who has completely surrendered to the effect of the powers of grace. Thus, the difference between Christ and every individual human being is reduced to a relative one; everyone can become Christ, and even the sinner is only "not yet" what he can become. Even the earliest teachers of the Church, such as Justin <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist</note> and Clement of Rome <note>A leader in the early church of Rome in the late 1st century AD</note>, used the expression in this sense that man becomes “deified,” and with greater or lesser boldness, all mysticism has held fast to this view, which forms its most important characteristic.

Just as there are dangers for the recognition of a personal deity, a strict <term>Doctrine of Immanence: the belief that the divine is fully present within the material world and the human soul</term> also carries dangers for the recognition of human personality. The closer man is moved toward the Absolute, the sooner the essential nature of his personal, individual existence is disregarded, and the more emphasis is placed on the divine Reason that is the same in all individual human beings. This Reason appears as the true substance of the human being, while the distinguishing individuality is seen as merely <term>Accidental: in philosophical terms, a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing</term>, something already abolished in essence and to be abolished through the activity of human will and divine grace. Almost by chance, Aristotle provided support for such a notion through the introduction of the <term>Active Intellect: (original Greek: *nous poietikos*) a concept describing the part of the mind that makes thinking possible</term>; this doctrine appears in its most developed form in Averroist <term>Monopsychism: the belief that all human beings share a single, universal soul or intellect</term>, which in any case links itself to Aristotelian concepts only superficially. For mysticism, where it received its most consistent formation, the thought of the unity of all rational souls must have been a highly welcome one; it appears now as the divine image in the soul, now as the substantial spirit, the objective Reason, or the idea permeating all things, which thinks itself within the human individual. # Introduction

[...as an] <term>Accident: in philosophy, a non-essential property or quality of a thing; here, the soul is seen as an outward expression of God rather than an independent entity</term> of the infinite, with which he strives to unite as closely and intimately as possible in order to reach his true form. Personality is a form of finiteness; mysticism strives beyond personality in the grasping of the Absolute and, for that very reason, cannot allow personality to count as the true and highest form of the human soul.

The perspective of the <term>Doctrine of Immanence: the belief that the divine presence exists within and throughout the physical world and the human soul</term> becomes most easily understood as it expresses itself in the realm of ethics. If God is truly one with man, then God cannot be viewed merely as the Master, nor man merely as the Servant who must fulfill that Master's commandments. The task is, rather, to return to God as the true essence of one's own soul. God Himself expresses Himself in the soul through moral action. But then, moral action cannot be understood as a series of individual, disconnected decisions and deeds, but rather as a lasting determination of man's essence. The mystic becomes indifferent toward the outward work; he is concerned only with the inner state of the soul, which conditions all external activity. This state of devotion to God—that is, to the true essence of the soul itself—is holy love and the pure <term>Vision of God: the direct experience and knowledge of the divine, often called the Beatific Vision</term>, mediated through man’s perfect renunciation of his own individuality and of his desire for the <term>Creature: a theological term for any created thing (people, objects, or earthly pleasures) as opposed to the Creator</term>, for everything that is not God. That which is foreign is to be stripped away; it is not individual requirements that are to be fulfilled, but rather a state of indwelling in God that is to be established. All action is conditioned, something individual and finite; the task, however, is oneness with the infinite. The ethics of the mystic thus have a predominantly negative character toward all duties arising from the nature of finite circumstances, and demand above all pure devotion to the highest good and its activity within the soul—a purely passive state. The significance of the law and of individual duty recedes here; reason and will are to become one with God in knowledge and love, to sink into the <term>Absolute Ground: the deepest, most fundamental level of reality where the soul and God are indistinguishable</term>, and to forget oneself in the contemplation of the pure light. Mystical ethics culminate in pure contemplation as a passive state of seeing.

# On the Value and Nature of Mysticism.

[...to] experience and witness the indwelling of God within oneself. God, who works through all things, works most powerfully in the soul. One must listen closely for this revelation of God in the soul. Alongside this, the significance of external revelation recedes—that which one only hears about through others, or through the written or spoken word. The mystic demands a direct communion of the soul with God, an inner light—not merely one shared by others—to illuminate his darkness. He becomes more or less indifferent toward the dogmatic fixation of religious concepts; his religion is the overflowing of his entire personality into the Absolute, an indwelling of the soul in God and God in the soul. The religious element does not appear in him in bursts, as one moment among others; it fills him completely and determines his entire personality. A single theorem is not enough for him; he must experience and witness God within himself. It is not artificial <term>Scholarship: the German word 'Wissenschaft' here refers to formal, academic theology or systematic study rather than the modern natural sciences</term> that brings him closer to God, but rather the simple gaze of the spirit into the Spirit. All his religious life is not the fruit of his own knowledge, but the effect of the revelation personally granted to him. Because of this immediacy of his <term>Intuition: 'Anschauung,' the direct, non-intellectual perception of truth or the divine</term> of divine things, he places little value on elaborate thinking; his piety is simple and unassuming; in contrast to the artificially developed systems of a dogmatic theology, he strives everywhere for simple intuition. Since mysticism strives for a penetration of the entire personal life by the Divine—instead of the lofty art of a developed scholarship which a person can possess without it bearing fruit for their inner life—the milder forms of mysticism take on the character of a simple, biblical, and practical Christianity. This form of faith seeks to gain living fruit from knowledge for the <term>Sanctification: the process of being made holy and more like God</term> of one's own soul and the salvation of others, returning from developed systems to the simplicity of original expression.

The essential communication of God to the human soul is, according to the mystical perspective, a continuous, ever-repeating process. Thus, the history of revelation is not viewed as a one-time occurrence or a single fact, but is generalized and spiritualized. The means of representing individual facts <note>The German *Facta* refers to the historical events or "deeds" recorded in the Bible.</note> told in Scripture as symbols of these general conditions and states of the human soul is the **allegorical interpretation** of them; through this, their actual and original sense is often quite forgotten. As long as there has been deep reflection on the internal connection of Christian doctrine, allegorical interpretation has been used to read general concepts of reason into the wording of the holy text. Initially, this spiritualizing interpretation was intended only for the initiated and the knowledgeable; however, mysticism as a whole, even in its more popular directions, generally does not know how to contend with Holy Scripture in any other way. Admittedly, <term>Rationalism: A theological movement that emphasized human reason and morality over supernatural revelation or mystical experience</term> also makes use of allegorical interpretation; yet here too, mysticism is clearly enough distinguished from all rationalist nature. It sees everywhere images and symbols of the one and absolute Being, while allegorizing Rationalism contents itself with partial truths, especially with moralizing wisdom.

With its principle of **inner experience**, mysticism makes itself independent of external authority to a high degree. Faith, in its sense, is a divine life worked immediately by God within the believer, and the mediating powers of the church, ecclesiastical doctrine, and tradition are something secondary in this process. But it easily happens that the mystic leans his high and transcendent <term>Intuitions: 'Anschauungen,' referring to direct spiritual perceptions rather than just intellectual opinions</term> of the relationship between God and the soul against the concepts given in church doctrine as if against firm supports; he views the church institutions as the means to generate and strengthen the mystical life. Thus, everything that exists in the church in the way of fixed forms is viewed and interpreted—spiritualized—according to its deepest meaning and its ultimate purpose. The more a mood of simple and modest piety prevails in the mystic, the more "churchly" he will be personally, without this churchliness being necessitated by the principle of his peculiar religious conduct. It is therefore quite compatible with that liberation from external authority that many men of a mystical bent [remain] on the ground...

That commonality of fundamental views is not contradicted by the profound differences in which the mystical principle has historically manifested itself. The <term>doctrine of immanence: The philosophical and theological idea that the divine presence is manifested in and through the physical world and human experience, rather than being entirely separate from it</term> everywhere yields a high enthusiasm, the consciousness of the immediate proximity of the Divine; and more than any doctrine that primarily focuses on the transcendence <note>original: *Jenseitigkeit*</note> of God in relation to all created things, there prevails in mysticism a high idealism, a freedom from the constraints of reality, and an elevation above rational sobriety. It is especially those natures possessed by an exuberant longing for the ideal who have turned toward mysticism. 

But this idealism can set for itself very diverse goals and can become active in minds of very different temperaments. Filled with the consciousness of the all-pervading power of divine life, one person might ruthlessly surrender to the logic of their thoughts and, on the foundation of those basic views, build a religious system of doctrine from the predominant perspective of pure knowledge, transforming all faith into knowledge. With the same consciousness, another might turn to the practical shaping of life, in order to fill as many people as possible with the longing for the salvation of the soul and to shape all conditions of the external world according to this single point of view. # Introduction

## Introduction.

...dence <note>The text continues the word "transcendence" from the previous page.</note> of the matter is always carried out under the predominant influence of one or the other principle. For no human individual can expand themselves into the universe.

In any case, a philosophical doctrine of immanence <term>immanence: the belief that the divine is manifested in and through the material world and the human soul</term> is very close to mysticism. The relationship of the finite to the infinite is, if not the fundamental problem, at least one of the problems of philosophy among others; thus, the question of the relationship between God and the world is also treated by philosophers and has been answered by many in the sense of immanence. Insofar as mysticism is a theory, any system that aims for the identity of the infinite and the finite, of thinking and being—of the "One in the Many"—must remind us of it most vividly. And the more such a philosophical system adopts a religious character, the more it coincides with mysticism—such as the later teachings of Fichte <note>Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814), a key figure in German Idealism.</note> or Schelling’s "Identity Philosophy" <note>Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854); his Identity Philosophy argued that the objective world of nature and the subjective world of the mind are ultimately one.</note>. But mysticism as such is by no means mere philosophy, not a pure theory; rather, it is a principle that governs and permeates the spirit in its totality. Its essential form of appearance is a specific type of religious conduct, which manifests in each individual case as a way of teaching, feeling, or acting, depending on the given occasion. The mystic is compelled by the relationship to the infinite established within their personality, while the kindred philosopher is moved by the logical consequences that arise with necessity from a certain basis of thought.

In mysticism, pantheism <term>pantheism: the view that God and the universe are identical; "all is God"</term> is, in a sense, of a sporadic, impulsive nature, developed only as far as the particular religious mood demands. Philosophical pantheism, on the other hand, follows a chain of concepts and strives for universal cultivation. In the former, the involuntary association of ideas prevails—one which rules over the thinker more than it is ruled by them; in the latter, it is critical labor, which accounts for itself through constant reflection. Only occasionally, and not by necessity, do they meet. The religious character of mysticism is the reason it places everything under the viewpoint of teleology <term>teleology: the explanation of phenomena by the purpose or "end" they serve rather than by their physical causes</term>, while the speculative pantheism of philosophy usually remains fixed on the relationship of causality <term>causality: the principle of cause and effect</term>.

# On the Value and Essence of Mysticism.

...ships of affinity. <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "relationships" (German: *Beziehungen*) from the previous page.</note> Not in their fundamental principle; for **Rationalism** <term>Rationalism: a philosophical movement that prizes reason and logic above all other forms of knowledge</term> presupposes a rigid **transcendence**; but certainly in their further implications. Mysticism and Rationalism are both un-church-like, and even easily anti-church, in their tendencies; historically, too, they stood close together in both the 13th and 18th centuries. <note>The 13th century saw a rise in mystical movements like the Beguines, while the 18th century was the height of the Enlightenment (Rationalism).</note> Both strive for freedom from authority and reinterpret sacred tradition—one into metaphysical truths, the other into moral wisdom. Both relocate the process of salvation into the innermost core of the person and maintain the essential "God-likeness" of human reason.

But Rationalism rests firmly on this earth, on the perceived, finite world, and on the concepts of the reflecting intellect. Mysticism knows truth to be in the soul, but as a light from above; for the mystic, the primacy of reason over faith is not the primacy of natural reason, but of reason illuminated by **grace**. Rationalism sees God outside of us and strives for God-likeness through "doing right" and the fulfillment of the law; mysticism sees God within us and demands **God-equality** through an essential indwelling in God. The former relates to tradition critically; mysticism, even while believing itself to be submissively faithful, treats tradition as a symbolic expression of truth. Both standpoints are equally unhistorical; they isolate the individual and detach them from the chain of historical connection. However, while Rationalism views everything by the analogy of the finite, mysticism has no sense or understanding of the finite. If the former directs its exhortations to the "empirical man"—the person as they are in everyday life—the latter appeals to the latent "image of God" within us, in order to draw us into the **Abyss of the Absolute** <term>Abyss of the Absolute: a mystical term for the infinite and unknowable nature of God into which the soul sinks during union</term> as if into our true essence.

We have previously demonstrated that mysticism, as such, is not a secret doctrine. However, it must be admitted that it is not for everyone. Its prerequisite is, in every way, a particular **virtuosity** <note>original: "Virtuosität", referring here to a high degree of specialized spiritual skill or talent</note> of religious conduct. For it is a fact that we are all, by nature, stuck in a system of fixed, one-sided intellectual concepts, beyond which the mass of people—whether they have a conscious relationship to the supersensible or not—never advance. Indeed, mystics have always been aware that their way is only for those who are most advanced and

...accessible only to the enlightened, and in this respect, mysticism has always carried a kind of **aristocratic character**. <note>The author uses "aristocratic" not to mean social rank, but a spiritual elitism where only those with specific internal experiences can truly understand the doctrine.</note> Everything Christian, of course, places the highest, unsurpassable demands on a person, provided that a complete **rebirth** <term>Rebirth (German: Wiedergeburt): a total spiritual transformation of the individual's nature.</term> of the whole person and a ruthless devotion to God are made the prerequisites for salvation. Mysticism is a life in the element of the **Infinite**; its eye is fixed on the **supersensible**, and on the sensible only insofar as the supersensible appears within it. <note>The "supersensible" refers to things beyond the reach of the five senses, such as the soul or the divine.</note> In this context, one must completely disregard the common usage of the word. Thus, the word mysticism was and often is used for any doctrine that allows a "beyond" or a "heavenly realm" to reach over into the world of the finite and natural, and which attempts to explain the processes of earthly appearance by enlisting forces other than those originating from nature. It lies in the nature of the mystical outlook that it is supported by a heightened life of feeling and imagination just as much as it produces the same. The mystic is accompanied by a constant consciousness of the **Divine** <note>original: "Göttlichen"</note>, which dwells within him and all things. This consciousness, the less it allows for a designation in rational and exact concepts, often expresses itself in word and gesture in forms that bear the character of **religious enthusiasm** <term>Enthusiasm (German: Schwärmerei): in the 18th and 19th centuries, this term often carried a negative connotation of "fanaticism" or "excessive emotion," which the author here seeks to distinguish from "true" mysticism.</term>. Even if the exact clarity of finite intellectual concepts is lacking in mysticism, this does not mean that a conceptual lack of clarity or the vague blurriness of feeling and mood necessarily takes its place. Rather, mysticism strives for a **definiteness** and **firmness of knowledge** <note>original: "Bestimmtheit und Festigkeit des Erkennens"</note> peculiar to itself, seeking a clarity of a higher kind. In many cases, it seeks—with earnest, even sober effort and not in vain—a systematic development of knowledge. If one wanted to make "emotional lack of clarity" the defining hallmark of mysticism, not a single one of its great leaders would remain who could still be rightly called a mystic. One may certainly use the term "mystical" for those phenomena—which do not even occur exclusively on religious ground—where the drive for the mysterious or the excitations of a morbidly heightened emotional life predominate and make a clear and prudent understanding of things impossible. # Introduction.

[...manifestations] together; we are dealing with a single expression that is used for two entirely different things. Certainly, <term>Mysticism</term> <term>Mysticism (German: Mystik): Here, the author refers to the disciplined, philosophical pursuit of internal union with the divine.</term> easily connects with that unhealthy over-tension of feeling; but this is only an occasional, secondary phenomenon, a degeneration such as easily attaches itself to any spiritual direction that undertakes to penetrate beyond sober superficiality. Religious devotion can be far removed from actual <term>Mysticism</term> and yet take on that one-sided emotional or fanatical form. In particular, that overstrained and ecstatic emotional devotion, which interacts in sensory immediacy with Christ or Mary or the saints as if with physically present persons, is quite the opposite of the mystical mood, for which the holy personages become conceptual abstractions instead. 

If, on the other hand, the mystical perspectives are one-sidedly exaggerated and grasped only in dark feelings rather than in conceptual form, we obtain a variant of <term>Mysticism</term>, which one can well distinguish from true <term>Mysticism</term> as <term>mystical fanaticism</term> <term>Mystical Fanaticism (German: mystische Schwärmerei): An emotional or irrational distortion of spiritual insight.</term> and—since this term already exists—as <term>Mysticismus</term> <term>Mysticismus: A technical term used by the author to denote a confused, overly emotional, or intellectually weak form of mysticism, as opposed to the rigorous "Mystik."</term>. <term>Mysticismus</term> in this sense is the necessary consequence when the clearly defined series of views that constitute the essence of <term>Mysticism</term> is imperfectly grasped by people of limited thinking power but unlimited longing for the Highest. 

The mystic as such is not an ecstatic, not a visionary. Many branches of <term>Mysticism</term> have fundamentally condemned the visionary nature as a form of interaction with the divine that drags the spiritual down into the sensory. The true <term>mystical ecstasy</term> <term>Mystical Ecstasy (German: mystische Ekstase): In this context, not a wild trance, but a profound "calm of thinking contemplation."</term> is the rest of thinking contemplation, which, sublime above everything finite, sinks itself through intuition and love into the absolute essence. However, it is a pure misuse of the word to describe saints and miracle-workers—especially of the Catholic Church—or people generally distinguished by personal devotion and a high intensification of religious feeling even to the point of <term>fanaticism</term> <note>original: "Schwärmerei"</note> as "mystics" for that reason alone and without the addition of essential characteristics, if they are thereby to be placed in a category of similarity with figures such as <term>Erigena</term> <note>Johannes Scotus Erigena (c. 815–877), a Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the unknowability of God.</note>, <term>Bonaventura</term> <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), a Scholastic theologian who integrated faith and reason into a mystical path.</note>, and <term>Eckhart</term> <note>Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328), a German theologian famous for his "sermons on the soul" and the concept of "God-birth" in the individual.</note>. The name <term>Mysticism</term> fits either one direction or the other, but certainly not both at once. For all common characteristics are lacking.

### On the Value and Nature of Mysticism.

After what has been said, it will be easy to distinguish mysticism also from more closely related directions, such as <term>Gnosticism</term><term>Gnosticism: A diverse group of ancient religious movements that emphasized "gnosis" (secret knowledge) of the divine as the path to salvation from the material world.</term> and <term>Theosophy</term><term>Theosophy: Literally "divine wisdom"; here referring to systems of thought that seek direct knowledge of the mysteries of being and nature through mystical insight.</term>. Mysticism clings with its essential interest to the Absolute and to its representation in the human soul; it nowhere enters more deeply into the details of finite appearances in history or in nature, since for the mystic, these have no independent validity. Quite the contrary, Gnosticism and Theosophy are stammering and clumsy attempts to point out how the Divine has realized itself in the processes of history or in the phenomena of nature. 

If a mature <term>Philosophy of History</term> follows the rule of Ideas <note>The author uses "Ideas" in the Platonic or Hegelian sense—the underlying spiritual or rational blueprints of reality.</note> in the individual great historical figures of heroes and nations, and in the states of religion and culture: then Gnosticism—lacking a clear recognition of facts and a sufficient development of concepts—clings to external forms and accidental or merely apparent relationships. These it undertakes to interpret mythologically as revelations of God or as <term>theogonic</term><term>Theogonic: Relating to the birth or origin of the gods.</term> and <term>cosmogonic</term><term>Cosmogonic: Relating to the origin of the universe.</term> processes. 

Theosophy stands in a similar contrast to a serious <term>Philosophy of Nature</term> <note>Naturphilosophie: A movement in German philosophy that sought to understand nature as a manifestation of the spirit, rather than just a collection of mechanical laws.</note>—which proceeds from the scientific knowledge of facts in nature and follows the rule of Ideas within it. Theosophy, with its dreamlike effort, attempts to demonstrate images of divine essential determinations and divine life-processes in the phenomena of nature by means of views of nature that have not been purified by critical thinking. Gnosticism and Theosophy both belong as little to the strictly religious as to the scientific field; they are attempts struggling with difficulty to break free from religious views, yet woven through with scientifically unclear theological ideas. They seek to illuminate the world of ideas with a "higher light," which they pass off as the light of true knowledge. That mystical elements can contribute to this process is self-evident; it is also natural that they are drawn upon with preference as the most suitable aid for grounding one's own world of ideas. This results from the fact that all these directions share a common underlying conviction: that all life and being of things is a divine life.

# Introduction.

...with what right <term>Eckhart</term><term>Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328) was a German theologian and philosopher. He is often considered the father of German mysticism for his profound and often radical ideas about the union between the soul and God.</term> can be called the central spirit of all mysticism. Indeed, all the elements of mysticism appear in him in such high perfection, and in such an appropriate development and connection with one another, as in none of his predecessors or successors. His harmoniously complete doctrine unites all the individual facets which appear separately in other mystics. Through the deep, principled foundation of his standpoint, he approaches the great scientific thinkers; yet, his entire teaching is merely the internally coherent <term>explication</term><term>The process of making an idea clear or developing it in detail.</term> of a simple, fundamental religious view. 

In his work, all theoretical interest rests upon the foundation of a high religious enthusiasm. The <term>dialectical</term><term>The art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions through logical argumentation.</term> sharpness of his definitions and the longing that presses forward toward the vision of God maintain a mutual balance. All religious conduct is determined by the logic of conceptual recognition, and all <term>speculation</term><term>In this context, philosophical or theological contemplation of the divine, rather than guesswork.</term> is determined by the fundamental religious mood. The deepest results for the advancement of Christian ethics are combined with the boldest ideas about the <term>Godhead</term><term>The essential nature of God, often used by mystics to describe the "inner" or "absolute" essence of the Divine that exists beyond our human descriptions.</term>, the divine persons, the essence and connection of the world and its relationship to the Absolute, and the soul and its high destiny. Nowhere else but in his work does the daring flight of ideas of <term>Johannes Erigena</term><term>Johannes Scotus Eriugena (c. 815–877) was an Irish Neoplatonist philosopher and theologian of the Carolingian Renaissance.</term> pair so well with the simple inwardness of <term>Saint Bernard</term><term>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) was a French abbot who emphasized a more emotional and personal love for God.</term>. 

The most unique and magnificent aspect of Eckhart, however, is the unity and wholeness of his way of thinking. Carried by a great and significant personality—whose living warmth touches the heart everywhere, and who everywhere bears witness to a fearless struggle with the highest problems of thought, into whose immeasurable depths he dives like a brave swimmer—his doctrine is a remarkable reflection both of the German intellectual life and the national character of the German conception of religion.

Secondly, the question presents itself to us: what significance and what value does mysticism have for religious life and for the advancement of knowledge? Only when this question is answered will it be possible to assign each significant representative of mysticism their proper place in history and to rightly appreciate the importance of their influence. ...mysticism—and not just in recent times—has a rather bad reputation and is condemned equally by almost everyone: by the religious as much as the irreligious. Much of this disparaging judgment is, of course, due to a false understanding of its essence and the confusion of accidental external features with the core of the matter. A simple observation shows that mysticism, as we have described it above and as it appears with common features in all its primary representatives, forms an indispensable element at least in all religion, and especially in the Christian faith.

If one wishes to properly appreciate the value of mysticism, one must not take one’s judgment from those forms where it is mixed with other elements, but rather from those in which it expresses itself most purely and fully. It must be admitted that mysticism, when pushed to the extreme, ends in dangerous errors, and even in its milder forms, it is never entirely free from a tendency toward them. Mysticism tolerates no estrangement between the soul and God; it regards separation as merely temporary and unity as essential. The finite, created nature of reason and will, or their stunted state through the power of sin, recedes behind their essential and indestructible divinity. Therefore, nothing is considered unreachable for reason and will, not even the Highest. Reason penetrates all the depths of the Godhead, and the will breaks through all the barriers of nature; man is able to become God himself. <note>The author is referring to the concept of 'theosis' or deification, a bold mystical claim that the soul can be transformed into the likeness of God through spiritual union.</note>

All mysticism perceives God as the indeterminate <term>absolute ground</term><term>In German "Urgrund," referring to the ultimate, underlying reality of God that exists before and beneath all created things.</term>, remaining distant even from all <term>predication</term><term>The act of assigning qualities or names (predicates) to something; mystics often argue that God is "beyond names."</term>, in which all things are one. By excluding all figurative representation and every parable from the right knowledge of this absolute ground, mysticism becomes <term>pantheism</term><term>The belief that God and the universe are identical, or that God is the essence of all things rather than a distinct person.</term>—to be sure, a pantheism that does not perceive God as the sum of natural things or natural forces, but rather as the one essence in all being, outside of which there is nothing at all. If God is to be granted one predicate above others, it is essentially **Reason**, and therefore He stands under the logical law of reason or the necessity of His own essence. God is the Unchanging; all specific occurrences and acts of will are excluded from Him; nothing remains but an eternal process, which is rather a rest eternally abiding within itself. With the separate existence of things, the separate existence of man also ceases. The contrast between God and man is not an absolute one; mysticism cannot recognize any fundamental or serious difference at all between the soul and its eternal origin. Not only in <term>Eckhart</term><term>Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328), a famous German Dominican theologian and mystic whose ideas about the "spark of the soul" often blurred the lines between the human and the divine.</term>, but in every consistent mystic, this doctrine of the identity of essence between man and God finds an expression that sounds like the deification of man and the belittling of God.

Just as with the doctrine of the immanence of God in reason, the doctrine of the immanence of God in the human will presents itself as an exaggeration or perversion of Christian doctrine. Mysticism tends to confuse finitude with sin, just as it equates the surrender of individuality with sanctification, and annihilation in God with blessedness. It prefers to draw the highest ideals and lingers mostly on the description of the state of perfection. The pain of sin, the feeling of divine wrath, and the misery of being separated from God do not find as powerful an expression in mysticism as the bliss of love, the perfect vision of God, and the divine clarity of the perfected ones. The boundary that separates the sanctified will of the creature from the essential holiness of the Creator is all too easily overlooked by mysticism; the Christian ideal of a horizontal blessedness and perfect sanctification is seen as something already realized and to be realiz— <note>original: "verwirkli-" (catchword for "verwirklichenden" or "verwirklichten")</note>

All mysticism, to a greater or lesser degree, is characterized by a disregard for the sensory and the finite, which is also transferred to the moral sphere. It strives for the most abstract, the highest universal in which all differences cease, and it easily sacrifices the fullness of life to a shadow-play of abstract concepts. Immersed in the admiring contemplation of the infinite light, it loses the power of sight for the light that is refracted in the individual things of reality. The highest glow of inspired feelings and the sobriety of subtle **dialectics** <term>Dialectics: Here referring to a complex, logical method of argument that seeks to resolve contradictions.</term>, which romps about in bare abstractions, alternate in a wonderful way. The higher it believes it sets its ethical goals, the deeper it condemns all seeking of reward and all external settling of accounts with God, the more easily it falls into the groundless and thoughtless; and if it speaks its final word, it ends in actual **nihilism** <term>Nihilism: The philosophical position that suggests life or the world is without objective meaning, purpose, or intrinsic value.</term>.

The mystic wants personal, immediate interaction with his God. Therefore, the authority of tradition, the community of believers, and the institution of the church count for little—easily far too little—to him. -># On the Value and Essence of Mysticism.<-

Mysticism itself leads down the opposite path. The mystic relies on the enlightenment specially granted to him, on the inner light he receives from grace, and on the intervention of the Spirit in his heart; mystical subjectivism easily turns into actual **fanaticism**. <term>Fanaticism (Schwärmerei): In this historical theological context, it refers to "enthusiasm" or a belief in direct personal inspiration from God that bypasses the written Bible or the organized Church.</term> He believes he possesses the Holy Spirit within himself and abandons himself to its guidance. If the mystic is consistent, then the priest holds no special privilege for him, the Church mediates no gifts of grace that he could not obtain more directly, and the discipline of the Church deserves no obedience. A heart that has surrendered itself to God <note>original: "Gott gelassen." Refers to the concept of *Gelassenheit* or "releasement," a central idea in German mysticism where the soul lets go of its own will to be filled by God.</note> possesses such rich treasures of knowledge in this oneness with God that it needs nothing more than to be fortified in God. Just like the institution, the dogma of the Church is held in low regard; it is not the doctrine as it generally prevails in the Church, but as it is established in the individual knowledge of the saints, that forms the foundation of life in God. Common to all mysticism is that it cannot accept even the revealed Word <note>The "revealed Word" refers to the Holy Scriptures.</note> as such; for the mystic, the history of revelation becomes a subject of allegorical interpretation, in order to find his own perspectives within the Word and to elevate the particulars of fact into the sphere of conceptual universality.

Mysticism moves in these directions whenever its principle is consistently applied. Of course, not all mystics have gone so far in all these respects. Alongside the extremes are those figures who, with a milder disposition—even if without satisfying the logical consistency of the thought—have prudently stopped before reaching the limit and have not followed the chosen path to its end. It is precisely in this middle region of mysticism that those spirits move who have had the greatest and most blessed influence on the development of the Church’s doctrine and life: a *Bernard of Clairvaux*, *Johannes Tauler*, *Thomas à Kempis*. Some closer, others further from the sharp edge of mystical thought, they have striven in mild, evangelical prudence to maintain a living unity with the collective consciousness of the Church, whereas others allowed themselves to be led astray into the wasteland of isolated paths. For this reason, they were able to become much-admired teachers of the Church and models of devotion. The bolder spirits, on the other hand, who

To be sure, to claim that mysticism is the only appropriate form of Christian knowledge, or that the personal conduct of the mystic is the absolute ideal of evangelical life, would mean in principle the abolition of all religious community, all Church. For on this contemplative immersion in God and enlightenment by God alone, no common doctrine, no comprehensive order of life, hardly even a school or sect, let alone a church, can be built. On the other hand, to deny mysticism all right on the ground of Christian life and Christian doctrine would mean misjudging and casting away essential elements of the Gospel of Christ. But when the time was fulfilled and God sent his Son into the world in the form of the man Jesus of Nazareth, God had ceased to be merely the Lord, standing over the world, his creation, and man, his image, as the strict, zealous lawgiver; the relationship to him was no longer an external legal service. 

Now divine essence had appeared in human form; in Jesus the Christ, the way was opened for all to become children of God and to know themselves as such. Since then, there is no longer an unbridgeable chasm between God and man; now human nature can be ennobled and introduced into God; now, through the gifts of grace he has bestowed upon his church, the Lord builds a body, of which he himself is the head, and to which he has called all to become members. 

This entire relationship of God to humanity—as it forms the common foundation of the doctrine of salvation <term>doctrine of salvation (Heilslehre): The branch of theology, also known as soteriology, that deals with how humans are redeemed.</term> in all historical forms of Christianity still worthy of the name—is irrational and possesses the character of mystical depth. No contrast is absolute here anymore. Finite and infinite, man and God, world and the kingdom of heaven, flesh and spirit, nature and grace: there are points in which they touch, in which the relationship of enmity passes into that of unity and community. 

The principle of the new divine life is faith; but faith is a recognition and knowledge and, at the same time, an experience and living-through—a knowledge whose object is simultaneously able to become the substance of my spiritual existence. Clearly, faith involves a specific relationship of reason to God and his revelation. What kind of knowledge should this be? Its object is called a mystery <note>original: "Geheimniss"</note> in the Scriptures. It does not lie on the path of natural experience; it cannot be measured by the categories of the finite intellect. Thus, the knowledge of God—

The **Johannine doctrine** <note>Refers to the theology of the Apostle John.</note> of the divine Word, which was in the beginning with God and, when the time was fulfilled, became flesh and dwelt among us and gave us power to become children of God; the **Pauline doctrine** <note>Refers to the theology of the Apostle Paul.</note> of Christ in us as the goal of our sanctification—the Christ with whom we die and are buried, whom we put on in faith, so that now it is not we who live, but Christ in us: these are the foundations upon which all later mysticism has built itself.

In everything Christian, the mystical thus forms an essential and indispensable element, yet only one element, which must not isolate itself in its independence without turning what is rightful within it into something wrongful. Alongside the mystical view of Christianity stands the **dogmatic-critical** view. The former individualizes the Christian; the latter brings the congregation together and unites it. The former develops, so to speak, a personal <term>virtuosity</term> <note>In this context, "virtuosity" refers to a highly developed, specialized personal skill or excellence in one's private spiritual life.</note> in the relationship of man to God and leaves each person to their personal communion with God; the latter establishes and maintains a common conviction and preserves the general rule of discipline and legal order; the former turns preferably to those who are advanced and convinced, while the latter offers "easy milk" <note>A biblical metaphor from 1 Corinthians 3:2 and Hebrews 5:12, referring to basic teachings suitable for beginners in the faith.</note> even to the immature and the weak. But it would be entirely wrong to perceive the relationship between a church dogmatic and an individualizing mysticism as one of absolute opposition.
