Since the **Formula of Concord** <note>original: "Concordienformel"; the 1577 Lutheran confession of faith that settled several doctrinal disputes.</note>, the dogmatics of the Lutheran Church have also explicitly recognized this fact in their wording by placing the "mystical" union with God <note>Often referred to in theology as the *unio mystica*, where the soul is said to be united with the divine.</note> at the end of the path of salvation as the final goal of even our earthly life.

The difference between dogmatic and mystical theology lies not in their goal, but rather in their starting point and their method. The first difference that catches the eye is their varying relationship to the Church. The dogmatic direction—represented in the Middle Ages by **Scholasticism** <note>The school of thought that sought to use logic and philosophy to defend and explain church doctrine.</note>—serves the Church and conveys a collective conviction among all members of the community regarding the facts of salvation. The mystic, as such, stands in a more external relationship to the Church. He may move within her grounds, value her highly as a means of education, and use her as a vehicle to carry out his activity; but ecclesiastical methods of salvation are never the highest for him, and he merely comes to terms with the Church where he does not simply distance himself from her with an air of superiority.

Because mysticism initially focuses only on the individual to point him toward the most direct path to his salvation, and because it finds this direct path not so much in connection with a communal order of life, but far more—or even entirely—within purely personal and individual life activities, it will never be able to place the Church at the forefront of its interest; indeed, it will often see itself forced to oppose her. While dogmatic theology emphasizes the authority of the collective consciousness of the Church to bind the individual to it with greater or lesser decisiveness, mysticism directs everyone to the work of **grace** <note>original: "Gnade"; in this context, the unmerited favor and divine influence of God acting within the person.</note> within themselves as a revelation of God granted specifically to them. The tradition of the doctrinal opinion that has become dominant in the Church is, for dogmatic theology, a strong bond and a reliable guide for orientation; for the mystic, his personal enlightenment and his inner experience count for far more. Mysticism, when established as a principle, results in the infinite right of subjective conviction over and against all authority.

# On the Value and Essence of Mysticism.

Subjectivism gives rise to the idea of immanence <note>The theological concept that the divine is present within the material world and the human soul, rather than being separate from it.</note>; any other idea could emerge from it just as easily. The mystic relates to God as if to his own true essence. According to the mystical view, God becomes man in each of us. Therefore, no external mediation is needed; on the contrary, it is a disturbing, hindering element. Only in the highest immediacy of the soul's relationship to God does the mystic find satisfaction. He wishes to cast off everything historical, every image and parable, every specificity of form under which the divine is to be perceived, in order to arrive at a pure, imageless contemplation. The dogmatic-ecclesiastical direction insists that it is itself this mediation, without which no one can reach God. From the outset, it conceives the entire relationship to God in the form of transcendence <note>The idea that God exists apart from and is superior to the universe; a "distant" or "other" holiness.</note>—a relationship to the Most High and Holy, which is originally still distant from me, and toward which one must mature through the gifts of grace administered by the Church. Thus, by necessity, the Holy becomes an authority that stands over reason, a law that confronts the will as something external and originally foreign; and the task is to gradually erase and overcome this foreignness through faithful submission.

The original opposition between immanence and transcendence—and what coincides with it, between immediacy and mediation—can be traced into all branches of doctrine. While the dogmatic direction in faith emphasizes more the side of submission to authority, the boundness to what is fixed by external tradition and ultimately guaranteed by divine communication, mysticism thinks of faith more as the freely active grasping of a content of life activated within the individual through the work of divine grace, for which the Word of God and the teachings of predecessors offer only further supports and securing boundaries. This same opposition continues throughout the entire doctrine of the path of salvation <term>Heilsweg: the theological steps or process an individual takes toward union with God or salvation</term>. The dogmatic direction first looks at man in his empirical state, as he has been shaped since the Fall of the first man <note>The biblical event of Adam and Eve's disobedience, which traditional theology views as the origin of human sin and separation from God.</note>. The separation between God and natural man is the first thing it pays attention to; it does not bridge the chasm, but holds fast to the idea of the infinite distance between the two sides, and its striving is directed precisely toward...

In the concept of virtue as well as sin, dogmatic theology holds more firmly to the legal norm, to which everyone must equally adapt their will. It therefore adheres more to the way the will appears in individual acts of doing or refraining—to the **actual sin** <note>original: *Thatsünde*; a technical term for specific sinful acts committed by an individual, as opposed to "original sin" which is seen as an inherited state.</note> and to good works. The mystic places more value on the internal state, which provides the foundation for all expressions of the will: the lasting and essential state of the will's direction. Just as it favors norms that apply to everyone, the dogmatic direction emphasizes the uniform paths of strengthening in goodness; it more forcefully stresses the gifts bestowed upon the Church to promote each individual on the path to their salvation, and to protect and strengthen the weak, tender germ of faith. 

For the mystic, on the other hand, the law is no longer the fitting expression for the Holy, which after all lies as a rational disposition and quality within the essence of the will itself. To him, the main thing is freedom from all mediation—and thus also from the law—the freedom which is the portion of those who have progressed, the life in the Absolute, and the right of **individuality**, by virtue of which each person must seek access to the highest goal in their own way and as *grace* leads them. Each of us is Christ according to our essence, if only we dare to be so: this is his exhortation. God redeems the sinner out of mercy when he accepts the grace offered in Christ through submission to the majesty of the Son of God, through the conviction and firm trust that Christ’s perfect fulfillment of duty—as a distinct, external person—benefits him and replaces his own deficiency: thus teaches **dogmatic theology** <note>Dogmatic theology refers to the official, systematic teachings and "dogmas" authorized by a church, often emphasizing external laws, historical events, and the "substitutionary" roles of Christ.</note>. God redeems the sanctified by virtue of the rational necessity of His own essence, once the human being has taken Christ into himself and God can no longer discover any difference between Himself and the sanctified human soul: thus teaches **mysticism**.

The capacity for understanding of the masses, the need for a common doctrine, for a formula that can be known by everyone, and the awareness of the historical mediation of their confession—through the acts of God and the development of human science under the influence of the divine spirit—conditions the tone and attitude of a dogmatic fixation of doctrine. **Dogmatics** moves within fixed, finite concepts, through which it seeks to express the **Absolute** <note>The "Absolute" is a philosophical term for the ultimate, unconditional reality or God, viewed as the source of all being, beyond human limitation.</note> according to its essence and attributes. It speaks of God as a specific substance, distinct from others, as an object in a world of objects which are His work, with a spatial and temporal effectiveness, and with exclusive, particular attributes. It considers the striving of man upward toward God from the viewpoint of a striving for **blessedness** <note>original: *Glückseligkeit*; this refers to a state of supreme spiritual happiness or "beatitude," often seen in dogmatic theology as the ultimate reward for the faithful.</note>, by grasping the infinite purpose through the analogy of finite purposes. It links even the most ideal goal—in form, if not in content—to the motivations of the natural life as the satisfaction of the drive for happiness. It holds as long as possible to the opposites of nature and grace, inclination and law, reason and revelation, setting them as independent forces against one another. The formula in which it captures the infinite content is **parable** and **representation** <note>original: *Gleichniss, Vorstellung*; in this context, it refers to using mental images, metaphors, or stories to understand God, rather than the direct, unmediated experience sought by the mystic.</note>; it cannot go beyond these without abandoning its own nature,

and it [Dogmatics] appears as the highest and final means to an end: making the **Infinite** accessible to the finite mind—at least when that mind is enlightened by **grace**. It seeks to speak the unspeakable, to draw human nature toward the **Mystery**, and to educate the will using effective, teaching-oriented motives. It aims to transfigure the mundane details of life through relationships that are relatable yet still express the **Ideal**. 

**Mysticism**, by contrast, seeks to move beyond mere formulas. The limits of human capacity, which are inherent to our earthly finitude, are bypassed or "flown over" rather than being carefully dismantled. The veil shrouding the ultimate **Mystery** may thin in places, but it only reveals an incomprehensible mist. 

The result is a constant demand for a type of knowing or doing that can never be satisfied. <meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the tension between systematic theology (Dogmatics) and the inward experience of the divine (Mysticism). [...is not a] requirement of religious life, but rather at times the death of the religious personality. Even the wise man, who united all human knowledge <note>German: *Wissenschaft*, which in this context refers to systematic, academic, or scientific knowledge.</note> within himself, would be like a child in matters of religion. Immediacy is the first prerequisite for a right relationship with God. Alongside this, systematic knowledge has its own special field and its peculiar requirements and needs. A true person must be able to rediscover that immediate relationship with God from every standpoint of mere cognition—that relationship which is called **Faith**. Far from being mere knowledge and cognition, faith rather permeates the entire life of a human being in all its expressions. 

If the principle of this life is to be expressed, language and its rigid concepts always present themselves as the only understandable form for its infinite content. The dogmatic approach is in danger of holding fast to the form while abandoning the content; mysticism threatens to make the content independent for itself and to collapse into formlessness. A healthy life in one’s earthly calling seeks to hold content and form equally, to combine them, and to develop them further in community. 

The finite concepts of dogmatics are the necessary and indispensable form for expressing any objective content of faith at all; yet the believer grows beyond this form through the experiences of their life. Each person experiences, in a unique way corresponding to their own capacity and spiritual individuality, that which cannot be shaped into a common article of faith in human words. If the formula becomes fixed and rigid, it loses its true meaning; an adherence to the "letter" sets in, which kills <note>A reference to the biblical phrase "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (2 Corinthians 3:6).</note>. The label itself acquires a value it does not deserve; that which is labeled disappears from the horizon; what should have been a means becomes the end itself. 

Mysticism keeps the formula in flux; it points to the finite nature within it; it stimulates one to penetrate the formula more deeply and to animate it more energetically. Life in faith is not a life of direct vision <note>German: *Schauen*, referring to "sight" or "contemplation" as opposed to belief.</note>. Faith is an anticipation of the Eternal in this earthly life—infinite in terms of its content, yet finite in terms of its form. To secure its full, living content, mysticism is a God-willed tool <term>Rüstzeug: literally "equipment" or "armor," used here to mean the spiritual resources or "tools" of the soul.</term>. Dogmatics has its own peculiar firmness and durability, not through external supports—for these would easily be swept away by the restless flooding of spiritual movement—

## Introduction.

[...not to] wash away—but by the inherent nature of the matter and the human spiritual constitution. It <note>Referring to "Dogmatics" or systematic church doctrine.</note> delineates a narrower field; but within this, it establishes itself with complete certainty, embracing it fully and penetrating it with absolute clarity. The mystical teachings offer the spectacle of a restless change, an infinite individual diversity. One system of teaching replaces another, only to give way in turn to a following one. Thus, they entwine themselves like delicate vines around the firm, persistent trunk of church doctrine, which alone—as the permanent element in the shift of the life circling around it—links generation with generation, provides a secure hold, and, where it does not overstep its rightful limits, is able to be "all things to all people." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:22: "I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some."</note>

The historical law is invariably the same. If a dogmatic system is overthrown by a spiritual movement that has advanced beyond it and progressed to higher forms of religious education, then the destined genius will appear to lay the foundations for a new dogmatic system—one which, after all, only goes deeper into the original and essential grounds of Christian ideas. Without the dogmatic formulation of the content of faith, there is no church, and the church has the promise that "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." <note>original: "Pforten der Hölle"; a reference to Matthew 16:18.</note> A humanity without a church would mean a humanity with only a legal community, but without a moral community; a world without the developing seed of the Kingdom of God within it. All truth, and most especially religious truth, we possess only through tradition and within it. All our thinking is a commentary on a given text, even in the field of science. <note>German: *Wissenschaft*, referring to systematic academic study or organized knowledge.</note> The core is ancient; that which is permanently added through the individual skill of even the greatest thinkers is, in each instance, only a very small amount by comparison. What is the value of the "presuppositionless" <term>presuppositionless thinking: the philosophical ideal of thinking without any prior biases or inherited traditions</term> thinking of the self-taught? It comes and passes away, as indifferent as the weeds by the roadside. So it is in science; and in religion? # Introduction.

...drawn upon in all ages of the Church. Striving from individual details toward the whole, its procedure is **analytical**. The mystical method forms the direct opposite to this. **Mysticism** places a unified foundational perspective <term>Grundanschauung: a fundamental core intuition or worldview</term> at the forefront and proceeds from there **synthetically** to the specific; it does not do this in a way that disputes or nullifies the details of historical tradition, but rather so that it draws upon them only as a subsidiary to the further expansion of its world of thought. It reinterprets fundamental facts as the expression of **metaphysical speculations** into the general processes of the Divine, and seeks to place even the less fundamental elements into immediate relationship with its highest principle—often somewhat forcibly—through the **allegorical interpretation of Scripture** <term>Allegorese: a method of reading the Bible where literal events are interpreted as symbols of deeper spiritual or philosophical truths</term> as conceptually general truths.

Pre-Reformation dogmatics <term>Dogmatik: the systematic study and formulation of church doctrines</term>, through its speculative tendency and its undecided relationship to Scripture, always retained a greater affinity with mysticism. Since the **Reformation**, mysticism has been as good as excluded from the ecclesiastical sphere, remaining effective only in individual echoes where it does not explicitly separate itself from the context of the Church. Since then, the functions that formerly fell to mysticism have been exercised by **scientific speculation** <note>In this 19th-century context, "science" (Wissenschaft) refers to systematic, academic scholarship and philosophy rather than just the natural sciences.</note>, which, originally emerging from a ground other than the religious, ultimately strives to mediate itself with the fundamental facts of religious faith. Herein lies the most essential advancement for the Church as well; and if the ecclesiastical office has the primary task of conserving what has been acquired, then on Protestant ground, the **theological faculties**—standing in connection with the broader world of science—have the task of further developing what exists.

The speculative philosophy of the modern era is a mysticism detached from the ground of **revelation** and brought into the form of science. Likewise, the dogmatic direction turns into **Rationalism** when it detaches itself from the authority of the revealed Word and instead relies entirely upon the critical insight of the natural intellect or the intellect trained by scientific methods. To mysticism, rational criticism is a distant concept. Just as it transfers heaven directly to earth, it distinguishes no "natural" from "supernatural" becoming here on earth. To the mystic, everything is an immediate act of God, a revelation of heavenly powers; therefore, nothing is so certain, so natural, and so self-evident as the **miracle**. Not only

# On the Value and Essence of Mysticism.

Mysticism accepts the wonders of the Holy Scripture and even those of legends without hesitation as proofs and representations of spiritual powers. By contrast, speculative and rationalist science <term>Wissenschaft: in this 19th-century context, this refers to systematic academic scholarship or "science" in the broadest sense of organized knowledge</term> unite in their common opposition to both dogmatics <term>Dogmatik: the systematic study and formulation of church doctrines</term> and mysticism. When these sciences carry out their basic principles with any consistency, they are unable to recognize an intervention of the infinite and spiritual within the finite world that acts only sporadically, rather than being active continuously in an ever-consistent form. In this, they are not swayed even by the testimony of the holy books. Science knows no reason why the principles of criticism, with which it otherwise views historical tradition, should not also hold valid when facing the holy scriptures of the Christians.

The contrast we have attempted to describe, between a mystical and a dogmatic direction, has existed at all times and from the very beginning of the Church. It appears already in the relationship of Paul to James, and of John to the Synoptics <note>original: "Johannes zu den Synoptikern." The "Synoptics" refers to the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, which share a similar narrative structure, often contrasted with the more philosophical and "mystical" Gospel of John.</note>. In describing this, we have intended to draw not so much specific individual figures, but rather an **ideal average** <term>Durchschnitt: here meaning a conceptual archetype or composite model rather than a mathematical mean</term>. Historical reality itself corresponds to this model only exceptionally and in its extreme forms; the most significant representatives of both directions are always determined by one of the two only in the main and predominantly, while incorporating elements of the opposite kind to a greater or lesser degree. The extremes may have worked more quickly, forcefully, and conspicuously in their own time; yet, far more has been contributed to the church's lasting treasury of ideas, institutions, and forms of life by the calmer and more moderate figures. These figures found their calling in the fusion of the legitimate elements from both opposing directions, albeit under the prevailing influence of one side or the other.

One must keep that relationship of opposition in mind in order to properly appreciate the one-sidedness and dangers of mysticism, but equally its high significance for the building of the **Kingdom of God** in the historical development of the Church as well as in the faith life of every individual. To a certain extent, the dogmatic-ecclesiastical view provides the firm skeletal structure for the Christian Church and produces the limbs and joints

Both complement each other and depend upon one another. Both directions have their dangers if they isolate themselves one-sidedly against the other, and these dangers lie on different sides for each. Even the Church, as long as it is administered by sinful human beings, and church doctrine, as long as it is mediated through the degree of understanding of individuals—who, no matter how called they may be, are still limited in their capacity—is close to the danger of overstepping its legitimate territory, of regarding objective orders as the highest purpose and bending the consciences of the congregation under such orders like a slavish yoke, which from one perspective are based on human ordinance. Whatever the nature of mysticism’s historical effectiveness may have been, it is easy to measure based on this. It stands at the forefront among the powers that have driven the Church forward in doctrine and life, kept the movement awake, and refused to tolerate the Church settling into a complacent possession of what has already been achieved. Every time the church-dogmatic view <term>Dogmatic: Relating to the official, established doctrines of the Church</term> attempted to close itself off in rigid formulas; every time living faith, upon which all "righteousness before God" rests, was in danger of being confused with a mere intellectual conviction regarding a system of theological tenets; every time the Church, acting as an institution, overstepped its assigned domain and did not see itself as called to the service of every individual soul, but instead demanded dominion so that it might be served; every time a dividing wall of externalizing forms was erected in this manner—forms that no longer served as a protective garment but as a concealing shroud that hid the truth and pushed itself between the Christian and his Redeemer: it was then, in every instance, that mysticism, with its life-oriented needs, most powerfully emphasized the right of the congregation over the institution. It emphasized the immediate relationship of every redeemed soul to their Redeemer and rescued the sacred from a state of rigid "otherworldliness" and estrangement. Mysticism has taught how to bring the sacred into personal life and to place the heart and conscience directly under the discipline of the Lord. Most heresies <term>Heresies: Beliefs or opinions contrary to orthodox religious doctrine</term> have formed from mystical perspectives. Where the mystical could not yet be grasped in pure thought, it has often surrounded itself with the wildest superstition and a colorful mythology. Pantheism <term>Pantheism: The belief that God and the universe are one and the same</term> and Emanatism <term>Emanatism: The idea that all things flow out from a divine source</term> easily slide into dualistic ideas; the peculiar position of mysticism toward revelation favors arbitrary interpretations or superstitious inventions in the field of sacred history; exaggerated spirituality alternates with a crude and common carnality of mind. Where ill-will was added, mystical delusions have defied all discipline and morality, as well as all sound reason, proving incompatible not only with the existence of the Church but also with the legal order of the state. Idle daydreaming and fantastic exuberance easily draw agreeable nourishment from mystical ideas. 

But one should not judge mysticism by such excesses. Genuine mysticism is the ripe fruit of a highly cultivated spiritual life, completely immersed in God. It can never become popular, never the property of the masses, without degenerating; but with its individual elements, it can permeate and enrich the treasury of the Church and deepen the devotion of the congregation, after it has gained power on ecclesiastical ground through influential figures who are truly seized by the life of the spirit. It expresses the one truth in more spiritual terms, less modeled on the analogy of earthly things; it places its main interest on different points of Christian doctrine than the specifically ecclesiastical science of faith. However, it is only the exaggerations of its teachings, or the arrogance of claiming to be in sole possession of an absolute truth, that truly abandon religious and Christian ground. A speculation <term>Speculation: Philosophical or theoretical reflection that goes beyond traditional religious observation</term> arising more from the pure impulses of thought has displaced and partially replaced actual mysticism among us. Instead, the spiritual interest is primarily occupied with the essential principles: the eternal significance that those facts (asserted by some and disputed by others) hold for the salvation of every individual.

# Meister Eckhart.

One is accustomed to speaking with reverence of *Tauler* and the "*German Theology*" <note>original: "deutschen Theologie," referring to the *Theologia Germanica*, an anonymous mystical treatise from the 14th century</note>, of *Ruysbroeck* and *Heinrich Suso* as bright stars in a dark age, and gladly recognizes them as teachers of a purer Christianity, as truly Christian-minded heralds of Christ, and as preachers of an authentic evangelical life in the midst of a Church hardening into external legalism. It would also not be easily disputed that they had a profound and beneficial influence on the development of the Church up to the Reformation and since the Reformation—partly through the deepening and inwardness of the Christian faith they sought and the numerous seeds of serious Christian speculation <term>Speculation: In this context, deep philosophical or theological contemplation regarding the nature of God and the soul</term> scattered within their works, and partly through their preaching of repentance and love grounded in faith, rather than the external obedience of the Church and "dead works" <term>Dead Works: Religious rituals or moral actions performed out of obligation or habit rather than from a living, spiritual conviction</term>. In exactly the same measure, one is accustomed to separating *Meister Eckhart* far from those men, viewing him as the author of an unrestrained and pantheistic speculation and as a kindred spirit to the "Brothers and Sisters of the Free Spirit" <note>A lay religious movement in the 13th and 14th centuries often accused of heresy for claiming that the soul can become so united with God that it no longer needs the Church or its laws</note>, finding in him the realization of the opposite of all Christian piety. It is one of the most essential merits of the collection of *Eckhart’s* surviving writings, published in 1857 and prepared by *Franz Pfeiffer*, to have made this conception—which *Schmidt* and *Martensen* had already previously opposed—impossible.

# Meister Eckhart.

[...insights] at their deepest level, exert a powerful influence through his thoughts for all subsequent time, and yet be forgotten by posterity itself. This same man, who until his death stood in the fullness of a grand activity as an official of his Order <note>Eckhart was a high-ranking member of the Dominican Order</note>, as a teacher and preacher, was already nearly forgotten by the 15th century and featured only in the heresy histories of the 14th century as the author of a strange heretical error, about which one knew more only from the papal bull <note>The bull *In agro dominico*, issued by Pope John XXII in 1329, which condemned several of Eckhart's propositions as heretical or "evil-sounding"</note> that condemned him. Even *Görres* <note>Joseph Görres (1776–1848), an influential German writer and theologian</note>, in the introduction to *Diepenbrock’s* 1829 edition of the writings of *Suso*, called *Eckhart* “a wonderful figure, half-shrouded in mist, almost a Christian myth.” *Franz von Baader* <note>A Catholic philosopher (1765–1841) credited with "rediscovering" Eckhart for the modern era</note> was the first to draw attention to him again. The only writings printed under *Eckhart's* name—appearing as an appendix to the edition of *Tauler’s* sermons published in Basel in 1521 and repeatedly in 1522—were small fragments of a comprehensive literary output, yet they had caught the attention of the Catholic *theosophist* <term>Theosophist: In this 19th-century context, a person who seeks direct knowledge of the divine through mystical insight or philosophical speculation</term>. And what was shared there deserved this attention in the highest degree. These fragments revealed the traces of a bold and powerful spirit, a captivating eloquence, and an undaunted flight of thought. It was primarily upon these that the two depictions of *Eckhart’s* doctrine were based: the diligent and conscientious work of *Charles Schmidt* (Studies and Critiques 1839, Issue 3, p. 663, and *Studies on German Mysticism* in the *Memoirs of the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences*, Vol. II, Paris 1847) and the spirited work of *Martensen* <note>Hans Lassen Martensen (1808–1884), a Danish theologian whose book helped establish Eckhart's academic reputation</note> (*Meister Eckart*, Hamburg 1842); and since these writings appeared, *Meister Eckhart* has stood before us in the clear light of day as one of the most remarkable thinkers of the Middle Ages. Even from those few fragments, *Schmidt* found justified ground for his judgment:

> “None of his predecessors surpassed or even reached him in speculative depth of spirit. All who have come after him have drawn from his well; they have made mysticism more ecclesiastical, more popular, and more practical; they have sought to remove the offensive elements of his bold consistency <term>Consistency: Here referring to the logical rigor with which Eckhart followed his radical ideas to their final conclusions</term>; but none has essentially added anything new to the daring structure.”

# Meister Eckhart.

**Pfeiffer’s** Publication <note>Franz Pfeiffer published a landmark collection of Eckhart’s German works in 1857</note>. It contains only in part previously unpublished material. More than a third had been printed before, but only the aforementioned parts under **Eckhart’s** name; much appeared under **Tauler’s**, and some even under **Rusbroek’s** <note>Jan van Ruusbroec (1293–1381), an influential Flemish mystic</note> names. The *Marrow of the Soul* <note>original: *Medulla animae*</note>, falsely attributed to **Tauler**, contains a frequently distorted reworking of several of **Eckhart’s** treatises. This partly corresponds with the treatise *Concerning Certain Principal Virtues* <note>original Latin: *de praecipuis quibusdam virtutibus*</note> found in **Surius’** <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a monk who translated mystical works into Latin</note> Latin paraphrase of **Rusbroek’s** writings. This same work is printed in its original form as *The Book of the Twelve Virtues* <note>original Middle Dutch: *Dat boek van den twaelf dogheden*</note> in the *Works of Jan van Ruusbroec*, Volume III, Ghent 1860. A number of **Eckhart’s** sermons appeared under **Tauler’s** name in the editions from Leipzig (1498), Basel (1521), and Cologne (1543). These are mostly the very sermons and treatises that were most frequently cited to strikingly illustrate both speculative and practical mysticism, precisely because they were the most significant and characteristic of the mystical spirit then available. 

Elsewhere in the writings of **Tauler** and other mystics, one finds not only numerous citations of **Eckhart** (where his name is usually not mentioned) but even word-for-word borrowings of short and long passages from **Eckhart’s** works. The same dependency appears in **Tauler’s** work *The Imitation of the Poor Life of Christ* <note>original: *Nachfolge des armen Lebens Christi*</note> as well as in the *German Theology* <note>original: *deutsche Theologie*; a famous anonymous mystical treatise later published by Martin Luther</note>. The external and internal connection between the leaders of German mysticism and **Eckhart’s** way of teaching and speaking is proven most irrefutably in both the form and content of their doctrine. As long as the source from which **Tauler**, **Suso**, and **Rusbroek** drew was unknown—or known only from small fragments—one could mistake their philosophical and theological systems <term>Philosopheme and theologumena: specific philosophical or theological propositions and tenets</term> for their own original creations. However, since a larger part of **Eckhart’s** writings has been made accessible (though still relatively small compared to the total of what he wrote), it has become clear that the uniqueness of these men’s influence is to be found far more in the personal elements of how they delivered this treasury of thought—which for all of them stems from a common source—and in their specifically ecclesiastical and practical impact, rather than in the original generation of thought.

# Meister Eckhart.

...and that the true author of both those purer evangelical principles in the moral sphere and those peculiar and lofty speculations is precisely **Eckhart**, upon whom they all depend. For the rest, however, they certainly softened **Eckhart’s** principles as much as was necessary to avoid drifting too far from the prevailing views of the Church. They even went so far as to allow the ecclesiastical elements of external "service of works" <note>the idea that religious deeds and rituals earn salvation</note>—even monasticism, the cult of Mary, and the veneration of saints—to regain a certain degree of entry into their understanding of Christian matters. The purer way of teaching in all these regards belongs entirely to **Meister Eckhart** and his purely speculative mysticism. 

They all share **Eckhart’s** fundamental errors; none of them is able, or even attempts, to oppose what is fundamentally false in **Eckhart’s** speculation with another, more correct principle. They repeat his entire doctrine and thus his errors as well, but with a different kind of interest. The speculation <term>Speculation</term> <note>In this context, high-level philosophical or metaphysical reasoning</note> that dominates everything in **Eckhart’s** work recedes in their writings, giving way to an interest in edifying devotion or the encouragement of a pious Christian life. However, because their overall disposition remains closer to the Roman Church, much of what is most fruitful and valuable in **Eckhart’s** teaching also recedes: the struggle against external legalism and the emphasis on evangelical freedom <term>evangelische Freiheit</term> <note>The spiritual liberty of a believer, a concept that would later become central to the Reformation</note>. With the softening of the speculative elements, these "practical" mystics also experienced a weakening of the purely evangelical perspective. To be sure, this softening made the reformative influence of these ideas on their contemporaries all the greater, in keeping with the spirit of the age; because they seemed less alien to the people of that time, they could count on a broader understanding in this form.

Very little is known about the circumstances of **Eckhart’s** life. We report on them according to the biography of **Eckhart** found in **Quétif** and **Echard’s** *Writers of the Order of Preachers* <note>original Latin: *Scriptores ordinis praedicatorum*, Volume I, folio 507</note>, to which only **Charles Schmidt**, in his second previously cited treatise, has been able to provide some supplements. # Meister Eckhart.

...points: the date of his retraction, February 13, 1327, and that of the papal bull, which condemned him and simultaneously identified him as already deceased, March 27, 1329. According to one account, he hailed from Saxony; according to another, from Strasbourg. He must have been born before the year 1260. That he reached a great age is evident from several traces (Pfeiffer, *Meister Eckhart* p. 627, line 11). We first encounter him in the year 1302 as a highly famous teacher in Paris. He belonged to the Order of Preachers <term>Predigerorden</term> <note>The formal name for the Dominican Order, known for its emphasis on preaching and scholarship</note>; at the College of Saint James, which belonged to his order, he held public theological lectures with the character and rank of a Master of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Magister der Heiligen Schrift"</note>. Albertus Magnus presided over the school in Cologne until 1280: that Eckhart might have heard the great teacher himself is therefore not impossible, though hardly probable. 

When the conflict between Boniface VIII and Philip IV of France broke out, the Pope—who was deeply angry with the Parisian faculty—summoned Eckhart and another teacher of the University of Paris, Remigius of Florence, to Rome, presumably to utilize them in his dispute against the King of France. Because the Pope did not want Remigius to obtain academic honors in Paris, he appointed him Master <note>original: "Magister"</note> in Rome by virtue of papal authority. It was likely the same reason that moved him to appoint Eckhart as a Doctor. At that time, Eckhart was able to see the dealings and nature of the Roman court for himself. An echo of the views gained then can be found when he later says that higher-ranking clergymen are by no means the more pious or blessed, precisely because they are most deeply drawn into earthly affairs. 

Eckhart was held in high regard at that time. When, in the following year, the Teutonic province of his order was divided due to its excessive size and a Saxon province was branched off from it, Eckhart became the first Prior of this new province. At the General Chapter <term>Generalcapitel</term> <note>A formal legislative meeting of the leaders of a religious order</note> of his order in Toulouse in 1304, he participated in his capacity as Prior in the election of the Master of the Order and was subsequently confirmed in his office by him. ...to appoint him to Bohemia with the full authority to reform the monasteries, even without a specific report to the Order’s chapter, according to his own judgment in both **head and members** <term>head and members</term> <note>original: "Haupt und Gliedern." This refers to a comprehensive reform of an organization from the leadership down to the individual members.</note>. In these high offices, Eckhart taught and preached in many parts of Germany, in Austria, in Strasbourg, and especially—up until the end of his life—in Cologne. A powerful movement of the spirit emanated from him; communities of the devout gathered around him. He preached particularly to the simple folk and to the nuns in the monasteries; in Cologne, he became the head of a far-reaching theological school.

It was a time of the most powerful stirring of hearts, especially in Germany. In wide circles, the religious education of the people had outgrown the institutions of the Roman Church; the need for heartfelt devotion could no longer be satisfied within the confines of the Church. Those most deeply moved by the longing for a truly holy life and for union with Christ also strived most for spiritual maturity, for liberation from the yoke of the priesthood and from external legalism. People wanted to taste and enjoy God’s grace for themselves, to seek the peace of God on their own terms, and not merely let the priest act on their behalf while living under Church discipline—a state in which the heart might remain inwardly unconverted. In this spirit, pious associations came together, separating themselves from the world and taking this *flight from the world* seriously. They did not wish to load themselves with a new yoke of external rules, as the often-corrupted monastic orders had done, but rather to inspire one another in free association toward devotion, works of Christian charity, renunciation, suffering with Christ, and prayer. Their flight from the world was also expressed in a peculiar, humble outward bearing and dress; their devotional exercises deviated from ecclesiastical methods; they did not require priests, and they rejected in principle <term>works-righteousness</term> <note>original: "Werkgerechtigkeit." The theological concept that salvation or merit is earned through outward religious acts rather than inner faith or divine grace.</note> and all merit derived from external works. <term>Waldensian teachings</term> <note>A movement founded by Peter Waldo in the 12th century that emphasized poverty and the Bible, often clashing with the institutional Church.</note> perhaps influenced this mindset; nor did they remain distant from the more dangerous doctrines of the <term>Brethren and Sisters of the Free Spirit</term> <note>A lay mystical movement often accused of heresy for believing that a soul united with God was above the moral laws of the Church.</note>. Yet there is no doubt that a true and genuine piety formed the fundamental character of these phenomena, even if it frequently degenerated into <term>fanaticism</term> <note>original: "Schwärmerei." Historically, this referred to an excessive, emotional religious zeal or visionary state that the established Church viewed as unstable or dangerous.</note>.

...because they found in the Church, instead of a support for their souls’ longing for salvation, a persecutor filled with grim hatred; because they lacked the support of a larger community and the regulating power of an established church order; and because a movement that saw itself excluded from the Church was necessarily driven toward sectarian excesses.

The Church’s stance toward these communities and their teachings had long been inconsistent. Even the Pope and the clergy <term>clergy</term> <note>original: "Clerisei."</note> could not fail to recognize that healthy and truly Christian motives lay at the movement's foundation. The communities of the **Beghards** and **Beguines** <term>Beghards and Beguines</term> <note>Lay religious groups in the 13th and 14th centuries who lived in communal houses and practiced devotions without taking formal, permanent monastic vows.</note> had emerged around the same time and from the same spirit as the two great orders, the **Franciscans** and **Dominicans**, with whom they also maintained ties. They were intended to satisfy nearly the same spiritual needs, but they embraced the principles of **evangelical freedom** and the **imitation of Christ** through a life of poverty <note>original: "Nachfolge Christi in einem armen Leben." This refers to the *Imitatio Christi*, a central medieval ideal of living simply as Jesus did.</note> more deeply and personally. Consequently, it was harder to reconcile their efforts with the institutional principles upon which the Church was built. 

While the two monastic orders—who also championed the principle of poverty—soon became powerful instruments of the Church’s authority, those pious associations remained outsiders. They were soon viewed with suspicion and eventually faced outright persecution. They had, after all, shown a tendency to claim a special status alongside the Church and to seek peace with God in a way that the Church, in its current state, could not sanction. The absolute power of the priesthood was clearly threatened by the greatest danger if movements like these grew stronger; they had to be restricted or suppressed if it proved impossible to make them serve the Church and its hierarchy. 

Nonetheless, despite all **bulls of condemnation** <term>bulls of condemnation</term> <note>Formal decrees or edicts issued by the Pope, named for the lead seal (bulla) attached to them.</note> and executions, this heretical direction spread among the Beghards and Beguines. It found constant nourishment in the growing corruption of the Church and its entanglement in worldly and political turmoil. The principle underlying this heresy was **evangelical poverty**, the renunciation of the world, and the rejection of the priest’s power to mediate salvation. It favored personal devotion over the rituals prescribed by the Church—

...fixed external rules and laws. The Church, however, in its struggle against these movements, eventually reached a point where any higher degree of piety was viewed with suspicion. A particularly deep, personal experience of the message of salvation, especially when it manifested as a desire to lead a holier life, was treated as heresy without further consideration. Not only for the bigoted or unrefined masses, but for the clergy <term>clergy</term> <note>original: "Clerus."</note> themselves, the personal piety of the **Quiet in the Land** <term>Quiet in the Land</term> <note>original: "Stillen im Lande." A historical term for humble, devout Christians who sought a personal relationship with God through quiet contemplation rather than public ritual.</note> was an object of mockery and contempt. Against these **"pietists, prayer-brothers, and prayer-sisters,"** <note>original: "Frömmler, die Betbrüder und Betschwestern." These were derogatory nicknames used by the established clergy to mock laypeople who practiced intense private devotion.</note> every kind of violence was permitted.

This climate eventually led to the total prohibition of Bible reading. While Pope Innocent III had once been inclined to allow the people access to the Scriptures, it was finally forbidden because of the supposed "danger of heresy" it brought with it. More accurately, the danger was that a Christian people well-versed in the Bible would no longer submit—passively and without a will of their own—to the absolute power of ambitious priests.

From an evangelical perspective, one cannot help but feel sympathy for the shifting efforts of the **Beghards** <term>Beghards</term> <note>Lay religious men who lived in communal houses and emphasized a life of poverty and prayer.</note> and similar communities, despite all the errors and delusions that became attached to them. Many of the accusations hurled against them were clearly invented by the frantic zeal of the **inquisitors** <note>original: "Ketzerrichter," literally "judges of heretics."</note>; the fact that they were driven by a holy aspiration was proven by the joyful deaths of so many victims during the harshest persecutions.

Nevertheless, the movement was not without the danger of severe moral lapses. Hypocrisy and malice sowed their weeds among the wheat here as well—all the more easily because a hazy fanaticism <note>original: "unklare Schwärmerei."</note> was all too tempting to these unproven souls, given the immaturity and lack of structure in the movement as a whole. Yet, the Church certainly had no full right to persecute these sects; it was the Church’s own neglect that caused the elements of a Christian life to flourish outside its own soil. The Church increased its guilt by failing to recognize what was legitimate in their efforts. Only the truth contained within these movements gave certain "heretical" directions the power to endure, inextinguishable amidst all persecutions, until they finally achieved a firm ecclesiastical organization in a more refined form during the **Reformation**.

# Meister Eckhart.

From entirely different starting points, Eckhart’s teachings arrived at the same destination as the efforts and attitudes of those pious associations. The **Beghards** and **Beguines** <term>Beghards and Beguines</term> <note>Lay religious communities in the Middle Ages that sought to live a life of poverty and devotion without joining a formal monastic order.</note> were for the most part poor, uneducated people; to the highly cultured teachers of the Church, trained in <term>Scholasticism</term> <note>The dominant medieval method of teaching and logic used to reconcile philosophy with Christian theology.</note>, they could only be objects of mockery, viewed as a raw and unlearned populace. With what contempt the investigating priests used to report on the **Waldensians** <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A movement that preceded the Reformation, emphasizing the Bible as the sole authority and practicing voluntary poverty.</note> and Beghards they examined! They noted how these people were utterly inexperienced in the simplest elements of scholastic disputation and theology, yet presumed to pass their own judgment—one that deviated from Church doctrine—on the deepest mysteries of religion! To be sure, these "heretics" often knew entire books of Holy Scripture, even the whole New Testament, by heart. From this knowledge of the Bible—which was by no means a mere external rote learning, but had been transformed into the very lifeblood of the inner person by souls hungering for salvation—they boldly held up their superior insight, drawn from the only valid source, against the arbitrary decrees of men. What a transformation must have occurred when a Master of Holy Scripture, a Doctor of the world-renowned **University of Paris**, a famous teacher of the Church well-versed in all the arts of Scholasticism, and a man in a high ecclesiastical position, gave a deeper foundation to the teachings of these poor and lowly people, setting a fully developed system of Christian doctrine against the system of Church dogma!

Johannes Eckhart possessed a vast and comprehensive erudition. In every point, one notices the influence of the school of **Albertus Magnus** <term>Albertus Magnus</term> <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a German Dominican friar and philosopher who was a key figure in medieval science and theology.</note> and **Saint Thomas** <term>Saint Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic philosopher and student of Albertus Magnus.</note>, whose teachings he repeated in many important respects. In his teaching post at Paris, he energetically defended the main tenets of this doctrine, as he himself repeatedly testified. Already as the "Master of Paris," as he is often called—a teacher at the world-famous university that dominated the science of the age—he enjoyed an outstanding reputation. With full right he could say of himself:

> "I have read many writings, both from pagan masters and prophets, from the Old and the New Covenant, and have sought with earnestness and with all diligence to find what might be the best and the highest virtue" (Pfeiffer, *Meister Eckhart* p. 483, l. 32).

# Meister Eckhart.

His diligence is tireless, his intellect incomparable. Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German Benedictine abbot and polymath.</note> describes him as a man well-versed in the Holy Scriptures and surpassing all the scholars of his time in Aristotelian philosophy <note>The philosophy of Aristotle was the framework for almost all medieval university learning.</note>, possessing a refined spirit and extraordinary eloquence. Eckhart is fond of quoting others, and he repeatedly references many of the most significant teachers of the Church, from Origen to Thomas Aquinas and Giles of Rome <note>original: "Aegidius von Colonna," a 13th-century theologian and student of Thomas Aquinas.</note>. He rarely disputes them, preferring instead to draw upon their methods of teaching to reinforce his own. He aligned himself most closely with Thomas Aquinas; however, he cites the Pseudo-Areopagite <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian mystic whose writings emphasized the "unknowability" of God.</note> and Augustine most frequently. 

The pantheistic-mystical element in the former, and the strict doctrine of faith and grace in the latter, lead him for the most part beyond the Thomistic <note>Refers to the system of Thomas Aquinas.</note> form of <term>Scholasticism</term>. Yet, the color and tone of his speculative thought possess, at the same time, a high and bold originality. He seems not to have known Scotus Erigena <note>Johannes Scotus Eriugena (c. 800–877), a philosopher who sought to synthesize Greek and Neoplatonic thought with Christianity.</note>, whose writings had been withdrawn from use since 1225; where he often coincides with Erigena, it is likely explained by indirect tradition and the similar foundations of his train of thought. However, Eckhart's speculation is much more substantial because its true conclusion and highest goal lie in the realm of ethical problems, which Erigena touched upon only with a light hand. 

Eckhart is not entirely dependent on any of his predecessors; he even allows himself to contradict Dionysius. Hugh of Saint Victor <note>A 12th-century mystic and scholar at the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris.</note> is a highly revered teacher to him; yet, when forced to oppose Hugh's opinion on the doctrine of the Eucharist <note>original: "Abendmahl," the Lord’s Supper or Holy Communion.</note>, he wonders how such a great man could ever speak so foolishly. The earlier great masters taught many things correctly, but they did not know the "right reasons" for their teachings. It is precisely in this direction that Eckhart wishes to supplement them; he wants to uncover the deepest meaning of their opinions and trace their teachings back to the most perfect and fundamental unity. Thus, he even declares outright that his teaching is "against all the masters now living." 

He seeks to penetrate to the very depths of the teachings of the Apostles John and Paul regarding the Triune God, the Word made flesh, and the justification and sanctification of man. At the same time, he carries the logical consequences of these thoughts further than any of his predecessors; the boundaries that the Church’s dogmatic formulation of doctrine might impose on his train of thought, he over-

<meta>This page continues the comparison between Meister Eckhart’s radical intellectualism and the more restrained Scholasticism of Thomas Aquinas and Albertus Magnus. <page-num>56</page-num>
<header>Meister Eckhart.</header>

he leaps, and he is not afraid to speak even the most challenging truths. The school of **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic philosopher who sought to harmonize faith and reason.</note> had taught that true blessedness rests in the act of knowing; **Eckhart** intoxicates himself with the joy of discovery and transforms the entire system of Christian doctrine into a system of speculative reason. He does not exempt any of the mysteries of Christianity—not even the doctrine of the Trinity or of Creation—from investigation by the light of reason. Indeed, he moves within this territory with a decided preference. **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> and **Thomas** had removed such doctrines from the judgment of reason, treating them instead as subjects of supernatural revelation. Reason, **Thomas** believed, could only demonstrate that these doctrines do not directly contradict reason; it could show that they are possible for thought, but not that they are actual facts. 

**Eckhart** adopts the more guileless standpoint of **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430), whose theological works often sought a deep, internal understanding of God.</note> and does not exempt even those mysteries from proof through speculative knowing. In this approach itself—quite apart from how the attempt is carried out—lies a reinterpretation of the doctrines of faith; for the historical facts of faith are thus drawn into the sphere of the universal as facts of reason. Divine history becomes a metaphysical process; the unique event that happened once and for all becomes an ever-recurring reality, a process fulfilling itself perpetually and without ceasing. 

As closely as **Thomas** brushes against this conception, he protected himself from it through a self-restraint <note>original: "Selbstbescheidung," a deliberate limitation of one's own inquiry out of humility or religious obedience.</note> that may indeed be an inconsistency compared to his usual <term>intellectualism</term> <note>The philosophical emphasis on the intellect as the primary faculty for reaching God.</note>, but which alone enabled him to become a Doctor of the Church. His relationship to the Church commanded him to stop at the right time. All the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Medieval academics who used logic and philosophy to defend and explain Christian dogma.</note> were primarily concerned with the objective institution of the Church and its contemporary state. They wished to give voice to what was the general ecclesiastical consciousness of their time; they sought to deduce the organically living institutions and forms present in the Church from first principles and to demonstrate their harmony with the essence of Christ’s religion. To defend and promote the Church, and to comprehend its foundations, was their most vital concern. Their thinking aimed toward a "church science," for which all dialectical tools and all knowledge—whether handed down from antiquity or newly won—were made fluid.

<page-num>57</page-num>
<header>Meister Eckhart.</header>

ought to become. Eckhart had, from the very beginning, a different position toward the Church. He did not intentionally adopt this position; rather, it fell to him as his lot, his special task, his unique calling, and the specific disposition of his brilliant mind. His goal was directed not toward the institution of the Church, but toward the salvation of the soul of the individual Christian. He wished to set forth the most direct path by which the soul might attain union with God. Whenever the Scholastics <note>The "Scholastics" were medieval theologians, such as Thomas Aquinas, who used systematic logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note> took this goal into consideration, they too drew closer to mysticism; however, they presented themselves as mystics who remained bound by specifically ecclesiastical and Catholic ideas. In Eckhart’s work, this mystical side became the exclusive and sole focus; his speculation <note>In a theological sense, "speculation" refers to deep philosophical contemplation of divine truths.</note> was required to serve this end alone.

The high flight of his metaphysics <note>The branch of philosophy that examines the fundamental nature of reality, including the relationship between mind and matter, and between God and the world.</note> is merely the naturally occurring correlate to his ethical views. In the treasury of knowledge available at that time, there were no other elements so well-suited to establish the foundation of his teaching on the right conduct of man toward God as the Neoplatonic-Dionysian <note>A school of thought derived from the philosopher Plato and the mystical writings attributed to "Dionysius the Areopagite," emphasizing that God is beyond all names and that the soul must ascend through "unknowing."</note> doctrine of the essence of God and His relationship to the created world. Eckhart necessarily highlighted these elements and emphasized them above all others; while they were present in the work of his predecessors, they had not yet reached the full development of which they were capable. In this lies, on the one hand, a great merit of Eckhart’s, but on the other, a primary source of his great and consequential errors.

In Eckhart, there is a mutual support between his lofty conception of the ethical task—which was eventually heightened to the point of empty abstraction—and a relentless drive for theoretical knowledge. And so, in the interest of strict logical consistency, Eckhart did not shy away from reinterpreting or even rejecting the most essential fundamental facts, not only of Catholic doctrine but of all Christian theology. The teaching of this man, though carried by religious enthusiasm, is in many respects not so much a Christian doctrine of religion as it is a metaphysical speculation colored by pantheism <note>The belief that God is identical with the universe or that everything composes an all-encompassing, immanent God.</note>, which in part only seemingly moves upon the ground of Christian concepts.

Eckhart’s method of teaching provoked no general offense until at least the year 1307; this is proven by the trust he enjoyed within his Order <note>Eckhart belonged to the Dominican Order, also known as the Order of Preachers.</note>. To be sure, in Paris he was not

taught much differently than he did later in Germany; he himself cites several statements that he made from his teaching chair in Paris, which prove the same high flight of ideas as his later style of preaching, including sentences that are found among those condemned by the Pope. But there, at the university, he had presented his propositions before an audience of scholars and had tested himself in the customary disputations and competitions. In Germany, however, he taught and preached "before the simple common folk," <note>original: "coram vulgo simplici"</note> and that made a great difference to the Church. What was considered heretical in this field, and what could still pass as official Church doctrine, was by no means fixed in itself. Even if one only accepted as Church doctrine what Saint *Dionysius* <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian philosopher whose mystical writings were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> and Saint *Thomas* <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian whose work synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian principles.</note> had taught, one could not do much to oppose a doctrine such as the one *Eckhart* presented. Sentences that strike us today as daring, incomprehensible, or even blasphemous, were at least much closer to the Church education of that time—the less one was accustomed to speaking strictly according to scripture, the more mystical speculation was the common property of the Church and determined the form and expression of its doctrine. 

But *Eckhart* now developed these teachings with bold consistency, and what is more, he developed them before the "immature" people <note>In this context, the "immature" (unmündig) refers to those who were not legally or educationally authorized to interpret scripture for themselves.</note>, before an audience of ignorant laity or simple monastics, in whom he either assumed or wished to awaken not formal knowledge, but a hunger and thirst for the knowledge of God and a true need for salvation. In doing so, he ignited a disposition that strove beyond the boundaries of the Church; he encouraged a very special, specific piety of the heart, a "following of Christ" that had little need for the Church’s institutional means of salvation, and a curiosity about divine things that was ill-suited for the common people. This changed everything, and *Eckhart* became a figure of suspicion. The pious who gathered around him were labeled with the traditional heretical name of *Beghards*. <note>The Beghards were groups of laymen in the Low Countries and Germany who lived in semi-monastic communities without taking formal vows; they were frequently suspected of heresy by the ecclesiastical authorities.</note> It was not his propositions themselves that were initially resented, but rather that he treated the deepest mysteries before such an audience. It was precisely this that made him dangerous, and the movement he stirred in people's souls was regarded as highly suspicious.

The doctrine that *Eckhart* presented did indeed coincide with the best and most genuine elements found in the spiritual disposition...

->Meister Eckhart.<-

the pious who stood outside the actual official Church were the dominant influence. The freedom of the enlightened from the law, the worthlessness of external works and outward church discipline, the longing for the most intimate union with Christ, and the assertion of the inalienable likeness of the soul to God: in all of this, Eckhart’s teaching met the disposition of those people. These doctrines had never been formulated before as they were by Eckhart; here, for the first time, they appeared not as the result of fragmentary reflection or a visionary delusion, but as a systematic speculation <note>In this context, "speculation" refers to rigorous, systematic philosophical and theological inquiry rather than mere guesswork.</note> on the basis of the scientific knowledge of the time. Their meaning became deeper, their content richer, and more fruitful for the shaping of life. They did justice in an outstanding measure to the noblest impulses of the religious life of that time and, in particular, to the national character of the German people. It is just as little surprising that they found immense acclaim as it is that the priesthood took the opportunity to intervene against the spread of these doctrines with all the means at its disposal.

Since the year 1307, we hear of Eckhart only where there is talk of measures of ecclesiastical persecution against him. In the year 1317, the Bishop of Strasbourg, *Johann von Ochsenstein*, condemned a series of propositions that were in vogue among the *Beghards* <note>The Beghards were lay religious groups who lived in communal poverty and devotion; they were often accused of heresy for their belief in the possibility of spiritual perfection on earth.</note> and were even preached by clergy and members of religious orders. These propositions, even if mixed with foreign components, are for the most part taken from Eckhart’s writings, though not without misunderstandings. That it was possible to put a teacher like Eckhart on the same level as the Beghards, without him ever having entered into an actual connection with them, is also shown by the example of *Ruusbroec* <note>Jan van Ruusbroec (1293–1381), an influential Flemish mystic whose writings on the soul's union with God were sometimes scrutinized by the Church.</note>, who was counted among the Beghards by the Chancellor *Gerson* <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), the Chancellor of the University of Paris, who was a famous theologian and critic of what he saw as mystical excesses.</note> and about whom the opinion later formed that he had been in contact with the Beghards for a time and only separated from them after he realized the reprehensibility of this sect. Clearly, the name of the Beghards also served Bishop Johann as a convenient label for a certain religious direction—not as a sectarian name in the narrower sense—in order to more easily target Eckhart’s teaching. Thus *Tauler* <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a Dominican monk and famous preacher who was a student and follower of Eckhart’s mystical tradition.</note> also defends himself

This persecution initially seems to have had no further consequences for *Eckhart*; at the very least, traces show that he still preached unhindered in *Strasbourg* after 1322. *Eckhart* then went to *Frankfurt am Main* as Prior. He preached there, as was his custom in *Strasbourg*, in nunneries. The opposing party used his close contact with the nuns to cast moral suspicion upon this noble man. In the heading of a collection of *Eckhart’s* sayings, we find him designated as Vicar <note>original: "Vicarius"</note> of *Thuringia* and Prior of *Erfurt*; whether he ever held this office and when, we do not know from reliable sources. The last years of his life were spent by *Eckhart* in *Cologne*, mostly as the revered head of a school of theology to which *Tauler* and *Suso* <note>Johannes Tauler and Henry Suso were Eckhart's most famous students and went on to become major figures in German mysticism.</note> belonged. He preached in the church of his monastery and taught at the university which had become so famous through the activity of *Albertus Magnus* <note>A celebrated 13th-century philosopher and scientist whose presence made Cologne a premier center for medieval scholarship.</note>. Serious accusations reached the General Chapter <note>The governing assembly of a religious order.</note> of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominican Order, known for its intellectual focus and role in defending Church doctrine.</note> held in *Venice* in 1325, alleging that certain brothers in the German province were delivering teachings in sermons to the common people that could easily lead uneducated and ordinary folk into error. *Gervasius*, the Prior of *Anjou*, was tasked with investigating the matter. We then learn that at the General Chapter in *Paris* in 1326, the Prior of the German provincial order was deposed. The conclusion is likely justified that *Eckhart* was this very Prior.

However, this was not the end of the persecution. The greater the success of *Eckhart’s* teaching activity in *Cologne*, the more violent the zeal of his opponents became. The Archbishop of *Cologne*, *Heinrich von Virnenburg*, who distinguished himself through his impetuous zeal in persecuting alleged or actual heresies, had already ordered the punishment of the Beghards and Beguines <note>Lay religious groups who sought lives of apostolic poverty and devotion, often operating outside strict clerical control.</note> through a rescript <note>A formal legal or religious edict issued by an authority.</note> in 1306, and many victims had fallen to his zeal as late as 1325. This same man brought charges before Pope *John XXII* not just against individual brothers of the Order of Preachers, but against the entire Order, claiming it was spreading false doctrine. # Meister Eckhart.

The Vicar <note>original: "Vicarius"</note> of the Pope found the accusations to be unfounded. On January 14, 1327, Nicholas protested against the fact that the Archbishop had heard false accusations against the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominican Order</note>, and the following day he renewed the protest against the proceedings of the Archbishop, who had meanwhile brought Master Eckhart before his religious court <note>original: "Glaubensgericht" — an ecclesiastical court or tribunal of the Inquisition.</note>. Also in January 1327, John Eckhart appealed from the inquisitors in Cologne to the Pope. On February 13 of the same year, Eckhart decided upon a conditional retraction. He declared, calling upon God as his witness, that he had always—to the best of his ability—abhorred every error in doctrine and every offensiveness in conduct, as such lapses would have contradicted his position as a Doctor of Holy Theology and as a member of the Order in equal measure. If, therefore, any error were to be found that he had written, taught, or preached in the past, publicly or secretly, in any place or at any time, directly or indirectly, out of lack of clarity or obstinacy of mind, he hereby expressly and publicly retracted it before all members of the court together and before each individual, because he wished such things to be considered as unsaid or unwritten from this point forward. Nevertheless, the verdict of the religious court must have been issued against Eckhart, and individual sentences of his must have been expressly condemned, or their author sentenced to a specific punishment. For on February 20, Eckhart appealed against the verdict of the inquisitors in Cologne to the Pope. The investigation, which the Papal Court initiated directly against Eckhart, and in which he himself had to admit to having taught certain propositions presented to him, took a turn that was unfavorable for Eckhart. In the year 1328, a Bull from the Pope appeared with the opening words: *In the field of the Lord* <note>original: "In agro Dominico"</note>, which, for the sake of the heretical Beghards and Beguines <note>Lay religious groups who were often accused of heresy for their mystical beliefs and lifestyle outside of formal monastic rules.</note>, forbade the preaching of a series of dogmas drawn from Eckhart's writings, though without mentioning Eckhart's name.

Teaching such audacious and enigmatic sentences was considered dangerous because of hypocrites of both sexes who lived heretically for the sake of financial gain, distinguished themselves through a peculiar way of life, and sought out a doctrine—that is, a falsified one—that corresponded to their lifestyle. Anyone who continued to preach such sentences should immediately incur the penalty of excommunication <term>Excommunication: A formal censure that excludes a person from the sacraments and the spiritual community of the Church.</term> and be punished for some of those sentences as heretical, and for others as suspicious of heresy and audacious. This Bull <note>The Papal Bull "In agro dominico," issued by Pope John XXII.</note>, therefore, initially only intended to prevent the further dissemination of the sentences because of the danger they posed to hypocritical minds, without, however, directly labeling them all as heretical. 

The Bull has mostly been misunderstood. The incorrect dating of it by the completely unreliable **Corner** (in *Eckhart's Corpus of Medieval History* <note>original: "Eccardi Corp. histor. medii aevi"</note> vol. 2, col. 1036) led **Mosheim**, **Gieseler**, **Ch. This also clarifies the true purpose of the Bull, the full wording of which we still do not know: for the reliability of the report given by **Heinrich von Erfurt** cannot be doubted. If only it would please **Pfeiffer**, in whose hands—alongside so much other valuable material—the Vatican documents relating to **Eckhart** are located, to share them, so that at last a full historical light might fall upon **Eckhart's** relationships to the **Beghards** <term>Beghards: A lay religious group that lived in semi-monastic communities without formal vows, often viewed with suspicion by the Church for their mystical practices.</term> as well as to the **Brothers and Sisters of the Free Spirit** <term>Brothers and Sisters of the Free Spirit: A loose-knit mystical movement in the 13th and 14th centuries that emphasized the soul's direct union with God, often accused of ignoring Church law.</term>!

### Meister Eckhart. 63

At the beginning of the year 1329, **Eckhart** died, and at the very least, any personal consideration for him ceased. On March 27, 1329, the Pope issued a new Bull <note>The Papal Bull *In agro dominico*, issued by Pope John XXII.</note>, which identified 28 propositions of the Master as heretical or suspected of heresy and rejected them as such. In this Bull, **Eckhart**—who is spoken of as if he were an obscure figure otherwise unknown to the Pope—is mentioned as already deceased. It relates that before his death, he confessed the Catholic faith and revoked and rejected 26 of those articles, as well as anything else he might have written or taught that could produce a heretical, erroneous, or hostile sense to the true faith in the minds of the faithful—insofar as it held such a sense. The Bull stated that this revocation should be valid as if he had revoked each of those articles and other teachings individually and specifically, as he had submitted both himself and all his writings and speeches to the decision of the Apostolic See <term>Apostolic See: The ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the Pope in Rome.</term>.

Whether these last words refer to a second, more explicit revocation by **Eckhart** made shortly before his death can at the very least appear doubtful. That it was not an unconditional, but a conditional revocation, is nevertheless evident from the wording of the Bull; and the first revocation mentioned above could very well have taken on the form presented in the Bull within a papal report. However, it is also not unthinkable that **Eckhart** submitted himself in all honesty to the judgment of the Church and revoked—not the propositions themselves—but everything in them that could lead to a heretical opinion.

**Eckhart** never speaks of the Church with anything but reverence, although he certainly emphasizes that the Pope’s power only reaches the boundaries of conscience. He recognizes only one true Church, the Roman one; he attacks neither its priests nor its institutions, but rather their claim to absolute authority. He knows something even higher than the Church, and that is **Christ** himself. He simply does not believe that the Church is the exclusive organ for the communication of all grace <term>Communication of grace: The theological concept of how God's favor or divine life is shared with humanity.</term>. He also acknowledges the sacraments and customs of the Church, but not as the ultimate and highest reality or as an absolute necessity to which one is bound; nor does he accept them in their traditional ecclesiastical sense, but rather with a reinterpretation into the spiritual realm. That **Eckhart**, what he held to be true,
