->### Meister Eckhart.<-

...that he would have labeled his teachings as false simply to please the Pope is something one cannot be persuaded to believe; but that he went as far as his conscience would permit for the sake of the esteemed head of the Church is something we may rightly assume. — Despite the Church’s censorship, **Eckhart** left behind an honorable memory, and even his opponents speak of him in a gentle manner. His "errors" were attributed by the Pope himself to an overly passionate drive for knowledge <note>original: *Erkenntniss*</note> that could not find satisfaction in the prescribed articles of faith. To the older ecclesiastical critics, he was—to one, a man of equally excellent character and spirit; to another, a man exalted beyond all praise; a third praises him as a man of the strictest conduct, a well-equipped teacher of the Church without equal among his contemporaries, as distinguished by his knowledge of doctrine as by his way of life and character. The historians of the writers of his Order <note>The Dominican Order, to which Eckhart belonged.</note> explain his errors by saying that the most outstanding spirits are not always the most cautious; one must believe that he was swept into these errors by an immoderate, unsober longing for a holy life. There must have been nothing to object to regarding his personal character if, despite the Church's condemnation of this "fallen" man, even his opponents judged him so mildly.

**Eckhart** died in the midst of the most violent persecution. Even over his grave, the Pope called out his cry of condemnation, though indeed with relatively mild words toward the author of the condemned teachings. But **Eckhart's** thoughts were not dead; only now did they truly come to life. Enthusiastic disciples carried them out into all the world, and although cast out by the Church, **Eckhart** remained "the Master," to whom many of the noblest, most pious, and most soulful men confessed their allegiance without fear and with the deepest reverence. Now **Eckhart** became "the Master" <note>original: *der Meister*</note> pure and simple for an entire generation of theologians; he was called the great, the high, the blessed, the divine Master—the Master from whom God never hid anything, who taught the truth at all times. People carried his individual sayings with them; the most inward and deepest things of God, and perhaps even the most strange and paradoxical in expression, were what people loved to associate with his name to...

Repeatedly, Suso <note>Heinrich Suso (c. 1295–1366), a devoted student of Eckhart and a famous mystic in his own right.</note> in particular remembers the holy, the blessed Master, who freed him from the trials, doubts, and anxieties of his soul; in his typical fashion, he sees him in visions, radiant with the light of transfiguration, and hears his assurance that the fullest contemplation of the divine light has been granted to him in the afterlife. Only now do the Master's thoughts gain power over the nation. His enthusiastic disciples spread them abroad and, through powerful preaching, ignite even sluggish hearts. Following the Master's very words most closely—often transcribing him directly or repeating his entire train of thought, though usually softening his harshness <note>original: *Herbigkeit*; referring to the challenging, paradoxical nature of Eckhart's original statements.</note>—these disciples shaped German mysticism upon an Eckhartian foundation as a specific treasure of the German nation.

But the Master's writings also continued to exert a most fruitful influence, albeit in a different manner. No doubt people tracked them down in obedience to the Pope's command <note>The Papal Bull *In agro dominico* (1329), which condemned several of Eckhart's propositions.</note> and marked them for destruction; yet many, at least, escaped this persecution. As a precious possession, they traveled in secret from hand to hand; godly souls exchanged them with one another and allowed themselves to be initiated through them into the mysteries of the divine essence; they became the foundational texts of a God-intoxicated piety. Naturally, they were often not labeled with the author's name; likewise, the writings of others—if only a similar spirit lived within them—were attributed to the high Master, and Eckhart's own writings sometimes circulated under different names. People never tired of copying them, making excerpts from them, highlighting important reflections, and reworking them into a new whole within a different context. We still have (in Greith, *German Mysticism in the Order of Preachers* <note>Karl Johann Greith (1807–1882), a scholar who documented the history of the Dominicans.</note> pp. 96–202) at least one treatise which—with the exception of a few passages borrowed from Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), another influential Dominican mystic and student of Eckhart.</note> or Suso—is composed entirely of longer and shorter excerpts from Eckhart and presents a structured system of doctrine in a clear brevity, such as Eckhart himself would hardly ever have provided. ->### Meister Eckhart.<-

Eckhart's eloquence is unanimously praised by all witnesses. What we still possess of his work proves a truly extraordinary power of language. His speech must have been captivating for those with more profound spirits. One would be completely mistaken to look to this "mystic" for an unclear expression of thoughts struggling with language, an overflowing of emotion, a wallowing in fantastical imagery, or a vague twilight that washes away sharp boundaries. Clear and definite, in striking, well-defined, and characterful turns of phrase, his speech builds itself up with mostly short, tightly joined sentences, like a building made of ashlar blocks <note>original: *Quadern*; squared stones used in masonry, implying strength and precision in his logic.</note>. There is a prevailing delight in the extreme and sharpest honing of thought; paradox is sought out rather than avoided. The speaker takes pleasure in turning prevailing, common opinions on their head, bringing distant ideas into close connection, and making the futility of common sense quite clear by confronting it, unprepared, with the unexpected, the strange, and even the shocking as the true and deepest understanding of the matter. The first version of a thought is never enough; it is surpassed by a second, sharper version, and then by a third, even bolder one. Indeed, one is right to speak of a daringness of expression, even where the thought itself does not strictly demand it. It is evident that the Master prefers the strongest expression, and that he deliberately highlights the contrast between his views and the flattening common perspective as drastically as possible in his wording. Yet he is never tasteless; he never lacks a sure and healthy sense of tact. Though his brusqueness might often offend the devotion of a religious soul, to many, the boldness of the thinker will seem to compensate for whatever he lacks in simple, plain piety.

Eckhart is the creator of philosophical prose in Germany. Excellent church sermons and mystical writings of edification with masterly language existed before him. But for his speculation <note>original: *Speculation*; in this historical context, it refers to deep, systematic philosophical or theological contemplation rather than mere guessing.</note>, he had to create the linguistic garment himself. And with wha—

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Meister Eckhart’s rhetorical and linguistic brilliance, specifically how he bridged the gap between Latin Scholasticism and the German language. The text picks up from the previous page's discussion of his daring expression.</meta>

->### Meister Eckhart.<-

5 *

...with such genius did he accomplish this! He was the first to attempt, in an exemplary manner, to forge German expressions for the philosophical concepts of the school <note>The "school" refers to Scholasticism, the dominant medieval system of theology and philosophy taught in universities.</note>. This is seen in Sermon 101 in Pfeiffer’s edition (pp. 324–328), which is partly a condensed translation from the *Summary of Theology* <note>original: *Summa theologiae*</note> of Thomas Aquinas (Part I, Question 15, Articles 1–3). He carefully distinguishes between synonyms, seeking everywhere a precision and certainty in language that cuts away all ambiguity. He did not disdain foreign words but used them only sparingly; occasionally, he uses the native German term alongside the borrowed one with the same meaning. However eccentric his speculation may sometimes be, the inevitable obscurity inherent in the subject matter is not increased by vagueness of expression; rather, it is reduced as much as possible through precise wording. His speech can sound so heartfelt, so gentle and sweet, only to storm forth again with the wings of inspiration, seizing the imagination and captivating all the senses. For his abstractions, for his chains of syllogistic reasoning <note>Formal logical arguments consisting of two premises and a conclusion.</note>, for the dialectical twists of his train of thought—for everything he found the appropriate, striking form; his expression, razor-sharp like his opinion, is the perfectly fitting garment of his thought. It is hard to say in which field he presents himself most perfectly: whether in the simple instructional tone of edifying devotion, when he holds before a simple Christian heart the reasons for its comfort, the greatness of its duties, and the love of its God; or in the heights of speculative discussion, when he undertakes to fathom the essence of the Godhead and all things through thought; or in the inspired portrayal of a perfectly sanctified life, where man has reached his highest goal—union with his God. His students have other merits; but in conciseness, liveliness, and sweeping momentum, he has been surpassed by none.

<margin>Eckhart was an extremely prolific writer. Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German Benedictine abbot and polymath.</note> still saw of his work: Commentaries on the *Sentences* <note>The *Sententiae* of Peter Lombard, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> and several books of Holy Scripture, a collection of dogmas, and sermons.</margin>

Even the famous Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa drew directly from the Master’s writings. ### Meister Eckhart.

“*Cusanus* <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), an influential German philosopher, theologian, and astronomer.</note> reported that he had seen many of *Eckhart’s* explanatory writings on most books of the Holy Scripture, many sermons and *treatises*, and furthermore several sayings drawn from his writings on John, here and there in libraries, which had been annotated and refuted by others. In Mainz, he also saw a short writing by *Eckhart* in which he responded to those who wished to attack him, by explaining himself and proving that his critics had not understood him. Nevertheless, the teacher—praising *Eckhart’s* spirit and his diligence—claimed he had never read that *Eckhart* taught the identity of the creature and the Creator; yet he wished that his books would not be made generally accessible, because the masses were not capable of understanding what he himself wove in, contrary to the habit of other theologians, although intelligent people could find much that is astute and useful in his books.” *Nicholas of Cusa* became one of the renewers of science precisely because he brought *Eckhart’s* speculation <note>In this context, high-level philosophical or theoretical reasoning.</note> into close relationship with the newly awakening efforts in the fields of mathematics and the natural sciences.

What we possess from *Eckhart* was all initially written for the purpose of edification <note>Spiritual instruction or improvement.</note> or has its purpose in the deeper foundation of ethical requirements. The form, too, is nowhere that of a coherent scientific lecture. All his speaking and writing has the purpose of moving the heart <note>original: *Gemüther*</note> and strives for general clarity. The fundamental character is theological discussion; he allows his view of divine and human things to be reflected in the most diverse texts taken from the Holy Scripture—though torn from their context—by virtue of the most arbitrary allegorical interpretation. The path is everywhere that of synthetic deduction <note>Reasoning that moves from a general principle to specific conclusions.</note> from that supreme principle, not the justification of this principle itself. In the devotion that animates these speeches and treatises, the element that is most prominent in all Pietist <note>A later movement in the Lutheran Church emphasizing individual piety and religious experience, though here used to describe a general focus on personal devotion.</note> movements—sorrow over sin—is almost entirely absent; instead, it is characterized by reveling in the abstract, in the pure, imageless contemplation of the highest unity. The most of Eckhart’s writings, especially his biblical commentaries, are likely lost forever. What remains to us are sermons and treatises, collections of passages extracted from Eckhart, and sayings preserved in tradition. **Pfeiffer** <note>Franz Pfeiffer (1815–1868), a philologist whose 1857 edition of Eckhart's German works rescued the mystic from relative obscurity.</note> spent 18 years collecting and brought together a not inconsiderable collection. Perhaps he wrongly excluded some manuscript material or texts printed in the editions of Tauler, or perhaps some included material cannot be attributed to Eckhart with certainty: yet this much is certain, that the conscientious manner in which he proceeded deserves the highest praise. In **Pfeiffer’s** collection, Eckhart stands before us for the first time in the full armor of his great spirit; the lost works can be more easily endured since we have enough material to grasp the uniqueness and significance of the man as a whole with certainty. We now know the deeper spring from which highly important elements have flowed that characterize the entire national culture of the German people. We recognize in Eckhart one of the deepest thinkers of all time, one of the greatest men of the German nation. The historical effects that have emanated from him can hardly be estimated too highly. # The Teachings of Eckhart.

### Preliminary Remarks.

The presentation of Eckhart’s teachings is made significantly more difficult by the fact that the Master only ever speaks about individual points of his circle of thought in a connected way. He strives to solve specific questions or remove particular difficulties depending on the specific occasion. If the form of the sermon <term>Predigt: A religious discourse intended for spiritual edification rather than academic debate.</term> and the devotional treatise is, in itself, poorly suited for a strictly scientific and interconnected system of thought <term>Gedankensystem: A structured, logical framework where every part supports the whole.</term>, the Master himself is also little inclined to develop his thoughts consistently in long sequences or to explicitly trace every detail back to the ultimate grounding principle from which it actually flows. 

Both his thinking and his speaking have an aphoristic, jumping quality; the fundamental vision <term>Grundanschauung: The core intuitive outlook or worldview that underlies his entire philosophy.</term> that encompasses every detail of his teaching shines through everywhere, and yet he presents his doctrines in the form of self-evident statements without delving deeper into the underlying reasons. At times, he leaps almost arbitrarily from one subject and turns to another, as his mood drives him. He tirelessly repeats those thoughts which he hopes will most powerfully take hold of the soul; however, he neglects the intermediate links that are indispensable for creating a conceptual whole if they do not promise immediate fruit for the religious and moral life. Thus, he has evidently not fully thought through a whole series of problems arising from his fundamental vision, nor considered a wealth of difficulties; many obvious contradictions in his statements remained hidden even to himself— <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the word "ge-", likely the beginning of "geblieben" (remained).</note>

It highlights how his "fundamental vision" is ever-present but rarely structured into a formal scientific framework.</summary>

# The Teachings of Eckhart.

...remained. He explores the interconnections of thought more thoroughly than those who usually write or speak for the edification <note>In a religious context, "edification" refers to the building up of the soul or spiritual improvement.</note> of readers and listeners; yet, at the same time, he is more guileless than is fitting for someone who undertakes to present a well-structured whole of scientific knowledge.

Eckhart himself described the principle of his entire way of thinking very well. Everything earthly is a parable. <note>original: "Gleichniss"</note> If you want the kernel, you must break the shell. If you want to find nature in itself, all parables must vanish (333, 24). It is a defect of nature, he says, that one must describe God with sensory images and specific predicates. God, however, is neither this nor that; He finds no satisfaction until He has withdrawn from all specific being into absolute unity. There, every blade of grass, wood, stone, and all things are one. "This is the very best, and I have become infatuated with it" (332, 31). <note>The original German "vergafft" suggests being completely captivated or "lost" in a gaze of wonder.</note> He always returns to this highest unity; to grasp it through thought and to permeate it through love is the constant goal of his exhortation.

But it is the spirit of pious devotion, not outward curiosity, that guides him. "I like to speak of the <term>Godhead <note>original: "Gottheit." In Eckhart’s theology, this refers to the absolute, undifferentiated essence of God that lies "beyond" the personal Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note></term>, because all our salvation flows from it" (301, 6). And along with God, he mentions the divine part of the soul, the uncreated and uncreatable light. "This light I am accustomed to touch upon everywhere in my preaching" (193, 17). God is not outside. One should not grasp God nor pay attention to Him outside oneself, but rather insofar as He is my own and within me (206, 2). You have all truth within you as your own being; why do you seek outside yourselves? Why do you not stay with yourselves and reach into your own treasure (67, 17)? No external authority, not Scripture, not dogma, can make you blessed; you must experience and live it all within yourselves (102, 34; 12, 30), when God and the Holy Spirit take you into His school (77, 16; 12, 34). What would it help us to speak much of divine nature if we did not find His image within us (657, 26)? — However high his speculations about God and the <term>essential unity <note>original: "Wesenseinheit"; the ontological oneness of the human soul's deepest core with the divine essence.</note></term> of the soul with God may soar, it is moral elevation that he strives for above all. "When I preach, I am accustomed to speak of <term>detachment <note>original: "Abgeschiedenheit." One of Eckhart's most famous concepts, referring to a state of being so "released" from worldly things and the "ego" that one becomes a pure vessel for God.</note></term> and that man should become free of his..."

**Eckhart** is well aware that his teachings are harshly criticized and grossly misunderstood by many. I know, he says at the conclusion of his magnificent little book "On Divine Consolation" (p. 447 ff.), that many an unspiritual person will say that many words I have written in this book and elsewhere are not true. And elsewhere the same man says: that person shows an all-too-naked self-love who wants to blind other people so that his own blindness might remain hidden. If someone dips a staff into water, the straight staff appears crooked to him; this happens because the water is coarser than the air. Nevertheless, the staff is straight in itself and not crooked, and it is also so in the eyes of one who sees it only in the pure element of air. **St. Augustine** says: He who recognizes inwardly, without all sorts of thoughts, without all sorts of sensory images and forms, what has not entered the soul through any outward seeing—he knows that it is true. But he who does not know it, laughs and mocks me, and I pity him. But such people want to gaze upon and judge eternal things and the works of God and stand in the light of eternity, while their hearts still flutter in yesterday and today, in time and space. **Seneca**, a pagan sage, says: Of great and high things one should speak in a great and high sense and with an exalted soul. ## The Teaching of Eckhart.

...add teachings; to know this is not necessary (284, 10), and he requires knowledge from those who are spiritually advanced, but faith from the uneducated (189, 14).

He is prepared for misunderstandings. Yet his soul is so full that he must share it. "Whoever has understood this sermon, I wish them well. If there had been no one here, I would have had to preach it to this wooden post" (181, 19). But he wants to make himself understood and strives for an accessible <note>original: "populären" — in this context meaning intended for the common people rather than just scholars.</note> presentation. "As I was walking here today, I considered how I might preach so clearly that you would understand me well, and I devised a parable" (192, 30; 336, 1). And so he also distinguishes between the popular pulpit sermon and scholarly investigation (69, 26). However, he does not believe himself exempt from the need for proof. "I will prove this to you with natural reasons, so that you can grasp it with your hands; and even though I believe the Scriptures more than myself, it will nevertheless be impressed upon you more deeply and better because it is proven to you" (4, 17). Speaking without explanation and proof would be like "a splash in the water" <note>An idiom meaning a futile or ineffective action; similar to "beating the air."</note> (216, 38).

Eckhart’s primary endeavor is to lead the soul out of all images and parables toward a pure and adequate contemplation <term>contemplation: "Anschauung" — direct, intuitive perception or viewing of a spiritual truth.</term> of the Absolute. He is not an absolute enemy of all parables; for spiritual things can only be communicated to the soul—in its state of being darkened by the body and the senses—through parables (196, 9). But he regrets this necessity and urges us not to stop at the parable, but to strip away everything pictorial. It is the habit of people that little appeals to them which they cannot grasp through sensory perception. And yet one should know that the truth is so pure in itself that it cannot be understood everywhere through the physical senses. Perception is, in a sense, a way to arrive at understanding (344, 33). Even the writers of Holy Scripture, the prophets, who received the revelation of divine truth through inspiration, had to take refuge in sensory images if they wished to communicate what they had seen, or else they had to remain silent. For partly the truth they beheld was beyond the capacity of their intellect to grasp, partly it could not be expressed in the images and forms of language, partly...

### Preliminary Remarks.

...it was so hidden that it could not be communicated at all (307, 20). If, however, Holy Scripture points beyond itself, then one must also not seek the highest truth within the rational concepts of science <note>original: "Wissenschaft" — here referring to systematic theological or philosophical study.</note>. Many arrive at a clear understanding and exact distinction through images and forms; but few advance beyond the self-satisfaction of rational knowledge to a pure contemplation <term>contemplation: "Anschauung" — direct, intuitive perception of spiritual truth</term>, in which all specific and particular mental representations are transcended (475, 35).

The Master’s fundamental premise is the divine nature of the soul, and from this he will not be moved. The soul demands the absolute highest and cannot endure that anything should be above it, even were it God himself (201, 37). Yet the highest element within the soul is reason. For this reason, he is far from assuming a fundamental opposition between revealed truth and rational knowledge. Instead, they essentially agree; the natural light of the rational soul and the teaching of the Gospel bear the same witness (421, 6). Reason must be purified under the influence of divine gifts; all knowledge here on earth is imperfect; but in principle, reason possesses the highest truth even now, albeit without clear definition or complete penetration. God did not wish to withhold anything from reason. It is an error, found mostly in dogmatic views and among theologians, to think that God only intended to reveal what is necessary for salvation <term>salvation: "Seligkeit" — can also mean blessedness or supreme happiness</term>. Rather, He has revealed everything to us; for this reason He became man, so that I might be born as God, just as He is. But some theologians do not understand that there is something so akin to God and so one with Him (233, 28; 234, 37). All our salvation proceeds from right knowing. That we should know God as much as we are able, and that we should know ourselves—that is God’s all-benevolent will (525, 40). Rational knowledge is eternal life (581, 6). He already defended the proposition of the primacy of reason among all the soul's powers while in Paris, evidently against the Scotists <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus, who generally prioritized the will over the intellect or reason.</note>, a point to which he frequently refers (270, 26; 138, 16). Holy Scripture does not find its significance in the facts it relates or the doctrines it proclaims, but rather in the fact that every person can fully live it out within themselves. ## The Teachings of Eckhart.

...from us in the same way. If you are in the right disposition, then everything that is said in the Old and New Covenant will be fulfilled in you (307, 2).

Eckhart quotes frequently and with pleasure; but he often interprets the teachings of the masters in a sense foreign to them and imposes his own meaning on their words. He is full of reverence for the great masters of former times, but he wants to supplement them and provide a deeper foundation for their teachings. Regarding the relationship of the persons in the Trinity to one another in particular, he says: "If the masters had understood it rightly, they would surely have proven it. They spoke of it and did not understand it" (176, 8). A true polemic is not found in Eckhart. Occasionally he mentions a quietist sect that strives to be free of outward works, and shows that this is impossible (53, 23; 19, 7). He criticizes people—evidently the Beguards <note>The Beguards were a semi-monastic lay religious movement in the Middle Ages, often viewed with suspicion or as heretical by the Church hierarchy for their claims of spiritual independence.</note> are meant—who place an undue value on a peculiar outward appearance and lifestyle in order to separate themselves from the world (564, 5). But apart from such subtle echoes, he avoids fighting those of different views. He acknowledges the Church and its worship without further ado. It is not his intention to found a new sect. The name "Friends of God" <term>Friends of God: "Gottesfreunde" — a loosely organized group of 14th-century mystics who sought a deeper, internal relationship with God while remaining within the Church.</term> appears frequently in his work, but it does not designate a specific community, but generally people of high piety and mystical orientation who stand on the word of the Lord: "I have called you not servants, but friends" (233, 24; 378, 5).

Eckhart also does not speak of the pagans <term>pagans: "Heiden" — here referring to the pre-Christian philosophers of antiquity.</term> with rejection. He considers well how much science and even the knowledge of God owes to the pagans, and what high virtues they have demonstrated. Often he quotes "pagan" masters and refers to Greek, but also to Arabian philosophers. Not infrequently he appeals to Aristotle, the "natural master," the master "who has spoken best of the soul"; to Plato, "the great priest"; he mentions with reverence Socrates, Tullius <note>original: "Tullius" — Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator.</note>, and Seneca. Using the example of Archimedes, who in mortal danger thought only of his circles, he shows how the soul should be gathered in God in order to shut itself off from everything earthly (13, 25); he presents the Heraclitean Cratylus as a model of perfect detachment <term>detachment: "Abgeschiedenheit" — a central concept in Eckhart's thought, meaning the soul's withdrawal from worldly concerns to focus entirely on God.</term>

# Preliminary Remarks.

...serve, who, according to the report of **Aristotle**, believed he should say nothing more, but only moved his finger (130, 17). <note>This refers to the philosopher Cratylus, who, believing that reality changes too fast for language to capture, eventually stopped speaking and only pointed.</note> He praises how even the heathens <note>Eckhart uses "heathens" (pagans) to refer to the great Greek and Roman philosophers like Plato, Aristotle, and Seneca.</note> sacrificed their lives and joyfully renounced themselves out of pure natural virtue (447, 1). He shows the great power of good habit and the practice of virtue through the example of so many pagan **masters**, who through practice possessed a greater experience and knowledge of all virtues than **St. Paul** or any other saint at the beginning of their conversion (48, 19). As an example and model of true poverty, he employs **Diogenes** in the barrel, who was permitted to say to the lord of the world: "I am a mightier ruler than you; for I have despised more than you have won. What you regard as great to gain, is for me too small even to despise" (576, 6). The pious urge for knowledge is represented by **Solon**, who, while dying, still wanted to learn something good in order to enjoy it eternally (15, 14). The heathens also achieved natural gentleness, love, and peacefulness (273, 24). 

But in this, **Eckhart** is by no means blind to the fundamental difference between everything Christian and everything pagan. The teaching of the pagan **masters** stands on the viewpoint of nature; the holy teachers have beheld the truth in a much purer light (270, 18). There is no virtue, however great, that could not also be worked out of mere nature; all outward works that have ever been found in the saints have also been found in the heathens. Only Christ is at a height that no nature can reach; with him, we are to rise again thoroughly and entirely. That is the true resurrection, where one does not die again (116, 9). And so he explicitly designates all virtue arising from mere nature as **vice** (106, 15). <note>This reflects the theological idea that without divine grace, even "good" actions are technically flawed because they are not directed toward the true God.</note>

For **Eckhart's** way of thinking, nothing is as characteristic as the figure of the **oxymoron**, in which he moves incessantly. The logical principle expressed by his student **Suso**, that speculative thinking must think two **opposites** <note>original: "Contraria"</note> as one, is not found expressed in such clear words in **Eckhart’s** writings; however, it forms a canon <term>Canon: a fundamental rule or principle by which something is judged.</term> that has indeed determined **Eckhart’s** thinking; and if in the work of **Nicholas of Cusa** this very principle is the animating soul

# I. The Soul.

The presentation of Eckhart's doctrine according to its own inner coherence must begin with his concepts of the soul, of its essence, and its powers. For his conception of the essence of the soul is the deepest foundation and the unifying principle of all his teachings. He himself indicates this through the high value he places on self-knowledge. If I knew myself as I should, he believes, then I would have the deepest knowledge of all creatures <term>Creatures: In medieval theology, "creatures" refers to any and all created things (animals, humans, objects) as distinct from the Creator.</term> (463, 20. 382, 33). No one can know God who does not first know themselves. It is the same path of stripping away the finite and the creaturely <note>original: "Abstreifung des Endlichen und Creatürlichen"</note>—the process of shedding worldly attachments—that leads to self-knowledge as well as to the knowledge of God (459, 25. 155, 21). In the essence of the soul, we can see and know God, and the more a person in this life approaches the essence of the soul with their understanding, the closer they are to the knowledge of God. Within yourself lies and dwells the truth. No one finds it who seeks it in external things. I find God most surely within my interior (617, 31. 12, 30).

He moves guilelessly within the prevailing <note>The German text breaks off here at "herrsche-", likely "herrschenden" (prevailing/dominant), as it transitions to the next page.</note>

He defines the soul as the **simple form** of the body (17, 32), which, being itself non-spatial and immaterial, completely permeates the body and is distributed whole and undivided in all parts of the body with equal power (116, 26; 268, 13). The body is made from the **four elements** <term>Four elements: Earth, water, air, and fire—the basic building blocks of the physical world in medieval science.</term> and is of an earthly nature, while the soul belongs to heaven; and yet they are so indissolubly connected that they are intended to remain together eternally (237, 4). The soul is created and has a beginning in time; but in itself, it is without matter and elevated above time, as its activities prove (631, 6; 671, 37; 509, 23; 412, 25). In its empirical <note>Based on experience or observation.</note> state, the soul is bound to the body and only attains the capacity for specific effective action through its union with the body. The soul, when separated from the body, has neither reason nor will; it is absolutely simple; it certainly contains the principle and the roots of its activities, but it does not actually exercise them (264, 15). Therein lies the difference between the soul and the spirit. According to its highest functions, the soul is **spirit**, and according to its lowest, it is **soul**, and thus there is a boundary line between soul and spirit within the single essence (397, 31). The soul is called spirit when it is elevated above all creaturely <note>original: "Creatürliche"; referring to all created things as distinct from the Creator.</note> things (121, 8), when it has forgotten the body and all individual effects mediated by the body and is gathered within itself (7, 15). The soul as the animating form of the body is susceptible to change. It is called spirit when it is elevated above space and time and all naturalness; yet even then, change still occurs within it (318, 25); for even then, certain forms and representations remain within it (320, 21). — The soul is more noble than all corporeal things. It is created, so to speak, in a middle place between **time** and **eternity**, touching both. With its highest powers, it touches eternity; with its lowest, it touches time. Thus it works in time and yet not temporally, but in the form of eternity, which it has in common with the angels. The soul is a simple power that conducts life into all the limbs through the intimate union in which it exists with the body...

The soul does not require the physical proximity of the object of its love and thought (383, 24). For this very reason, one must clearly distinguish the <term>ground of the soul: the deepest, innermost essence of the soul that remains untouched by external things</term>, from which all powers flow, from the powers themselves and their functions. Everything the soul performs, it performs through its powers. It understands with the reason, remembers with the memory, and loves with the will; it performs all of this with the powers, not with its <term>essence: the core 'being' or 'substance' of the soul as it exists in itself</term>. All its activity is attached to an organ; for example, the power of sight is attached to the eyes, and so it is with the other senses. In the essence, therefore, all activity ceases, because there all powers are silent. ### 1. The Soul and its Powers.

No created thing <note>original: 'Creatur' — in medieval philosophy, this refers to any created being, such as a person, animal, or object, as opposed to the uncreated God.</note> is able to penetrate into the ground of the soul; instead, it must remain outside within the soul's powers (4, 29). Therefore, the perception of finite things is ill-suited to our true essence, just as multiplicity is ill-suited to simplicity. If it were the case in this life that we always had a mirror before us in which we could see and recognize all things in a single vision in one moment, then neither action nor knowledge would be a hindrance to us. But since we must turn our focus from one thing to another, one thing cannot be present within us without the other being hindered. The soul is so bound to its powers <note>original: 'Kräfte' — the faculties of the mind, such as memory, will, and intellect.</note> that its attention is scattered among them; without this, the powers could accomplish nothing. However, the more the soul scatters itself in attention to external things, the weaker its purely internal activity becomes (14, 8).

3. Thus the soul is a middle-ground <note>original: 'ein Mittleres' — a bridge or mediating entity.</note> between God and the creature (395, 1), turned on one hand toward the eternal and on the other toward the transitory. In itself, the soul shares a common light with the angels, through which it recognizes God; this light created within it is reason <note>original: 'Vernunft' — referring to the higher intellect or the spark of divine understanding.</note>, which ceaselessly pours the wisdom of God into the soul. But when the soul is poured into the body, it becomes darkened (410, 35). With its higher powers, the soul touches eternity—that is, God—and with its lower powers, it touches time; through this, it becomes changeable, turned toward the material, and stripped of its nobility (170, 11). The soul has, in a sense, a double face: one face is turned toward this world and the body, which it enables with various skills, and the other is directed straight toward God. There, God works unceasingly with His light within her, but she is unaware of it because she is not "at home" with herself (110, 21; 250, 36; 59, 4; 488, 31). Consequently, the word "soul" takes on a double meaning. First, in a narrower sense, it designates the animating principle of the body—the empirical soul, bound to the body as if in a prison. Second, it designates the true essence of this principle, which is itself elevated above space and time, simple and unchanging, and relates to nothing lower, finite, or material. The word "soul" in the former sense designates the basis of its effects, but not the nature of the soul itself. For the soul in its own right has nothing to do with that which is changeable. ->I. The Soul.<-

There is no name for the indeterminate <note>original: 'bestimmungslose' — meaning without specific attributes or definitions; a state of pure potentiality.</note> essence of the soul. One calls it "soul" just as one calls someone a "carpenter"; it is clear that one does not then designate him by his essence—for then one would rather have to call him a "human being"—but rather by his trade. Some have called the soul a "fire" because of its power, its warmth, and its radiance; others call it a "spark" of a heavenly kind, others a "light," a "spirit," or a "number." One wishes to name it with something that is simple and indeterminate; but even the highest and simplest things do not reach the "ground of the soul" <note>original: 'Seelengrund' — a central concept in Eckhart's mysticism, referring to the innermost, absolute core of the human being where the soul and God are one.</note> (89, 3).

This, then, is the true essence of the soul, which is capable of no designation at all: its simple ground, the highest unity of all its powers. The concept of this unity is already familiar to *Plotinus* <note>A third-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose ideas deeply influenced Christian mysticism.</note>; but with *Eckhart*, it becomes the starting point and center of all his teaching, and there is no other concept he has impressed upon us as diligently as this one. However, this concept of the soul-ground only receives its full meaning when we include *Eckhart's* doctrine of knowledge.

## 2. Knowing.

One should not look for a systematic theory of knowledge in *Eckhart*. He does not touch upon the logical-dialectical disputes concerning the relationship between the "universal" and the "individual" <note>This refers to the 'Problem of Universals'—a major medieval debate over whether general concepts like 'humanity' exist in reality or only as names.</note> which so constantly occupied Scholasticism <note>The dominant philosophical and theological system of the medieval universities.</note>. He designates the universal as the generating principle of the individual, as that which alone truly constitutes the essence within the individual. But for him, this is not the result of laborious investigation, but rather a self-evident prerequisite. His interest leads him to other areas. In his work, the purpose of edification and moral rebirth through religious knowledge stands in the foreground; he leaves behind the academic wisdom of the "school" that turns away from life. Yet even here, he cannot deny the school of *Albertus* <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a German Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> and *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential thinker of the Scholastic period.</note>; he is an *Aristotelian* in the same sense as they are, and wherever the occasion arises, he reproduces the teachings of the *Aristotelians* down to the very wording. Insofar as he has to express himself on the relationship of the universal to the individual, of knowing to its objects, and of form to matter, he is a *Realist* <note>In this context, a 'Realist' believes that universal concepts have a real existence independent of the mind.</note> in the strictest sense of the word. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the soul and its faculties. [relationship] between [essence and knowing], he has not achieved anything of independent value in the doctrine of the essence and processes of knowing; but his concepts—drawn from the philosophy of the Arabs, from *Albert* <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a German Dominican friar and philosopher who was a teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> and *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Italian theologian and philosopher.</note> and in part also directly from *Augustine*—regarding the activity and validity of rational knowledge <note>original: 'Vernunfterkenntniss' — knowledge attained through the power of reason or intellect.</note> are highly significant for the formation of his worldview. His high regard for reason and knowing as the soul’s most elevated function is the foundation for what is most unique and valuable in his thoughts. Because of this, his remarks on the subject are quite numerous, even though he never wrote a dedicated treatise on it. They all reach the same conclusion: what his predecessors saw as merely one part of a larger whole becomes, for him, the most important part. Knowing is the highest act; reason is the best thing. The soul is driven by an irresistible urge toward the highest universal—the "absolutely simple"—and the tool used to grasp, enjoy, and merge with this simplicity is no longer just one specific faculty of the mind, alongside which others might exist, but the soul itself in its complete essence.

Eckhart distinguishes between different aspects of the soul: "sensuality" <note>original: 'Sinnlichkeit' — the realm of physical senses and instincts.</note> or the "outer man," the powers of the soul (divided into lower and upper), and the "soul-ground" <note>original: 'Seelengrund' — the innermost, divine core of the human being.</note> (12, 30). Similarly, he identifies three types of knowing: sensory, rational, and supra-rational (297, 21).

1. All knowledge begins with sensory perception. Through its lower powers, the soul is tied to the five senses, which must allow whatever is to be known to enter the soul. Sensory perception deals with material and physical objects (130, 40). Eckhart attempts to explain how the senses work, though he uses the limited scientific understanding of his time. When the soul's powers touch a creature <note>original: 'Creatur' — in medieval thought, this refers to any created thing (animal, plant, or object) as distinct from the Creator.</note>, they extract forms and likenesses from these things and pull them into themselves. A created thing can only enter the soul through these forms. These forms—or images of things—must necessarily enter the soul from the outside via the senses (5, 8). All sensory perception

Without such a medium, one could say with equal justification that one sees everything and nothing (107, 12). The stripping away of the material is the precondition for all perception. If I wish to gain a representation <term>Vorstellung</term> <note>A mental image or concept</note> of a thing, such as a stone, I by no means pull the coarse matter into myself, but rather separate it outside (83, 11). The visible is seen only by means of the invisible; the eye would see nothing physical had it not something non-physical <note>original: 'Unkörperliches' — an incorporeal or spiritual element</note> that enabled it to see (394, 28). The eye and the soul are a mirror in which everything is reflected that is held before it. Therefore, I do not see a hand or a stone, but rather the image of it. Yet I do not see this image by means of another image or any kind of medium, but rather without a medium and without an image. The image is its own medium, just as movement might be the cause of movement but is not itself moved, or as magnitude <note>original: 'Grösse' — size or greatness</note> makes other things large but is itself without size (142, 26). To be sure, my eye perceives color by means of light; but the color itself does not enter the soul. To perceive color, my eye must first be free of all color. Thus, external things are first spiritualized, and they are present to the soul only through their forms. — Eckhart has nothing to say regarding specific physiological processes in this regard; thus, like Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian philosopher whose works on the soul heavily influenced medieval scholasticism.</note> or Albert <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), Eckhart's predecessor in the Dominican order.</note>, he attributes the receiving of forms into the soul to the activity of an angel, who imprints the image received from the senses onto the higher powers of the soul (116, 31). He does not explain how we come to have the representation of something material at all; we find no indication of a distinction between higher and lower senses.

Each sense organ has a specific sphere of perception by virtue of a special affinity for a particular quality of things (333, 12). All individual senses are rooted in the common sense <term>Gemeinsinn</term> <note>Latin: 'sensus communis'—the faculty that integrates the data from the five individual senses into a single experience.</note>, which in itself simply grants hearing, seeing, feeling, and tasting to the other senses. All perceptions of the outer senses are carried into the common sense (538, 10), which represents the single sensory consciousness as the bearer of all perceptions.

The process of separating out all that is coarsely material from things is carried out by the senses; but even more must be stripped away, and therefore the process is continued by the other powers of the soul, beginning with the so-called lower powers. From sensory perceptions come thoughts; from thoughts comes rational knowledge; and from this arises the steady, calm contemplation of the Absolute (80, 38). The senses provide a disordered multiplicity of representations <term>Vorstellungen</term> <note>Mental images or ideas of external objects</note>; these are ordered by desire and unified in the empirical understanding, termed "discretion" <term>Bescheidenheit</term> <note>In this context, the Middle High German 'bescheidenheit' refers to the ability to discern or distinguish, rather than the modern sense of modesty</note> (383, 14; 139, 14). In contrast to the senses, which are bound to place, time, and matter, there stands first the "expansive" power—discretion or integrity—the empirical understanding, also described as the inner sense or the faculty of thought, which outgrows all limitations. Above this, as one of the three highest faculties of the soul, stands reason <term>Vernunft</term>, the "imageless" power; specifically as "seeking" reason, which is still subject to change, increasing and decreasing. But the highest is the resting reason, which stands unchanging in the pure and simple essence (304, 31; 80, 30).

— The linguistic usage here is not entirely fixed. Understanding <term>Verstand</term> and reason <term>Vernunft</term> are often used with the same meaning to describe the higher faculty of knowledge, but they are also used for the lower faculties. Reason, sometimes used in contrast to understanding, also serves as a designation for the highest unity of the soul, which is elevated above both knowing and willing as separate faculties, and whose activity can be described as a supra-rational knowing.

The faculty of thought has the specific task of stripping away even the last remnants of the sensory—the categories of space and time—from things. Nothing hinders the soul so much in attaining true knowledge as space and time. For they are the ground of all determination and distinction. In truth, all time is contained in the "Now," and all space in the "Here," and only in the form of eternity are things known in their true essence (222, 24; 296, 13). In thinking, I also represent to myself things that are not physically present, so that I know them just as well or even better than if I saw them with my eyes (270, 11). If I saw a person twenty years ago, even if they are dead, I still have a mental representation of their form as if they stood before me. This power does not require matter; but it is still imperfect in that it abstracts the form from the matter. Reason strives to go even beyond this (132, 17).

To further explain this striving of reason beyond all boundaries of finiteness, Eckhart delves even deeper into the nature of cognitive activity. Following the prevailing style of the time, it would likely have been natural for him to connect this to the frequently used terms of **possible** and **actual reason**. Indeed, these terms are not foreign to him; but he uses them only exceptionally, once or twice, and then not so much to ground his theory of cognition on them, but rather to establish his doctrine of the path to salvation by means of knowing. The terminology of the School <note>Referring to Scholasticism, the dominant philosophical and theological system of the medieval universities</note> is so indifferent to him that he handles it quite arbitrarily and uses the same term with a completely changed meaning. At one point he says: the **possible reason** <term>mögliche Vernunft</term> <note>In Scholasticism, the capacity of the human mind to receive knowledge</note> recognizes things in their own natural light, while the **active reason** <term>wirkende Vernunft</term> <note>The faculty that transforms sensory data into abstract concepts</note> recognizes them in God (110, 35). At another time, he distinguishes the **possible reason** as a capacity for reason before any reality of knowing; the **active reason**, which proves itself self-active in the processing of the representations mediated by the senses; and the **passive reason** <term>leidende Vernunft</term>, as the faculty of receptivity, which receives its content partly from the active reason and partly from God. One must not think here of the common meaning of these terms as they had been developed especially by Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath whose interpretations of Aristotle deeply influenced Western medieval thought</note> and adopted by Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the influential German Scholastic and teacher of Thomas Aquinas</note>. At least in this passage, reason is not called "possible" insofar as it relates to the sensory world; the passive reason is distinguished from the possible and is directly a higher faculty than the active reason. Eckhart’s meaning certainly remains unclear; even the writing of an unknown mystic regarding actual and possible reason (found in Docen, *Miscellany on the History of German Literature* I, p. 140) provides no intelligible explanation. — The difference from **Averroistic** <note>Followers of Averroes, who proposed that there was only one "active intellect" shared by all humans; Eckhart differs by focusing on the individual soul's internal path to God</note> ideas is clearly evident...

## 2. Cognition.

...enough. According to Eckhart, the soul is a single essence in all its cognitive functions; nothing approaches it from the outside. The individuality of souls is tied to the lower powers (511, 23); but the soul overcomes this barrier from within. The **active reason** <term>wirkende Vernunft</term> <note>Also known as the "agent intellect," this is the faculty that actively processes sensory information into abstract thoughts.</note> is the energy of its own inner disposition; it is not to be thought of as a force that comes to the personality only from the outside—being itself impersonal, identical, and a unified power in all people. Rather, it is the reason's own inner development that elevates finite individuality into the sphere of pure self-relation (where knowledge reflects upon itself) and finally unites it with the **absolutely simple**, which lacks all specific characteristics and thus even those of personality.

The "real" or "**active**" **reason**, Eckhart teaches, abstracts forms from things, stripping them of matter and "chance," that is, all **accidental** <term>accidentiell</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidental" refers to qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or size.</note> determinations. In this way, it hands them over to the **passive reason** <term>leidende Vernunft</term> <note>Also called the "patient intellect," this faculty receives and stores the concepts processed by the active reason.</note>, and the latter gives them its own spiritual form. Without the help of the active reason, the passive can do nothing. But once the passive reason has been fertilized by the active, it retains and recognizes things. The active reason is still bound within certain limits. It cannot give what it does not have, and it cannot hold two ideas simultaneously, but only one after the other. The air, for example, allows for several perceptions at once—it possesses light and warmth simultaneously—but you can perceive them only one after the other. The **possible reason** <term>mögliche Vernunft</term> is not, however, inactive; it too exerts certain effects, ordering and moderating all processes in the active and passive reason to some extent, so that they conform to the rational disposition of the spirit. The passive reason takes its name from the fact that, without independent activity, it only receives what is delivered to it by either the active reason or the **absolute spirit**, which takes its place. For when the active reason of a person fulfills its task in the right way, it is replaced by the absolute spirit; God takes its place, and God Himself then performs the functions in the soul that the reason previously performed (19, 21; 37. 17, 1). This is the foundation of the **doctrine of salvation** <term>Lehre vom Heile</term> as Eckhart shaped it. Here, however, we are initially concerned only with the question,

# I. The Soul.

...how the active reason, through the process of cognition, prepares this state of fulfillment with the absolute spirit.

Reason must always direct itself toward something specific; the faculties—whether they be memory, reason, or will—always seek to cling to a specific object. But the true object of reason, its fortress, is the essence—not "accident" <note>original: "Zufall"; in medieval philosophy, an "accident" refers to a non-essential quality of a thing, like its color or shape, rather than its core being.</note>, but the mere pure essence in itself. When reason recognizes a truth, it clings to it, rests upon it, and makes a rational statement about that object. So long as reason has not actually found the truth and the essence, nor grasped the foundation well enough to form a certain judgment, it remains searching and wavering, without support or rest; it labors and casts off what is false. Therefore, reason never comes to rest in this life. All that is known is a mere nothing compared to the full truth. Even though the truth exists in the ground of the soul, it is nonetheless veiled and hidden from reason.

For this reason, reason waits restlessly and prepares itself for what shall one day be known to it, but which is currently still hidden. Just as matter does not come to rest until it is filled with all forms, so reason finds rest only in the essential, all-encompassing truth. In this alone is it self-sufficient; and yet this truth is repeatedly withdrawn from it, so that its diligence may be awakened and it may be spurred to advance ever further, to reach ever higher, and to grasp the true, boundless good—never finding satisfaction in finite things, but longing ever more intensely for the highest good (20, 20). The soul possesses all things within its understanding, each thing according to its diversity. But it also has the potential to recognize all things as a single unity, and it soars above all multiplicity into simplicity, rising from distinguishing rational knowledge into **unknowing** <term>Nichterkennen</term> <note>A central concept in mysticism where the mind moves beyond intellectual concepts to experience a direct, wordless union with the Divine.</note> (540, 14). That is the goal. The other powers of the soul are a tool with specific functions intended to help reason ascend into this highest **vision** <term>Anschauung</term> (126, 16).

3. Before we describe this highest vision itself, let us consider the relationship in which cognition in general stands to the world of things in *Eckhart’s* thought. The natural light of reason is so noble and so powerful that everything created is too small and too narrow for it. It is in itself nobler than everything physical, and even the lowest and most common of physical things, when illuminated or brightened by this light of reason, is thereby ennobled and raised above all physical things, becoming brighter and purer than the sun. For reason separates temporality and physicality from things (228, 36). The soul is the place of all things; but she herself is without place (515, 38). The soul can perform wonders with her natural light. She is so powerful that she separates what is joined as one. Fire and heat are one; yet in reason, they are separated (255, 39). As a thing exists in the ground of my soul, it is there in its highest and noblest form; there, it is nothing but an image (83, 13).

Form is nobler than matter. Yet the soul possesses the power to have the forms of all things imprinted upon her (90, 24). Thus, things are indeed possessed by cognition in a spiritual rather than a natural form; but through this, they attain their own true form of existence. The spirit transforms the raw material of what is perceived by making it its own possession; but the form it thereby grants is the things' own essential form. Likeness is the condition of all cognition. If the spirit is to take the multiplicity <note>original: "Mannichfaltigkeit"; the diverse and varied nature of the physical world.</note> of all things into itself through cognition, it must carry all things in principle within itself; it must be, in a sense, all things—a <term>Mikrokosmus</term> <note>Microcosm: the philosophical idea that the human being is a "little world" containing the essence of the entire universe.</note> (589, 17). 

The spirit carries within itself the comparison of all things (97, 31; 139, 10). If the form that the spirit grants to things and their own essence are one and the same, it follows that the essence is what is most knowable. That which has the most essence is also what is most clearly recognized (99, 8). On the other hand, whatever eludes cognition—such as coarse matter and individuality—also possesses no true essence. There can be no talk here of a "thing in itself" <note>original: "Ding an sich"; a reference to Immanuel Kant’s concept of an object existing independently of our perception, which the author here argues does not apply to this mystical-rational framework.</note> as the presupposed ground of our sensory perceptions. Behind the appearance of the manifold, the sensory, and the material, the only essence is the universal <note>original: "das Allgemeine"; the shared, essential nature of a category of things.</note> itself, which the understanding grasps. ## 4. Thinking unites the manifold.

The spiritual form that things take on in cognition is thus that of universality, and being as a universal is the true being of things. Furthermore, what one is to recognize, one must recognize in its cause (264, 1; 308, 26). The progress of cognition is thus the ascent to ever-higher causes until finally reaching the absolute "origin" itself (101, 10). There must, therefore, be a first principle that carries and holds all things (389, 33). Every effect flows from power, but power flows from the essence (210, 22). Thus, the goal is to penetrate to the essence of all essences, and that is once again the most universal of all. Thinking is an ever-ascending abstraction, until finally all mutually limiting definitions and all differences are excluded. From all partial truths and individual insights, the soul strives with power upward toward the subject of all predicates, for whom no predicate is any longer sufficient—toward the most abstract pure being, which for that very reason is also non-being; toward the "super-essential essence" <note>original: "überwesentlichen Wesen"; a term from mystical theology describing God as being beyond the human concept of "being" or "existence."</note>, which is also no longer an "essence," insofar as essence is still a definition, and in which essence is not so much negated as it is elevated and transfigured. Only now is this the form of being completely worthy of the spirit: that it be immersed in the cognition of the Absolute. Eckhart dwells on nothing with such decided preference as on the description of this state of pure cognition of the absolutely most universal concept. Yet the soul does not reach this concept with any specific power or activity. Reason, insofar as it is still a power distinct from other powers of the soul, is not the adequate organ to raise itself to the Absolute. # 2. Cognition.

...[according to the] capacity <note>The German text begins with "mögen," the second half of "Vermögen" (capacity/power), completing the sentence from the previous page.</note> of the one who understands and not according to its own nature (484, 36). Everything that enters the soul is grasped by it in a limited way (153, 21). All knowledge of the intellect is simultaneously a distinguishing; thus, finitude still adheres to all knowledge. Only when one recognizes everything in everything has one risen above the intellect (648, 10). The things that one otherwise recognizes as perishable are then recognized as imperishable, and one grasps them as they are, entirely without parts and in unity. What is otherwise far is near there; all things are there in an eternal present. What happened on the first day and what will happen on the last day—that is a present moment there (98, 18).

The cognition of the Absolute is a forgetting of all things finite, a "not-knowing"—that is, not a "not-yet-knowing," but a "no-longer-knowing," and thus an intensified knowledge <note>original: "potenziertes Wissen"; this refers to a higher state of awareness that transcends standard intellectual logic.</note> (10, 5; 15, 5). In this not-knowing, all the labor and effort of cognition comes to rest, and the soul attains its full, blessed satisfaction. To know nothing in this sense means to know everything.

It is important for the entire further development of the system to note that this definition of the thought process is simultaneously linked to a determination of value. The individual and the finite are the essence-less and the null; the universal is the true essence within things. Therefore, the universal is the better, while the individual is the worthless. The more universal a concept—the greater its scope and the poorer its content—the higher the value ascribed to it. The nobler a thing, the more it shares itself with others, and the more common <note>original: "gemeinsam"; here meaning shared or universal rather than "ordinary."</note> it is. The Absolute is the best, for it is in everything (135, 35; 262, 30; 279, 27). I would rather give up my eye than my life, for I can live even without an eye; and I would rather give up my life than my essence, for essence is more universal than life (333, 16; 279, 32).

— *Eckhart* does not see that this example would sooner prove the opposite valuation; that it should say: because I am unable to preserve the better, the "more," I content myself with the lesser, the poorer in value—not as if I assigned it a higher value, but in order to hold onto at least something instead of losing everything. — Thus, this determination of value is also transferred to the ethical sphere. The Absolute, although it is simultaneously the most devoid of content, is grasped as the highest good,

# I. The Soul.

...and the principle of good will—love—is described as the striving to be as universal as possible; that is, to be as free of specific content as possible, inclined as little as possible toward specific things, and instead turned toward the All and Unity. 

Another consequence is even more important. Cognition presupposes a likeness between the knower and the known, and it brings about equality. Even sensory perception signifies a real union between the perceiver and the perceived. Eckhart himself places a special emphasis on this: "If you could rightly understand this," he says, "you would understand my view and the basis of my entire way of thinking." A piece of wood neither acts nor suffers anything by my seeing it. Likewise, my eye in itself remains the same whether I open or close it. Nevertheless, if I direct my gaze at the wood so that I see it, each remains what it is, and yet both become one in a certain sense, so that one might call the eye 'wood' and the wood has, in a way, become my eye. <note>This analogy illustrates the Scholastic theory of perception, where the 'form' of an object enters the mind without its physical 'matter,' creating a temporary identity between the observer and the object.</note> For in the act of seeing, the wood has become mere form, and my eye, in the act of seeing, likewise has no other content than this very form. If, however, the wood were immaterial and of a thoroughly spiritual nature, so that it were entirely suited to the eye's power of sight, one could truly say that in the act of seeing, the wood and my eye formed one single being. If this applies to physical things, it applies even more so to spiritual things. Now, the form under which the wood becomes an object of sight is a distinguishing property of the eye. In this regard, my eye is more closely related to that of any animal across the sea that I have never seen than my eye and my ear are to each other (192, 32). It is upon this that the power of cognition rests: establishing a true identity between the spirit and the object (502, 31); and this occurs at the highest level when the soul contemplates the Absolute. The soul itself becomes the Absolute (God) by knowing the Absolute (380, 3; 157, 10).

### 3. The Soul in its Essence.

...of the soul, a new and finally correct understanding has been gained. The soul in its temporal form of appearance is not the true soul. In its act of knowing, it has shown what it truly is. In the act of cognition, it divests itself of all finitude and materiality; it sheds space and time and retains only the pure essence. This process, which it begins in sensory perception and in reflective thinking, it must—driven by the inner necessity of its rational <term>disposition<note>original: "Anlage." Refers to the soul's inherent potential or natural capacity to reach God.</note></term>—continue until the very end. With an unstoppable urge, it strives to grasp the highest, most general, and absolutely simple concept; this "Simplicity" is therefore present in it from the very beginning as its disposition, its essential form, to which it only needs to return. In its <term>ground<note>The "Ground" (Seelengrund) is a central concept in Meister Eckhart's mysticism, referring to the innermost core of the soul where it is unified with God.</note></term>, the soul is thus that "Most General" itself; this, however, is the Absolute, or to use another expression: God. The soul in its essence is God, and despite all veiling and distortion, it remains essentially God.

The relationship to sensuality is only a preliminary stage for the soul. That which can fill the noblest part of the soul never enters through eyes or ears; there is no place for it other than the <note>Eckhart often speaks of the "nameless" quality of the divine and the soul's core, which transcends all categories of human language.</note> "nameless place," which is the place of all things. Everything sensory is merely a guide and assists the soul in a specific way, though it is veiled in color, sound, and physicality. It is merely an exercise of the senses through which the soul is awakened and its slumbering natural disposition is called into activity (131, 3). When the soul remains in the pure light of reason, it has no relationship to the material and no susceptibility to it (132, 30; 229, 1; 304, 8).

Everything that is to be known must be known by means of images abstracted from objects. However, the soul only possesses such images of external things, not of itself. Therefore, it knows all other things, but not itself. Because of that mediation through images, it knows less about itself than about any other thing (5, 18). The soul is therefore something unutterable and incomprehensible, just like God (89, 23). The soul does not age. The rational soul is eternally young. The more one finds the principle of one's own activity within the soul, the closer one stands to one's highest origin, to one's birth; and that which is near its birth is called "young" (255, 3). The soul in itself is still just as young as when it was created, and the age that befalls it, comes...

2. As those forces which elevate the soul to the Absolute, Reason and Will are specifically considered, along with their activities: Knowledge and Love. Knowledge and love are the two feet upon which the spirit should stand and with which it should step over all that is transitory, so that its feet are not soiled by the dust of the ephemeral (684, 8). He asserts with them that Reason is closer to the Absolute than the Will; yet he also cannot ignore that the Will, in some respects, has a more direct relationship to the Absolute than Reason. ### 3. The Soul in its Essence.

In this regard, the will is superior to it when it draws its impulses in full freedom only from its own essence. However, the highest is indeed Reason, provided one no longer grasps it as a specific, distinct power. There is a Reason in a higher sense which forms the ultimate unity of the soul—the unity from which Reason and Will, as distinct and separate powers of the soul, take their origin. This Reason has the Absolute <note>The "Absolute" refers to God in His purest, most unconditioned state.</note> and no other content; it is the Absolute itself, no longer anything particular, but a totality persisting within itself.

Eckhart mentions on several occasions the fierce disputes conducted in Paris regarding the question of the priority of Reason or Will, in which he also took part. We find the following pronouncements from him on the matter: Our bliss does not consist in the fact that God is in us—for He is in all creatures, but they do not know it and are therefore not blessed—but rather in the fact that we recognize and know how near God is to us (220, 35). My bliss depends on this: that God is rational <note>In the medieval sense, "rational" (vernünftig) refers to the divine Intellect or the capacity for spiritual understanding.</note> and I recognize that (270, 40). The core of the primary concept and of eternal bliss lies in knowledge. A master taught in Paris with loud shouting and clamor, seeking to prove the opposite. Then another master, surely a better one than the best Paris has, taught: Master, you shout very loudly. Had God not said it in the Gospel, one might give much weight to your screaming and shouting. Our Lord spoke: "This is eternal life, that they may know You as the true God" (138, 15) <note>original quote from John 17:3: "Haec est autem vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te, solum Deum verum."</note>. I taught in the school <insert>in the College of Saint James</insert> <note>The *Collegium St. Jacob* (Saint-Jacques) was the famous Dominican center of study in Paris where Eckhart held the chair of theology.</note> that Reason was nobler than Will. Then a master in another school taught that Will was nobler than Reason; for Will takes things as they are in themselves, while Reason takes them as they are within it. That is true. An eye is nobler in itself than an eye painted on a wall; <insert>thus one might consider things to be nobler than the images of things reflected within the Reason</insert>. But I say nonetheless that Reason is nobler than Will. The Will grasps God under the veil of goodness; Reason grasps Him unveiled, stripped of goodness and of being (270, 26). Knowledge leads and illuminates the Will and precedes its expression, which is Love (98, 27); one cannot love God without having first known Him (273, 37).

# I. The Soul.

Knowledge <note>original: *Erkenntniss*—the act of spiritual knowing or cognition</note> is a bedrock and a foundation of all being; love can only cling to knowledge (84, 13). Some say that blessedness <note>original: *Seligkeit*—a state of supreme spiritual happiness or beatitude</note> does not lie in knowledge, but in the will alone. These people are wrong; for if it lay in the will alone, there would be no union with God. But God and I are one; that can only take place in the act of knowing (206, 10). The will has two functions: desire and love. The function of Reason <note>original: *Vernunft*</note> is simple, and therefore it is better; its function is knowledge, and it does not come to rest until it grasps its object without a veil. Therefore, it precedes the will and announces to it what it then loves. As long as one desires things, one does not have them. When one has them, one loves them, and the desire falls away (106, 30). Reason is the head of the soul. Those who promote the most foolish doctrine say that love takes the first place; but those who promote the best doctrine say properly and in truth that the core of eternal life lies more in the intellect than in the will. Reason goes straight toward God. For love is directed toward the Good; Reason, however, grasps the cause by which the Good is good. Love seizes God insofar as He is lovable; Reason rises higher and seizes Him insofar as He is Being <note>original: *Wesen*—the essential nature or substance of a thing</note> (108, 13; 121, 17).

Other passages sound different only in appearance. If one understands Reason as the theoretical power opposed to the will—either as the lower or the higher faculty of knowledge—then the will is either superior or equal to it. Thus, the will is even called the supreme power of the soul in contrast to Reason as a power of lesser value. Both must work together; Reason must be fertilized by the will to fulfill its purpose (591, 23). In the theoretical power of Reason, there is no full rest. For in the activity of Reason, a movement of external things toward the soul takes place, and through this movement, the image of these things is imprinted and formed into the soul, so that it is the beginning of a movement of the soul into the substantial form of the soul and the true essence of the things that appear in the images (214, 24). The theoretical power is not as uninhibited as the will; for otherwise, it would sink without ceasing into the indeterminate Godhead <note>original: *Gottheit*—the ultimate, impersonal essence of God</note>.
