### 3. The Soul in its Essence.

Eckhart never tires of describing this uppermost part of the soul again and again, and of tracing all individual phenomena of the life of the soul back to it. Here lies the center of his teaching; both what is of highest and imperishable value in his work, as well as his grave errors, are rooted here.

The supreme reason <note>original: *Die oberste Vernunft*</note> — which, following the allegorical explanation of several biblical passages, is also called the "man in the soul" in contrast to the lower part as the "woman in the soul" <note>This gendered allegory, common in medieval scholasticism, represents the active/spiritual faculty versus the receptive/sensory faculty</note>, a usage that has been not uncommon since the time of the Lombard <note>Refers to Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), whose *Sentences* was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages</note> — the supreme reason is the original essence and the goal of all the soul's development. All the powers of the soul are servants of this reason, intended to raise it above low things and help it upward into the "origin." Yet when the soul stands before its origin, the powers remain outside, and it stands there naked and nameless, stripped of all definiteness (469, 36). This uppermost part of the soul is exalted above time and knows as little of time as of the body. Past, present, and future are one there. In eternity there is neither a yesterday nor a tomorrow; there is only an eternally present moment. The animal perceives within place and time; man perceives beyond place and time. The "now," the smallest unit of time, still has something of time about it; it is related to time and borders on time. Therefore, it must pass away. It is the same with space. What is across the sea is just as present to the soul as what is right here. ...true knowledge, on the other hand, gazes in an **eternal Now** <note>original: *ewiges Nu* — Eckhart's term for a timeless moment that participates in eternity</note>. To be or to have something specific means not to be or have everything; strip away all specificity, and you are everything. Nothing, therefore, hinders the soul’s knowledge of God as much as time and place. Time and place are fragments, and God is one. Therefore, if the soul is to know God, it must know Him beyond time and space. In the soul’s supreme power, which is akin to the divine nature (63, 29), God shines unveiled. Nothing enters it but God, and it remains in God without ceasing. By means of this power, man grasps things not as objects, but as they are in God; in this power, all things are equal. Their material matter is stripped away; nothing but what is beautiful and lovely in them remains (199, 25). This power is a light that never goes out, even in the state of mortal sin; it always preserves within the spirit the possibility of turning back to God; for even in hell, the nature of the soul remains divine (395, 20; 11, 31). Pleasure and pain touch only the lower powers; the **spark** <note>original: *Funke* or *Fünklein* — the indestructible divine core of the soul</note>, a light of divine likeness, remains turned toward God at all times and never separates from Him; it struggles unceasingly against everything non-divine. It is not a particular faculty; nameless, without qualities, neither this nor that, neither here nor there, it shares the nature of the Absolute (79, 6; 113, 33). What the little spark is, it is through another—through God—and it is one with Him. The unity flows into it, and it flows back into the unity. Here, the soul receives all its life and essence. Only this is entirely in God; everything else remains outside (306, 8).

Elsewhere, the little spark is also called "created by God" (581, 23; 113, 34; 412, 30). But because it is essentially one with God, Eckhart is not consistent in this; to distinguish it clearly from everything finite, he also calls it **uncreated** and **uncreatable** <note>original: *ungeschaffen und ungeschöpflich* — This was a controversial point in Eckhart's theology, suggesting that part of the soul is not a created thing but part of God's own essence</note> (193, 16; 286, 17). Where the soul has its natural, created essence, he says, there is no truth. However, there is something above the created nature of the soul.

# I. The Soul.

You have no fellowship with nothingness. Everything that is created or **creaturely** <term>creaturely: relating to created beings as distinct from the Creator; often implying a state of limitation or "nothingness" compared to God</term> is nothing; but to this [the soul's ground], all being-created or the possibility of being-created is distant and foreign. Thus, it is generated from God's own essence in such a way that it does not take on a creaturely particularity, but remains "All in All" just as God Himself is. Therefore, it carries within itself the reflection of all creatures, but without the specific form of being an "image" and is exalted above this form; it is so close to God that it constitutes an inseparable, single One with Him (286, 17).

This supreme power is entirely without outward expression and performs no specific function; it is an image of God, and yet is not an image itself, but rather a principle or faculty to present and elevate the soul's pure image. In this presenting, it remains without image; in this elevating, it encompasses all images and the images of all images. There, the soul in its steady progress is free from every specific form of activity, and for that reason, it should remain purely within itself. For truth is in it, and yet not as its own property or in any other sort of particularity (584, 38). The divine image imprinted upon the soul relates to itself without mediation in the innermost part of nature; and the innermost and highest part of nature presents itself most truly in the form of the soul without any mediation, neither through will nor through wisdom; if wisdom mediates here, then it is the form of the soul itself (68, 39). The "spirit" <note>original: *Gemüth* — the totality of the higher soul-powers, encompassing mind, heart, and disposition</note> is a dwelling place of ideal forms and rational conceptions. There, God is grasped according to His personal distinctions <note>This refers to God as the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>. But if one penetrates deeper into the innermost essence of the soul, one finds the **Reason**, which alone makes possible an adequate knowledge of God (585, 34). The little spark <note>original: *Fünklein*</note> is free from all names and stripped of all forms; reason and love cannot penetrate it, power and particularity remain outside—indeed, even God Himself, insofar as He bears personal particularity within Himself, stays out (46, 3).

Gradually, this postulated totality transforms back into the form of a specific power. # I. The Soul. — 3. The Soul in its Essence.

...point of indifference for all specific spiritual faculties, where the opposition between reason, will, and memory—like every other opposition—is meant to be superseded <note>The German "aufgehoben" is a key philosophical term meaning both to cancel and to preserve at a higher level, often translated as "sublated" or "superseded"</note>. In this way, the striving to penetrate the Absolute by means of the most abstract concepts gains a problematic dominance that empties the content of faith, even though the requirements of the will and—we would add—feeling had an equal right to be asserted. It is very similar with **Schleiermacher** <note>Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768–1834), an influential German theologian known for emphasizing "feeling" in religion</note>, where the faculty intended as the totality of the soul (excluding all one-sided powers) sinks unnoticed—through the use of the term "feeling"—to the meaning of feeling as a power coordinated alongside reason and will, excluding them rather than being superior to them and subsuming them within itself. 

Nevertheless, in **Eckhart** as in **Schleiermacher**, the intention itself is a valuable pointer, capable of leading us onto the right path toward understanding how, in religious behavior, it is not a specific function of the spirit, but rather the human being in the totality of their personality who is able to live in Gott. **Eckhart** states directly that knowing is grounded in the rational nature of our soul, but is not the soul's essence; it is rooted in this essence and is a part of the soul's life. This knowing lies beyond time and space, beyond the "here and now." In this knowing and living, all things are one and the same, a supreme, all-encompassing universal. 

But in this very same context, he describes the soul's deepest essence as the **spark of the intellect** <note>original: "Fünklein des Verstandes"</note>, which never goes out. It stands in opposition to lower knowing—the knowing of external things, the intellectual and sensory knowing that remains caught up in similarities and differences (39, 7). This is the fateful turning point in **Eckhart’s** teaching, which, instead of a rich personal life, brings in its wake an abstraction driven to the highest degree. Ultimately, it allows only a "delirium of the imagination"—a reveling in the inconceivable universality, in the thought of the Ineffable—where there is nothing definite left to think and all specificity dissolves, as the only apparent expression of immediate life.

He compares this to Schleiermacher’s use of "feeling," arguing both aim for a total soul-experience but risk reducing the soul to a single, narrow function.</summary>

## II. Essence and its Revelation.

### 1. The Concept of the Absolute.

It is the rational nature of the soul which compels cognition to rise above every specific concept to the concept of the Absolute. The Absolute, as the ultimate goal of thought, is thus to be understood as that which is purely universal and without determination. **Eckhart** strives to draw this conclusion in the fullest and highest sense, and in this, he allows no other consideration to lead him astray. The concept of God the Trinity <note>original: "Gottes des dreieinigen"</note> cannot be the concept of the Absolute; for in the Absolute there is no distinction, yet the three Persons are distinct. Furthermore, alongside and outside of God, there is also that which is not God: the world of creatures. If the soul wishes to press forward to the Absolute, it must also ascend beyond God the Trinity and beyond the one God in the three Persons to the concept that encompasses God and all things within itself. The organ of this ascent, however, is the "spark" <note>The "Seelenfünklein" or "little spark of the soul" is, for Eckhart, the uncreated part of the human spirit that is capable of direct union with God.</note>.

The spark sheds everything created and desires nothing but God, as He is in Himself without addition. Therefore, it is not satisfied with Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, or with the three Persons insofar as each remains in its particular individuality; but it is also not satisfied with the simple divine nature which brings forth the three Persons, nor with the simple divine essence <term>Wesen|The fundamental, underlying substance or nature of being, distinct from outward appearances.</term> remaining within itself, which neither communicates nor receives. Rather, it wants to know from whence this essence stems; it wants to penetrate into the simple ground, into the silent wilderness <note>A famous Eckhartian metaphor for the "Godhead" (Gottheit), which is the undifferentiated source behind the Trinity.</note> into which no distinction has ever gazed. ## 2. The Godhead.

God, then, is not the Absolute. If a fly had reason, God—with everything he is as God—could not satisfy the fly's striving (281, 32). The Absolute, the most universal concept, which also encompasses God within itself, is called the **Godhead** <term>Gottheit|In Eckhart's theology, the 'Godhead' is the hidden, undifferentiated source of the divine, whereas 'God' refers to the Trinity or God in relation to creation.</term>.

Eckhart draws attention to this distinction between God and the Godhead more often than to almost any other of the deepest mysteries of his teaching. A similar distinction had once been proposed by Gilbertus Porretanus, who claimed that the **divine essence** <note>original: *divina essentia*</note> or the one **deity** <note>original: *deitas*</note>—as the form through which God is God—must be distinguished from God himself as the divine persons. After heated negotiations conducted in 1147 and 1148, in which Bernard of Clairvaux was particularly active as an opponent of this view, it was declared reprehensible by Pope Eugene III. Eckhart did not so much renew this specific doctrine; rather, he was led by the principles of his own way of thinking to a similar conception, which, however, goes far beyond what was established by Gilbertus.

Gilbertus was prompted by realist perspectives to view what is common to the three persons of the Trinity as a "universal" standing above them. He ascribed to this universal concept an independent essence—a concept that has reality in the persons but no substantiality in itself. Eckhart, however, seeks the most universal concept of all, which not only encompasses the three persons but also goes beyond the unity of these three—beyond what Gilbertus calls the **deity** <note>original: *deitas*</note> and Eckhart calls the divine nature. He seeks the concept under which the personal God and the divine nature, and on the other hand God and the creature, can be subsumed. Eckhart’s "Godhead" is therefore an even more comprehensive concept than Gilbert’s *deitas*. Eckhart's representation relates similarly to the proposition of Peter Lombard, according to which the essence—the **divine essence** <note>original: *divina essentia*</note>—which is to be distinguished from the persons...

It situates Eckhart's controversial distinction within the historical context of medieval scholastic debates involving Gilbertus Porretanus and Bernard of Clairvaux.</summary>

### II. Essence and its Revelation.

...is, which itself neither begets nor is begotten <note>This continues the thought from the previous page regarding the "divine essence" (*divina essentia*), which remains static and undifferentiated compared to the "acting" persons of the Trinity.</note>. Eckhart expands the idea, which was only hinted at there, into a broader context.

The **Godhead** <term>Gottheit|Eckhart's term for the absolute, hidden, and undifferentiated "ground" of the divine, which exists beyond the Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</term> in Eckhart's view is that **super-being** <note>original: *Uebersein*. This refers to a state of existence that transcends all human categories of "being" or "existence."</note> which Pseudo-Dionysius <note>A 5th-century Christian philosopher whose "apophatic" or "negative" theology argued that we can only say what God is *not*, rather than what He *is*.</note> describes through a heap of negations—the "nothingness" of all determinacy, the negation of every negation and of every predicate whatsoever. For this reason, it is inexpressible and unthinkable, impossible to grasp through the representations of the cognitive faculty, and accessible only to the pure intuition of the highest reason. — **Essence** <term>Wesen|In this philosophical context, essence refers to "pure, undetermined being"—the most basic form of existence before it is shaped into a specific thing.</term> (pure, undetermined being) is the most universal predicate; everything finite is a departure from essence. In essence, there is no opposition: neither love nor sorrow, neither white nor black (264, 12). God’s characteristic property is essence (263, 10). But the Godhead is also exalted above essence, insofar as even essence still contains a certain determination. God—it should be noted that where Eckhart does not specifically have to emphasize the difference between the two concepts, he mostly uses the word "God" for "**Godhead**"—God, then, as the **Absolute**, is neither essence nor reason (282, 30). It would be just as wrong to call God an "essence" as it would be wrong to call the sun "pale" or "black." This does not mean that essence is denied to God; rather, it is attributed to Him in a more valuable and higher sense. For in God is everything, yet not in exclusive determinacy, but in a higher and more universal form (268, 35; 82, 28). **Non-essential essence** <note>original: *unwesentliches Wesen*</note>—that is, essence which lies beyond the defined concept of essence and has become completely void of content, the being which is simultaneously non-being—this alone lies beyond God and beyond every distinction (283, 38). Even the predicate "He is," when applied to God, would be an alien addition (659, 17).

The Godhead, therefore, has no predicates at all. God is without will, without love, without justice, without mercy, even without divinity—without anything, in fact, that has been written about Him or can be attributed to Him in linguistic expression. Any "good" that one might wish to attribute to or state about God completely nullifies the concept of God. If I add anything to God, I turn God into an **idol** <note>original: *Abgott*. Literally an "off-god" or "false god." Eckhart suggests that any human description of God creates a limited mental image that is not actually God.</note> (590, 24). The highest cause is neither light nor darkness.

## 2. The Godhead.

All predicates <term>Prädikate|Philosophical attributes or characteristics assigned to a subject, such as "good," "wise," or "powerful."</term> are foreign additions to the bare divine essence. Its nature is to be without nature. Whoever thinks of goodness, wisdom, or power, obscures and darkens the essence within their thought. Even a single predicate attributed to the essence abolishes the concept of the essence (160, 30). Once everything is set apart, subtracted, and peeled away, so that nothing remains but a single "Is," that is His true name (108, 31). God is nameless, for no one can speak of Him or understand Him. In this sense, a pagan master <note>Likely a reference to a Neoplatonic philosopher like Proclus or the anonymous author of the *Book of Causes*, whom Eckhart frequently cited.</note> says: what we understand or say of the ultimate cause, we ourselves are that much more than the ultimate cause is; for it is beyond speaking and understanding. If I now say: "God is good," that is not true; rather, I am good, but God is not. Even more: I am better than God. For what is good can also become better, and what can become better can also become best. Now, God is not "good," therefore He cannot become "better." And because He cannot become better, He cannot become "best." All three are equally distant from God: good, better, and best; He is beyond it all. If I say further: "God is wise," it is not true; I am wiser than He. Or: "God is a being," it is not true; He is a being transcending all being, and a non-being at the same time... You should understand nothing of God, for God is beyond all understanding. A master says: "Had I a God whom I could understand, I would never hold Him to be a God" (318, 31; 163, 19). God is therefore the Not-God, the Not-Spirit, the Not-Person, the Not-Image—a pure, unmixed, clear One without any duality (320, 28).

God is a "nothing" to Himself and a "nothing" to the sum of all creatures (506, 30); but at the same time, there is nothing negative in God; He is the comprehensive unity of everything positive (321, 6). God is One, but One is the negation of all negation. Unity is more abstract than goodness and truth; it signifies the absence of all predicates. By denying God a predicate, one makes a negative statement about Him; this negation is itself negated in the statement: "God is one" (322, 9) <note>This "negation of negation" is a key concept: to say God is "One" is to deny that He can be limited or divided by any specific qualities.</note>. The unity of God is without ground; rather, it is its own ground. It is an origin of the bottomless depth, a roof of the limitless height, and a circumference of the inconceivable width (525, 31). And with this single predicate, Eckhart lets the matter rest; the expression, which so closely...

## II. The Essence and its Revelation.

The idea that unity and multiplicity are equally present in the Absolute is not found in **Eckhart**. Multiplicity is merely a derivative state.

Just as it is without attributes, the Godhead is also without activity. God and Godhead are as distinct as heaven and earth. God acts; the Godhead does not. It is the simple "Ground," the "silent desert," the "impenetrable darkness," and the immovable rest (527, 23; 389, 2). God has a history; God becomes and "un-becomes" <note>original: *entwird*. This is a central Eckhartian term for the soul letting go of its own identity to merge with the divine.</note> or passes away (180—181). The Godhead, on the other hand, has left all things to God; it is so poor, so naked and empty, as if it were not. It has nothing, it wants nothing, and it needs nothing; it works nothing and gives birth to nothing (532, 30). The Godhead thus remains enclosed within itself, without revelation; it does not communicate itself and does not appear. It is related to nothing but itself; remaining within itself, it is the darkness into which no perception or knowledge penetrates (528, 24; 529, 3). If one moves beyond all that is finite, and thus also beyond the divine persons <note>Referring to the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>, to the highest all-encompassing unity—that immobility devoid of light and revelation, which is the common essence of the persons—then one finds God "de-spirited" <term>entgeistet|A state where the soul moves beyond even the "spirit" to reach the absolute essence of God.</term>, deprived of all attributes and modes of operation, even those of a spiritual nature (670, 30). There, personality, light and darkness, matter and form, all cease to exist (517, 2). And this pure nothingness is intended to be the highest and best, the goal of all longing, the object of all pure contemplation!

### 3. Essence and Nature.

With this concept of the Absolute, the final, most abstract unity would now be reached, but now every kind of expression or relationship to something else would be excluded. Many paths lead into this "desert Godhead," but none lead out. **Eckhart** stands here before the same problem in which every extreme monistic <term>monism|The philosophical view that all of reality is essentially one single substance or principle.</term> way of thinking necessarily entangles itself—a problem which many distinguished thinkers before and after him have tried in vain to solve. It is the task of deriving a world of multiplicity from the abstract One, or at least demonstrating how there can be something else and something limited besides the Absolute without contradiction. **Eckhart** has a specific perspective...

### 3. Essence and Nature.

...possessed and set forth concerning the relationship of the simply One to the Many; however, that this relationship is thoroughly contradictory is evident at first glance. Modern thinkers <note>Likely referring to 19th-century German Idealists like Hegel.</note> have understood the Absolute from the outset not as resting Being, but as **living movement**, so that it is driven through its inherent **negativity** toward an **explication** <note>An unfolding or making explicit what was hidden.</note> of the moments slumbering within it. The old Master [Eckhart] has the same intention; but the available means for the systematic execution of his fundamental idea are still far more inadequate.

According to Eckhart, the Absolute lacks all predicates and all activities; it is **pure Being**, which, as completely indeterminate, can also be called **Non-being** with equal right. However, the concept of the Absolute was attained through continuous abstraction. Therefore, all the gradually shed determinations must, in a certain sense, be contained potentially within the most general concept, and within the highest unity there must somehow be a **principle of differentiation** from which the other differences then flow in a steady progression. Eckhart finds this principle of differentiation in the distinction between the **divine essence** and the **divine nature**—between "being-in-itself" and "being-for-others," as we would say today. They are distinguished as **matter** and **form**. Just as there is no matter without form, there is also no divine essence without divine nature, which is to say, without the principle of **revelation**. Form, however, is the revelation of the essence (530, 37; 681, 32). The essence neither acts nor suffers, the nature does not suffer, but it *acts* (191, 19). Nature is the out-streaming of the Godhead, while the essence is the ground of this out-streaming that remains within its own depths (669, 31). The fact that we ascribe matter, form, and activity to God arises from our confinement to the senses, which are incapable of purely spiritual vision. The highest contemplation of God must discard all such categories in order to reach the pure, undifferentiated unity. But if we wish to make God and the world comprehensible when descending into multiplicity, those categories are indispensable (681, 30; 513, 9).

The Absolute is not merely the negation of all definiteness, but it is above all the unlimited **capacity** <note>original: *Vermögen*. In this context, it refers to the potential or power to become all things.</note> that lacks no kind of being (26, 5). In it, nothing is determined; but all determinations can flow from it, insofar as it is the...

## II. Essence and its Revelation.

**Potential** is the ability to determine oneself. Within this unity, all multiplicity is potentially included; everything individual slumbers within it, not as many distinct things, but in an all-encompassing unity, and not as something truly existing for itself, but according to its **inherent potential**. Everything is <term>sublated</term><note>The German term is *aufgehoben*, a central concept in German philosophy meaning that something is simultaneously canceled out, preserved, and lifted to a higher level.</note> in the <term>Absolute</term>, but only the finitude in everything is negated (541, 23); rather, the "essentialness" is preserved here, and this sublation of individuality is an elevated and better form of existence for all things. The Absolute is therefore to be thought of as the conclusion of an absolute **process**, as the goal of all essence. The first beginning exists for the sake of the final goal. God himself does not rest where he is the first beginning, but rather where he is the goal and the resting place of all essence—not that this essence is annihilated there, but rather it is brought there to its highest perfection.

What then is this final goal? It is the **hidden darkness** of the eternal Godhead, which is unknowable, was never known, and never will be known. There, God remains unknown even to himself; the light of the eternal **personality** (the possibility of forming a person) has shone into it, but the darkness (of the Absolute) is not accessible to the light (288, 21) <note>This is an intentional inversion of the Gospel of John 1:5, suggesting that the primal "Godhead" is so deep that even the "Light" of the divine persons cannot fully penetrate its mystery.</note>. God **externalizes** himself and flows back into himself again (515, 27); that is his history. This **eternal becoming** is the work of eternal nature, and therefore it is without beginning and without end (497, 30).

The Absolute, insofar as it has enclosed within itself all the richness of diversity, is called the **form-rich light of divine unity**. In itself, it is simple and yet both **essence** and **nature**. As **essence**, it rests in pure being, in immobile stillness. There, its light encompasses the "All" as a simple unity—not in such a way that it takes the specific form of any creature, but rather, in this immobile stillness, it is only its own form. As **nature**, it is the unity of the divine persons, the possibility for the Godhead to become a person; only in the "persons" <note>In Christian theology, the "Persons" refer to the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> is there activity, production, labor, and birthing. For the **essence** does not work and does not give birth. The essence is the all-embracing unity of the divine persons and of all things; it contains the forms of all things within itself in simplicity and according to their essence, and by means of this simple "image," it dwells within all things. **Nature**, however, is the nature only of the divine persons, not of things; created things have a part in the **essence**, but not in the **divine nature**. Essence and nature are not...

## 4. The Divine Persons.

The nature within God is the ground of the divine personality and thus of all manifestation of God, of all revelation; it is the simple <term>Being-in-itself</term><note>German: *Ansichsein*. A philosophical term describing a thing as it exists independently of our perception of it.</note> of the persons, from which they emerge, each with its own particular nature (670, 22). The absolute essence of God is unity. This unity cannot reveal itself. This is God’s "impotence," but at the same time his highest "power" <note>Eckhart often uses paradoxes to show that what seems like a limitation in God (the inability to be divided) is actually a sign of his absolute perfection.</note>. What the unity itself could not reveal, the three persons have revealed, and indeed all in the same way because of the unity of their essence—most of all to themselves, because it is their own natural essence (390, 14). The essence cannot reveal itself insofar as it is essence; the persons, insofar as they reveal the essence, are the form of the essence (681, 30). It is exactly like the difference between humanity and a human being. The common nature of all humans is called "humanity"; humanity can do nothing or produce nothing in itself, but only within a human person. Likewise, the Godhead has all things enclosed within itself; but it does not work or give birth in itself, but rather through the persons (632, 30).

Eckhart reproaches the <term>Scholastics</term><note>The "Masters of Paris," the medieval academics who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note>, the "Masters of Paris," for dwelling too much on the workings of the Trinity and therefore failing to penetrate to the Unity (504, 1). In the doctrine of the Trinity, however, he feels at one with them; admittedly, even if they said the right thing, they did not have the right understanding and could therefore not correctly prove their doctrine (176, 8). Eckhart evidently wants to present the church's teaching and make it understandable from the deepest grounds. In doing so, he aligns himself most closely with Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential philosopher of the Scholastic period.</note> by deriving the process of person-formation in the Godhead from the activity of divine Reason,

### II. The Essence and its Revelation.

However, his doctrine takes a very peculiar turn because he places the impersonal Godhead before all divine persons, and he expressly and most vigorously contests the absolute status of those persons. Consequently, the persons become instead stages of the absolute process, and they essentially appear only as "modes" <note>In philosophy, a "mode" is a specific way in which a substance exists or is experienced.</note> of the divine substance, which extends beyond them all.

The charge of <term>Tetratheism</term><note>The heretical belief that there are four divine entities: the Father, Son, Holy Spirit, and the divine essence itself. This was a common accusation in medieval theological debates.</note> could be leveled at *Gilbertus Porretanus* with good reason. *Eckhart’s* doctrine of God is a purer, more pronounced <term>Monism</term><note>A philosophical view that everything in existence can be reduced to a single substance or principle.</note>; the Trinity of the persons appears only as a "contingency" <note>German: *Zufall*. In a philosophical context, this refers to an "accident"—a property that a thing possesses but which is not part of its core, unchanging essence.</note> of the essential unity. This unity is impersonal as such, and one cannot ascribe "reason" to it any more than one could ascribe any other property.

Eckhart distinguishes between the **unbegotten essence** and the **begotten essence**, the **un-natured nature** and the **natured nature**. The unbegotten essence is self-sufficient without acting or begetting; the Godhead communicates itself to no other (528, 24). The Absolute as nature is reflection into itself. Through the act of this self-reflection, nature becomes a person, and as a person, nature is called **Father**. This self-reflection is "knowledge"; therefore, the Father is pure intellect who perfectly perceives himself (6, 8; 269, 39). The object of this knowledge is the **Son** or the **Word**, the second person in the Godhead; and the love between Father and Son, as their eternal mutual relationship to one another, is the **Holy Spirit** as the third person. Eckhart expresses himself in this way: In God there are two things: **Essence** and **self-relation** or **relationship**. It is not the Father’s **essence** that begets the Son in the Godhead. For the Father, insofar as he is the **essence**, looks only into his bare essence; there he finds himself in all his fullness without any distinction, without Son and Holy Spirit, and sees only his unique absolute essence. However, if the Father wishes to behold himself and relate to himself in another person, then the Father’s essence begets the Son through this self-relation; and because he has eternally had his joy and delight in this, this self-reflection had to take place eternally. Therefore, the Son is eternal like the Father. From the delight and the love, however, which Father and Son have for one another, the **Holy Spirit** springs forth, and because this love between Father and Son has been eternal, so is the Holy Spirit—

This eternal Word does not originate in the Father’s personal reason (at the stage where the Father has already become a Person), but rather in His natural capacity; otherwise, the eternal Word would be its own origin, for understanding and the Word are one and the same (336, 19). It is, therefore, the act of begetting the Son through which the Father and the Son simultaneously receive their personality; for this reason, the Father can even be described as a <term>creature</term> <note>German: *Geschöpf*. In the unborn essence (prior to the formation of the Persons), the Father exists as an impersonal essence, and thus not yet as "Father." However, this unborn essence is simultaneously the root of His personality—the capacity to reveal Himself to Himself as both essence and Person. Through this capacity, the process of person-formation has taken place from all eternity. Within the essence, the three Persons are one. The "born essence" is distinguished from the "unborn essence" as the God who constantly generates Himself in three Persons (499, 16).

The unborn essence is also called the <term>un-natured nature</term> <note>German: *ungenaturte Natur*. This refers to the divine nature as it expresses itself through the specific characteristics of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>. The un-natured nature is the inactive Absolute, from which the natured nature nonetheless proceeds. The birth of the Son takes place within the natured nature. In the un-natured nature, the Persons are one; in the natured, they are distinct (537, 29).

In Eckhart's mysticism, the "Godhead" refers to the primeval, undifferentiated essence of the Divine, while "God" refers to the Divine as He manifests in the Trinity.</note>. Unity reveals itself in Trinity with distinct rational certainty; the Trinity then returns into Unity and sheds all distinctions and all knowability (517 ff.). The Godhead, like a mother, holds all things enclosed as a simple whole within its womb; but as such, it does not give birth. The Father, as the principle of personality within the Godhead, does not have things within himself, and therefore he is called Father; but he bears them out of himself like a mother, and the Absolute One penetrates everything that he begets (672, 6). The Trinity is, as it were, the heart of the divine nature. Just as all limbs receive life from the heart, so the Godhead performs everything it does by means of the Persons. But the heart of this heart is the high power of Unity, in and with which they are capable of all things (525, 12).

The Godhead, conceived of as nature, is in Eckhart's view absolute knowledge as pure relation to itself (670, 1). This impersonal knowledge is what Eckhart calls "Fatherliness" <note>German: *Väterlichkeit*</note>, the mere capacity for the act of self-knowledge in which the Person of the Father arises. In the act of self-recognition, the Son is given as the object, and the Spirit is given as the relationship—completing the duality into unity—between the Father and the Son (174—176). In the act of self-knowledge, the Father posits himself as his own object, and by holding himself as "another" over against himself, he distinguishes himself as a Person from this Other as another Person (670, 3). For, according to the fundamental premise of <term>Realism</term> <note>A medieval philosophical school holding that abstract concepts or "universals" have a real existence. The Son, now as the perfect counterpart of the Father, is a knowing and rational being just as He is; through this opposition, both become Persons, and it is the Son who first reveals the Father as Father (198, 17). The Son is exactly like the Father, except that he is born (that is, begotten) of him, while the Father is unbegotten. The process through which the Godhead determines itself as a <term>Trinity</term> <note>German: *Dreiheit*</note> of persons is an eternal, supra-temporal, and necessary one—a *becoming*, not a *doing*; it does not arise from a free decision of God, which he could just as well have omitted, but is established along with God as the necessity of his essence. If he were to cease it for a single moment, he would deny himself (336, 31; 290, 25). The begetting, like the act of creation, does not happen merely in the past, but is happening perpetually (437, 27). The Persons are eternal; they have no "before" or "after." They are not held by the Absolute as if by something outside of them; they are *in* the Absolute (677, 23). The Son is not "born" [as a finished event]; rather, he is *now* being born, and this *now* is an eternal becoming. For the Father always remains identical to himself in his eternal begetting. If one wished to attribute an "action" to him, it would have to be understood such that what he has ever done, he does now, and what he does now, he has done eternally. For him, there is neither future nor past (672, 27). And because in this event no serious essential distinction is made anywhere, but all the manifoldness of form does not actually depart from the unity of essence and always flows back into it, this process is also called a *play* <note>German: *Spiel*. This is frequently connected to the definition common among the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Medieval theologians and philosophers who used logic to systematize Christian doctrine.</note> since *Abelard* <note>Peter Abelard (1079–1142), a famous philosopher known for his work on the Trinity and logic.</note>, according to which Power is assigned to the Father, Wisdom to the Son, and Goodness to the Spirit as specific attributes (538, 21; 497, 20; 332 ff.; 511, 2; 248, 30; 386, 34), although a direct link between this view and Eckhart’s other descriptions cannot be proven.

As the Persons emerge from the <term>Absolute Ground</term> <note>German: *absoluter Grund*. In Eckhart's thought, the "Ground" is the ultimate, undifferentiated reality of God that lies beneath even the distinction of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>, they by no means fall out of it; rather, the Absolute remains in them and expresses itself through them. Eckhart takes great pains to clarify how the Absolute and the Person are formally distinct, yet essentially one. The most decisive statement on this is found in the following passage: "Nature cannot exist without there being something whose nature it is; and the Person of the Father—with whom the other two Persons are given—cannot exist without there being something whose Person he is. Therefore, neither can exist without the other, and neither is the origin of the other. Nonetheless, they possess specific characteristics and relate to one another as distinction and indistinctness <note>original: *reden, unreden*. These terms literally mean 'speaking' and 'unspeaking,' used here to describe the tension between the expressed Persons of the Trinity and the silent, hidden Essence.</note>. Where they turn in equal measure into the ground of their particularity, there they retain their own characteristic essence; there, the distinction does not cancel out the indistinctness, nor the latter the former. This 'outgoing' from the ground of particularity is the eternal process. Change-less rest does not cancel out this process. The process inherently contains the state of being separate, while change-less rest contains the state of being indistinct. Rest must have a substrate; this is the eternal process, which constitutes the power and the potential within the ground of particularity. This makes the Father 'Father' and the Essence 'Essence,' yet not in such a way that the Father is the result of a process; rather, it is an eternally proceeding standstill (682, 16)." The distinction between the Persons is always resolved back into the unity of the essence; thus, the river has flowed back into itself (387, 38).

...divine Persons as simultaneously remaining in the stillness of a unity without attributes <note>original: *prädikatlose Einheit*. A unity that cannot be described with adjectives or "predicates" because it is beyond all human categories.</note>. **Eckhart** did not find a suitable expression for the idea of "absolute negativity" in God, and this connection between the One and the Many, between stillness and movement, remains a complete contradiction. **Eckhart** went to great lengths to avoid every misunderstanding, to refute every possible objection, and to answer every question that arose. But the concepts he uses are not clear enough, and his method is too aphoristic <note>A style of writing using short, pithy, or disconnected statements rather than a sustained, systematic logical argument.</note> in character for his earnest efforts to have succeeded. Through **Eckhart’s** methods, it was impossible to reach a concept of a "living personality" in the divine. In fact, he teaches an "essential Trinity" <note>original: *Wesentrinität*. This refers to the Trinity as it exists within the divine essence itself, rather than how it relates to the created world.</note> as the prerequisite for the Godhead <note>German: *Gottheit*. For Eckhart, the "Godhead" is the silent, unchanging, and undifferentiated source, while "God" refers to that source as it becomes active or personal.</note> becoming manifest to itself, occurring before any revelation to the outside world. However, if the interests of rigorous conceptual science are not satisfied by the fact that the three stages in the Godhead’s process of self-knowledge are called "Persons," it is even less likely that the traditional Church concept of the Trinity can be rediscovered in these moments of divine activity, which are designated as "Persons" in name only. Nevertheless, one can find in **Eckhart’s** presentation of the Trinity a middle ground between the perspective of **Thomas [Aquinas]** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic teacher who emphasized the logical distinctions between the divine Persons.</note> on one hand, and the perspective that—starting with **Lessing** <note>Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1729–1781), a dramatist and philosopher who interpreted the Trinity as a developmental step in human consciousness.</note>—has paved the way for a deeper understanding of this doctrine in modern German philosophy, especially in **Hegel** <note>G.W.F. Hegel (1770–1831), who viewed the Trinity as a dialectical process of the Spirit unfolding.</note>.

When **Eckhart** uses the term "God," he uses it—aside from those instances where it stands for "Godhead"—to designate the Absolute as a Person, much like its usage in common speech. By the expression "God," one is not to think of the unity of the three Persons, the divine nature—for this itself precedes personality—but rather the concept of God the Father lies at the foundation. This is not, however, in the sense that the Father is a specific person distinct from the Son and the Spirit, but rather insofar as He encompasses them both. ### 5. God.

...person united in one conception. In this sense, *God* is the bearer of divine attributes <note>original: *Prädikate*. In philosophy, these are the properties or qualities assigned to a subject.</note>, insofar as they are common to all three persons (541, 15).

*God* is the absolute *Being* <term>Being (Wesen): Eckhart often distinguishes between the hidden, undifferentiated Godhead and "God" as He exists in relation to himself and the world.</term>, insofar as it has already entered into a series of determinations. *God* has a history, albeit in a timeless sense; he is a substance that serves as the foundation for a series of processes. *God* becomes and unbecomes; this strange-sounding sentence is evidently the same one that appears in the 1317 Bull of Condemnation by the Bishop of Strasbourg against the Beghards <note>A lay religious movement in the Middle Ages often accused of heresy for their mystical beliefs.</note> in the form: the heretics claimed, "God will be in a certain state of loss" <note>original Latin: *Deum fore in quadam perditione*. In the context of the Eckhartian way of teaching, this long-enigmatic sentence gains its recognizable meaning, even through the distortion. — *God's attribute is Being.* *God* recognizes nothing except *Being* alone; he knows nothing but *Being*, he loves nothing and thinks of nothing but his *Being* (262, 37). But the highest attribute belonging to *God* is that he is *Reason* <note>German: *Vernunft*. In this context, it refers to the divine intellect or the capacity for self-awareness.</note> that thinks itself. He is a living, existing, substantial *Reason* that understands itself, exists and lives within itself, and is identical with itself (188, 29). If we understand *God* as *Being*, we understand him only in his outer court. His temple is *Reason*. *God* is a *Reason* that lives in self-knowledge, remaining solely within itself, where nothing external ever touches him. There he is alone in quiet rest and recognizes himself within himself (269, 35; 527, 12). Thus, as a rational *Being*, rather than as a Creator, human *reason* recognizes him in its truest form (69, 7). This *Reason* establishes the necessity of his action; whatever is established within it must emerge as his expression, and nothing in *God* is mere whim; everything is a necessary consequence of his rational *Being*. *God* is good; but that is not what makes me blessed <note>German: *selig*. Refers to the state of ultimate spiritual happiness or beatitude.</note>. I would never desire that *God* make me blessed out of his goodness; for then he might perhaps choose not to do it. My *blessedness* consists solely in the fact that *God* is rational and that I recognize this (270, 38). *God* is the *Truth* (57, 30); the most proper attributes one can assign to *God* are *Word* and *Truth* (271, 11). God's *Reason* is essentially this inner action upon itself, and in this lies God's *blessedness* (272, 5). Furthermore, *God* is infinite, beyond space and time. *God* in all his working has no shadow of temporality or change—

What God actually is remains impossible to say (112, 33).

## 6. The Creation.

For the manifest, personal God, who is essentially Reason <note>original: *Vernunft*. In this context, it refers to the divine Intellect or Logos through which all things are ordered.</note> and Goodness, the world of creatures is the necessary completion of His essence. He cannot remain alone; He must communicate Himself. Because He possesses a particularity, another particularity must stand over against Him. The Son is not this required "Other"; for He is the same in essence as the Father—He is indeed another person, but not another *thing* than the Father (675, 28). <note>The author is likely referencing the Latin theological distinction between *alius* (another person) and *aliud* (another substance).</note> But the Son must be understood as the Principle of this "otherness." It is the same process that produces, on the one hand, the divine persons who remain in essential unity (the inner-divine life), and on the other hand, the world of creatures who proceed from God into a—though only seemingly—separate existence.

The eternal process within God is the cause of all creatures. Were it not for the three Persons with their distinct particularity within the Godhead, the Godhead would never have been revealed, and God would never have created creatures. If one could say that one aspect in God were nobler than another, His Reason would be this nobler thing. Through Reason, God is manifest to Himself; through it, He returns into Himself; through it, He goes out of Himself into all things. And were there no Reason in God, there could be no Trinity, and thus the creature would never have proceeded from God (313, 5). The Godhead only becomes manifest through the things that stand lower than it (541, 2). Just as God is eternal, so all things have been eternal in Him, but they were nothing in themselves. When creatures came into being and their created existence began, God was not God in Himself alone, but in the creatures (in relation to the creatures as their <term>immanent</term> <note>Existing or operating within; inherent.</note> essence) He was God (281, 26). God is the absolute One; He knows nothing but Himself alone. God could never know Himself without also knowing all creatures (254, 15); He knows and loves Himself in all things (379, 32). One cannot, therefore, properly speak of a time before the creation of the world. Before the world was created, God was heaven, hell, and all things (589, 25); thus there was no time, but all distinct things have existed from eternity in their absolute <term>ground</term> <note>original: *Grunde*. Here referring to the Divine Intellect or Logos.</note>—with its gaze fixed upon the essence of the world as it stood in uncreated simplicity, without any form, within the Father (589, 6).

In this birth, all things have <term>emanated</term> <note>original: *emaniert*. Flowed forth from the divine source.</note> (254, 9). God has created the world in such a way that He is still creating it without ceasing. For all past and future being is foreign and distant to God (437, 30). God creates the world in an eternally present Now. The time that passed a thousand years ago is as present and as near to God as the time that is now. What God created six thousand years ago, He creates even now (266, 27; 207, 1). God has stood eternally in immovable <term>detachment</term> <note>original: *Abgeschiedenheit*. A key concept in Meister Eckhart’s philosophy, referring to a state of being perfectly still, self-contained, and free from worldly attachment.</note> and still stands in it. # 7. The World of Ideas and the Sensible World.

Connection with the dogmatic understanding. He boldly contrasts the more suitable expression of truth against the unsuitable one, and he frames dogma within the context of his highest metaphysical assumptions regarding true being.

*Eckhart* does not teach an eternity of matter. The eternal world is not the world of <term>creatures</term> <note>original: *Creaturen*. In medieval theology, this refers to all created things—humans, animals, and objects—as distinct from the Creator.</note>. In God, the world exists eternally only as the ideal principle of a world. At the foundation of all finite being lies a world of ideas, of <term>prototypes</term> <note>original: *vorgehenden Bilder*. Literally "preceding images." These are the divine blueprints or "exemplars" in the mind of God.</note>. In this, *Eckhart* is entirely a student of *Thomas* <note>Referring to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican philosopher and theologian.</note>. Things are created according to the likeness of these images, not directly according to the likeness of God himself. The infinity of the divine essence spreads out in a brilliant, luminous fullness of particular forms, which, however, remain as such within God and are thus held together in the unity of his essence. It is only through the departure from God—by taking on a different, spatio-temporal form of existence, passing into a real multiplicity and finiteness through mutual limitation, and becoming material and perceptible to the senses—that this finite world of creatures arises; and of this world, it is certainly not true that it is eternal.

In the doctrine of the ideal world, *Eckhart* intends only to repeat the doctrine of *Thomas*. The primary passage in which he discusses this in a coherent presentation is partly a literal translation and partly a condensing or expanding adaptation of the relevant section from *Thomas’s* <term>Summa</term> <note>original: *Summa (I, Quaest. XV, Art. 1—3)*. Referring to the *Summa Theologica*, Part 1, Question 15, Articles 1 through 3, which discusses how "Ideas" exist in the divine intellect.</note>. We repeat the essential content of this passage because, although it is not Eckhart’s original property, it expresses his opinion and cannot be dispensed with for the whole of his teaching.

The essence of all creatures has eternally been a divine life in God as the origin of ideas, of the prototypes. Now, the prototype can exist in a soul in two ways: as a model, according to which I represent an image in sensory material; and as a universal concept, under which I cognitively encompass individual things. In both ways, prototypes must exist in God. For all generation adheres to a common schema, and every thing arises from another of its kind according to this schema. Humans beget humans, lions beget lions, and fire begets fire. Thus, we find

Since God has created the world, there must have been an eternal <term>preceding image</term> <note>original: *vorgehendes Bild*. This refers to the Platonic "Idea" or the "Exemplar" in Scholastic theology—the blueprint of a thing existing in God’s mind before the thing itself is made.</note> in His reason, according to whose likeness He created specifically these <term>creatures</term> <note>original: *Creaturen*. In this context, it refers to all created things, including plants, animals, and inanimate objects, not just living beings.</note> and not others, the images of which He did not possess within Himself. — Now, everywhere, the final purpose is that which is actually intended. According to *Aristotle*, however, the final purpose of the world is the Good, and this is the order of all creatures directed toward God. Therefore, the world order must have been eternally known and intended in God, the first cause. If God has the image of the world order within Himself, then He also has the specific image of every single creature. Therefore, there must be as many images in God as there are particular gradations in creation; thus, the rose has its own particular image, the violet another, and likewise the human, the angel, and all other things. — It is marvelous how the multiplicity of images can be reconciled with the simplicity of the divine essence, in which all things belonging to Him are one. This can be understood as follows: God sees the image as a mirror of His own essence, according to which He shapes the sensible thing, but not as an external determination foreign to Him that enables His reason to act. In all the plurality of images, He sees only the reflection of His own essence. God knows His essence as fully as it is knowable within Himself, and insofar as the creatures have their likeness in the divine essence. This likeness, which unites the creature and the divine essence, is called the preceding image. For this reason, there must be as many images as there are stages of creation that have their likeness in God. The preceding images are the essence of God—not as it is in itself, but insofar as it is a mirror in which the essence of all creatures is reflected. Thus, there are many images and yet only one mirror, one essence. — The preceding images are the principle of creation and simultaneously the principle of the knowledge of creatures; what God knows, He therefore knows through the mediation of these images. Evil and the bad are without essence; rather, they are a <term>deprivation</term> <note>original: *Beraubung*. Corresponding to the Latin *privatio boni*, the theological idea that evil is not a "thing" but a lack or hole where a good should be.</note> of essence, just as blindness is nothing in itself but rather a deprivation of sight. Therefore, God does not recognize evil and sin in themselves, but in the image of the <insert>virtues</insert> <note>original: *Tu-*... The word is truncated at the page break, likely intended to be *Tugenden* (virtues).</note> opposed to them.

In philosophy, these are the specific qualities or states of a substance—like the "redness" of a rose compared to the rose itself.</note> as well as the <term>substances</term> <note>original: *Substanzen*. In this sense, God has all things hidden within himself. In their simple nature and also in the nothingness from which they are created, <term>creatures</term> <note>In the sense of all created things—stars, stones, and souls.</note> are incomprehensible: an impenetrable darkness, void of light and distinction (528, 4). All things are in God insofar as they have been eternally in God—not in coarse materiality, as we are now, but as the art is in the master. God looked upon Himself and saw all things. Therefore, God was not as manifold as things are now with their distinctions. Although creatures are now manifold, they are nevertheless only one image in God (502, 22).

From this <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The world as it exists in the divine mind or intellect, rather than the world we perceive with our senses.</note>, one must, in Eckhart’s sense, clearly distinguish the "created world." The former is eternal in God, the latter is temporal; the former is of the same essence as God, the latter is without essence. Were there neither time nor place nor <term>otherness</term> <note>original: *Anderheit*. The state of being "other" or separate from God.</note>, then all would be one essence. Time separates; eternity unites. Time is the cause of aging and fading. In eternity, everything is eternally young (87, 30; 88, 2). Physicality is a falling away from essence, a mere accident and a deterioration (117, 29). All things have emanated in time in a finite form, but in eternity they have remained infinite (390, 30). Nature and "naturalness" are not the same. Naturalness is assumed in time, while nature is eternal in itself (466, 30). In the eternal emanation, in which all things have emanated without themselves (as mere possibility without a specific existence for themselves), they became an eternal <term>Now</term> <note>original: *Nu*. Eckhart’s famous term for the "Eternal Now," a moment transcending time where past and future are present.</note>; but in time they are from nothing

All creatures have no essence, for their essence depends on the presence of God within them. Should God turn away for a single moment, they would come to nothing (136, 23). Whoever sees God recognizes that all creatures are Nothing. If one holds one creature against another, it seems beautiful and is something; but if one holds it against God, it is Nothing (222, 34).

### 8. God and the Creature.

Eckhart shows the clear intention to avoid <term>pantheism</term> <note>original: *Pantheismus*. The belief that the universe and God are identical, or that God is merely the sum of all things.</note>. He emphatically rejects the error that sensory-finite things in their totality express the essence of God. He protests against such an interpretation of his teaching in the strongest possible terms. God created the world: this does not mean that creatures sprang from the essence of God like the eternal Word of the Father <note>The "Word" refers to the second person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ, who Eckhart distinguishes from created things.</note> as a birth from God’s nature; for then the creature would be God, which no sensible person can accept—rather, the nature of creatures refutes this as something impossible and false (325, 24). The nature of the three <term>Persons</term> <note>Referring to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the Trinity.</note> cannot also be the nature of things. For then all things would have to be God in the same sense that God is God, and that is impossible (669, 10; 673, 20). But certainly, on the path that Eckhart takes, pantheism cannot be avoided even with the most earnest intent.

### 8. God and the Creature.

Being in God exists without real differences, where the world is a simple entity and essentially equal to God, and the multiplicity of things is only established in an ideal form as a possibility; yet there is also a finite <term>being-for-itself</term> <note>German: *Fürsichsein*. A philosophical term for an object existing as an independent, self-contained entity.</note> of things which, as such, are outside of God—that is, they are essence-less and naught. Now, one can well understand how the world, in the first sense, is in God, but not how the world, in the second sense, can be "outside" God. Indeed, outside of God there is nothing but <term>Nothingness</term> <note>Eckhart frequently uses "Nothingness" to describe the state of any created thing if it were to be conceptually or actually separated from its divine source.</note> (321, 11). Eckhart then draws the consequence that therefore the world, insofar as it exists "in itself" and is not thought of as being in God, is absolutely Nothing. Nevertheless, the reality of these finite things constantly asserts itself, and the problem arises to define more closely how these things can, after all, participate in the Essence—that is, in God. Eckhart’s explanations on this point are extremely numerous, yet they are hardly of sufficient clarity. Fundamentally, he does not escape this unmediated contradiction. Eckhart asserts just as much that things have full equality with God, insofar as their essence is concerned, as he asserts that they fall completely outside of God and are an essence-less appearance, insofar as material things are meant that exist in space and time.

1. According to the first view, as we have seen, the world is co-posited in the concept of God, and God has expressed his innermost essence in things. God is All, and All is God. This is because the builder is not the <term>sufficient cause</term> <note>The complete reason why something exists. God, however, gives nature everything: both form and matter (610, 29). God is the center of all things (273, 5); the Godhead holds all things within itself, but undivided in a single essence (541, 12). Insofar as God is in all things, he is the "soul of all souls" (529, 34). He is the nature of all natures, because he possesses the nature of all natures within himself, undivided. He is the Light of lights, the Life of the living, the Being of beings, the Reason of the rational (540, 5). Had God ever placed a work outside of himself, he would not have been God. God performs all his works in such a way that they remain <term>immanent</term> <note>original: *immanent*. ## II. The Essence and its Revelation.

Things are made from nothing, but the Divinity has infused them, so that they are full of the Divinity. Otherwise they would come to nothing (529, 21). God has all things hidden within Himself, but not as this or that specific thing, but as One in unity (333, 10). All creatures are in God and are His own Divinity and signify His fullness (322, 22). God has enclosed everything in everything within Himself; there everything is one and one is everything in everything (391, 14). What I recognize of creatures in God, I perceive nothing there but God alone. For in God there is nothing but God (83, 16). God is a <term>Being</term> <note>German: *Wesen*. In Eckhart’s philosophy, this refers to the ultimate, fundamental reality or "is-ness" of a thing.</note> that has the essence of all creatures within Himself (83, 7); He is more intimate to things as their reason and their nature than they are to themselves (10, 36). How God is in things can be very well understood if we substitute the word *Being* for *God*. As *Being*, *God* is in all things (613, 13). God has all things in a perfect form within Himself (321, 14); therefore, things in God are nobler than they are in themselves (530, 8). God is not in things with His personality, nor with His nature. Person and nature are one in Essence, and thus, as Being, God is in all places, and in every single place, God is whole. Now, because God is without parts, all things and all places are a *Place of God* <note>German: *Gottesstatt*. A term implying that every location is a dwelling place for the divine presence.</note>. Thus, all things are full of God according to His essence without ceasing (389, 24). God was and is eternally Father; but since He created creatures, He is Lord (433, 15), an expression that brings to mind Tertullian <note>original: *advers. Hermog. 3*. A reference to Tertullian’s treatise *Against Hermogenes*, where he argues that "Lord" is a relative title God acquired only after creation began.</note>.

It is a consequence of the same viewpoint, by virtue of which the indwelling of things in God and God in things is maintained, that the creature is credited with expressing God's essence, leading upward to God, and being a way to God (374, 28). Whoever knew nothing but creatures would not need to pay attention to any sermon. Every creature is full of God and is a book that preaches Him (271, 33). God is in all things with His essence, His activity, and His omnipotence. All creatures are the *footprints* of God (11, 6). And indeed, this refers specifically to particular, actual things. God communicates Himself to all things, and yet to each in a different measure. God gives equally to all things, but the things receive differently according to the measure of their capacity. 3. Let us look back at the line of thought just presented. According to the highest principles of Eckhart’s way of thinking, the world is to be understood as an <term>emanation</term> <note>A "flowing out" from a divine source, a central concept in Neoplatonic philosophy where the universe is seen as an overflow of God's essence.</note> of God. Particular existence—multiplicity and finitude—is only appearance, an appearance that is <term>sublated</term> <note>German: *aufgehoben*. A philosophical term meaning that something is simultaneously canceled out, preserved, and lifted to a higher level of meaning.</note> for God and within God. And yet, a certain reality of finite things forces itself upon Eckhart as well, and he goes so far as to make the finite world, in its very finitude and by means of its finitude, a revelation of God. The eternal ideas, in which the essence of God is reflected and in which things participate (having been created according to their likeness), are meant to form the bridge between the Godhead and the world of creatures. But this only pushes the difficulty further away. For the images are *in* God, while the things are *outside* of God. This chasm cannot be bridged. If in truth there is only the One, how can the Many exist in any sense? And if the Many possesses any kind of being, how can God be the **Absolute**, since He must simultaneously be conceived as the all-encompassing One, outside of whom there is absolutely nothing?

...for whom is it? When Eckhart distinguishes two aspects within things: the Universal in them—the <term>essence</term> <note>German: *Wesen*. In Eckhart's thought, the "essence" is the true, divine reality of a thing, whereas its "existence" as a physical object is secondary.</note>—and the Particular—the <term>non-being</term> <note>German: *Nichtseiende*. One might think that the **appearance of multiplicity** arises in the human intellect, and many of Eckhart's statements seem to suggest this. What appears to us as <term>temporal</term> <note>Existing within time, as opposed to the "eternal" state of God.</note> is, in God, eternal. God sees all things as One; the division is in our perception. God speaks only one word: Himself; we hear two: **God** and the **creature** (207, 31). The essence of the soul is receptive to the inflow of divine light, but not in such a pure and clear way as God is able to give it; rather, it is received only in a veiled manner. One sees the light of the sun well enough as it shines upon a tree or another object, but one cannot grasp the sun within itself. Thus, divine gifts must also be measured according to the one who is to receive them, not according to the one who gives (95, 9). Whatever the soul grasps, it grasps in a **finite form** (153, 21). Every knowable thing is grasped and understood according to the measure of the capacity of the one understanding, not as it is knowable in itself (484, 36).

Nevertheless, Eckhart is far from viewing the finitude and <term>multiplicity</term> <note>German: *Mannichfaltigkeit*. The individual human soul belongs precisely to this plurality of finite beings, and as long as it remains within this finitude and does not become like God, it remains trapped in the perception of this untrue and essence-less plurality. To Eckhart, this plurality is considered—if not as true "being"—then at least as something independent of the human intellect. Every thing first "enjoys itself" in this individuality, from which it then (as we shall see later) strives to escape. In every thing, its <term>ideal prototype</term> <note>German: *ideales Urbild*. The perfect "idea" or "blueprint" of a thing as it exists in the mind of God.</note>—the Divine within it—mixes with its undivine finitude, which clings to it as **negation** and **distinction**. ### 8. God and the Creature.

...was bound to appear as a task that could only be posed and attempted on the ground and with the tools of the <term>critical philosophy</term> <note>The school of thought founded by Immanuel Kant, which examines the limits and structures of human understanding.</note> of **Fichte**. He sought to solve it through the <term>primacy of practical reason</term> <note>The idea that moral action and the will take precedence over theoretical knowledge in understanding reality.</note>. In this view, the absolute spirit becomes an organized realm of **Egos**—of finite subjects—in order to overcome finitude through the moral will. Yet, there is indeed an inkling of this thought when **Eckhart** states: If the soul could recognize God as perfectly as the angels do, it would never have entered the body (170, 14).

But if it does not stem from the makeup of the human intellect, where then does the **appearance of finitude** originate? The process of knowledge within God leads only to a self-reflection in God, and everything that appears in this mirror must remain essentially <term>immanent</term> <note>Existing or remaining within; in this context, everything in the "mirror" of God is still part of God's own being.</note> in God. A principle outside of God can never be acknowledged by a way of thinking such as Eckhart’s. The differences within God are not suited to derive anything extra-divine from them. Eckhart bypasses this difficulty. He must, after all, admit to something existing outside of God: the evil creaturely will, or **sin**. As little as he occupies himself with this concept in a detailed or independent way, he nonetheless cannot avoid it. In simple adherence to established church doctrine, he identifies the origin of evil as the **Fall of Man**—a decision of the **free will**, which God gave to man as the "seal of God-likeness." To be sure, he did not attempt to explain how this free will, originating in God, could fall outside of God. From the Fall, Eckhart wishes to explain every extra-divine and ungodly form of existence; only with the Fall did multiplicity and conflict enter into things (497, 2). But he cannot be entirely earnest about this either. To him, as to all his predecessors, evil is nothing positive, but only a <term>privation</term> <note>original: "Privation". From the Latin *privatio boni*, the philosophical theory that evil is not a "thing" in itself, but merely the absence or lack of the good.</note>, a defective good. And since defectiveness stems from finitude, it is rather **finitude** that is the cause of evil, not evil that is the cause of finitude.

The ground of the **sensory world** cannot be found outside of God; nor does it lie within the absolute process. There remains, therefore, only one explanation: the world is created by God, an act of the **divine will**. But even this ex—

He concludes that evil is not a substance but a lack of good, and that the physical world's existence must ultimately be an act of God's will.</summary>

Eckhart’s <term>concept of creation</term> <note>original: Schöpfungsbegriff; the theological framework for how the world was made.</note> is entirely unclear. He distinguishes creation from the trinitarian process, and yet the Son is the archetype of all becoming, and in the Son all things have “flowed out.” The world, whose principle is the Son, is the world of ideas; the term <term>emanation</term> <note>original: dèr Emanation; the philosophical idea that the world flows out from a divine source like light from a candle.</note> must be applied to this all the more, since creation is rather the work of the entire <term>Trinity</term> <note>The Christian doctrine of God as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>. Creation out of nothing can only be the creation of finite <term>creatures</term> <note>original: Creaturen; any created thing, including humans, animals, and objects.</note>. However, precisely in relation to these, Eckhart tends to represent creation not as a free act, but as a necessary process within God. God’s creating is timeless; how then can temporality arise from it? The <term>creatures</term> have “assumed” temporality; but from where could they have taken it? Not from God, for in God there is no time; and not from themselves, for they did not yet exist; and even less from a third party, for no such thing exists. Furthermore, God gives an equal amount to all <term>creatures</term>: to each, his entire essence. Only the <term>creatures</term> receive differently according to their various capacities. Thus, the diversity is actually not created by God, but rather the <term>creatures</term> are already different before God calls them into existence. It is beyond doubt that the finite world cannot be explained through Eckhart’s <term>concept of creation</term>.

Eckhart stops at a mere contradiction. God is everything, therefore he is also the essence of things, and things are nothing outside of God. And yet, things possess something else whose origin cannot be sought in God. He encompasses both in a single intuition. He calls <term>matter</term> <note>original: Materie</note> a coarse, corporeal thing; it is said to be brittle and obstructive, so that the purposes of nature are not perfectly realized (150, 39). Time and place are forms of non-being. And yet, according to the monistic <note>A philosophical view that all of reality is composed of one single substance or principle.</note> fundamental view, even material, spatio-temporal being is not absolutely the opposite of the essence. In what sense Eckhart sometimes attributes a certain being to the finite, and at other times regards it as absolute non-being, remains unclear. When he tries to derive the finitude and imperfection of things from the <term>Nothing</term> <note>original: Nichts</note> from which they were created, the contradiction is somewhat hidden from him by the ambiguity of the word <term>Nothing</term>.
