"God creates things out of ***nothing***" therefore means: God creates out of the fullness of His divine essence. On the other hand, *Eckhart* also uses the word ***Nothing*** to describe the untrue, void existence in contrast to the true Being of the Absolute. However, *Eckhart* cannot admit to a ***Nothing*** in this sense acting as an independent principle outside of God. Even if it occasionally appears as though the ***Nothing*** from which God created the world were something other than the richness of the divine essence—as if this ***Nothing*** were a specific explanatory ground for limited existence in time and space, for materiality and multiplicity, in short, for all the qualities of the finite <term>creature</term> <note>original: Creatur; in Eckhart’s thought, this refers to any being that is not God.</note>—the two different meanings in which he uses the word clearly flow into one another.

It is always the same unresolved difficulty whenever the reality of the finite and the individual is to be maintained alongside the sole essentiality of the infinite and the universal. Just as the world of <term>creatures</term> lacks an understandable foundation in the principles of Being, so too, as we shall see, does the realm of finite personalities; and the origin of evil remains equally uncomprehended, even though without it, the very core and center of the system—the <term>return of the soul</term> <note>original: Rückbildung der Seele; the mystical process of the soul returning to its divine source.</note> into God—would lack its justification. *Eckhart* teaches that because the absolute process must fulfill itself, there is a multiplicity of <term>creatures</term> and finite personalities, and therefore sin and evil exist. Nevertheless, he does not dare to designate finiteness and evil as something good, even in a relative sense, nor to derive them directly from the will of God. Yet, he knows of no opposing principle from which they could originate. ***The Master*** <note>original: Der Meister; a standard way of referring to Meister Eckhart.</note> was able to encompass these contradictions within a single intuition; but he lacked a sufficiently powerful drive for clear <term>dialectical thinking</term> <note>original: dialektischen Denkens; the logical method of resolving contradictions through reasoned argument.</note> to attempt to resolve the contradiction through scientific speculation; his tendency toward a certain form of religious-ethical enthusiasm was far too predominant.

## 9. The Realm of Creatures.

The structure of the realm of creatures is only executed in the broadest outlines by *Eckhart*; he lacks any independent interest in the glory and significance of the primary forms of natural existence. It is here most of all that later <term>theosophy</term> <note>A tradition of mystical philosophy seeking direct knowledge of the divine, often through nature.</note>, especially in *Jacob Boehme*, supplemented his teaching. Despite all his lack of clarity, lack of formal education, and confusion, *Boehme* cannot be denied the great merit of having brought about the dawn of a deeper understanding of nature by weaving together the teachings of *Paracelsus* <note>A Swiss physician and alchemist who saw the human body as a reflection of the cosmos.</note> and *Eckhart*. He was the first to make the bold attempt—often in a childish way, yet instructive for those who followed—to interpret nature throughout as a symbol of the spirit and to bring its most important phenomena into alignment with spiritual processes from the perspective of <term>analogy</term>.

In *Eckhart's* work, we find the following ideas expressed regarding nature as a whole. In God, the perfections of all creatures, which are scattered and divided among them, are collected and united. If there were a creature that possessed all the advantages of all creatures according to their essence and number, God would have created nothing more than that one creature alone (324, 6). God

9. The Realm of Creatures. 145

[God] could not stop at creating only one kind of creature; for a single kind would not have been able to express the fullness of His essence. Therefore, He created a variety of creatures, so that their indefinite multitude might express God—though, of course, even in this way, they cannot do so exhaustively (173, 23). In this abundance of creatures, each individual participates in the divine essence according to the measure of its capacity; this results in a ladder of beings <note>Often referred to as the "Great Chain of Being," a traditional philosophical model where all things are ranked in a hierarchy from inanimate matter up to God.</note> which stand partly closer to and partly further from the Godhead.

The underlying view here is that of the doctrine of <term>emanation</term> <note>The idea that all things "flow out" from a single divine source like light from a sun or water from a spring, rather than being created "out of nothing."</note>, according to which things are distinct based on the sequence in which they have flowed, either more directly or more indirectly, from the divine essence. Like the circles created by throwing a stone into water—which grow larger but also weaker as they move further from the center, with each subsequent circle arising from the one before it—so do the various systems of things exist at an ever-increasing and more indirect distance from God, their original source. Thus, from the Father first emanates the Son <note>In this mystical context, the "Son" represents the first and most perfect expression of God's intellect.</note>, who is the cause of all subsequent emanations; then the highest angel and the entire angelic world from the highest to the lowest (who himself still stands at an infinite distance from all matter); and by means of the angels, all other creatures then emanate. The first emanation is so powerful: if there were a thousand worlds or more, their capacity to receive would reach its end before the power of the first emanation to act upon them all would be exhausted—just as the expanse of the water would fail before the strength of the stone’s original impact failed to produce ever new and wider circles (165—166).

In particular, there are three main distinctions among creatures. Some participate in the absolute essence only through mere inorganic existence; there are others who also possess life; and thirdly, there are those who are images of God through reason: the angels and the human soul (660, 18; 479, 19). — The basic elements of all <term>creatureliness</term> <note>original: Creatürlichkeit; the state or quality of being a created being as opposed to the uncreated Creator.</note> are also enumerated in the following way: In the order of things, that which encompasses always stands higher than that which is encompassed. Thus the angels, themselves graded from highest to lowest, stand higher than the heavens, and the heavens higher than fire,

### 10. The Angels.

Only faint traces of the developed doctrine of angels by Pseudo-Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite was a highly influential mystical theologian of the late 5th century whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined how the Middle Ages understood the ranks of angels.</note> are found in Eckhart (110, 14; 153, 25). Generally, he did not pursue this doctrine to any great extent. Nevertheless, within the world of existence, the angels occupy a significant position for him as the mediators between the purely spiritual world of Ideas <note>In this context, "Ideas" refers to the eternal archetypes of all things existing in the divine mind.</note>—with which they are also often identified (111, 1)—and the world of material things. They serve, in a sense, as the "handles of God" to govern the finite creature. In their ranking among themselves, they proceed from the being of the highest angel, who is most closely related to God, toward those lower angels who become increasingly similar to the material creature—though even the lowest remains exalted at an infinite distance above everything physical.

The angels are created out of nothing; they are purely spiritual beings who lack the "soul-principle" <note>Eckhart distinguishes between the 'soul,' which gives life to a physical body, and the purely intellectual spirit of an angel.</note> because they are not related to any body. Their essence is <term>Reason</term> <note>German: *Vernunft*. For Eckhart, this is the faculty of direct spiritual understanding.</note>, and through this, they enjoy the unceasing contemplation of the divine light (677, 38; 647, 17; 682, 40; 162, 18). The number of angels is infinitely large, corresponding to the infinite fullness of the Godhead. Every angel has its own special nature and receives the totality of nature in a particular way. The closer an angel is to God, the higher its rank; each receives from God as much as it is capable of receiving (276, 31; 135, 25; 400, 21). The angel is a spotless mirror in which the divine light is reflected without clouding. Thus, the angel stands free and immaterial in the middle between God and matter. Being itself an image of God, the angel illuminates its entire being with the image of God (103, 24; 162, 2). The angels are nobler by nature than the soul; for they sprang first from the divine spirit and remain within it, while the soul must pour itself into the body (395, 12; 173, 19). Higher than all creatures, they have neither time nor change in their essence. They also perceive in a light that is beyond time.

### 10. The Angels.

The works they perform in God are timeless. But in their action upon finite things, they possess a shadow of temporality (162, 10; 133, 28).

Nevertheless, in another respect, the angel is not perfect, and the soul can rise higher than he. The highest angels themselves are only somewhat, and yet not entirely, similar to the soul in its highest power, the <term>little spark</term> <note>German: *Fünklein*. Eckhart’s famous term for the "spark of the soul" (scintilla animae), the innermost part of the human spirit that remains in direct contact with the Divine.</note>. This similarity consists in knowledge and love; but a goal is set for them beyond which they cannot go, whereas the soul can indeed penetrate further. If the soul reached the highest standpoint still possible here below, man, through his free capacity, could attain infinitely higher than the angels and all created rational beings (36, 5). The mode of knowledge of the angel, who sees everything under the form of eternity <note>original: "Form der Ewigkeit" (Latin: *sub specie aeternitatis*).</note>, is by no means the highest; for in this vision, the finite is still present as such (587, 35). The angels can therefore progress in knowledge and love, and they increase in these until the Last Judgment. The lowest among them is then almost as wise as the highest was when he was created. But what the angel possesses comes to him without effort; the soul, by contrast, attains it only through its labor. Therefore, the growth of the soul is something far more glorious than that of the angel, and one bit of knowledge gained by the soul is worth ten of the angel's (639, 12).

The highest angel is closest to the first <term>emanation</term> <note>The process of "flowing out" from the Godhead into created existence.</note> and possesses so much likeness to God and divine power that he preserves and cares for the entire world and the angels who are lesser than he. His activity occurs constantly in God as an essential being, not as an external deed; he remains in God and persists constantly within Him (321, 40). He acts as the highest creature with divine authority, just as the <term>Steward</term> <note>German: *Truchsess*. A high-ranking court official who administers a territory on behalf of a king.</note> governs the land by the king's authority (124, 20). Through him, all the activity of God passes into things. The angelic mover turns the heavens and thus becomes the impulse for all the activity of nature. From a single spark of the angel, everything on earth lives (212, 12; 257, 3). The angels dwell with us, serve us, and protect us. But their activity does not hinder their untroubled blessedness. For their activity and the will of God are one and the same. ### 11. The Human Being.

The angel is a specific kind of created being; the soul, by its very design, is an absolute totality. If one compares the angel with the soul in its empirical, everyday state, his purely spiritual essence stands far above it; but if one compares him with what the soul is capable of and destined for—what it inherently and inalienably is—the soul cannot be compared with the angel at all, but only with God Himself.

When God created all creatures, they were so lowly and so narrow that God could not move within them. Therefore, He made the soul so like Himself and so appropriate that He could communicate Himself to the soul (136, 34). He created it according to the highest perfection and infused all His clarity into it in its original purity (286, 13). God created nothing that was His equal except for the soul. Just as one cannot assign a form or shape to God, one cannot assign one to the soul; and just as God is immortal, He has also bestowed immortality upon the soul (394, 10). The soul is nobler, mightier, and greater than all creatures (395, 12). All creatures are the footprints of God <note>original: "Fussstapfen" (Latin: *vestigia*). This refers to the "traces" of the Creator found in the physical world, which are less direct than the "image" found in the soul.</note>; but the soul is by nature fashioned after God (11, 6). ### 11. The Human Being.

Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher whose *Summa Theologica* is cited here.</note> distinguishes between a representation of the Trinity by way of a trace <note>original: "repraesentatio trinitatis per modum vestigii"</note> and another by way of an image <note>original: "per modum imaginis"</note> (S. th. I, Qu. 45, Art. 7). God is in the soul with his nature, his essence, and his divinity, and yet he is not the soul (180, 39). Man, according to the highest part of his inner self, stands closer to God than to the creatures. By nature, he stands within the created order; through his reason, he is more like God than any other creature (351, 16). The soul is not created like other things in some arbitrary form, but in God; it is formed with God, and God's image is imprinted upon it (179, 25). Therefore, it is the noblest creature <note>In this context, "creature" refers to any "created thing," including humans and angels, rather than just animals.</note> that God has ever conceived. For God reached between the Godhead and the divine nature into his eternal essence and made the soul from nothing. And if one asks how great the soul is, one should know that its greatness cannot be filled by heaven and earth, but only by God himself, whom the heavens of all heavens cannot contain. Therefore, whoever wishes to measure the soul should take God as the standard; for the ground <note>German: *Grund*. A central term in German mysticism (the *Seelengrund*) referring to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where it meets God.</note> of God and the ground of the soul are one essence (413, 21; 467, 13). The soul is inexpressible and incomprehensible like God; what the soul is in its ground has never yet been known (89, 23; 236, 8; 305, 1). Nowhere is God so truly present as in the soul. In all creatures there is something of God, but in the soul, God is present in a divine manner; for it is his resting place (230, 36; 207, 3). Even in hell, this nobility of its nature remains with the soul eternally (11, 31). It is created between time and eternity, and it partakes in both (95, 24); it is a middle ground between creature and Godhead (395, 1). God is bound to no place; neither is the soul. God shapes all things according to the conceptual purpose <term>Zweckbegriff: the divine blueprint or teleological idea of a thing</term> he holds within himself; in the same way, the soul also acts. Of everything that can be said of God, the soul carries something similar within itself (386, 10). The image of the Trinity in the soul is primarily attached to the three highest powers: reason, will, and memory, which represent the three persons of the Godhead (318, 1). Memory resembles the Father, reason the Son, and the will the Holy Spirit. The highest form of the soul, however, the spark <note>German: *Funke*. Often called the "little spark of the soul" (*Seelenfünklein*) in mystical tradition, it represents the uncreated part of the human spirit.</note>, corresponds to the unmanifest Godhead, which is the soul's highest object.

## II. The Essence and Its Revelation.

God speaks his Word in all creatures; but no creature can perceive him, except for the rational creature (479, 19). Likeness to God is the prerequisite for the knowledge of God <note>original: *Gotteserkenntniss*</note>. Why does my mouth or my ear not recognize the heavens? Because they have no similarity to them. The eye, as Saint Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) was a highly influential Cistercian abbot and mystic whose writings often focused on the soul's intimate bond with God.</note> observes, is similar to the heavens: round, pure, and clear as they are, occupying the highest position on the body, and inaccessible to external influences. If God were foreign to the soul, he would not be accessible to it. Everything else I know, I know through images in a mediated way: God is known directly, and therefore God must be the "Thou" to my "I", and I must be the "Thou" to God's "I" (139, 10).

The soul shares the light of reason <note>original: *Vernunft*</note> with the angels (410, 35); only the angels and the human soul are created in God’s image and perceive him as rational beings (616, 39). The soul has a rational, knowing essence; therefore, where God is, there is the soul, and where the soul is, there is God (267, 11). In other words: as soon as God is, he beholds within himself the eternal image of the soul. God is pure self-consciousness: thus, he is the archetype <note>original: *Urbild*</note> of the soul. God is the form of the soul and the "soul of souls" (658, 21). Everything that is an object of the divine intellect is the soul. The idea of humanity stood eternally at the throne of God; this idea is the Son of God. The soul implicitly contains all creatures within itself; it is the necessary complement to God. God cannot understand himself without the soul (582, 30).

In its pure essence—free from time, space, and nature—the soul is as immutable as God (318, 30). It has no further difference from him other than that it is created and is not its own cause (581, 23). If the soul could entirely cast off its state of being "born" and "created," it would be exactly the same as the Son of God. Whatever the soul possesses, it holds as a fief <note>original: *Lehen*; a feudal term for land or rights held on condition of allegiance. Here, it signifies that the soul’s attributes are not its own property but are held as a gift from God.</note>; nothing belongs to it as its own, but everything is given to it (671, 35; 511, 29). What exists in God through his own essence does not exist in the soul through its own essence. What the soul is, it has from God, and it has flowed out from him in such a way that it did not remain within the [divine] essence, but received a foreign essence that took its origin from the divine essence. ### 11. The Human Being

...[heaven] and on earth and gives life to all things; rather, the soul bestows movement and life upon the body (394, 18). Everything the soul possesses is therefore grace; man is God by grace, just as God is God by nature (531, 36). But this does not satisfy the soul; it is its deepest resentment <note>original: *Ingrimm* — a term suggesting a fierce, inward fury or a state of being "at odds" with its limitations</note> that it is not entirely as God is by nature (542, 9).

The alien essence that the soul has taken on is clearly its finiteness in the form of individuality. Eckhart does not explain how the soul arrives at this form. The soul in itself is not an individual personality, but pure knowledge; rather, if one wishes to reach the true essence of the soul, individuality must be absolutely transcended <note>original: *aufzuheben* — a central term in German philosophy meaning both to cancel out and to lift up to a higher level</note>. Nor do we obtain certain information from Eckhart regarding the reason for the fragmentation of the inherently simple soul into a multiplicity of powers. It is the same difficulty that we encountered in the doctrine of the creation of creatures <note>original: *Creaturen* — referring to all created things as opposed to the uncreated Creator</note>. Only the striving is visible everywhere to let the concept of purpose serve as an explanation, and to explain the diversity of the soul and of souls from the destiny and task of the soul. If man could remain in unity, it is said, so that he practiced all the functions that all creatures have ever practiced, that would not be as good. For the highest power would draw the lower ones into itself, so that man could perform nothing but a divine work. But that cannot be, and therefore the highest power looks to God for its salvation and pours it further into the lower powers, so that they have knowledge of good and evil. That was the state of Adam before the Fall (496, 29). The splitting of the soul into powers and the origin of the individual personality, which after all depends on the lower powers (511, 23), is thus a component of the eternal world order and belongs to God’s original purposes. Even Adam before the Fall possessed this splitting of the soul into many powers. The infinite value of individuality—irreplaceable and incomparable—is explicitly asserted (519, 11; 260, 24).

The soul has an eternal pre-existence in God. In the groundless substance of the Godhead <note>original: *Gottheit* — often distinguished by Eckhart from "God" as the silent, inactive essence behind the Trinity</note>, human nature stood immutable and unveiled in a radiant light, to radiate for the delight of all creatures (591, 34). "I," says Eckhart, "stand in the ground of the eternal Godhead; there God performs all His works, even before He has gained personality <note>Eckhart distinguishes between the 'Godhead' (the absolute, undifferentiated essence) and 'God' as the Trinity of persons</note>, through me, and all that is understood is what I am. God has made all things through me, when I was in the groundless ground <note>original: *grundloser Grund* — often translated as the 'Abyss' or 'Unground,' referring to the bottomless nature of the divine essence</note> of God. I was there bare and free of all determination, uncreated" (581–583; 182). Everything that is in God, is God. Since my image has been eternally in God, as it still is and must always be, my soul has been eternally one with God and is God Himself, and thus I find myself standing in God in such a high manner that I have eternally been God in God (619, 13).

Thus the soul is identified with the Word <note>original: *Wort* — the eternal Logos or Son of God</note>, which was eternally with God; in the human being, all creatures <note>original: *Creaturen* — all created things</note> are created (589, 25). Between the Son of God and the soul there is no difference; the Son is the archetype <note>original: *Urbild* — the original pattern or primary image</note> of humanity (266, 4). When the Father gave birth to all creatures, He gave birth to me, and I flowed out with all creatures and yet remained immanent within the Father. Thus we are one single Son, whom the Father has eternally begotten (285, 14).

The individual human being is not the whole of humanity. If I now cast off what separates me from other people—all individual differences—and return to my pure essence, then what remains is the essence that has eternally stood in God as the counter-image of His essence, as His Son (157 ff.). Therefore, the soul is co-posited in the concept of God; and if this is extended to the individual personality, which in its essence coincides with that archetype, then God has His Godhead from me. I only understand myself in the highest sense when I understand myself no differently than that I am the essence from which God takes His essence or His own Godhead (588, 37).

And here Eckhart boldly draws the final, extreme consequence. Once the distinction between the soul in itself and the individual soul is lost from sight, and since God is soul-like by His nature, then the soul is God Himself, and I am the creator of all things. Indeed, the soul lies even beyond "God" in the simple Absolute, and she must rid herself of even "God" <note>Eckhart famously suggests that to find the 'Godhead,' one must leave behind the concept of a personal 'God'</note> if she is to reach her true form. Were I not, then God would also not be (283, 37). <note>This bold statement suggests that God and the soul are so interdependent that one cannot exist without the other in the "eternal now."</note>

The way **Eckhart** defines the relationship of the soul to God is entirely analogous to his teaching on the indwelling of God in creatures. His gaze remains focused one-sidedly on the simple essence within every appearance; finiteness and the individual form of existence <term>Daseinsform: the specific, limited way a thing exists in the physical world</term> are overlooked or described as mere nothingness. The attempt to bring the fact of finite personality into harmony with the doctrine of the absolute ground of the soul is not made; the harshness of his statements about the true essence of the soul—which cannot be intensified any further—stems simply from the fact that the rational personality as such is posited as a manifestation of the Absolute. Then, the finite personality, because it shares "personality" with the former, is confused with it without further ado.

If **Eckhart** thus strongly opposes an external, Judaizing <note>original: *judaisierenden* — In this 19th-century academic context, this term refers to a theological view that emphasizes a strict, legalistic distance between the Creator and the created, as opposed to the mystical union Eckhart favored.</note> conception of the relationship of the soul to God, a false consequence drawn from half-true premises has nevertheless led him to the outermost limits of the opposite error, where it threatens to dissolve into a wild, nonsensical fanaticism. Only the health of his moral feeling and the depth of his religiosity ensured that this remained merely a false philosophy, a theory presented with high enthusiasm. Indeed, **Eckhart’s** conception of the ethical shows the disturbing influences of this error on many points; but precisely in the decisive questions, he paused with noble discretion. It is precisely the unmistakable deep and genuine aspects of his teaching on the soul which have had the greatest lasting effect in **Eckhartian** ethics and have placed it so far above all the conceptions of his contemporaries.

## II. The Essence and its Revelation.

Natural science is far from **Eckhart’s** mind. He lacks almost everything required for a scientific understanding of nature. We may dismiss his individual remarks on natural things—mostly concerning the heavens and celestial bodies, which typically arose from the superstitions of his time—as worthless for characterizing the man and his teachings. Aside from angels and humans, no <term>creature: in this context, any created thing, whether a stone, plant, or animal</term> captured his interest, which was essentially religious. However, what we must add to the description of his doctrine of creatures is the conclusion of his theory of the absolute process: his doctrine of the return of all things into God.

1. The process of knowledge within God <note>Eckhart views God’s self-awareness as a dynamic internal movement that results in the creation of the world.</note> is the reason why God created an infinite abundance of things in which he beholds and reveals his own richness. These things, however—though it is not clear in what specific sense—did not remain within the essence of God, but instead took on a "foreign" essence. This state of "being outside of God" cannot persist. If every creature flowed out from God as its ultimate origin, then it must also return to God as its ultimate end, because nothing can sustain itself outside of him. All the activity of creatures, every event in the world of things, points toward this goal; this is the purposeful destiny that runs through every realm of existence.

God has done all things for his own sake; he is the cause of all things, and just as he acts according to the "likeness" of the first cause, so all creatures act according to that same likeness. This is the love they have for God (529, 17). God holds all things as if by a bridle, guiding them to act according to his likeness. Therefore, nature always strives toward the highest goal (94, 14). The Father speaks the Son eternally in eternity and, in him, pours out all creatures. To all of them, the call is issued to return once more into that from which they flowed. All their life and essence is nothing but a pressing and hurrying back to the one from whom they proceeded (93, 13). All creatures, in all their activities, want to reveal God as truly as they can; but they cannot fully reveal him. Just as my mouth proclaims and reveals God, so does a stone; and this revelation through action is clearer than that through words. Yet even the highest angels, with their activity striving upward toward God, do not reach the efficacy of God himself (92—93). All creatures bear within themselves the mark of divine nature,

All <term>creatures: in Eckhart’s thought, this refers to any created thing—animate or inanimate—rather than just animals</term> are with God, and the essence that they possess is given to them by God through his presence within them. The three Persons <note>The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the Christian Trinity.</note> have imprinted their own image upon all rational creatures. Therefore, everything is in motion, and the meaning of this movement is a continuous <term>ennoblement: the process of making something spiritually more refined or "noble"</term>. Nature makes no leaps; it always begins its work at the lowest level and strives upward toward the highest. Just as the colors of the rainbow transition imperceptibly into one another, so too in nature, effect follows effect without interruption (124, 3, 15). All things, even the lowest, strive out of <term>multiplicity: the state of being many or divided</term> toward unity (439, 20). To become like God is the common longing of every creature. This is why the heavens revolve; this is why humans and beasts feel desire. God is Love, and he is so worthy of love that everything capable of loving must love him, whether it is a joy or a burden to them (31, 6). # 12. The Return into God.

Everything that is active works for the sake of the ultimate goal, in order to find peace and rest at its destination (285, 36).

For this reason, there is a constant change of forms in nature. Wood burns to become fire, indeed, to become all things. The wheat grain decays to pass into new forms. The plant that my parents ate helped build my body (333, 31). This is the true significance of the human being in the order of all things: that they are the essential means for God's highest purposes. The soul is a tool <term>Rüstzeug: literally "equipment" or "armor," here used to mean an instrument or vessel</term> of God (402, 32; 526, 2). God cannot act without the soul, and the soul cannot act without God (529, 30). The love that God has for the soul has so overcome Him that He created all <term>creatures: all created things, both living and inanimate</term> so that He might reveal His glory to the soul through them (405, 39). If the soul could know God fully like the angels, it would never have come into the body. If it were able to know God without the world, the world would never have been created. Therefore, the world is created for the soul's sake, so that the eye of the soul may be practiced and strengthened to endure the divine light (170, 14). This is the striving of all things: to be transformed into human nature. The moral person should carry all things upward to God, back to their first origin. All creatures are made for the sake of the human being. This can be seen in all creatures, how one creature benefits another: the ox benefits from the grass, the fish from the water, the bird from the air, the beast from the forest. Thus all creatures benefit the moral person, and one creature after another is raised up to God by a moral person (459, 16). By its very design, the human being is the sum of all creatures. When one speaks of a human, one speaks of all creatures; all creatures are gathered within the human (273, 10). Every creature is a human being whom God must by nature love (587, 33), and this human being is God (522, 3) <note>original: "und dieser Mensch ist Gott." This refers to the mystical union where the human soul becomes one with the Divine.</note>. In human nature, all creatures change their name and are ennobled; in human nature, they lose their nature and return to their origin. And this happens even in a physical way. The food and drink that a person enjoys become flesh and blood within them. In this way, on the day of resurrection, all things will rise with the human body and become spiritual. In human nature, every creature attains eternity (390, 38).

### III. The Union of the Soul with God.

The explanation of the path by which the soul attains union with God is the primary task that **Eckhart** set for himself in his teaching and preaching. It is here that his opposition to the doctrine of the contemporary <note>The 13th and 14th-century Catholic Church</note> Church is mainly founded. Not external mediation <note>such as sacraments or the institutional hierarchy of the church</note>, but an essential unity with God is the goal he sets before all human endeavor as the highest—yet also as attainable and to be attained by everyone. All metaphysical and psychological doctrines serve this center of his circle of thought. His entire remaining theory initially holds only the value of an indispensable precondition; one must pursue all other matters simply to grasp this point clearly; one must teach about God and things so that the developmental process and the destiny of the soul may be understood correctly. However, this should not be understood as if the practical aim of edification and exhortation and the purely theoretical interest fell completely apart. On the contrary, the laborious and careful consideration of purely theoretical problems can only be understood as driven by a curiosity that finds satisfaction in knowledge itself. But this drive for knowledge and the practical aim of the theory do not contradict each other; for it is **Eckhart's** view that the soul can only reach its <term>salvation: Heil</term> through rational <term>knowledge: Erkenntniss</term> <note>Eckhart often identifies the "spark" of the soul with the intellect, suggesting that understanding is a divine act</note>, indeed, that pure knowledge is itself salvation.

The reunification of the soul with God, the absolute...

# 1. The Soul in its Empirical State.
11

**Being** <note>original: "Wesen" - often refers to the ultimate essence or divine reality</note>, as we have seen, is the final purpose of all that occurs. The soul holds this central position in the midst of the absolute process, being simultaneously the highest and most perfect revelation of God and the means by which all things are led back to God. The soul takes the entirety of all things into itself in order to carry them up into God; by means of the soul, Being returns to itself from its state of <term>externalization: Entäusserung</term> <note>A term describing how the divine essence "goes out" of itself to become the material world</note>. Thus, God's activity is, in the highest sense, an activity in and with the soul; that the soul should reunite with God and that all things return through it to their origin is the final purpose of all happening. How **Eckhart** conceives of this activity of God proceeding within the soul, we shall present in the following as his doctrine of **salvation**.

## 1. The Soul in its Empirical State.

We have seen in the preceding sections what exuberant glory **Eckhart** ascribes to the soul where it remains in its true essence, and how he places it in the immediate proximity of the **Godhead** itself. But the soul has not remained in this glory. As we find it in reality, it exists in the form of the finite personality, the sensory-spiritual individuality, bound to a body with its sensory organs and activities, fragmented into a multiplicity of powers and functions, through which the soul-unity—remaining imperishable in its deepest ground—only glimmers. And even if, as is at least left open by **Eckhart**, this entire finite form of the soul's existence is grounded in the essence of the absolute process as a necessary stage of the revelation of **Being** and as a point of transition for the realization of the absolute purpose, yet even that original glory of the soul, which it had still preserved in its connection with the body and in its relation to the infinite multiplicity of material things, has been completely disrupted by the effect of the <term>Fall: Sündenfall</term> <note>Referring to the biblical Fall of Man and the entrance of sin into the world</note>. **Eckhart** does not speculate about sin; he does not seek to explain or comprehend it; he accepts it as a fact. In his concepts of the great interconnections of the universe, he has no open place for sin. Thus, we have hitherto from

### III. The Union of the Soul with God.

...lose sight of, and only when we describe *Eckhart’s* relationship to church dogmas in detail will we be able to go into his statements about *sin* more closely. Here it is enough for us that *Eckhart* recognizes only a factual state of *sin*, which he does not attempt to explain further from its ultimate causes, but which for him becomes the starting point for describing a *re-formation* <note>original: "Rückbildung" — the process of stripping away worldly forms to return to the soul's original divine prototype</note> of the *soul* into *God* and to draw the path on which it is sanctified again. His doctrine of *salvation* needs *evil* as a starting point, and these are, in brief, his statements about it: *Man* as an *individual personality* was originally created pure and perfect and gifted with *freedom of the will*. There he turned his will toward himself instead of toward God, and instead of wishing to dissolve his individual existence through his will, he wanted to assert his *selfhood* <term>Selfhood: Eigenheit</term> <note>Eckhart uses this to describe the selfish attachment to one's own ego or "I" in opposition to God</note> against God. Through this, not only was human *nature* disrupted and corrupted, but *creatures* also became disobedient to man and at odds with one another; strife and *evil* entered the world. But even *sin* was not able to abolish or corrupt the *essence of the soul*. Just as it is only externally bound to the *body*, but essentially free from the *body* and the *senses*, so it is also only externally a *multiplicity* of *powers* and *activities*. If it reflects upon itself in a *pure image-free thinking* <note>original: "bilderfreies Denken" — a state of meditation or contemplation that does not rely on sensory images or concepts</note>, it finds itself again as what it originally is and must always remain: a simple, spiritual, supersensible being, free from space and time. Only in its earthly *finitude* is the *soul* subject to the consequences of the *Fall* and corrupted by the evil direction of the will turned toward *selfhood*. But the *core* of its essence has remained free from such *corruption*. The *nobility of divine nature* is inalienable to it, and it can return at any moment to what it ought to be, into this deepest *ground* <term>Ground: Grund</term> <note>A foundational term in German mysticism referring to the absolute, uncreated essence of the soul where it is identical with God</note> of its being, which is also the *ground of the divine being*. Toward this, an inextinguishable *longing* spurs it on. For the essence and life of all *creatures* depend on their seeking *God* and chasing after him; but above all, this is the case with the *soul*. Just like a person who hides themselves and reveals their hiding place by clearing their throat, so *God* has betrayed his presence through the *longing* for him in the *soul* (301, 3 ff.). For the *soul* is so impetuous that it finds rest nowhere but in its *origin* (101,

## 2. Human Freedom.

1. The task set before the soul—namely, to achieve full union with God—is fulfilled as the soul returns to its own true essence and casts aside everything that tends to obscure this true nature. The assumption is not that the soul is thoroughly corrupted; it is explicitly emphasized that one should not linger in lamentation over one's sin, nor ever imagine oneself to be far from God. Eckhart considers it the more appropriate exhortation to remind every Christian how near God and His grace are to them, and that they can reach God at any moment, as soon as they simply desire it. He explicitly rejects the misery of sin and the alienation from God it causes, as well as the fear of God, His justice, and the punishment for sin; or rather, he assigns them very little significance in the process of obtaining grace. 

Man should not fear God; at times, fear is even harmful. There is only one kind of "right fear," and that is when one fears losing God (287, 27). Man should in no way and never believe himself to be far from God, neither because of his sin, nor his weakness, nor any other thing. If your sin prevents you from believing yourself near to God, you should nevertheless believe that God is near to you. For great harm lies in man pushing God away into the distance. Whether man distances himself from God or approaches Him, God never distances Himself; He always remains nearby, and if He cannot remain within <note>i.e., inside the human heart or soul</note>, He still moves no further than just outside the door (561, 23). 

What separates man from God is only the external and non-essential; in his essence, he is already one with God. Even if this unity is to some extent latent—a mere possibility—in man's natural state, it can become the most energetic reality <note>Eckhart uses the distinction between "possibility" (potential) and "reality" (actualization)</note> in the next moment. It is not actually a matter of acquiring something positively new, but rather of removing an obstacle, a bond that holds us back...

2. How then do we shake off the obstacle and tear apart this bond? **Eckhart** directs us first to our free will and our thinking reason. Together, these are the seal of our <term>likeness to God</term> <note>German: "Gottähnlichkeit"; the concept that humans are created in the image and likeness of the Divine</note> and the original glory of our nature. To the mystic, for whom the close kinship of the soul with God is the highest of perspectives, no complete separation can be admitted even in the soul's natural state. In the <term>ground of the soul</term> <note>A central Eckhartian concept referring to the innermost essence of a person where they are one with God</note>, God is always present; the **spark** <note>original: "Fünklein"; Eckhart’s famous term for the eternal part of the soul that remains in contact with the Divine</note> is a permanent dwelling-place of God. The longing for God never vanishes from the soul, and even in all sensual desire, this striving upward toward God reveals itself. For we only desire what is good, or what appears to be good. Therefore, the will has the possibility to turn away from all finite and <term>creaturely</term> <note>Refers to things created by God, as opposed to the Creator Himself</note> things and to direct itself entirely toward God, the highest good. 

And in the same way, thought simply cannot stop striving beyond the sensible and the finite. Reason always possesses the capacity to overcome all boundaries of time and space in this direction toward the supersensible and the eternal—to cast away all thinking in images and parables, all specific ideas and forms, and only to come to a halt at the "Most Universal," the Absolute. The pure recognition of the Absolute, however, is already life in the Absolute; there, man has arrived at his true home, at his true essence, and is able to maintain himself within the pure essence through pure contemplation of that essence. **Eckhart's** teaching is intended essentially to be an inspiration toward this free willing, which no longer wills anything specific, and toward this pure thinking, which no longer thinks anything specific. He insists on this exclusively, as if everything else were already established by it. 

The abstraction of thought and the renunciation of the will regarding all finite things is itself already the essential cause of sanctification. In thinking, where one no longer embraces anything else, one has only the pure essence—that is, God Himself—left as the sole content; in the will, where one is free of every finite purpose, one desires only the absolute good itself. And thus one has received God as a life-giving power into one's own soul. Once all creaturely essence is cast off and everything finite is removed, then...

## 2. Human Freedom.

...we find ourselves again in our true essence, which is God. For God is himself the <term>Nothing of all determinacy</term> <note>In mystical theology, God is often described as "Nothing" (Nichts) not to mean he doesn't exist, but because He is beyond all "things," definitions, and limits</note>, which remains where all determinacy vanishes. Thus, the shell is burst; God is the light that rises within us. Where we ourselves no longer think and will, there God is the one willing and thinking within us; His reason takes the place of our reason, His will takes the place of our will, and His fullness takes root within us as soon as we have become completely empty through the expulsion of all <term>creatureliness</term> <note>German: "Creatürlichkeit"; the state of being a "creature" (a created thing) as opposed to the Creator</note>.

The pantheism which thinks of the Absolute as the one infinite substance and all phenomena as necessary effects of the absolute cause can admit no independent causality outside of the Absolute, and thus also no freedom of the human will. The pantheism of the Master <note>Referring to Meister Eckhart</note> is of a different kind. His Absolute is not strictly "personality" in the human sense, but it is Reason—the possibility of grasping itself through thought as a person, and thus the necessity of entering into the process of person-formation. What holds the world together is not blind causal necessity, but the highest rational purpose, which organizes itself into a system of purposes in a descending hierarchy. Within this system, man stands as the central bearer of this organism; he must therefore have the capacity for spontaneous action, and be able to freely set and realize his own purposes. Therefore, in *Eckhart*, we find a decisive doctrine of freedom, far removed from all determinism. Admittedly, one cannot claim that the great difficulties arising from this juxtaposition—on one hand, the single absolute Being in whose sphere of power everything falls, and on the other, the world of individuals endowed with freedom—have been fully resolved.

It was natural for the mystic to emphasize human freedom so emphatically. The more thoroughly man is brought into proximity with the divine essence, the more he must be free, just as God is free; the more decisively moral independence must be maintained as an inalienable disposition of human nature. For the mystic, the Absolute is therefore the ground of a world of finite personalities, upon whom it bestows the power to assert themselves as finite beings over against the Absolute, or to turn back toward their origin—thus either promoting or hindering God's purposes. God is then the over-

God foresees everything and has predetermined everything from eternity; nothing, not even evil, can happen against His will. Yet, the independence of human souls is by no means considered abolished by this; man does not simply dissolve into the infinite substance. Instead, he is like a <term>God in miniature</term> <note>A reference to the concept of the "microcosm," where the human being reflects the entire divine order on a smaller scale</note>, and his will possesses an inalienable freedom to decide for God or for his own <term>self-will</term> <note>German: "Eigenheit"; the tendency to focus on one's private, separate ego rather than on God</note>.

3. **Eckhart** adopts this position with absolute decisiveness. The fact that the soul stands higher than all other things rests upon its freedom; it recognizes that no one can conquer it, and even God Himself does not wish to conquer it by force (512, 3). The will—this upward-striving power—constantly reaches for the highest and most ideal: the truth in which God exists within Himself. This power is so free in its aspiration that it will suffer no compulsion (103, 1). The will is free and independent of everything material (130, 37). God has predestined us all for His eternal <term>bliss</term> <note>German: "Seligkeit"; a state of perfect happiness or salvation in the presence of God</note>; He has shown this to us by giving us our free will, so that we may do good and leave evil aside (453, 4). Naturally, the doctrine of a total corruption of the soul through sin cannot apply here, for that would render the soul incapable of any cooperation with the working of grace. According to **Eckhart**, nature is not inherently bad; reason is always directed toward the divine, and where it has been perverted or corrupted by evil habits, it is the task of education to guide and direct it from early youth (569, 10). And although one does not find in **Eckhart** expressions as strong as those in **Tauler** <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a German mystic and student of Eckhart</note>—who repeatedly and explicitly defends nature against the accusation that it is the seat of corruption, arguing rather that "good is natural to man, while sin is against nature," and "to err is not human, but devilish"—the foundation for these **Taulerian** statements is nevertheless to be sought in **Eckhart’s** teachings. If God destroyed nature, he teaches, then it would happen...

[It] springs from the heart of the Godhead <note>original: *Gottheit*. The earth cannot flee the heaven; whichever way it turns, the heaven retains its power over it and fertilizes it, whether the earth likes it or not. So God does to man. He who thinks to flee from Him, runs into His lap; for all corners are open to Him. Whether it pleases you or causes you pain, whether you sleep or wake: God does His part (287, 29). All the gifts that God has given us in heaven and on earth, He has given for the sake of only one gift; with all of them, He only wishes to prepare us for the gift that He Himself is. And all the works that God has performed in heaven and on earth, He performed to be able to work one work—namely, to make us blessed (569, 36).

If we are not ready, we spoil the gift and God within the gift. This is the reason why God cannot always give to us as we ask of Him. The fault lies not with Him; for He is a thousand times more eager to give than we are to receive. It is only we who do Him violence and injustice by hindering Him, through our lack of readiness, in the work that is necessary to Him by His nature (570, 22). God adorns Himself with all charm and woos the soul; He stakes His entire Godhead to please the soul. For there He will have no rival (148, 22; 323, 30). Be certain of this: God does not cease to give us everything; even if He had sworn an oath against it, He still could not refrain and would have to give to us. It is much more necessary for Him to give to us than for us to receive. And the greater the gift, the more gladly God gives it (149, 9, 19). God loved us when we did not exist and when we were His enemies. God is so in need of our friendship that He cannot wait until we ask Him: He goes out to meet us and begs us to be His friends (62, 7). God caresses us and begs us entreatingly; He cannot wait until the soul adorns itself and detaches itself from the creature <term>creature: original *Creatur*. In mystical theology, this refers to any "created thing"—the material world or worldly attachments—that is not God.</term>. It is a certain, primary, and fundamental truth that God is as driven to seek us as if His entire Godhead depended on it—as indeed it does. God can do as little without us as we can without Him; for even if it were the case that we could turn away from God, God could never turn away from us. Therefore, I will not ask God to give to me; I will also not praise Him for what He has given me; rather, I will ask Him to make me worthy to receive, and I will praise Him because it is His nature and His essence that He *must* give. To take that away from God would be to take away His very own essence and His very own life (60, 10). God loves the soul so powerfully that anyone who took away God's ability to love the soul would be taking His life and essence, and—if one were permitted to say so—would be killing God. For in the same love with which God loves the soul, the Holy Spirit springs forth, and this love *is* the Holy Spirit. If God loves the soul so powerfully, the soul must indeed be something great (141, 33). Earnest longing and self-denying humility work wonders. God is capable of all things: but He is not capable of refusing anything to the person who is humble and full of earnest longing. The <term>spark of the soul</term> <note>original: "Fünklein der Seele." A central concept in Meister Eckhart’s teaching, referring to the innermost part of the human spirit that remains eternally connected to the divine.</note> does not go out; the knowledge of God within it never vanishes so completely that a person could not rise up and turn toward God out of sin. For God’s purposes, everything that happens is a means. That humanity should be saved is the ultimate purpose of all God’s deeds. Therefore, God’s <term>counsel of grace</term> <note>original: "Gnadenrath." As diverse as the human temperament is, so diverse is the way to God; God draws one person to Himself through joy, another through pain and suffering. Often God exhorts us to do good through various hardships that He sends us; if we could understand them and conduct ourselves as we should, we could attain grace (367, 11). God gives to each person, at every moment, that which is best for them. To teach and warn us, He often takes from us both physical and spiritual goods. If one wants to cut a coat for someone, it must be made according to their measure; the one that fits one person does not fit another at all; one measures each person according to what suits them. So God gives to each the best, according to how much they can perceive and what furthers them most (575, 6; 576, 26). The Lord works partly by means of the creature, and partly without the help of the creature. Grace reaches the soul veiled in word and preaching; but it acts purely and irresistibly where the Holy Spirit, without any external mediation, speaks into the receptive heart, and the heart understands it and receives it willingly (200, 35).

Grace; but grace itself is entirely and thoroughly God's work in us. But freedom and grace are by no means in opposition to each other. This is precisely the certain sign of the light of grace in the soul: when a person, through their free will, turns away from transitory things and toward God, the highest good (385, 6).

*Eckhart* cannot speak of a <term>predestination</term> <note>original: "Prädestination." The theological doctrine that God has foreordained all things, especially the salvation of certain souls.</note> in so far as it is meant to impair human freedom. God gives His spirit to those whom He has eternally chosen (530, 4; 48, 38). Therefore, man must constantly watch and lift his reason toward the highest things and into the eternal rules that God has written from eternity concerning all those who should be saved or lost. Therefore we should pray every day that the eternal rules and laws be fulfilled in us (481, 27). But whether God has chosen someone or not should not cause a person any unrest; he should view all these things purely as a matter of God's honor, not his own welfare, and entrust them to the divine <term>omnipotence</term> <note>original: "Allgewalt." *Eckhart* nowhere addresses the peculiar difficulties of this doctrine; he knows only the element within it that inspires devotion. The point of view from which *Eckhart* considers the whole question of the relationship between freedom and grace is a purely speculative and ethical one. Thus, in this area, we receive from him only approximate answers that certainly characterize the direction of his thinking and the nature of his devotion, but which bypass the difficulties inherent in the matter. According to *Eckhart*, it is the innate drive, inseparable from its nature, that drives the soul forward until grace gains space within it. In this respect, everything depends on the will—whether it chooses to follow this drive or not. But how it happens that some have this will and others do not, *Eckhart* does not discuss; the freedom of the will is for him the ultimate ground of explanation. He contents himself with these propositions: Everyone can be saved as soon as they will it, and God can save no one without their will; but everything positive in the work of grace is God’s work; the will can only clear the obstacles out of the way.

## 4. Faith.

According to *Eckhart*, the actual seal of <term>God-likeness</term> <note>original: "Gottähnlichkeit." The concept that the human soul contains a spark or image of the divine.</note> in man is <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "Vernunft." In Eckhart's thought, reason is often the highest faculty of the soul, capable of perceiving God.</note>. To reason, therefore, is attached the entire movement in the soul which leads to the detachment of the free will from everything created and from sin, and finally to the full reunion of the soul with God. The expression **faith**, on the other hand, appears in the <term>doctrine of salvation</term> <note>original: "Heilslehre." Soteriology, or the study of how humanity is reconciled with God.</note> as *Eckhart* develops it only exceptionally, and it certainly has a much smaller significance here than in the doctrine of the Church of his time, and even more so than in the later Protestant Church.

The mystic insists on a full possession and knowledge of God; thus, in this sense, faith appears to him as a state of relative estrangement from God and, for that very reason, as a still imperfect standpoint that must be overcome. Faith presupposes instruction by men, a divine revelation carried out in specific historical facts, and further ecclesiastical tradition; but life in the truth, in the full knowledge of God, is an immediate reception from the Holy Spirit. There, all <term>metaphor</term> <note>original: "Gleichniss." This refers to indirect ways of speaking about God through images, parables, or analogies.</note> and thus all expression in words ceases in the immediate vision of truth. A revelation that happened to others in the past can only be a guide to experiencing the same or an even higher revelation in one’s own heart. Therefore, Eckhart calls, in inexhaustibly new variations, for one to advance beyond all specific, ecclesiastically fixed versions of doctrine, beyond Holy Scripture itself, and even beyond the human appearance of the Lord, in order to reach the pure contemplation of the Absolute. All of that, he says, is only an image, only a metaphor, a conceptual veiling of the truth. All metaphors, all specific doctrinal content must be cast aside; only in the darkness of the <term>wilderness of the Godhead</term> <note>original: "wüsten Gottheit." A famous Eckhartian term for the silent, undifferentiated essence of God that exists beyond the Trinity of persons.</note> does the soul find its rest. Admittedly, in this way, the content of religious knowledge remains without any positive definition, entirely empty; and the highest standpoint of religious contemplation, which Eckhart never tires of describing with enthusiastic speech, is the immersion of the spirit into <term>pure nothingness</term> <note>original: "reine Nichts." In mysticism, "nothingness" does not mean non-existence, but rather a reality so far beyond human categories that it cannot be called a "thing."</note>.

Eckhart recognizes three standpoints in the contemplation of God, among which that of faith is the lowest. Those who stand on the standpoint of faith know no more of God than they can grasp in rational concepts. The second standpoint is that of grace; but even this is still marked by the deficiency that God is not grasped here any more deeply than as He satisfies the soul’s longing, grants inner refreshment, devotion, bliss, and the like. Above both stands a third standpoint, that of perfection—the adequate seeing of God in divine light (245, 1). Similarly, a distinction is made between the children of the gods, the gods, and the fathers of the gods. The children of the gods are those who read or hear Holy Scripture, and understand it in their innermost being and in good works

Thus, the highest standpoint that the soul can and should occupy is not the standpoint of faith in this sense; and beyond the salvation mediated through faith in the teachings of the Church, *Eckhart* knows another and more perfect one. Faith still allows its object to remain outside; to it must be added inner bliss and, finally, immediate contemplation. But *Eckhart* does not wish to dispute the relative right of faith for those who are not able to penetrate further. He by no means intends to combat the Church, which demands faith. Those who are unable to follow the high flight of his speculations he refers to the simple faith in the triune God, although it is a duty to earnestly strive for understanding (174, 35). If you cannot comprehend the depths of the divine nature, then believe in *Christ* <note>original Latin: "Christum."</note>, follow his holy example, and let yourself be redeemed; for *active Christian faith* protects against damnation (498, 22). But faith also has its right in another sense. Faith is the preliminary stage of *knowledge* <term>Erkenntniss</term> <note>original: "Erkenntniss." This refers to a deep, experiential spiritual realization or "gnosis," rather than just intellectual facts.</note>. But if faith is merely a preliminary standpoint, then the soul must step further forward. Encompassing everything—the sensory with the external senses and the spiritual with the spiritual faculties—and stripping away everything else, only then does the human being become "all creature," and only then has the human being truly come to themselves and is ready to enter into God. That we do not find God is because we seek Him in parables <note>German: *Gleichnissen*; this can also mean "likenesses," "images," or "analogies." That the soul moves in representations and grasps its God in representations comes from the fact that it attends to too many things. Sinking into the Godhead, it loses all perception (513, 31). Even in special revelations from God, in visions and ecstasies, one should not seek the right knowledge; for they often deceive and, in any case, they shroud pure knowledge in sensory forms and representations, in sounds and images (559, 5. 240, 21). We should recognize and love the Eternal Word as it is distributed under the priest’s hands at the altar; we should recognize it as it flows to us through the preacher as through a channel; we should understand it in all the friends of our Lord who live within Him. But we should also understand it as it is spoken by the bare Godhead <note>German: *blosse Gottheit*. This refers to the divine essence stripped of all names, attributes, or distinctions of the Trinity.</note> directly into the bare soul, and how it cannot be captured in any words. There, the soul recognizes the Eternal Word better than all the teachers of the Church can express. What one can put into words is all too slight; the Eternal Word has instructed the soul in all of that in a single moment. 3. Thus, **Eckhart** rejects faith as a lower stage insofar as it signifies a submission of reason to the authority of a traditional doctrine; he demands an immediate communion of the soul with God and independence from every external testimony. Of course, faith then also signifies something higher to him: all transcendent knowledge, especially insofar as it simultaneously becomes a determining ground for the will. But the church's doctrine of <term>justification: *Rechtfertigung* — the theological process by which a person is made righteous or "right" in the eyes of God.</term> through faith is as foreign to him as the church's concept of faith itself. He skips too easily over purely external acceptance based on authority to the opposite extreme: the evaporation of all content of faith into an intuition whose object is without any positive definition. The middle ground between these extremes—the living, highly personal experience of a specific, factual content of revelation—remains untouched by him. It is a very similar relationship that causes the doctrine of justification to recede entirely in **Eckhart’s** work. In his thought, the entire doctrine of salvation takes a different turn from the very beginning than in the ecclesiastical doctrinal system. In the foreground of his view stands not sin, but finitude and <term>creatureliness: *Creatürlichkeit* — the state of being a created, limited being rather than the infinite Creator.</term> as the condition of human nature that must be overcome; the goal to be strived for is not merely peace with God, but full unity with the divine essence. He regards the natural state of man as a state of <term>estrangement from God: *Gottentfremdung*.</term>, of "being-outside-of-God"; it is not a feeling of God's wrath, but of "being-other" than God—a feeling of imperfection, not of depravity—that drives one beyond this state. <header>5. Justification.</header>

The mystic is not satisfied with the mere external forgiveness of sins, in which an essential transformation of the person would not simultaneously be established as a condition. Just as the concept of faith was distorted in the prevailing view of the Roman Church, so too was the concept of <term>justification: *Rechtfertigung* — the theological process by which a sinner is declared righteous before God.</term>. Eckhart stands in opposition to the mechanical flattening of these concepts. However, he skips all too quickly over every intermediate stage and describes a state in which every boundary between the Creator and the creature, the saint and the sinner, is blurred. This exuberance dominates the mystic's entire way of thinking in this area and hinders its fruitfulness for a truly religious need. This is the true seat of mystical <term>enthusiasm: *Schwärmerei* — a 19th-century term often used to describe religious fanaticism or excessive emotionalism.</term>, and indeed, no one has drawn the final consequences of this fundamental view as unabashedly and with such full awareness of their significance as Eckhart himself.

## 5. Justification.

In Eckhart’s work, the doctrine of the justification of the sinner before God is not linked to the concept of faith; he regards justification as the immediate consequence of right and perfect <term>penance: *Busse* — can mean both the act of penance and the internal state of repentance.</term>. The first thing that grace effects in us is that it moves our free will to turn away from sin and toward a sorrow over sin, which has led us so far away from God and from the eternal, immutable Good of the Godhead (218, 10). For the first step on the way to the kingdom of God is <term>conversion: *Bekehrung*.</term>. No one is good who has not changed their old ways (101, 30). In fact, we have two things to cast off: not only that which we do not have by nature—sins and faults—but also that which we *do* have by nature, our <term>selfness: *Eigenheit* — the quality of being attached to one's own ego or private will.</term> (155, 18). At the beginning of conversion, fear permeates the soul because of sin; only afterward does love drive out fear (245, 29). As long as you have sorrow in your heart, even if it be for the sake of sin, you are, so to speak, in labor; you are still in the process of giving birth. Once the birth is complete, all pain ceases and perfect joy enters (41, 18). This pain is penance. It is a gift of grace when penance manifests itself in painful tears, first out of—

Penance that remains without tears is imperfect and the sign of a hard heart (362, 28). Penance should be so powerful within us that we would rather suffer a thousand deaths than commit even a minor sin. He who says he has true penance and yet persists in sin speaks untruthfully and increases his sin (453, 8). An unexpiated sin, even in an otherwise most holy life, causes a person to be eternally lost. No prayer of the saints could help the person; indeed, even if Christ Himself fell at His Father's feet with Mary His mother, the soul could never be helped <note>original: "nimmer Rath werden" — literally "never be advised," meaning no remedy or salvation could be found for the soul in that state.</note>. But whoever has committed a thousand mortal sins and recognized them, casting them off in true penance and serious <term>amendment of the will: *Willensbesserung* — a conscious turning of the inner intention toward the good</term>, would be blessed with the blessed (454, 5).

True penance alone enables us to truly receive God within us. Through it, we recognize every sin and achieve a state where God finds a <term>reflection: *Widerschein* — an echoing image or radiance</term> in us of all that we seek in Him (659, 27). However, there are two kinds of penance; one is temporal or sensory, the other divine and supernatural. Temporal penance sinks ever deeper into pain; it leads the person to despair and makes no progress, and thus it remains fruitless. Divine penance is quite different. As soon as a person feels displeasure at their sin, they rise to God and begin diligently turning away from all sins through an unchangeable <term>resolve of the will: *Willensentschluss*</term>. There, they grasp a firm trust in God and gain great security; from this comes a spiritual joy that lifts the soul above all pain and misery and fastens it in God (558, 3). 

The fruit of true penance is the forgiveness of sins. All sins for which one has felt true penance, God has forgotten, and we should no longer think of them (451, 11). The more seriously one regards the sins, the more quickly God is ready to forgive them. For everyone is most eager to remove what is most repugnant to them. Therefore, the more numerous and greater the sins are, the more gladly and quickly God forgives them (558, 18). Of course, Eckhart does not say that God forgives sin out of regard for Christ’s merit; rather, He forgives it because of the person's inner state; even less does he find the reason in what the person does, but rather <note>The sentence ends abruptly here, continuing onto the next page.</note>

With this, the will also attains the *unlimited* capacity so that everything becomes possible for it, and it can manifest what has been received in a holy life (242, 26. 37, 15. 667, 34).

For union with God, likeness to God is required; therefore, everything must be cast off that is not God in us, and this happens in <term>detachment: *Abgeschiedenheit* — a central concept in Eckhart's thought, referring to a state where the soul is "cut off" from worldly distractions to be open only to God</term>.

God loves nothing but Himself or His likeness in all things. He has never descended and never descends into a foreign will, but only into His own will. Therefore, man must first gather himself inwardly and enter into the deepest <term>ground of his own soul: *Seelengrund* — the spark or essence of the soul where Eckhart believed the divine and human meet</term>, in order to drive out everything ungodly. The soul has divided and scattered itself in external things through its powers, each of which exercises its own peculiar function; thereby it has become all the weaker in its inner activity, for every divided power is imperfect. Therefore, if it wishes to act powerfully within, it must call all its powers home again and gather them from their dispersion in things for inner activity, in order to recognize the single, infinite, uncreated, eternal truth.

Reason and memory must be taken back into the ground of the soul, and abandoning all other functions, we must arrive at a <term>unknowing: *Nichtwissen*</term> of all finite things. For perceiving and knowing <note>referring to sensory perception and intellectual categorization</note> scatters and disturbs. What is familiar and intimate to you is in truth your enemy. This unknowing, however, is not to be understood as ignorance, but as a potentized knowledge, an unknowing that has passed through knowledge—a supernatural knowledge (13—15).

The soul, which is unified in itself but divided into a multiplicity of powers through its connection with the body, is purified as it gathers together what is scattered and externalized. It has a power to summarize everything introduced into it by the senses into one, and in practical conduct to climb up to a simple, self-collected life. If it is to know God, it must have no fellowship with "nothingness" (222, 29). <note>Eckhart frequently argued that compared to the absolute existence of God, created things are essentially "nothing."</note> Creatures are something that separates us from God. To a sick person, food and wine do not taste good, not because the food fails to touch the tongue directly, but because it touches the "coating" with which the illness has covered the tongue. As long as that separating layer is not removed, God cannot please us as He is in Himself. As long as we do not leave the creatures, receiving pleasure and pain through them, we remain far from God (298, 16). All creatures carry something bitter within them. No matter how charmingly God has equipped them, He has nonetheless coupled them with pain and suffering. For every creature is denied this: that any single one could possess everything that could fully satisfy a human heart. If I had everything I could desire, but my finger hurt, I would have no full happiness. Bread is very pleasant to a person when they are hungry; but if they are thirsty, it would be as worthless to them as a stone. Clothes are welcome when one is freezing; but if one is too hot, they provide no joy. So it is with all creatures;

None is so pleasant that it would not become loathsome through long observation. The soul can find no satisfaction in creatures, which are finite, material, and transitory (300, 11. 374—375. 406, 1, 13). Light and darkness cannot exist together, nor God and creature. If God is to enter into you, the creature must necessarily go out of you (12, 8). Where the creature ends, only there does God begin. Now God desires nothing more from you than that you go out of yourself, as you are encumbered with the created, and let God be God in you. The slightest image of a creature that clings within you is as large as God; for it deprives you of a whole God. As soon as this image enters, God must withdraw with all His divinity. But as soon as this image goes out, God goes in (66, 26). Whoever leaves things insofar as they are a null, accidental being, acquires them insofar as they are a pure essence and eternal (67, 33). Whoever has left all things in their lowest form and where they are mortal, receives them back in God, where they are truth (233, 8). To be empty of all creatures means to be full of God, and to be full of all creatures means to be empty of God (487, 10). It is like an exchange in which the goods correspond exactly to the price paid: as much as you rid yourself of all things, just so much, no less and no more, does God enter into you with all His being (546, 14). Whoever wants to receive all things must first give all things away (574, 36).

3. A good person should stand thus: my work is not my work and my life is not my life. A distinction must be made between humanity and the human individual. God did not take on the nature of a specific individual human, but humanity—He assumed the general human nature. <note>This refers to the doctrine of the Incarnation, arguing that Christ's divinity united with the universal essence of being human rather than just one person's biography.</note> Humanity in the highest sense is equal to the angels and related to the Godhead. Therefore, I should cast off the individual and grasp myself as humanity.
