### III. The Union of the Soul with God.

<term>The detached person: *Abgeschiedene* — in the tradition of Meister Eckhart, someone who has spiritually withdrawn from worldly desires and self-centeredness</term> clings least of all with their will to themselves. All love in this world is built upon self-love; if you had abandoned this, you would have abandoned the whole world (204, 38). The detached person desires nothing more for themselves; indeed, they no longer desire anything individual or specific at all; their will has become entirely one with the will of God; they have ceased to will altogether. This is God's purpose in all things: that we surrender the will. Nothing brings a person into their true <term>disposition: *Beschaffenheit* — the fundamental state or quality of one's soul</term> more than the surrender of the will. That alone would be a perfect and true will: that one has stepped entirely into God's will and is without a will of one's own (555). God has never shared Himself, and never shares Himself, with a foreign will. He shares Himself only with His own will. Wherever He finds that, He gives Himself into it and pours Himself into it with all that He is (570, 30).

The person who stands thus in the will of God wants nothing other than what God and God’s will is. Were they sick, they would not want to be healthy. All pain is a joy to them, and all multiplicity is something unmixed and simple, provided they truly stand in the will of God. Indeed, even if the pain of hell were attached to it, it would be joy and bliss to them. Such a person is free of themselves and has gone out from themselves; they are dead to themselves and to all <term>created things: *Creaturen* — in medieval theology, anything that is not God</term>, and they regard themselves as little as someone else a thousand miles away (311, 39). Detachment is therefore a state of perfect *passivity*. God seeks <term>rest: *Ruhe* — a profound, divine stillness that is the very nature of God</term> in all things, for the divine nature is rest. In all created things, nothing is as similar to God as rest; the soul can offer nothing dearer to God than rest. God requires nothing more than that one gives Him a quiet heart (152 ff.). 

Everything in the soul should be silent, and the soul itself should be silent, otherwise God cannot speak within it (15). The detached person receives neither sorrow nor pleasure from created things; the multitude of earthly impulses and worries has been brought to silence. The soul has become immovable. True detachment is nothing other than the spirit standing as immovable against all external fates—love and suffering, honor, shame, and blasphemy—as a strong rock stands firm against a gentle breath of wind. This immovable detachment brings a person into the greatest likeness to God; for that God is God, He owes to His immovable detach-

Thus the soul has made itself capable of receiving God. If the heart is to be prepared to the highest degree, it must stand upon pure nothingness; for therein lies the greatest *receptivity*. If I wish to write upon a white tablet, nothing written upon it—no matter how glorious—could be there without hindering me in my writing; if I wish to write well, I must erase everything on the tablet, and it never serves me so well for writing as when it is completely empty. Likewise, the human heart must be empty if God is to write within it (490, 13). That darkness and that "unknowing" of the detached person is actually an unlimited capacity to receive—a capacity that lacks no kind of being <note>In this mystical context, "being" refers to the specific, limited existence of objects in the world.</note> and in which you are to be perfected (26, 5). Everything that is to receive and be receptive must be naked and bare. He who is "poor in spirit" is therefore receptive to all that is spiritual and to all spirit. To be naked and bare, to have nothing, and to be empty transforms the course of nature; emptiness makes water climb uphill; a cup that was empty of everything, even air—without a doubt it would forget its nature, and emptiness would carry it upward toward heaven. Thus, being *poor and empty of all created things* carries the soul upward to God, into God; and just as emptiness does, so too do likeness and the fire of desire (429 ff.). In detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit: the central Eckhartian concept of "releasement" or "cutting away" from the world to be alone with God</term>, nothing can dwell except God, who is absolutely simple and immaterial; therefore, it is receptive to nothing but God (484, 29). God’s natural, proper dwelling place is unity and purity; and these are provided in detachment. Therefore, through detachment, I compel God to enter into me, and God must necessarily give Himself to a detached heart (484, 15). God desires so greatly that you leave yourself behind in your creaturely nature, as if all His own bliss depended upon it. Ah, dear person, what harm does it do you to allow God to be God in you? (66, 36).

## 7. The Birth of God in the Soul.

In *detachment*, the soul sheds everything that is not God; what then remains—its own true essence—is God himself, conceived as the most universal and abstract reality, as Being = Nothing. <note>In mystical theology, "Nothing" does not mean non-existence, but rather a "No-thingness" that is so beyond human categories it cannot be defined as a specific thing.</note> This *self-annihilation* is the condition for the highest *operation of grace* by God. God is then in the soul as he is in himself, and God performs his eternal work in the soul just as he performs it timelessly and beyond time within himself. This work of God is the *begetting of his Son*. Thus, the Son is born in the soul, and the soul itself becomes the *Son of God*. The *birth of the Son in the human soul* is *Eckhart's* positive expression for the *operation of grace*, the condition of which is provided in *detachment*.

The expression was not newly coined by *Eckhart*; it has been found since the earliest days of the Church as a designation for the *entry of God into man and of man into God*. The distant inspiration for this is provided by the biblical concept of *rebirth*. <note>Referencing John 3:3, "Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God."</note> But only with *Eckhart* does the concept of the *birth of God in the soul* become the *centerpiece of the entire doctrine of salvation*. For *Eckhart*, the *forgiveness of sins* is only a preliminary stage of the *state of grace*; he demands something higher. Between the person justified by God and God himself, not even a shadow of a separation may remain. Therefore, everything that separates must be done away with in *detachment*. *Eckhart* takes this requirement in the very strictest sense; he outdoes himself in ecstatic descriptions of the state of *detachment*. In the person who has satisfied these demands, the same process must now repeat itself which has taken place in God from all eternity. This is conceived as an *act of God upon man*, which He can perform once man has made himself capable of it—yet, for that very reason, it is also an *act of man*. In truth, the *birth of the Son in the soul* is merely another expression for that which is already established in *detachment*. For if man is emptied of all other content, only his eternal essence remains as the *Son* whom the *Father* has begotten from eternity. *Detachment* creates, so to speak, the empty space which God then fills through the *birth of his Son*. The thought is that after

Eckhart elevates this "birth" above simple forgiveness of sins, viewing it as the ultimate goal of the Christian life.</summary>

1. The birth of the Son in the human soul—this actual and highest form in which God reveals himself to every individual soul—is thought of as being entirely identical with the eternal, immanent process of the begetting of the Son within the Godhead. And just as with the eternal begetting of the Son, the expression of the "speaking of the Word" is used here in exactly the same sense (77, 9). — God does nothing but beget his Son; in this work he consumes all his power (254, 19). And as it is said of God, so it is said in turn of the soul, that it begets the Son (256, 3). For this purpose God created the soul: that his only-begotten Son be born in it (401, 5); toward this he hunts and drives, as if all his Divinity depended upon it (190, 10). Why is all Scripture written, and why did God create the nature of the angels and the whole world? For this reason alone: that God might be born in the soul (104, 30). The Father has all his joy and delight in this work of the birth of his Son; this birth prepares such great pleasure for him that he spends his entire power and all his nature upon it (166, 29. 185, 38). The Father loves nothing but his Son and everything he finds in the Son; only because each of us can become this Son has he loved us from all eternity (159, 30). No creature <note>original: *Creatur*; in mystical thought, this refers to any finite, created being as opposed to the infinite Creator</note> is capable of this work except the soul alone. All perfection, light, grace, and blessedness <term>Seligkeit: the state of perfect happiness or spiritual joy in God</term> must necessarily come into the soul with this birth, and in no other way. In it you find all good; neglecting it, you neglect all good. Everything else passes away; this alone makes you essential <note>original: *wesenhaft*; meaning to possess true being or substance rather than being a mere fleeting shadow</note> (10 ff.). — As a result of this birth, man becomes the Son of God himself. You are born there as the child of the heavenly Father, and he gives you all the authority of his Son (9, 39). God’s Son is the soul’s Son, and in this, God and the soul have one and the same Son, namely God (401, 15). Between the only-begotten Son and the soul, there is no difference (266, 5). Each of us shares in this destiny in the same way. From eternity I have been the Son of God according to my destiny; however, I was not yet so in reality. Out of this simplicity he has begotten me from eternity as his only-begotten Son into the same form of his eternal Fatherhood, so that I may be a father and beget him from whom I am begotten. The soul is like the echo, which lets the received call of a voice resound back in the same way. God begets his only-begotten Son into the highest part of the soul, and as he begets his Son in me, I beget him again back into the Father (286, 21). In the Word, which the Father must speak by virtue of his nature, he speaks my spirit and yours and the spirit of every human being in equality with that Word. In this speaking, you and I are one Son out of God's nature, just like that Word. For the Father knows nothing but this Word; in it, he knows himself and the whole divine nature and all things, and what he knows therein, that is equal to the Word, and it is by nature and in truth that very same Word. 2. Eckhart now also gives more detailed descriptions of how one is to conceive of this birth. It is described as the highest ecstasy <term>Verzückung</term>, as Saint Paul experienced it himself and as it was granted to the disciples on the feast of Pentecost (652, 26). It happens beyond time and space in eternity (101, 19), not perhaps in a specific moment—this year, this month, or this day—but at all times; that is, beyond time in the vastness where there is no "here" or "now," neither nature nor thought (110, 28). It therefore presupposes a soul that has raised itself above time and stands in an eternally present "Now" (105, 10. 266, 32). The birth takes place in the innermost essence of the soul, in the little spark of reason <term>Fünklein der Vernunft; Eckhart's famous term for the uncreated part of the human mind that can unite with God</term> (110, 26). The body, too, is in a quiet stillness so that no limb moves; for the eternal Word is born simultaneously in the spirit and in the body. ### 8. Sanctification.

The birth of God in the soul, the highest effect of grace <term>Gnadenwirkung; the internal influence of divine favor upon a person</term>, occurs in the beyond, the supra-temporal; but while it is itself presented as a passing moment, its effects extend not only to the supra-temporal essence of the soul but also to its temporal form of appearance. All the powers of the soul and the body itself participate in these effects; they manifest themselves in the entire earthly life and action of the human being. Through that birth, the human being is fundamentally changed; this at least it has in common with rebirth in its biblical sense. It is the conclusion of that movement which began with conversion, penance, and the forgiveness of sins acquired through these, and which has led in detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit; the state of being free from worldly attachments to make room for God</term> to receptivity for the entire fullness of the divine communication of grace. This complete change of the inner essence must all the more give the impetus for a completely changed form of action, as the supra-temporal <note>that which exists outside of or above time</note> and the temporal essence of the personality by no means fall apart; instead, the former is thought of as working through and determining the latter. The infinite capacity of the will gained through justification <term>Rechtfertigung; the process by which a person is made or declared righteous in the eyes of God</term>—which in detachment first proved itself in a negative sense as the capacity to purify oneself from everything non-divine—thus attains its positive content in sanctification <term>Heiligung; the process of becoming holy through God's grace</term> as the capacity to fill oneself with everything divine. Only here, as a result of that rebirth, is the will enabled to merge completely into God's will. We will have to consider the manifestation of the sanctified will in more detail in a special main section presenting the Master's <note>referring to Meister Eckhart</note> ethics...

Sanctification begins only with the completed rebirth. Far from being able to fold our hands in our laps after attaining grace, it is rather only then that the right activity, well-pleasing to God, begins (121, 9). Only after the disciples had received the Holy Spirit did they then begin to act virtuously. When the saints become saints, only then do they begin to act virtuously and then they gather the treasure of eternal glory. What they did before serves only to make satisfaction for their sins and to divert punishment from themselves. Therefore, there can be no question of being allowed to quietistically <note>Quietism refers to a form of religious mysticism that emphasizes a state of passive, devotional contemplation, which Eckhart here argues against in favor of active virtue.</note> rid oneself of all activity in the state of grace (53, 23). Rather, if we have become God's son through this birth, then all our life also becomes divine, and the divine principle implanted in us works itself out in works of love and justice. A remnant of imperfection, of course, remains even after that birth in those who have received grace, because the infinite fullness is not able to enter entirely into the finite personality. Even St. Paul after the time when he was enraptured <note>referring to the Apostle Paul's vision of being caught up to the "third heaven" in 2 Corinthians 12</note> and St. Peter after the day of Pentecost were not free from minor faults (645, 25. 653, 2). But this imperfection is there only like a chance occurrence, an accident <term>Accidenz; in philosophical terms, a non-essential property that can change without changing the core nature of a person</term>, while holiness is the essence <term>Wesen; the true, unchanging inner nature of a being</term>. He to whom the eternal light has been granted in the birth can no longer fall. Free will, to be sure, remains. The rapture happens neither in such a way that the free will is touched by it, nor in such a way that it would not be touched by it; in a sense, it happens in a higher sphere that lies beyond the free will. Only indirectly and only in a certain way is it suspended through rebirth; for whoever has beheld God in that height of grace can no longer fall. It would be mortal sin and heresy to believe the opposite. Just as little as the heavenly Father can leave his Son, so little can he leave the soul in which he begets his Son (652, 11). The human being in this state can never and in no way be separated from God, and never fall into a mortal sin nor willfully commit even a lesser sin (10, 14).

...leaves behind some imperfection in the powers of the soul, and the task of infinite perfection remains even after it. This birth is itself a super-temporal moment <note>A moment existing outside of ordinary time.</note>, which appears to us like a sudden and momentary lifting of the soul into the realm of the timeless and divine; however, the effects on finite life itself emerge only gradually. In their earthly appearance, the human being—in whom the image of God has been restored in principle—is still afflicted with a remnant of finiteness. But that which is given immediately with the birth, and which therefore (like the birth itself) actually takes place in the realm beyond time within the person in whom God gives birth to His Son—that is the union with God.

If one does not wish to thoroughly misunderstand *Eckhart*, if one does not wish to find simply blasphemy and fanatical exaggeration in his strange, even unheard-of sounding statements about this union, then one must keep in mind that according to *Eckhart*, man already participates in the absolute essence in the deepest <term>ground of the soul<note>original: "Seelengrund" — the innermost core of a person where Eckhart believed the soul and God are one.</note></term> during earthly life. Alongside this, however, all the diversity of finite activities of the <term>soul’s powers<note>original: "Seelenkräfte" — the mental and spiritual faculties such as will, memory, and intellect.</note></term> can quite well exist without the human being being transformed into the Godhead "hide and hair" <note>An idiom meaning "entirely" or "completely." Eckhart is arguing that while the soul's core is unified with God, the person's human personality and physical nature remain.</note>. Thus, the union with God is initially nothing that manifests itself in outer appearance; it is only a complete sinking of the soul's ground into the absolute ground—a state felt in temporal life, but actually occurring beyond it, in which the bodily-spiritual form of the human being does not directly participate. In this union, man himself has become the Absolute, but only as he has actually been from eternity; only the obstacles and bonds have been removed which prevented him from truly taking possession of his true and original dignity. But even alongside that union, the entirety of finitude continues to exist in man; initially, one does not disturb the other. This is the highest expression for the concept of the <term>state of grace<note>original: "Gnadenstand" — a theological term for the condition of being in harmony with God's will and receiving divine help.</note></term>; but it always refers primarily to the <term>spark of the soul<note>original: "Fünklein" — the "little spark," Eckhart's famous term for the uncreated part of the human spirit that remains eternally in contact with the Divine.</note></term>; it is this alone of which that perfect unity with God is predicated, and the strangeness lies perhaps more in the expression than in the thought. Yet Eckhart knows very well that here on earth, imperfection is and remains our lot. He describes an ideal for which we must strive; he portrays it as completed and immerses himself so deeply in this depiction that it appears to him as something real and present. But fundamentally, he remains very well aware that the permeation of the entire human being by the divine life always remains merely a task in this temporal existence, and that fulfillment is reserved only for the afterlife. One must not view this as a contradiction in the Master's teaching; they are only two different ways of expressing the same thought. When Eckhart explains the essence of <term>sanctification<note>The process of being made holy or being purified from sin.</note></term>, the experience of inextinguishable human imperfection predominates; when Eckhart speaks of the <term>working of God's grace<note>original: "Gnadenwirkung"</note></term>, his fundamental view of the ideal possibility of a perfect union with God predominates.

Eckhart cannot bear to stop at the intermediate stages; he presses forward relentlessly toward the final goal, and the highest ideal alone satisfies his insatiable longing. He wants to inflame every Christian with the same desire; hence the exuberance of his expression. To him, no <term>justification<note>In a theological sense, the act of being made right in the eyes of God.</note></term> is enough in which I would be accepted into grace through someone else’s merit, no grace in which God still stood before me as "Another," no likeness in which a remnant of inequality still remained. Precisely in contrast to the external settlement with God through the church’s means of grace—as the <term>Roman Church<note>The Catholic Church and its sacramental system.</note></term> alone knows them—his mode of expression takes on this cutting sharpness, and his thought assumes this visionary excess. This is his most urgent admonition everywhere: that one should not underestimate oneself and one's own worth. The highest is attainable; it is unworthy to be content with the lower. Or who, in earthly matters, would be satisfied with a few miserable pennies when an immeasurable treasure was due to them by right? (230, 39)! This, above all, he feels called to shout to his contemporaries: why do you need the priest? Why are you satisfied with an external justification? Why do you walk along comfortably and cheerfully in everyday busyness, or make for yourselves self-invented rules about completely indifferent things, and torment yourselves with inventively devised agonies? ...in the former, man [sinks] into the sea of things from which he is not essentially distinct; in the latter, a crudely materialistic way of thinking seems to push itself forward, which especially allows the moral dangers of the doctrine to emerge most strongly. Eckhart was the first to allow the doctrine of the **substantial union** of man with God to emerge within the grand context of a <term>speculation<note>In this context, "speculation" refers to deep philosophical or theological contemplation aimed at understanding the nature of the divine.</note></term> that overcomes all opposites as the ultimate result. Here, for the first time—without impairing the moral content <margin>•</margin> of the doctrine—it proved to be the necessary consequence of a coherent whole of religious and speculative thoughts. We certainly do not intend to deny the gaps and shortcomings of these thoughts, as they are found in all human intellectual life. In this point, Eckhart’s spiritual originality reaches its peak. Here the secret of his personality is revealed, and this is the crucial point that conditioned the entire structure of the Master’s world of thought, all his borrowings from existing systems of doctrine, the modifications he made to them, and all his own further developments. —

1. The Church’s doctrine of salvation stops at the concept of **grace**; for Eckhart’s understanding of the relationship between the soul and God, grace is no longer the appropriate expression. Grace is still something <term>created<note>original: "Creatürliches" — In medieval theology, a "creature" is anything that is not God. By calling grace "created," Eckhart suggests it is a tool or a bridge, but not the final destination.</note></term>, a relationship of God to that which is not He himself, an "affection" of God, but not God Himself. Grace presupposes that the person to whom it happens is still outside of God, still stands beneath God. We must move beyond that (306). The grace with which God works in the soul and draws it into God is a created thing; in leading the soul to its destiny, grace stands higher than the soul; but in regard to what the soul is capable of, the soul stands above grace (529, 37). In grace, one sees God, but from afar. As long as grace as grace is within us, we cannot see God. The soul still stands low as long as it remains at the standpoint of grace. Therefore, it should ascend within grace until it is perfected and goes beyond grace; there it recognizes God (139—140). The light of grace shines for man on the path to his salvation; but there is a higher light into which man should raise himself (460, 22). The soul is to become God beyond grace; it should come to a height—

...is, I have it from no one. But if I receive it from another, it is not mine; it belongs to the one from whom I received it (209, 26). Love can never exist on a footing of equality between a lord and a servant; they remain eternally distant and unequal (266, 5). Therefore, we should strive so that we do not need to beg God for His grace and divine goodness; rather, we should strive to take it for ourselves without even asking Him for it (614, 35).

The soul only achieves this perfect freedom in union with God. The prerequisite for this union, however, is that God begets His Son within the soul. Then, God does not only beget me as His Son; He begets me as Himself, and Himself as me, and me as His being and His nature (205, 9). Whoever is God’s Son is one with God, just as the Son is one with the Father in essence and nature. You do not hold this from God as a <term>fief<note>A "fief" (German: *Lehen*) refers to land or rights held from a superior lord in exchange for service. Eckhart is arguing that our divinity is an essential possession, not a conditional grant from a superior.</note></term>, for God is your own (158, 28). Therefore, unity with God consists in God being born in the human person at all times—that is, God’s image constantly reveals itself within them (198, 12). In this birth, I am one with God; there He cannot exclude me, and there the Holy Spirit receives his essence, his work, and his becoming from me as much as from God (55, 24). Now, if <term>detachment<note>The German *Abgeschiedenheit* is a central term for Eckhart, meaning a state of being "cut off" or "set apart" from worldly desires and self-will, creating a void that God can fill.</note></term> is perfect and the entire finite individuality has been surrendered, then God enters into the person—not partially, but in His full abundance. The human person in their individual existence has ceased to be; they have become "all in all." When all imperfection, finitude, and everything negative is driven out, and with it all distinction, we become like God; we become all in all, just as God is all in all (41, 12). Where I possess Christ's life more than my own life, there I possess Christ more than myself; there, I am more truly called "Christ" than I am called John or Jacob or Ulrich. And just as this occurs beyond time, I am transformed into God (592, 11). When I have so passed away into the absolute Being that I no longer perceive anything in myself or in all things but that Being, then my soul has lost its name. What remains is the pure Being that has eternally begotten the Son in the Father; thus, I am born as a new person in that Being and perform all my works beyond nature, in a divine nature. Thus, I become one body with Christ...

### 9. Union with God.

...and one spirit with God; I am lifted up with all my powers into the **uncreated Good** <note>German: *ungeschaffene Gut*. In mystical theology, this refers to God as the ultimate source who was not Himself created.</note> and draw all things with me into the **absolute Simple** <note>German: *absolut Einfache*. A philosophical term for the divine nature, which is perfectly unified and contains no complexity or parts.</note>. There I understand myself as nothing other than a **son of God**, and thus the **eternal Word** is born in me without ceasing (584, 4–19). One spirit with God and one body with Christ, that is true unity (522, 12).

2. Through this, the most intimate fellowship—indeed, the most perfect unity—is established among all those who are united with God. In the **kingdom of heaven**, everything is in everything, everything is one, and everything is ours. Whatever grace Mary possesses, I have just as much, provided I am in the kingdom of heaven; and I do not have it as something flowing to me from Mary, but as my ownmost property, which comes to me from no stranger. What one person has there, the other also has, and not as if from the other or in the other, but as in oneself, so that the grace that is in one is entirely and as belonging specifically to them in the other (39, 35). All the works that all the saints and all the angels and Mary, the Mother of God, have ever performed—from these I will receive eternal joy as if I had performed them myself. Everything that God has given to his only-begotten Son, he has then given to me just as perfectly as to him (56, 5. 412, 36. 137, 2).

The unity with God is furthermore a unity not only of **essence** <term>essence<note>German: *Wesen*. The fundamental nature or substance of a thing; what it is in itself.</note></term>, but also of **action** <term>action<note>German: *Wirken*. Often translated as "working" or "activity," referring to the divine operations in the world.</note></term>. Where a person is lifted above time into eternity, there they perform one and the same work with God; they work with God what God worked thousands of years ago and will work thousands of years from now. For in God there is no time, and all His doing is one work (190, 29). The soul should not believe itself to have reached its goal until it works in equal power with God. Then it performs with the Father all His works (161, 30). When a person is one with God, they bring forth all **creatures** <note>German: *Creaturen*. All created beings in the universe.</note> with God; thus they bring **bliss** <note>German: *Seligkeit*. Often translated as "salvation" or "beatitude," referring to the state of eternal happiness in God.</note> to all creatures to the extent that they are one with God (199, 12). And on the other hand, it is no longer the person themselves who acts, but God is then, in this person, the actual actor of their deeds. God takes the place of reason and the will, and all the person's doing is rather a doing of God within the person (467, 10).

But on the other hand, the unity that we should have with God is not merely a unity of action, but of essence...

This **breaking through** <note>German: *Durchbrechen*. A central term in Meister Eckhart’s mysticism, referring to the soul's movement beyond its identity as a "creature" to return to its uncreated source in God.</note> of all the barriers of finitude is far more glorious than the original proceeding forth from God. In the latter, I behave as a **creature** <note>German: *Creatur*. In this theological context, it refers to any being that has been created by God, which is inherently limited compared to the Creator.</note>. But in that breaking through, in which I desire to stand free and **void** <note>German: *ledig*. This implies being empty, detached, or unencumbered by worldly desires or even personal will.</note> in the will of God—void even of the will of God and all his works and of God himself—there I am above all creatures, neither God nor creature; I am what I was and what I now am and shall remain forevermore. There I receive an impulse that shall carry me up above all angels. In this impulse, I receive such rich fullness that God, with all that he is as God and with all his divine activities, cannot suffice for me. For in this breaking through, I receive the realization that I and God are one. There I am what I was; there I neither decrease nor increase; there I am an **unmoved cause** <note>A reference to the philosophical concept of the "unmoved mover," here describing the soul’s state of perfect stability when unified with the divine source.</note> that moves all things (284, 11). Where God and the spirit have lost their distinguishing characteristics, there I am the Son of God, whom God has begotten from eternity; where I am, there is God, and where God is, there I am. There is no more intimate union than that between God and the soul (590, 32. 267, 4). God is one and the same as what I am; God’s essence is my life; therefore, what is God’s must be mine, and God’s **substance** <note>German: *Substanz*. The essential reality or "stuff" that makes something what it is.</note> must be my substance. This does not mean *becoming* God, but *being* God. In the eternal, unchanging Being, there is nothing but God in God. There, only the uncreated spirit lives in the soul; and this uncreated eternal thing is nothing less than God. To be *like* God still sounds of strangeness and separation. But such [separation] does not exist between God and the soul; therefore, the soul is not like God, but is entirely one with him and the very same as he is (439, 11. 204, 20. 377, 26. 532, 11. 620, 19. 163, 35). God is what he is, and what he is, that is mine, and what is mine, that I love, and what I love, that loves me and draws me into itself, and what has drawn me into itself, that I am more than I am myself. Therefore, love God, and you shall become God with God (392, 31). But the unity with God is not like the unity produced by love—a unity merely of activity—but like that which **knowing** <note>German: *Erkennen*. In mystical theology, "knowing" or "cognition" is often considered more fundamental than love, as it represents a total identification or merging of the knower with the object known.</note> produces: a complete merging of the one...

Between man and God there is no difference; there is pure unity, closer than that of the three persons in the Godhead, who are, after all, several <note>Eckhart argues that while the Trinity consists of three distinct "persons" (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), the union of the soul with the divine essence is even more absolute, reaching the "One" beyond distinction.</note>. It is highly characteristic of Eckhart's conception of the relationship of the soul to God that he almost never uses the daring and often so poorly portrayed parable of the relationship between bride and bridegroom <note>German: *Braut und Bräutigam*. This refers to "Bride Mysticism" (Brautmystik), a tradition that used the erotic imagery of the Song of Solomon to describe the soul’s love for God.</note> for the union of the soul with God. The parable has its good biblical foundation in both the Old and New Testaments; but as it was and is used most often in ecstatic devotion—and particularly by mystics—it leads to offensive images and descriptions that correspond as little to the essence of the matter as to a sober religious feeling. For Eckhart, the parable was almost unusable. For him, unity with God rests essentially on the immersion of the **knowing reason** <note>German: *erkennende Vernunft*. For Eckhart, the intellect or reason is the highest part of the soul, the "spark" that is uncreated and capable of reaching the divine essence.</note> into God; all sensual fire of love can only lead away from it. But at the same time, this love is a relationship from person to person; the union with God in the Eckhartian sense presupposes precisely the stripping away of personal individuality and the merging with the impersonal Absolute. Therefore, while Christ may indeed appear once as the **bridegroom** <note>German: *Bräutigam*.</note> to whom God has betrothed the soul from eternity as his lawful spouse (288, 6; cf. 402, 38; 407, 12), Eckhart otherwise prefers other parables more characteristic of his conception. The soul unites with God as food does with the body. Just as food becomes eye in the eyes and ear in the ears, so the soul becomes God in God. It unites with every divine power, just as power is in God, and God unites with the soul just as every power is in the soul; the two natures flow together in one light and the soul is **annihilated** <note>German: *zu nichte*. This describes the mystical death of the self, where the individual "I" vanishes so that only God remains.</note> as it reaches its highest form. What it is, it is in God. The divine powers pull it into themselves, as the sun pulls all creatures into itself (531, 25; 113, 24; 226, 31). <header>### III. The Union of the Soul with God.</header>

...however many loaves of bread there may be, it is still only one body—so too we are transformed into God (205, 21). The soul is united with the naked Godhead, so that it can no longer be found therein as a distinct being, any more than a drop of wine can be found in the middle of the sea (467, 6; 566, 35). Just as fire transforms whatever is fed into it and brings it into its own nature, so we are transformed into God (206, 15).

The person who is thus united with God is called a *deified* <term>vergotteter: a person who has undergone "deification," the process of becoming divine by grace</term> or a *God-formed person* (643, 38; 240, 14). It is still the same soul, but in a different state; for the old way of being is entirely gone and dead. The soul has regained its true essence and stands in its original innocence. Reason and everything that can be grasped through concepts remain outside; the soul is received into pure unity. That which the highest soul-power <note>Eckhart believed the soul had various "powers" or faculties, such as memory and will, but the "highest" power was the spark of reason that could touch the divine.</note> previously performed, God now performs in the person; the soul, however, stands naked and free of all things. One might well say: this person is God and man. He has attained through grace everything that Christ possessed by nature. The body is so permeated by the glorious essence of the soul that one might say: this is a divine person (127, 25). He is more God than creature (185, 1).

*Eckhart* speaks of five standpoints that the soul can occupy. The standpoint of the *Devil* is satisfaction in sensuality; the standpoint of *Nature* (that is, of a consciousness perceiving itself as a universal "I") is that of devotion and selfless love, which nevertheless cannot rid itself of finite images and mental representations; the standpoint of the *Angel* is that of a vision of all things under the form of eternity <note>German: *unter der Form der Ewigkeit*, often referred to in Latin as *sub specie aeternitatis*—viewing things from a timeless, divine perspective.</note>, free and unhindered by passions. At the standpoint of the *Spirit*, one seizes the infinite substantiality of one’s own soul and perceives oneself as Christ. But whoever is directly enraptured into the *divine standpoint* understands himself in no other way than as being the essence from which God takes His own essence and His own Godhead (586, 21 ff.).

Under the guidance of her confessor, she strives to move beyond the distresses of her conscience, advancing from the legalistic to the evangelical, from the evangelical to the mystical

Soon, she grows in her experiences of grace beyond her confessor, so that she is now in a position to guide him, and finally she reaches the ultimate height, which she announces to her confessor with the words: “Sir, rejoice with me; I have become God.” Her rapture is then described. This young woman—named in tradition Sister Catherine <note>original: "Schwester Katrei." She is the protagonist of a famous 14th-century mystical treatise once attributed to Eckhart, though now thought to be by one of his followers.</note>, and called Master Eckhart's daughter <note>In a spiritual context, "daughter" refers to a female disciple under a master's guidance, not a biological child.</note>—goes into a corner of the church. There she reached the point where she forgot all finite things and was raised so far above herself and all created things that she lay there until the third day and was presumed dead. Had it not been for her confessor, they would have buried her. Only on the third day does she come to herself and say: "Oh, poor me, am I back here again?" What she experienced, however, she cannot communicate to anyone. — Eckhart intended to present his ideal here through a concrete image. This, he wants to say, is what you could achieve; however, the specific details of the depiction are hardly meant to be taken seriously. The "daughter" is only proven true through the repetition of this rapture; the confessor calls this her "remaining God." Nowhere does Eckhart's teaching style appear so off-putting or like a fanatical extreme as in this portrayal; however, one must keep in mind here as well that Eckhart does not intend to describe actual psychological states, but rather that the whole thing serves only as a *poetic fiction* <term>poetische Fiction: a literary or pedagogical device used to illustrate a concept rather than record a literal historical event</term>, an image, an example in which his doctrine of perfect *detachment* <term>Abgeschiedenheit: the state of being "cut off" from worldly desires and even from one's own ego to be open to God</term> and of deification is presented concretely and vividly. It is only an ideal that he draws; he did not mean to say that it has been realized or is even realizable. But certainly, the ideal itself is wrongly conceived and is more a product of religious enthusiasm than of sober reflection.

4. Eckhart describes the union with God as something realized in certain individuals. His purpose in doing so is essentially to direct longing and drive toward the highest goal; he is mostly prompted to such extreme intensification by his polemic against the prevailing shallowing of spiritual life. Yet his full, positive seriousness is only present in the description during moments of intense emotion. Upon calmer reflection, his statements sound significantly milder and more sober, and he not infrequently adds weakening restrictions to his most extreme explanations, which then—

<header>### III. The Union of the Soul with God.</header>

...undoubtedly bring his teaching closer to the common understanding in essential points.

A certain tempering of the thought is already evident in the fact that man is not meant to be God in exactly the same way as God Himself; for God is God by nature—that is, through Himself—while man is so only by grace—that is, through a gift from God (185, 2. 382, 8. 398, 34). <note>In medieval theology, "nature" refers to what a being is by its own essence, whereas "grace" is a supernatural gift bestowed by God that allows a creature to participate in divine life.</note> What God possesses by nature, the soul possesses by grace; God Himself does not ascribe any further difference between Himself and the soul (531, 36. 533, 16). Yet this one distinction is thoroughgoing: man is simply not the **Absolute**. <note>The "Absolute" here refers to God as the ultimate, unconditional reality that exists independently of all other things.</note> And this is now described as the deepest pain of the soul: that it can never, under any circumstances or in any way, become the Absolute itself. The face of the soul is flushed with anger; no one can comfort her in her suffering. She even rages against God Himself. If she were the Creator and God were created by her—as the soul is indeed created by God—she would surrender herself and become a **creature** <term>Creatur: a created being, as opposed to the uncreated Creator</term> and give the other the power to become God. Indeed, if it were a pain for God from which He could not escape, that He derived His essence from the soul, she would wish for Him to annihilate her and for her to become nothing, just to spare Him the feeling of inferiority. But to thus deprive Himself and elevate another in His place is simply against the nature of the Absolute; the soul, in turn, is unalterably bound to its status as a created thing. In the soul, the creature attains the "form of eternity"—that is the soul's destiny. Therefore, nothing remains for the soul but to hold itself completely unworthy of God in the deepest humility, in the feeling of its own imperfection, to renounce, and to surrender. Thus the soul desires to go out of itself, and thus its pure essence can enter into God (542, 9).

The soul, therefore, cannot become the Absolute itself. Just as a drop is lost in the ocean, but the ocean is not lost in the drop, so it happens to the soul when God draws it into Himself: the soul becomes divine, but God does not become the soul. <note>This "drop and ocean" metaphor is a cornerstone of mystical literature, illustrating how the individual self is absorbed into the Divine without obliterating the Divine’s distinct, infinite nature.</note> There, the soul loses its name, its power, and its activity, but not its being; the soul remains in God as God remains in Himself (314, 20). The soul becomes God in a higher way than through the mere form of grace. There, she has lost herself and flows in a stream into the unity of divine nature. But however much she sinks into that unity, she still [cannot reach] the absolute ground...

...never encompass. Therefore God has left her <note>In German, "soul" (Seele) is a feminine noun; the author maintains this personification.</note> a little point where she returns into herself and finds and recognizes herself as a **creature**. This precisely is the soul’s essence: that she is not able to fathom her Creator (386, 39). This rational nature of hers—to understand herself—can never be lost to the soul; she can never become nothing (506, 25). It is not the highest bliss of the soul to completely lose her creaturely nature, such that she would cease to recognize, love, and feel. Rather, to enter into God and yet, as something distinct, to possess an "undistinguished unity" as a creature—and to do so with the full energy of feeling and loving—that is the highest bliss. For if she were entirely absorbed into God, she would completely disappear; in God, every creature is something infinitely small and vanishing, like a **dewdrop in the sea** (662, 20). 

The Elect, who turn their recognition toward God, flow into the same "Nothing" as the damned. But the torment of the damned is the consciousness of this Nothing into which they sink ever deeper, and which they are yet unable to comprehend. The blessed also pass through this darkness of the Nothing; but in this Nothing, they do not see mere void, but rather the infinite fullness of the divine being, which they cannot encompass. There, the soul sinks ever deeper into the **ground of Nothing**. But in this sinking, her substance remains and does not come to naught. For the "nothing" which sinks can never encompass the "nothing" into which it sinks (522, 18). And for this reason, Eckhart can add a restriction to the sentence "the soul becomes God in God": *insofar as it is possible for a creature at all* (356, 23). This is exactly what Eckhart aims for when he describes the little word <term>quasi: Latin for "as if" or "in a certain sense"</term> as that which all his preaching leads toward. This little word describes what children in school call a "by-word" <note>original: "Beiwort." In medieval German, this could refer to an adjective, an adverb, or a parable/example. Eckhart uses it to suggest that the soul exists "alongside" or "in relation to" God's Word.</note>, that is, an example or a parable. Thus, we should be a "by-word" to the Word (271, 10).

---

The soul, therefore, does not perish entirely in the darkness of the absolute essence. There remains for her a remnant of finitude, which at the same time gives her the guarantee of eternity. Everything about her individual being that is divine and rational shall remain hers eternally. Through the barrier of her consciousness, the soul remains always aware of herself as a finite being in the midst of the encompassing infinity of the Absolute, with which she has united.

He uses the linguistic metaphor of the word "quasi" to show that the soul's union with God is a likeness or participation rather than a total disappearance of the individual.</summary>

<page-num>214</page-num>
<header>III. The Union of the Soul with God.</header>

It remains Eckhart’s conviction that the highest perfection of which one can speak can indeed be achieved (642, 28). However, he does not claim with full earnestness that it is entirely attainable here in this earthly life. All <term>bliss</term> <note>German: *Seligkeit*. In a medieval context, this refers to the state of perfect happiness and salvation found in God's presence.</note> that we possess here below is, after all, only a foretaste; the full enjoyment of it will only be granted to us in the hereafter. It begins here, and it shall last eternally. Grace, as we have it in this life, and bliss, as we shall one day have it in the eternal life, relate to one another as the blossom relates to the fruit (323, 5. 377, 15. 382, 18). What is still hidden from us now shall one day be revealed to us. One cannot reach the full vision and knowledge of divine activities while in this body; but the striving toward it, the love, remains with us (238, 13. 619, 21). Here below, such a union with God—where all striving and all change would cease—cannot occur (252, 3). The body, before it is <term>transfigured</term> <note>German: *verklärt*. This refers to the "glorified body" believed to be received after death, which no longer hinders the spirit.</note>, can never follow the upward flight of the spirit (655, 2. 668, 11).

Therefore, the sense in which alone one can speak of a union between man and God is explained as follows: When man frees the divine image—which God has impressed upon his nature—from all its veils and coverings, then the image of God is revealed within him; that is, God is born in him. For the Son is said to be born of the Father because he reveals the Father as such. Through this awakening of the divine image within himself, man makes himself equal to God. For the <term>archetype</term> <note>German: *Urbild*. Eckhart suggests there is an original, uncreated "blueprint" of every person that exists eternally within God's own essence.</note> of man is equal to the archetype of God, which God is according to His pure essence. The more man resembles God in this way, the more he is one with God. In this sense, it is said: **M a n** is born in God, in that man’s archetype shines with the same light as the archetype of God. This equality of the archetype constitutes the unity of God with man. Therefore, when it is said that man is one with God, one is thinking of his archetype, through which he is equal to God, and not of his created essence. In this, one disregards his "creatureliness"—not as if it did not exist at all, but because in this specific relationship, it is not present (198, 13).

But certainly, despite all these limitations and considerations which he does not wish to suppress, Eckhart dwells with particular fondness on portraying an absolutely perfected state,

# 9. The Union with God.

...in which he, on the one hand, removes all barriers between God and the soul, and on the other, allows no distinction between the <term>here and now</term> <note>German: *Diesseits*. Nevertheless, one must interpret Eckhart's thoughts in such a way that the complete union of man with God is regarded by him only as the highest ideal—one which he feels called to hold up to his contemporaries (who are often preoccupied with external matters) as the only legitimate goal of their striving. Thus, the exuberance of his claims lies more in his expression than in the underlying thought itself.

When he chooses, for the most part, to disregard the finite limitations of all our striving and the inevitable imperfection of all things earthly, this pertains not so much to his doctrine or its fundamental concept, but rather to the delivery of this doctrine and its educational purpose. Eckhart believes he is more effective when he presents and allows us to visualize the ultimate goal of striving as something realizable and already realized, rather than speaking—as is actually his opinion—only of an <term>infinite approximation</term> <note>Eckhart suggests that while we never truly "become" God in a literal, numerical sense, our journey toward Him is a never-ending process of becoming more like Him.</note> toward this ideal as the highest we could hope for. 

This will emerge even more clearly in Eckhart’s teaching on moral activity. At the same time, it should not be denied that a certain mixing of the human and the divine is already visible in the basic framework of his way of thinking—specifically in his definition of the essence of the soul.

## IV. On the Moral Life.

In the presentation of Eckhart's teaching on the way leading to union with God, we have become acquainted with the fundamental <term>principle</term> <note>German: *principielle Seite*. This refers to the core theoretical framework of Eckhart's philosophy regarding morality.</note> of his conception of the essence and the actual content of morality. However, Eckhart is not satisfied with merely describing the God-like life in general terms; he also attempts to show in detail how the divine principle—received into the spirit under the influence of <term>grace</term>—reveals itself in various activities and in the overall state of the soul, unfolding, so to speak, into its individual components. We shall group the thoughts which Eckhart expresses on this subject—some in a structured form and others scattered and isolated—under the perspective of a doctrine of the moral life.

### 1. The Prerequisites of the Moral Life.

When Eckhart undertakes to describe the performance of moral acts under the conditions of earthly life in detail, a great difficulty arises for him: he regards everything that alone could provide the positive basis for a moral determination of actions as something "non-existent" or "that which should not be." According to Eckhart, the principle and prerequisite of all moral action is the being of man in God—that is, at the same time, the elevation above space and time and all earthly conditions and circumstances: pure <term>detachment</term> <note>German: *Abgeschiedenheit*. This is one of Eckhart's most famous concepts. It describes a state of spiritual "cutting away" from worldly desires and even from one's self-will, to allow God to act through the soul.</note>. To him, the earthly has no independent value anywhere; it is much—

It highlights the central paradox of Eckhart's ethics: that true moral action requires "detachment," or the spiritual elevation above the very earthly conditions in which the action takes place.</summary>

# 1. The Prerequisites of the Moral Life.

...more a thing that must be constantly <term>negated</term> <note>In this context, to negate means to deny or suppress the urges of the physical world in favor of spiritual ones.</note> and overcome; and the will, insofar as it relates to the sensory individual, is precisely not a moral will, but a natural, and therefore immoral, will. In this way, however, the whole of earthly life, with its physical and spiritual needs that can be set aside by no act of will, would be a negation of the moral life. The first task of morality would, accordingly, have to be the abolishing of this earthly life itself. 

As long as man is on earth, the activity of the senses, the variety of perceptions, the intricate play of the soul's powers, the multiplicity of cares and desires, and the fragmentation of the single collective spiritual power into nothing but individual occupations directed toward the sensory never cease. The <term>peace of the soul</term> <note>German: *Seelenruhe*. A central concept in mysticism referring to an inner stillness that remains undisturbed by external events.</note>, which ought to remain immovably fixed in the one absolute ground, is always disturbed anew. The unalterably constant will—which, when it is in unity with the divine will, alone corresponds to the concept of the moral will—is disturbed by ever different and ever new temptations from both within and without. 

New resolutions are required time and again; the struggle does not come to a standstill, the conflict leads to no final victory, and the laboriously won spiritual concentration is always turned back into distraction by the necessity and care of the earthly. The diversity of inner and outer goods, all of which want to be equally preserved, leads to recurring collisions—to a <term>conflict of duties</term> <note>German: *Streite der Pflichten*. This refers to the moral dilemma where two ethical requirements seem to contradict one another.</note> from which the conscience cannot always bring itself back pure. 

Against these consequences, which lie within the very concept of <term>finitude</term> <note>German: *Endlichkeit*. The state of being human, limited, and mortal, as opposed to the infinite nature of God.</note>, even the <term>mystic</term> <note>A person, like Eckhart, who seeks a direct, personal experience of God or ultimate reality.</note> cannot close his eyes. If he acknowledges them, as <term>Eckhart</term> <note>Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328), a German theologian and philosopher known for his radical views on the soul's union with God.</note> indeed does, then he seems to be faced with an alternative: either to give up his ideal of the moral life, or to give up earthly life as the site for the realization of this ideal.

The Master, who despite all his monastic constraints does not entirely lack a view for the significance of earthly life itself—even in the details of its external conditions—decides in the face of this difficult and apparent alternative for neither one side nor the other. His deep moral feeling urges him to hold fast to both sides simultaneously. He does not yield the slightest from the rigor of his moral ideal; but on the other hand, he attributes to earthly life with all its—

# IV. On the Moral Life.

...human imperfections an infinite and incomparable significance.

The strict consequence of the mystical standpoint would be <term>Quietism</term> <note>A 17th-century mystical movement (later declared heretical) that advocated for a state of perfect passivity and the suppression of the individual will to allow God to act alone.</note>, this caricature of the God-devoted will. Indeed, the demand the mystic places on the will amounts to us giving up the will, ceasing all our own wanting and doing, so that God alone may rule within us. Self-annihilation and complete passivity remain as the only duties where the tendency toward absolute unity asserts itself so boundlessly. And yet, that seemingly compelling consequence is not present in truth; a deeper speculation can admit the premises without acknowledging the conclusions that lead to absurdity.

Truly, the soul would like to be God; truly, it wished that there were no creatures <note>In medieval theology, "creature" refers to anything created by God, including inanimate objects and humans, not just animals.</note> at all, but only God, as He was in eternity before the creation of creatures, so that it could enjoy the divine nature in its unity just as it once did. But in that case, God would have lacked an object for His love; and yet it is the nature of the Good that it communicates itself <note>original: "dass es sich mittheile". This refers to the Scholastic principle *bonum est diffusivum sui*—the idea that goodness naturally pours itself out or shares itself with others.</note> (543, 1). Since God must create a world of the finite in order to be truly and perfectly God, man must become a sensory-finite individual personality, and the goal of this finite existence is to mediate the return of the soul, and with it all things, into God. With this, the infinite task that the soul must fulfill in this earthly life is already expressed: not only that it should itself break through the barriers of finiteness, but that it should also subject all finite things, as far as it is able, to its power and draw them upward with itself. The salvation of the human soul thus simultaneously encompasses the salvation of all creation. Man is commanded to work—in thinking, feeling, and doing—to spiritualize all things, so that they may become spirit again, as they were by their nature from the beginning (533, 5).

The soul is divided dualistically into a transcendent essence and a finite form of appearance. ## 2. Work and Disposition.

Following his own premises, **Eckhart** teaches us that when it comes to the concept of the moral, we must turn our gaze away from the **external**—the activity that manifests in the physical world—and direct our focus exclusively toward the **internal**, the source from which all individual activities spring. In doing so, he turns most decisively against the view that had become dominant in the Roman Church. That view wrongly treated the **external** element of the "work" as something independent in human conduct and assigned it a moral **value** even when separated from the internal state that supported it: the moral **disposition** <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "Gesinnung." This refers to the inner intent, heart, or attitude of a person, rather than their outward actions.</note>. For the Master, when an external work is detached from its ground in the state of the human will, it is worth absolutely nothing. It is his highest principle in moral **judgment** that the work in itself—viewed as an external event carried out by a person—is something completely indifferent. Human **action** only receives moral value through the corresponding **disposition**, the quality of the **will**; consequently, only the will, and not its outward expression in a "work," can be called moral or immoral.

1. **Eckhart** holds the highest possible ideas regarding the power of the **will**. The will is eternal by its nature, while its expression in a work is temporal and finite. Morality consists in that **eternal** element of the will, not in its **temporal manifestation** within a work. The will, when it is truly earnest, is incredibly powerful; but then it must be more than a mere desire or a simple inclination. It must not say: *I would like to*, but rather: *I will*. Many a seemingly insignificant act, once performed, is more pleasing to God than many a seemingly significant work that another has performed long and often, provided that the insignificant act happened from the perspective of eternity. # IV. On the Moral Life.

...consequently, one who has raised themselves into eternity in a **moment** <term>the moment</term> <note>original: "Nu." In the tradition of Rhineland Mysticism, the "Nu" is the "Eternal Now," the timeless instant where the soul and God meet.</note> achieves more in the eyes of God than all temporal actions are able to achieve. For in that moment, all time is contained (304, 11). A person should therefore never be frightened so long as they find within themselves the **will** for what is good, and they should not be grieved if they are unable to fulfill it through outward works. They need not think themselves far from virtue; for virtue and all morality lie in the **good will**. You can lack nothing if only you have the right will. But to will powerfully and with your whole heart—that is up to you, and neither God nor any creature can take that from you. What I will to have, I already possess. If I never did anything evil, but had the will for evil, I would bear the sin as if I had committed it. In the mere earnest **will**, I could commit a sin as great as if I had killed the entire world, even if I had not moved a finger to do so. 

With the **will**, I am capable of everything. I can bear the hardships of all people, feed all the poor, and perform the works of all humanity, and whatever else you can imagine: if you do not lack the will, but only the power, then in truth, before God, you have done it all, and no one can take it from you. For to **will** to do something as soon as I am able, and to have actually **done** it, are the same in the eyes of God. In **love**, two things must be distinguished: the essence of love and its "work"—that is, the mere outward expression of the essence of love. The true seat of love is only in the will. Whoever has more will, also has more love (552 ff.). God does not look at the nature of the works, but only at the nature of the love, the disposition, and the **spirit** <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "Gemüth." This difficult-to-translate term refers to the seat of one's emotions, character, and innermost soul.</note> within the works. For He is not concerned with our works, but only with our spirit in all our works—namely, that we love Him alone (560, 34). 

A person who has nothing to give can still be charitable; for they can give through their will (607, 34). Every person is judged according to the purposes they set for themselves; their value is determined by the goal they strive for. Whoever sets a goal lower than God is not worthy of God; but whoever loves God can only be rewarded with God, and God wishes to give Himself as their reward (608, 31). The same applies to actions; their character is determined by the **intention** toward which the actions are directed (297, 11).

## 2. Work and Disposition.

> If someone gave a hundred marks of gold <note>A "Mark" was a traditional medieval unit of weight for precious metals, later becoming a currency. Here, it signifies a vast sum of money.</note> for God's sake, that would be a great deed and would appear to be a great deed. But I say: if I have the earnest will to give a hundred marks if I had them, in truth, I have paid them to God, and God must respond to me as if I had actually paid him a hundred marks. And conversely: were the Pope to be slain by my hand and it happened without my will, I would go to the altar and read Mass <note>The "reading" or "saying" of Mass is the central liturgical act of the Catholic priest.</note> just as I usually would (56, 39). He is not called virtuous who performs virtuous works, but he who performs them in a manner corresponding to virtue. Whoever gives alms <term>alms</term> <note>Charitable gifts given to the poor as a religious duty.</note> reluctantly and not with a joyful heart performs a virtuous work, but not in an appropriate manner. It is not outward suffering that makes a patient person; rather, it only shows and reveals whether the person is patient, just as fire shows whether a penny is made of silver or copper. A patient person would be called patient even if no outward suffering ever befell them (611, 36). All the value of outward suffering comes and flows from the value of the good will. Everything, therefore, that the good man is ready and desires to suffer for God's sake, he truly suffers in the presence of God (444, 8).

2. To speak more closely about the relationship of individual actions to the enduring essence of the spirit, **Eckhart takes the occasion** of a controversy that must have caused a stir and in which his opinion differed from that of all the scholars of his time. It is Eckhart's claim that in the state of mortal sin <term>mortal sin</term> <note>In Catholic theology, a "grave" sin that destroys the state of grace in the soul.</note>, good works can be practiced which, if the person is then accepted back into grace, serve to further their spiritual progress. We present his explanation of this thought in brief. All good works, he says, like the time in which they happen, pass away in themselves absolutely without effect. To no work does the predicate "holy" or "blessed" belong; evil and good works pass by equally without effect. Holiness, blessedness, and goodness are only externally attributed predicates of the work and the time in which it happened, and do not truly belong to them. A work as such is nothing in itself; it does not exist for its own sake, nor does it know anything of itself. As soon as the action has happened, it has come to nothing and passed away like the time in which it happened; it is neither here nor there, and the spirit has nothing more to do with it. If the spirit is to act further, then...

# IV. On the Moral Life.

...it happens with other actions and at another time. Therefore, good and evil deeds pass away in the same manner; they have no permanence in the spirit, no essence or place in themselves, and God likewise can do nothing with them; for in God, neither time nor temporal action exists. However, the performed deed does have a negative value <note>In this mystical context, "negative" refers to the process of "negation" or stripping away—the act of clearing out internal distractions or intentions to make room for God.</note> for the spirit. For through the deed, the spirit frees itself from a concept or an intention that had occupied it; this liberation brings it closer to its true essence, and thereby it becomes more blessed and better. Only in this figurative sense can a work be called blessed and good. Strictly speaking, only that person is blessed in whom the fruit of the work remains—not as a "work" or as "time," but as an eternal effect identical to the spirit, and therefore as the spirit itself. Since work and time are nothing in themselves, he who loses them loses nothing.

— But are good works possible in the state of mortal sin <term>mortal sin</term> <note>In traditional theology, a grave sin that separates the soul from God's saving grace.</note>? Yes; for the fundamentally good ground of the spirit cannot be extinguished, and out of this ground, good works can be practiced even outside the state of grace. Such works cannot earn the kingdom of heaven, but even less can they harm the spirit; rather, their effect remains eternally in the spirit. If the person then attains grace, everything that was previously in them by nature is ennobled through grace; the fact that they previously rid their spirit of mental concepts through these works now facilitates their union with God. Should they perform those works now, they would require time, which can now be used more effectively and profitably. The expression of the spirit in actions thus possesses a truly ennobling power that works eternally within the spirit (71–74). — One need only think of the skills acquired through diligence and earnest effort, or the proficiencies gained through habit, which can serve the person who later receives grace as a means for a beneficial influence on themselves and others, to find this line of thought justified.

This corresponds entirely to what Eckhart <note>Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328), a German mystic and philosopher whose teachings often emphasized the "inner work" over external rituals.</note> teaches about the significance of so-called "good works" as known by the Church. ## 2. Work and Disposition.

...[practices and actions] have been established and ordered for the purpose that the outer man <note>In mystical theology, the "outer man" refers to the physical body and the sensory soul, while the "inner man" refers to the spirit or the spark of the soul.</note> might be turned toward God through them, being made ready for a spiritual life and for all that is good; so that he might remain within himself and not turn toward anything inappropriate, so that when God wishes to work within him, He finds the person ready and does not first need to draw him up from estrangement within the realm of the senses. It is only so that the person may be preserved from self-estrangement and from all that is ungodly that those external exercises were devised: praying, reading, singing, keeping vigil, fasting, kneeling, acts of penance, pilgrimages, and mortifications and self-punishments of all kinds. Therefore, as long as a person still feels weak and estranged from God, those exercises are useful to him. However, as soon as he perceives <term>true devotion</term> <note>German: *wahre Andacht*. In this context, it refers to a state of focused, internal awareness of God's presence that transcends mere ritual.</note> within himself, let him boldly abandon all external matters, even those exercises to which he may have bound himself by a vow that no Pope or Bishop could release him from. For no one can release a person from a vow through which he has personally bound himself to God; and yet, simply entering a religious order nullifies all such vows, because in principle one there commits oneself to everything that is holy before God. In exactly the same way, the state of true devotion nullifies all vows; for there God works within the person, and His work is better than all the actions of <term>creatures</term> <note>The term "creatures" refers to all created things, including humans and their independent efforts, as opposed to the uncreated God.</note>. If this applies to educated and knowledgeable people whose eyes God and the Holy Scriptures have opened, how does it stand with the simple layman who has made a vow? Well, if he finds that it hinders him and that he would be more greatly advanced if he were free of it, let him boldly free himself from it; for the work that brings you closer to God in a higher measure is always the best. One should look more toward the fruitful effect and the inner truth than toward the external work (22, 18 ff.). The external discipline of life finds its justification in the fact that the body and the flesh always struggle against the spirit. The body is bold and strong here below, for it has its home here; the world helps it; this earth is its fatherland; all its relatives help it here: food, drink, and physical comfort. The spirit is a stranger here in exile; in heaven are all its kin and its entire lineage; there it is well-befriended. That one might come to the aid of the spirit in its banishment and [strengthen it] against the flesh...

# IV. On the Moral Life.

...to some extent bring an end to this conflict, so that the body does not achieve victory over the spirit, one applies the bridle of <term>penitential exercises</term> <note>German: *Bussübungen*. These are physical acts of atonement, such as fasting or specific prayers, meant to discipline the body.</note> and burdens it so that the spirit may be able to defend itself. But if you wish to bind and burden the body a thousand times better, then apply to it the bridle of love. With love, you overcome it most quickly; with love, you burden it most heavily. And for this reason, God pursues us with nothing so powerfully as with love. 

It is exactly the same with love as it is with a fisherman’s hook. The fisherman does not catch the fish unless it is caught on the hook. But once the hook has seized it, the fisherman is certain of the fish, no matter how much the fish struggles. The same holds true for love: whoever is captured by it wears the strongest of fetters and yet carries a sweet burden. Whoever has taken this sweet burden upon themselves achieves more and is furthered more by it than by all external practices and <term>mortification</term> <note>German: *Kasteiung*. The practice of self-denial or physical discipline to subdue physical desires.</note>. Nothing makes you so much God’s own, and God so much your own, as this sweet bond. Whoever has found this way should seek no other. Whoever hangs upon this hook is so captured that foot and hand, mouth, eyes, heart, and everything that is within the person must belong to God. And therefore, you can overcome that enemy <note>Refers to the "outer man" or the egoistic physical nature mentioned in the previous section.</note> with nothing better than with love. Therefore it is written:

> "Love is strong as death, firm as hell." <note>A translation of the German "die Liebe ist stark wie der Tod, fest wie die Hölle," referencing the Song of Solomon 8:6. In many English Bibles, this is rendered as "love is strong as death, jealousy is cruel as the grave."</note>

Death separates the soul from the body; but love separates everything from the soul. It does not tolerate anything that is not God or godly. Whoever is caught in this net and walks in this way—whatever they do, it is rather love that does it, and to love the action belongs; whether they do something or do nothing, it matters not. Indeed, the most insignificant act of such a person is more useful to themselves and to all people, and more pleasing to God, than the collective practices of all those who possess little love. <header>2. Work and Disposition.</header>

...specific actions, even if one performs them for God’s sake and without any selfishness, insofar as they are bound to certain rules, to time and number, to "before" and "after," take away a person's freedom and therefore hinder them from the right and true life. Inward rest in the contemplation of the wonderful nature of God and in love for Him surpasses all outward activity in value and loveliness. For that rest clings to the noblest powers—to reason and will—and its object is the most glorious and highest; outward activity, however, takes place in the changeable and the sensory. That contemplation and love are lasting, while the work is transitory. Inward rest makes us similar to God, whose rest is not disturbed by His eternal activity; our outward activity, however, brings constant unrest with it. The former is without need and is self-sufficient; the latter makes us dependent on external things. Even in works of mercy performed for God's sake, care and sorrow are attached. That rest is without hindrance and opposition, which are nonetheless inseparable from activity. Only rest is desired for its own sake, while activity is desired only as a means to an end.
