### IV. On the Moral Life.

...the powers peculiar to us; the powers that serve us for external action are common to us and the animals, namely <term>sensuality</term> <note>German: *Sinnlichkeit*. In this context, it refers to the bodily senses and physical impulses shared by all living creatures.</note>. The exercise of the <term>inner man</term> <note>German: *innerer Mensch*. A concept in Christian mysticism referring to the spiritual core of a person that is capable of direct communion with God, as opposed to the "outer man" who deals with the physical world.</note> begins here below and lasts eternally. The outer life, by contrast, in works of mercy, has an end where there is no longer misery or poverty: in eternity (328, 37ff.). If the soul is satisfied with such external works of virtue, it is not like a free daughter, but like a subservient maidservant (353, 3). God does not reward according to the length, greatness, or quantity of works, but according to whether they are accomplished in God; for the soul is an <term>instrument of God</term> <note>German: *Rüstzeug Gottes*. Literally "God's equipment" or "tool," suggesting the soul does not act on its own but allows God to act through it.</note>, in which He works His works (402, 29). All those works that do not stem from your innermost being, to which you are prompted by external causes, are dead works before God. For only that thing lives which has the cause of its movement within itself (158, 38). Difference, number, and parts, finitude and definiteness—all this and its like, just as with all analogies in general, is foreign and distant from God Himself; this constitutes the character of works. They cling to and persist in that which is good, which is <term>creaturely</term> <note>German: *Creatur*. Refers to anything created (humans, animals, objects), which the mystics often contrasted with the uncreated nature of God.</note>, yet they are entirely blind to Goodness and Light in itself (435, 34). The work is creaturely and finite and falls within time. Therefore, works are too small and worthless for God to be required to reward them. Only the works that God performs in us without our contribution—where the soul only <term>suffers</term> <note>German: *leidet*. In mystical theology, "suffering" often means "undergoing" or being "passive" and receptive to God’s influence rather than experiencing pain.</note> and God alone acts—these God must reward with Himself, because they are purely divine and infinite (480, 1).

It is absolutely necessary to correctly determine the value of works. For as a preliminary stage, they certainly have their significance, but one must not concede more to them than that. One must take careful note of how we are prompted to perform external works. For both the angel and the devil give us counsel. The angel advises us only what is necessary and does so in a gentle, pleading manner, something like this: "Look, you must still set this aside, and do this, and leave that"; his counsel is deliberate and sensible, and a quiet peace comes into the soul through his counsel. The counsel of the <term>evil enemy</term> <note>German: *böse Feind*. A traditional term for the devil.</note>, however, commands superfluous works of special holiness, such as excessive fasting, <term>vigils</term> <note>German: *Wachen*. The practice of staying awake for prayer during the night.</note>, genuflections, and lamentations, and he commands them in a harsh tone, something like: "If you cannot do it, then you are lost," or "then you are neither good nor perfect."

## 2. Work and Intention.

Such unusual works of virtue performed without prudence and right understanding are the Devil's counsel; before him the soul is terrified and without peace. But God demands no works at all from us; he performs the work of grace upon our soul, and works are then the simple consequence of the state in which our soul has been placed (633, 18). — In essence, we have here before us Amsdorf’s doctrine <note>A reference to Nikolaus von Amsdorf (1483–1565), a colleague of Martin Luther who provocatively claimed that "good works are harmful to salvation" if they lead to pride or reliance on one's own merit rather than faith.</note> of the **harmfulness of good works**. —

Two men in particular prepared the way for Eckhart's teaching on the worthlessness of external works: **Abelard**, the moralist, who redirected focus from the deed to the intention, and **Saint Bernard**, whose deeper understanding of the moral life underlies Eckhart's explanations throughout. But neither in consistency nor in fundamental depth can any of Eckhart's predecessors be compared with him. The opposition to the Catholic doctrine of the merit of good works was never voiced so forcefully before Eckhart, nor grasped so fundamentally at its root. Eckhart would have to be considered a highly significant *Reformational spirit* even if he had brought no other truth to light but this one. Eckhart’s teaching is a living renewal of **Pauline doctrine**. Just as the Apostle Paul stood in opposition to Pharisaic <term>righteousness of the law</term> <note>German: *Gesetzesgerechtigkeit*. The belief that one can be made right with God simply by following religious rules or legalistic traditions.</note>, Eckhart develops his thoughts in opposition to Catholic <term>sanctity through works</term> <note>German: *Werkheiligkeit*. The idea that salvation or holiness is earned through performing specific religious deeds or rituals.</note>. He is quite naive in this opposition; even here, he does not have the slightest intention of opposing the Church, nor the awareness of how deeply he has become estranged from the Church's view. Indeed, a purer understanding of the value of works had always been represented to some degree by the teachers of the Church, and the perversions are much more to be blamed on the Church’s hierarchical practices, to which theory then tended to prove all too compliant and submissive after the fact. In fact, Eckhart believed he was merely holding consistently to what the best teachers had always taught and what the Church could not help but acknowledge—at least outwardly—as the deepest foundation of its own existence. A remnant of Church-bound tradition, however, reveals itself even in Eckhart, especially in the fact that he still [regards] the purely external exercises himself...

# IV. On the Moral Life.

...seems to attach too high a value to the preparation for true Christian freedom.

The negative aspect of what Eckhart teaches regarding the value of external works strikes at the heart of the matter and remains an indubitable truth. Now, however, the task arises to represent the essence of morality in a positive sense. In many respects—as we may note right here at the outset—Eckhart approaches, even in these positive determinations, the genuinely evangelical doctrine <note>German: *evangelische Lehre*. In this historical context, "evangelical" refers to the core teachings of the Protestant Reformation, specifically the emphasis on faith and grace over ritualistic works.</note> and post-Reformation consciousness. But even in his statements about works, one can recognize that he is unfamiliar with the fundamental moral forces of the objective world; his gaze, therefore, clings too exclusively and one-sidedly to the subjective quality of the will. As a result, this will must lack its actual content—the object toward which it is directed. He cannot sufficiently disavow the medieval man and the monk within himself, and he holds fast to the opposition between the internal and the external in too rigid and harsh a form. That mystical tendency toward "The One" <note>A reference to the Neo-Platonic concept of the absolute Unity of God, which Eckhart believed the soul must return to by stripping away all diversity and "creaturely" things.</note> robs moral life of all distinctness. It cannot be expected of him that he would have grasped the essence of a harmonious morality—one that makes it possible to let all earthly circumstances appear in the transfiguring light of a divine calling.

### 3. The Inner Work.

All external activity relates to a created existence. But creatures—and our relationship to creatures—insert themselves between man and God as an intermediary, whereas the relationship ought to be an immediate one. The work that is meant to place man in the right relationship with God, or to correspond fully to Him, cannot be an external work. Instead, it can only take place in the interior of the soul, where God Himself touches the soul’s essence directly. This gives rise to the concept of the **inner work**.

The inner work can only be accomplished in a state of <term>detachment</term> <note>German: *Abgeschiedenheit*. This is perhaps Eckhart’s most famous technical term; it describes a state of being so "cut off" from worldly desires and the ego that the soul becomes a perfect, empty vessel for God’s presence.</note>—that is, in a state where man surrenders everything, including himself, in order to become receptive to God’s activity. If you wish to live, and if you wish for your works to live, then you must be dead and brought to nothingness <insert>in regards to all things</insert>...

### 3. The Inner Work.

...must have become nothing. It is the nature of the creature <term>creature: any created thing as opposed to the Creator</term> to make something out of something; but it is God's nature to make something out of nothing. Therefore, if God is to do something in you or with you, you must first have become nothing. Go therefore into your own ground <term>ground: the "Seelengrund," or the deepest, most essential part of the soul where it meets God</term> and work there; the works which you perform there are all living (189, 26). Detachment <term>detachment: German "Abgeschiedenheit," the state of being "set apart" from worldly desires and the self</term> itself, understood as a state that is continuously renewed, is the inner work. However, in detachment, the purely negative relationship to things is more emphasized; it is the complete emptying of the spirit of all finite content, which is the condition for being receptive to God. 

In the inner work, by contrast, one thinks more of the positive relationship to things that has become possible again through that emptying; it is therefore the principle of all morality <note>German: *Sittlichkeit*</note>, even insofar as this reveals itself in the specific relationships of earthly life through a particular way of acting toward finite matter. Detachment is the mere turning toward God, which conditions the receptivity for salvation; the inner work is detachment insofar as it also involves a preparation for earthly action. Into the soul of the detached person, God enters through the birth of His Son. This birth is conceived as an act of God and as a singular event, while the inner work is conceived more as an act of man and as a recurring event; but in fact, they belong together. It is only that the birth of the Son in the soul is thought of simply as a drawing of the soul into the Divine, whereas the inner work expresses the corresponding decision of the will, which then becomes fruitful in the individual actions of one’s earthly calling <note>German: *Beruf*, which implies both a professional occupation and a spiritual vocation.</note>.

The task is not to be hindered by the external busyness that life brings with it. But one is free from such hindrance when one turns all of one's activity in a well-ordered manner toward the one goal, the absolute ideal. External busyness is thereby ennobled and raised to a higher standpoint by working inwardly within oneself with reason and deliberate reflection; there, one stands in the midst of things and yet is not immersed in things. One then stands near the goal, as if standing sublime above everything finite at the circumference of eternity. Without acting externally and being active in time, no one can come to God—

# IV. On the Moral Life.

...come; rather, for this very purpose we are placed in time: that through temporal, rational action we might become closer and more like God. And to this belongs the requirement that one should unceasingly raise one's reason to God, not in the form of distinct, finite mental images, but in the form of pure, ideal truth. Whoever acts in this sense rises up, free and unburdened by all intermediary things, into God; the light that shines within him and his action are entirely one and the same <note>original citation: (49, 19)</note>. If a person is to accomplish this "inner work," he must gather all his powers within himself, as if into a corner of his soul; he must close himself off from all particular images and forms and arrive at a state of forgetting and <term>unknowing: "Nichtwissen," a state of mystical ignorance where the mind is emptied of worldly concepts to encounter God</term>. It must happen in stillness and in silence, if the Word of God is to be heard within him <note>original citation: (14, 31)</note>.

In the freedom from all finite images and from everything external lies the contrast between the inner work and the outer work. All outer action is finite and temporal; for this very reason, there is also an inner work which neither time nor space can encompass or limit. In it is contained everything that is God, that is divine, and that is like God—whom neither time nor space can enclose. No one can hinder this inner work, any more than someone could hinder God. This work shines and radiates by day and by night; it rumbles and sings God’s praise in ever-new ways. God does not love the outer work <note>This suggests that God does not value the external deed for its own sake</note> which time and space encompass, which is limited, which can be hindered and overcome, and which becomes weary and old through time and repetition. The true inner work is to love God, to will the Good and "Goodness" in itself. 

We have a clear example of this in the stone. Its external activity is to fall down and lie upon the earth. This activity can be hindered, and it does not fall at all times nor without ceasing. But another work is more internal to the stone, and that is its constant <term>striving: "Streben," the innate inclination or "weight" of an object toward its natural place</term> downward. This is innate to it, and neither God nor <term>creature: any created being or thing</term> nor anyone else can take it away. The stone performs this work without ceasing, night and day. Even if it lay still for a thousand years, its striving would be no less and no greater than it was on the first day. ### 3. The Inner Work.

...evil, which is unlike God and goodness. And the more evil and unlike God the work is, the greater the revulsion it inspires; conversely, the more difficult and God-like the work is, the easier, dearer, and more welcome it becomes <note>original citation: (434, 1)</note>.

The inner work is also divine in the following respect: it is modeled after the very essence of God. Just as all creation added to God—even if there were a thousand worlds—would not be better than God alone by a single hair’s breadth, so too the goodness of the inner work is not increased by its length or width, its quantity or its size. It possesses its goodness within itself. Therefore, the outer work can never be insignificant if the inner work is great, nor can it be great or good if the inner work is small or non-existent. For whoever has the inner work always enclosed within themselves: all its greatness, breadth, and length is drawn and taken from nowhere else but from God and in God’s heart. God loves the Son and is born as the Son in the <term>bosom of the heavenly Father: "Schoosse," a term describing the internal, eternal generation of the Word within the Trinity</term>. This is not the case with the outer work; rather, it receives its divine goodness from the inner work, but only as it is externalized and estranged from its essence into a lower form of manifestation of the Godhead—one that is hidden within distinction, multiplicity, and parts, as if behind a thick veil <note>original citation: (435, 22)</note>. —

To summarize everything, *Eckhart’s* teaching on the inner work is as follows. The love that reveals itself in outer works is not the ultimate ground of morality; it is merely a consequence of the inner work. This inner work is a constant, ever-renewed resolution of the will to renounce one's own will and to surrender oneself entirely to God. It is, therefore, far more a state of <term>rest: "Ruhe," a technical term in mysticism for the soul's stillness that allows God to act</term>—restoring itself from all the distractions of the outer world—than an activity. This rest encompasses an unceasing inclination and longing toward God and a struggle against all that is ungodly. Yet this inclination and striving should, in every moment, already be a satisfied stillness, a pure passivity, in order to let God act within us. This rest of the will is at the same time pure knowledge; the will ceases to act as a separate power of the soul and passes over into <term>pure contemplation: "reine Contemplation," the intellectual and spiritual vision of God</term>, in which the soul, in the totality of its being, has God Himself as the Absolute as the sole object of its adequate vision. # IV. On the Moral Life.

...of the spirit is the principle of true morality, which then reveals itself in its consequences as a connected series of external activities within the created world. Only this internal state is good and involves <term>blessedness: "Seligkeit," a state of supreme spiritual happiness or salvation</term> and God’s pleasure; the works that are its consequences are not good in themselves, but only insofar as the inner work expresses itself through them. For that inner work and its outward fruitfulness in deeds are an inseparable and cohesive unity. —

It is clear that this Eckhartian concept of the inner work comes closest to the <term>Evangelical concept of faith: in this 19th-century German context, "evangelisch" refers to the Protestant doctrine of justification by faith alone</term>, if one is willing to set aside the mediation through the historical facts of revelation, which certainly belong as a necessary concrete object to the ecclesiastical concept of faith. Yet *Eckhart* incorporates the moral transformation of the entire human being more decisively into the inner work because it originates from the will. In contrast, with the concept of faith—where one usually thinks first of the theoretical faculty of the spirit—moral renewal tends to appear only, to a certain extent, as a second and additional element.

## 4. Virtue.

The inner work is a continuously unfolding resolution of the will. By establishing a permanent state of the spirit, it becomes the source of virtue. The inner work is the foundation; virtue is the consequence. The former describes the way in which the principle of a divine life is established within—a life capable of proving itself even in the individual tasks of one’s <term>earthly calling: "Beruf," referring to one's daily work or station in life seen as a God-given vocation</term>. Virtue, on the other hand, is that lasting quality of the spirit from which the correct and moral form of all actions, and all relationships of the spirit to the external world, necessarily arises as if from its own principle.

1. The inner work was defined as a constant inward turning toward God and a turning away from all that is ungodly. Virtue can have no other content. It is a constant remaining in God; its foundation is the love of God. Everything belongs to virtue that purely and exclusively...

## 4. Virtue.

Love for God is active within the soul (495, 22). However, Eckhart uses the strongest possible terms to guard against the view that the good is only good because it is God's will; rather, it is God's will because it is good and rational, and God can will nothing except what is good. He vehemently contradicts any way of thinking—whether unconscious or explicit—that would separate God, reason, and goodness, thereby making the moral law appear as the accidental whim of divine caprice. Love can only relate to God insofar as God himself is good and just, the <term>archetype: "Urbild," the original model or primary pattern</term> of all virtue and morality. Everything else is regarded as completely indifferent compared to this one and highest purpose.

Morality is its own highest purpose. The truly virtuous person does not love the good for the sake of some other goal, but for its own sake. The just are so earnest about justice that if one could even imagine that God were not just, they would not value God "the worth of a bean" <note>original: "nicht einer Bohne Werth"; a common medieval idiom meaning something is utterly worthless</note>. Indeed, they stand so firmly in justice and have surrendered themselves so completely that they heed neither the torments of hell nor the joys of heaven, nor anything else. Even if all the torment of those in hell, or all the torment ever suffered on earth or yet to be suffered, were attached to justice, they would not care in the slightest, so firmly do they cling to God and to justice (203, 28). If the devil were just, the just person would love him insofar as he was just, and not a hair’s breadth more. The just person loves nothing specific or particular in God; and if God were to give him all his wisdom and everything he could offer except himself, the person would not heed it and it would not please him. For he wants and desires nothing; he has no <term>finite ends: "endliche Zwecke," specific, limited goals or rewards in the material world</term> for the sake of which he would do anything. Just as God acts without finite ends, so too does the just person; and just as life is its own highest purpose, so the just person is determined by no finite ends in his actions (146, 10).

2. Therefore, virtue is incompatible with any kind of <term>seeking of reward: "Lohnsucht," a mercenary spirit or the desire for divine payment in exchange for good deeds</term>. The inner work is the person’s ever-renewed renunciation of self. How, then, could virtue coexist with a person desiring something for themselves in their actions? God is the absolute purpose; surrendering oneself to Him is the prerequisite—

### IV. On the Moral Life.

...foundation of all virtue. How could the virtuous person have any other purpose in mind than God himself? Virtue is selfless; it desires nothing for itself, it is not practiced with regard to anything else, nor for any reward to be expected. All those who guard against coarse sins, who would like to be good and perform their good works for God's honor, but nonetheless with the intention that God give them something in return or do what is pleasing to them: all these are like the merchants whom *Jesus* drove out of the temple <note>Referring to the Cleansing of the Temple in Matthew 21:12–13; Eckhart frequently used this as a metaphor for "spiritual merchants" who trade good deeds for divine favors.</note>. They want to give one thing for another and, as it were, conduct a trade with our Lord. But they are deceived in this trade. For everything they have and are able to achieve, they have from God, in order to achieve it all for God's sake. Therefore, God would owe them nothing to give or do, unless He chose to do it voluntarily and for free. God does not seek His own; in all His working He is detached and free, He works from love alone. So too the person who is united with God; he stands detached and free in all his actions; he performs them out of love and without an external purpose, solely for the glory of God; he does not seek his own interest therein, and God works it in him (34, 10).

One cannot condemn the <term>desire for reward: "Lohnsucht," the mercenary spirit of doing good only for gain</term> with harsher words than *Eckhart* has done. If any particular thought prevails or if any personal benefit is sought, it is no longer a virtue; rather, it becomes the opposite, a "**vice**" <note>original: "Untugend"; literally "un-virtue"</note> (a "splendid vice" <note>original: "glänzendes Laster"; a reference to Augustine’s *splendida vitia*, the idea that even the "virtues" of the prideful or godless are actually sins</note> in the sense of *Augustine*). And all virtue by its natural state is so constituted (106, 13). However, *Eckhart* counts as false desire for reward not only the consideration of earthly goods and temporal well-being: he also includes the striving for heavenly bliss within it. He finds in this latter pursuit only a finer and all the more dangerous <term>eudaemonism: a moral philosophy that defines the "good" in terms of what produces happiness or well-being</term>, which virtually cancels and destroys the moral character of all actions. The harshest expressions of *Fichte* <note>Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814), a German philosopher who emphasized duty and the "pure will" over personal happiness</note> against such a disposition are already found in the old Master, who is only even more rigid and abrupt in his consistency. For the formula "the good for the sake of the good" cannot yet satisfy him, insofar as the good has a specific, distinguishing content; instead, it transforms for him into the demand: become the Absolute itself and act in the manner of the absolute Being.

### 4. Virtue. 237

Virtue consists in this: that one acts from one's own innermost essence without any foreign consideration, and in acting, desires nothing at all except the acting itself. Therefore, just as an action can no longer be considered moral if it was done out of fear of hell, just as little can an action be considered moral which is determined by a consideration of eternal bliss. The desire for bliss is no better than any other <term>eudaimonistic: the ethical theory that personal happiness or well-being is the highest good</term> motive. Whoever seeks God and something else besides does not find God; but whoever seeks God alone finds God, and indeed not God alone, but everything God is able to offer in addition. If you do indeed seek God, but it happens for your own benefit or for the sake of your salvation, in truth, you are not seeking God. Seek God for God’s sake, truth for truth’s sake, and justice for justice’s sake. Once truth, justice, and goodness have truly taken hold of a person—even if all the torment of hell were attached to it—that person could never turn away from it even for a moment (58, 8). We should be so serious about virtue that the greater the torment associated with it, the greater our love for virtue would become (62, 15). 

As long as you still perform your works for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, or for God, or for your eternal bliss—that is, out of an external motive—you are not yet on the right path. People will praise you for it, but that is not the best way. If one were to ask a truly moral person, who acts out of his own <note>The term used is "Grunde" (ground), a central concept in Eckhart's mysticism referring to the deepest, uncreated part of the soul where man and God are one.</note> ground: "Why do you perform your works?", he could not answer otherwise than: "I act in order to act" (66, 7). 

Some people look at God as they look at a cow, and want to love Him as they love a cow. You love the cow for its milk and cheese, and generally for your own benefit <note>This is a famous analogy used by Meister Eckhart in his sermons to illustrate "mercenary" love toward the divine.</note>. All those who love God for the sake of external wealth or internal refreshment do the same; they do not love God in the right way, but rather they love Him out of self-interest. Every motive and every intention that is something other than God in Himself—however good it may otherwise be—is nevertheless only an obstacle to reaching true morality (70, 16). Whoever loves God so that something else which is not God might be granted to them acts like someone who seeks something by the light of a candle. Once he has found what he was looking for, he throws the candle away. As Judas

# IV. On the Moral Life.

If God could be sold, such a person would buy him. If what he desires is granted to him—whether it be devotion, spiritual refreshment, or whatever else might please him—he no longer concerns himself with God Himself (147, 18). God rewards all good, and what you give up for His sake, He returns to you a hundredfold. But if your intention is focused on this compensation, you achieve nothing; for in truth, you have given up nothing. A person should desire no reward, neither understanding and knowledge, nor emotional stirring and devotion, nor even peace of soul, but only God’s will (177, 2). The righteous person desires nothing at all in his works; for those who desire something and act for the sake of an external purpose are <term>servants and hirelings: those who work only for wages rather than out of love or duty</term>. If you do that which is capable of <term>forming you into God: the German "einbilden" here refers to the mystical process of being shaped into the divine image</term> with the specific intention that it accomplish this, the work becomes downright sinful through this alien secondary intention and actually removes you from God (189, 16). In the righteous person, nothing should act but God alone. If anything external drives you in your acting, then your works are <term>dead works: actions performed without spiritual life or grace, regardless of how "good" they look</term> (190, 17). If I had a friend and loved him with the intention that he should do me good and fulfill all my wishes, I would not be loving the friend, but rather myself. Thus, true love for God consists in being free of all selfishness and loving God alone for the sake of His goodness—for the sake of all that He is in Himself (259, 17). Whoever leaves earthly house and home, but does so with the intention of saving his soul, how little and how slight a thing has he actually left! (260, 4). The true and perfect essence of the spirit is to love God for His own goodness, even if heaven and hell did not exist (517, 22). <term>Servile fear: fear motivated by punishment rather than love</term> is when one avoids sin out of fear of the torments of hell and not out of love for God. Such fear squints with one eye at God and with the other at the torment. Mere natural fear, in which one fears things that harm our nature, is entirely indifferent and deserves neither reward nor punishment. For it is not a matter of free will; nor was it given to nature so that nature might be preserved by it, but rather it is a disturbance of nature that entered through <term>original sin: the inherited state of imperfection and separation from God</term> (368, 6). —

Such thoughts were not unheard of before Eckhart; however, no one had clothed them in such strong expressions. <note>Peter Abelard (1079–1142) was a famous medieval philosopher and theologian known for emphasizing the importance of internal intention in ethics.</note> Abelard also commands us to love God and not merely what He can give;

### 4. Virtue.

Saint *Bernard* <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic</note> calls only that love authentic and true which is free from any regard for a reward; he finds the deification of the soul only in the fact that one desires everything solely for God's sake. But while *Bernard* doubts whether a human being in this life can ever rise to this standpoint, *Eckhart* denies the moral character of any action taken from any other standpoint. He demands this pure love not merely as an ideal toward which one should gradually strive, but as something that must be fully realized right here on earth.

*Eckhart* finds true selflessness only in the relinquishing of all specific mental images and in the retreat into the <term>pure Nothing: in mystical theology, this "Nothing" (Nichts) is not a void of non-existence, but a state of being stripped of all "thing-ness" and ego to become one with God's essence</term>. However, it is impossible to arrive at a positive principle of the good will from this pure Nothing. If *Eckhart* merely rejected the carnal idea of sensory paradisiacal delights as the sought-after compensation for earthly renunciation, who would disagree with him? But in the face of this extreme sharpening of his thoughts, one might uphold the viewpoint of *Hugh of Saint Victor* <note>A 12th-century Saxon philosopher and theologian</note>: that a striving for the kingdom of heaven and blessedness should not be considered a motive foreign to moral action, so long as we only expect from blessedness that God give us Himself. — Furthermore, when *Eckhart* himself seeks to influence the moral decision of the will through the idea of an expected reward (as he often does), he makes—if not a theoretical—certainly a practical concession. This nonetheless implies the principle that such a directed action, even if it does not possess the highest value, still possesses some *value*.

3. There is, however, a second point to consider regarding *Eckhart's* definition of the essence of virtue. Virtue itself does not consist in a specific way of acting, nor does it derive its value from external works. It is just as valuable and just as good in the smallest work performed in the right way as it is in a thousand works; its value does not consist in the quantity of works. For if it were good because there were many works, it would not be good through itself (611, 20). Virtue, furthermore, is the constant, enduring <term>disposition: "Gesinnung," the internal moral orientation or "heart" behind an action</term> that remains the same; it cannot be present one moment and gone the next. Virtue truly exists only where not just individual virtuous acts are performed, but where the Good has become a permanent part of the character—

## 4. Virtue.

...think <note>The text likely refers here to a student of writing or art who must first consciously think about the rules before they become automatic</note> and imprint its image firmly upon himself. But once he has learned the art, he no longer needs to pay attention to every single detail; then he writes freely and unbound, practicing effortlessly the art that has become his second nature. Thus should man—after first practicing like a pupil—be so permeated by the God dwelling within him, so transformed into the form of the God he loves, and so established in Him, that the radiance of the God present within him shines out from him without any effort (549, 20). —

In *Eckhart's* teaching on the essence of virtue, we have before us a line of thought of immeasurable significance. It is well worth the effort to pause here for a moment. It is precisely here that the Master's teaching remains of high value even for our contemporaries. Let us briefly recall, in a few main features, the development of moral theory in the epoch that has just passed. Until *Kant*, a more or less openly acknowledged eudaimonism <note>Eudaimonism: an ethical theory that measures the "goodness" of an action by how much it contributes to human happiness or well-being</note> was generally accepted; in investigating the nature of the Good, one asked what purpose the Good served. The conviction that the Good is its own highest and ultimate end broke through powerfully with *Kant*, and all external considerations—except for the moral law itself—were banished from the realm of ethics. 

But for the father of modern German philosophy, the concept of "law" remained the highest expression of morality. Virtue consisted in the victory—which had to be fought for anew every single time—of the will obeying the law over resisting natural inclinations. The more difficult the victory won, the higher the value of the good deed. According to this view, the will holds the Good outside itself as a power that is initially foreign to it, as a rigid law to which it must submit in every given case. This law is formulated as a general principle obtained through abstract thought. Here, one certainly finds moral actions—each isolated for itself, each starting over from the beginning—but not a moral state of the entire human being. It is the standpoint of pure morality, of a strict service to the law that recalls the manner of the Old Covenant <note>Old Covenant: the author refers to the biblical legal tradition (the Law of Moses) which is often contrasted in Christian theology with an internalized "New Covenant" of the spirit</note>, with the only difference being that the content of the law originates from the legislation of thinking reason, rather than from revelation, and that it does not also extend to more or less

# IV. On the Moral Life.

...accidental forms of action, but refers solely to the fundamental relationships in the interaction of free beings with one another and with the entire external world. Rationalism <note>Rationalism: A philosophical movement emphasizing reason as the primary source of knowledge; here, the author suggests it views morality too much like a set of rigid, external rules</note>, even in theology, is essentially based on this external conception of morality as a legalistic action.

Schiller was the first to break the spell of these purely moral perspectives with lasting effect. This deeper conception of the ethical is his most personal possession; even in his pre-Kantian period, in the poem "The Artists" <note>original: "die Künstler"</note>, he knows that the law only "slowly drives faint blossoms," and he demands an education toward morality which gradually immerses the entire person in the element of freedom; to him, duties appear as a "slavish escort." The principle of a truly ethical worldview then dawned on him all the more clearly through his study of Kant; though the religious side of the matter remained foreign to him, he placed art in the place of religion, tasking it with the education of humanity—something he believed religion could not achieve. In this, he erred; but this demand for a genuine morality <term>Sittlichkeit</term> <note>Sittlichkeit: A German term for "ethical life" or "morality" that implies a living, social, and internal habit rather than just following abstract rules</note> instead of the Kantian ideal of virtue is the permanently significant element within it. If we set aside that error, the ethical ideal has hardly found a more beautiful or complete expression anywhere than in Schiller’s poetry. Who does not remember that incomparable poem: "The Ideal and Life" <note>original: "das Ideal und das Leben"</note> and especially the verses:

> "Take the divinity into your will, and it descends from its world-throne. The strict fetters of the law bind only the slave-mind that scorns it; with man’s resistance, the majesty of the god also vanishes."

We add only the prose passage found toward the end of the treatise "On Grace and Dignity" <note>original: "über Anmuth und Würde"</note>:

> "Love alone is thus a free sensation, for its pure source flows from the seat of freedom, from our divine nature. Here, it is not the small and lowly measuring itself against the great and high, nor the sense looking up dizzily at the law of reason; it is the absolutely great itself, which finds itself imitated in grace and beauty and satisfied in morality. It is the legislator himself, the God within us, who plays with his own image in the world of the senses."

— This ethical content in all his crea—

## 5. The Virtues.

A classification of the "one virtue" into many individual virtues—based on the varying relationship of the will to the external or internal world—is not found in **Eckhart**. Just as he always describes only the *form* of the virtuous will without designating a positive content for it, he also lacks the possibility of allowing the concept of virtue to unfold into its individual parts. He knows and names various virtues, but he does not present a principle for their division. The unity of all virtues is so predominant for him that he does not allow for any essential difference between them. There is only one morality <term>Sittlichkeit</term> <note>Sittlichkeit: Referencing the internal, lived ethical life rather than a set of external rules</note>, and for the ethical person, only one supreme point of view remains valid. Their striving should not be directed toward individual manifestations, but toward the essence of virtue itself. All virtues are necessarily interconnected (116, 2). If one virtue seems more important to you than the others, and if you value it above others, then you do not love it insofar as it belongs to morality, and God is not yet at work in you. As long as this is the case, a person is not yet truly ethical; for the ethical person loves and practices all virtues insofar as they belong to morality (190, 22).

Eckhart names the four cardinal virtues: wisdom, temperance, fortitude, and justice, and alongside them the three "divine" virtues of faith, hope, and love (244,

But he also lists twelve virtues in a quite arbitrary order, namely, in addition to those <note>Likely referring to the four cardinal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, discussed previously.</note>, the following six: humility, patience, fear, gentleness, mercy, and compassion (343, 1); in this instance, justice has been omitted, as its name in *Eckhart’s* work usually signifies morality <term>Sittlichkeit</term> <note>Sittlichkeit: A German term for the shared ethical life and customs of a community, but used here by Eckhart to mean the general state of being moral.</note> in general.

In this entire field, the greatest confusion reigns within *Eckhart’s* writings. Love and justice sometimes denote individual virtues, and at other times they are the principle of all virtue. Love, in particular, is identical with God, and as much as we dwell in love, so much do we dwell in God (377, 39). Love grants all virtues the ability to bear the name of virtue (606, 33). Where love is, it works great things; where holy and perfect works do not appear, love must be meager or not present at all (378, 17). If the soul were to strive for other virtues before love, it would have no virtue at all (352, 35). In all the impulses where we are stirred to love, nothing else drives us but the Holy Spirit. The goal toward which love directs all its outward effects is goodness, and this goodness is God. Just as my eye cannot speak, and my tongue cannot recognize colors, so love can direct itself toward nothing other than goodness. Nothing can be called good unless it happens in love. Love, however, should be pure, free, and detached <note>original: "rein, ledig und abgeschieden"; these are central terms in Eckhart's mysticism, referring to a soul emptied of worldly attachments and personal desires to make room for God.</note>; it should not be directed toward myself or my friend or anything outside itself, but only toward goodness and toward God himself (61, 4). Therefore, love extends to everything in the same way. If you love one person more than another, that is wrong; and if you love your father and your mother and yourself more than another, that is wrong; and if you love the state of bliss <term>Seligkeit</term> <note>Seligkeit: Often translated as "blessedness" or "salvation," referring to the ultimate state of spiritual joy in God.</note> more in yourself than in another, that is wrong. Every limb serves the whole body and, at the same time, every individual limb specifically, just as it serves itself and no less. It should be even more so in the kingdom of grace. What you love, you shall love in God; in Him, your neighbor is just as much the object of your love as you are yourself (208, 26). Among the other virtues, Eckhart discusses **humility** and **patience** most frequently. Since he places less emphasis on the consciousness of sinfulness <term>Sündhaftigkeit</term>, humility signifies for him rather the awareness of **creaturely finitude** <term>creatürliche Endlichkeit</term>—the willingness to receive from God and to surrender one’s own will. Whoever wishes to receive from above must necessarily keep themselves low in right humility (137, 22). The soul must strip itself of everything that does not belong to its essence; if we are to penetrate into **God's ground** <note>In Eckhart's mysticism, the "ground" (Grund) refers to the deepest, uncreated part of the soul where it is one with God.</note>, we must first go into our own ground in pure humility (225, 31). 

True humility is when a person remains aware of what they are by nature: a "something" created out of nothing. That in one's actions and omissions one does not choose for oneself, but instead waits for enlightenment through grace to find the right path—that is the true **humility of nature**. In contrast, **humility of the spirit** is when one attributes the good that God works within them to themselves as little as they did when they did not yet exist (295, 21). 

Now, this humility also manifests itself toward other people. The righteous consider themselves the most unworthy people on earth; therefore, they are able to humble themselves beneath all people (478, 3). In true humility, where one remains silent while others scold, one truly overcomes. To answer others back until they must be silent is not to overcome, but to be overcome (639, 7). 

—Moreover, the humility that Eckhart preaches is a very **proud humility**. He seeks to awaken nothing so eagerly in his listeners as the high consciousness of their own calling and their own **likeness to God** <term>Gottähnlichkeit</term>. He has at times given this proud consciousness a daring expression, and if he has neglected one virtue in his preaching of Christianity, it is precisely that of humility <note>The author suggests that Eckhart's focus on the soul's inherent divinity can seem at odds with traditional, self-effacing humility.</note>.

Eckhart is tireless in his praise of **patience**. To him, it is only another expression for that total surrender of one's own will and interest, that boundless...

### IV. Of the Moral Life.

**Surrender** <term>Hingabe</term> <note>In the context of German mysticism, *Hingabe* implies a total yielding or abandonment of the self to God.</note> to God forms the essence of virtue. From this it follows immediately that a person receives everything in the same way from the hands of God, that in **pure passivity** <term>reiner Passivität</term> <note>This does not mean "doing nothing," but rather being perfectly receptive to God's action within the soul, without the interference of one's own ego.</note> they willingly allow whatever God sends to wash over them, and are as joyful in suffering as in prosperity. The righteous hunger and thirst so greatly for the will of God, and it pleases them so well, that they wish to want or desire nothing other than what God decrees for them. And if God wished to release them from it, they would not want to be released. Whatever God gives to the righteous person—sickness, poverty, or whatever else it may be—that person prefers it to anything else because God wills it. If it were not God’s will, in that same moment it would also not be theirs. If God's will pleased you, then you would be just as if you were in heaven, regardless of what happens or does not happen to you. For to those who desire something other than God's will, what happens is quite just: they are always in misery and distress, they are often subjected to violence and injustice, and they find suffering everywhere (146, 32).

And one should accept willingly and joyfully not only external suffering—hunger, thirst, cold, shame, and the like—but also spiritual deprivation and sadness. If God wanted to annihilate us or throw us into **Hell**, we should not want nor desire that God preserve us in our being or protect us from Hell; rather, we should let God do with us exactly as He wills, as if we did not exist. God should be just as powerful in everything you are as He is in His own uncreated nature (293, 31). We deafen God night and day saying: "Lord, Thy will be done." And then when God's will actually happens, we are angry and it does not suit us at all.

When *our* will becomes *God’s* will, that is good; but when *God’s* will becomes *our* will, that is far better. If your will becomes God’s will, and you are sick, you would not want to be healthy against God's will, but you would still *wish* that it were God's will for you to be healthy. And if things go poorly for you, you would *wish* it were God's will that things went well. But when **God’s will becomes your will**: if you are sick, then [you say] "in God's name"; if your friend dies, "in God's name." It is a certain and necessary truth: even if all the pain of Hell and Purgatory and the world depended on it, the pious person would gladly suffer it eternally with God's will and would forever consider it his eternal bliss <term>Seligkeit</term>, and [grant] all the saints their bliss...

It highlights the distinction between merely aligning one's will with God and the higher state where God's will entirely replaces the individual's desires.</summary>

## 6. The Virtuous State.

While Eckhart does not provide a detailed explanation of the essence of virtue in itself or of the various specific virtues, he does depict, in many strokes, how the moral person conducts themselves amidst the circumstances of this earthly life. He first sets forth the highest and most ideal requirement: that a person should no longer be touched at all by anything sensory or finite. Secondly, however, he moderates—or rather, clarifies—this demand by demonstrating to what extent and to what degree such involvement in the machinery of finite things is inseparable from earthly life, and how the divine principle then proves itself within the moral person in relation to the earthly.

1. First, then, the state of the moral person is described as **perfect passivity**, **indifference** <note>In this context, "indifference" refers to *Gelassenheit* or detached equanimity—a state of being unmoved by worldly gains or losses.</note> toward all things except the One Absolute, and an **immovability** and **closedness** against all impressions from without. We are to become more immovable than the "Nothing" we were before we were created—that "Nothing" which needed nothing, was capable of nothing, and resisted everything except the divine power. It was this power that made the Nothing "movable" when God created all things out of nothing. The soul should gather all its powers into its free will so that it remains unhindered by itself and by all things; it should be completely absorbed into the **immovable God**, who was never moved by any of the workings of the **Trinity** <note>original: *Dreieinigkeit*</note>, nor ever stood in need of such activity. The soul must sink itself so completely into the **groundless ground** <term>grundloser Grund</term> <note>Eckhart’s term for the absolute essence of the Godhead, which is "groundless" because it has no cause and is beyond human understanding.</note> of the **divine Nothing** <term>göttliches Nichts</term> <note>A concept in "negative theology" where God is called "Nothing" because He is no-thing; He transcends all categories of being that humans can name.</note> that nothing has the power to pull it out, so that it never turns toward the lower things and, as far as is possible for creatures, remains as steadily within it as...

Well then, noble soul, go out of yourself, never again to return; enter into God, never again to step out of Him, and hold yourself fast there, never again to turn toward the creature <note>In medieval theology, "the creature" refers to any created thing, as opposed to the Creator.</note>. Do not burden yourself with what is announced to you; do not let yourself be led astray by what lies before your eyes, and do not delay yourself with any kind of servitude or external performance. This immovability results in a perfect indifference <note>original: *Indifferenz*; in this mystical context, it refers to *Gelassenheit* or "releasement"—a state where one is equally unmoved by worldly success or failure.</note> toward everything external and freedom from all affects <note>original: *Affecten*; these are the passions or emotions that disturb the soul's equilibrium.</note>. 2. But this abstention from all activities and all affects is not a standpoint to be realized on earth. This earthly life is the necessary passage in the divine process toward a higher form of life, and therefore all the consequences that necessarily arise from the form of earthly existence are themselves morally justified. One only needs to pay attention to that which is the unavoidable result of sensory existence to see that the demand for that perfect immovability cannot be fulfilled for the external life. Therefore, the actual task, even according to the Master's <note>Referring to Meister Eckhart.</note> view, is to transfigure the earthly in itself while still here. Then the struggle is transformed into delight, and what man must win with great effort now becomes a joy of the heart <note>original: *Herzensfreude*</note>, and only then does it become truly fruitful (53, 14). 

So also say some well-meaning people, that one should become so perfect that no joy can move us and that one should be untouchable by joy and sorrow. In this, they are not right. There was never a saint so holy that he could not have been moved. But this much is granted to the saint even here on earth: that nothing is able to move him *away from God*. ## IV. On the Moral Life.

...and grace: if someone were to challenge a person's faith or anything else they held dear, if that person were completely seized by grace, they would remain indifferent in joy and sorrow. But it is well for the saint that nothing is able to move him out of God; and even if the heart is tormented, as if the person were not in a state of grace, the will nevertheless stands firm in God and says: "Lord, I in you and you in me!" Whatever then touches the person does not hinder eternal bliss, as long as it does not reach the highest peak of the spirit <note>original: *obersten Wipfel des Geistes*; in mystical theology, this is the 'spark of the soul' or the highest faculty where the human and divine meet.</note>, up there where it stands in unity with God’s most beloved will (52, 18). A good person can quite easily be a good person and yet be touched and waver by natural love for father and mother, to a greater or lesser degree, and yet not fall away from God and goodness. And yet, he is good and better to the degree that he is less or more delighted and touched, and becomes aware of natural love and affection for father and mother, for sister and brother, and for himself. Nevertheless, if a person could accept this as God’s will—insofar as it is God’s will that man should have this imperfection, especially through God’s justice because of the sin of the first man—and even regardless of that, would gladly do without it because it was God’s will: then he would be quite right in his mind and would certainly be comforted in his suffering (427, 22).

Therefore, because a person is moved, he does not lose divine enlightenment. For everything temporal is moved within time. But certainly, the less a person is movable, the more he is already placed out of time and into eternity. Only when we set our foot upon all creatures <note>In this context, 'creatures' refers to all created things or worldly attachments.</note> do we first reach the hem of the Godhead: and that is called a spiritualized naturalness (641, 17; ibid., 32). Immovability never becomes so much a part of a person's essence that the living stirrings of the sensory nature could not be awakened without the participation of reason. But as soon as it is seized by reason, it vanishes, and the person stands indifferent as before; and then the person is not a person after the human fashion, but is a deified person <note>original: *vergotteter Mensch*; a central concept in Meister Eckhart's thought, referring to a soul that has been transformed by grace to share in the divine nature.</note> (643, 26). ### 6. The Virtuous State.

The root remains unshaken. Thus, one must sometimes use harsh words that outwardly appear as agitation; but the inner self should remain fixed in the One (666, 31). The natural **physicality** <note>original: *Leiblichkeit*; our bodily existence and the sensations that come with it.</note> is constantly seized by joy and sorrow, and it never loses this capacity. But the **will** stands with **equanimity** <note>original: *gleichmüthig*; a state of mental calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation.</note> in both joy and sorrow, and the capacity for any inappropriate action is taken away from the person to whom eternal light is given (667, 6). The soul is by nature skillful, while the body is unwieldy and material. That this material unwieldiness should be as skillful as the spirit's ideal nature is not granted to a body before the **transfiguration** <note>original: *Verklärung*; in Christian theology, the glorification of the body in the afterlife, making it like the spirit.</note>. The eye’s own specific purpose is to see colors, and the ear’s is to hear sounds. In this, there is no fault, no obstacle to becoming a partaker of the eternal truth. As true as it is that one should be free of such things, yet it cannot be. One thing I tell you, and let this be enough: that the will and love should fall out of balance—that will be taken away from you. Even more: even the mere *possibility* of going astray with will and love is taken away from the soul, and thus its capacity has become its very being, an essential power. The true sign that it has become your being is this: that whatever you do outwardly never brings disturbing **representations** <note>original: *Vorstellungen*; mental images, thoughts, or perceptions of the external world that can distract the mind from spiritual focus.</note> into the depths of the soul (668, 10).

3. That, then, is the actual task: not that a person should withdraw entirely with all their powers from the changing gears of things, but rather that the spirit should not be consumed by the unrest of this activity, by the multiplicity of these cares, or by the movement of this struggle. If the outer man can never be at rest, then instead, in the deepest essence of the soul, in the <term>Spark<gloss>original: *Fünklein*; in medieval mysticism, this refers to the 'spark of the soul' (seelenfünklein), the innermost core of the human being that remains eternally in contact with God.</gloss></term>, this rest shall reign, immovable and unshakable. Let the soul simply not cling with pleasure to any representations or to any desires; let there always be only the striving and the longing for rest in God. Let only the Spark of the soul be at all times with God and united with God. Therein lies the condition of the virtuous person. But this manifests in every individual expression of a person's life, as all powers of the soul and body are determined by it. Just as the light goes out from the sun and is first communicated by the sun to the air, and from the air is further bestowed upon all that is receptive to light, exactly so is it in the soul.

## IV. On the Moral Life.

God births his Word in the soul, and the soul receives it and offers it further to its **powers** <note>original: *Kräfte*; the various psychological and spiritual faculties of a human being, such as memory, will, and intellect.</note> in manifold ways: sometimes as a desire, sometimes as a good intention, sometimes in works of love, sometimes in gratitude, or however else it may take hold of you. All this is God’s working in you, and you should view it as his and not as your own (21, 33). A right order should exist in the soul; that is, the lower powers should subordinate themselves to the higher ones. When a lord wants to organize his people, the servant is under the knights and the knight is under the count; for they all desire to have peace, and therefore each one helps the other. In this same way, every power should be subject to the others and help them strive, so that there may be nothing but peace and rest in the soul (160, 38). The **outer man** <note>The physical, sensory self that interacts with the material world.</note> can be busy, while the **inner man** <note>The spiritual self that remains focused on the divine.</note> stands entirely **free** <note>original: *ledig*; detached or unencumbered by worldly affairs.</note> of it and is motionless. Just as the door turns on its **hinge** <note>original: *Angel*; a classic mystical metaphor for the soul's stillness—the door moves, but the center point remains fixed.</note>—so that while the door moves, the hinge remains motionless—so it is here. The person who loves God uses the powers of the soul in the outer man no further than the five senses necessarily require. The inner self turns toward the five senses no further than as a guide and leader, ensuring they do not turn toward animal pleasure. The soul leaves all higher powers to the inner man, and when the inner man turns to a high and glorious object, the soul also draws back the powers it had lent to the five senses; the person is then called "free of the senses" and **ecstatic** <note>original: *verzückt*; a state of being "carried away" or in a spiritual rapture where one is unaware of the physical environment.</note> (489, 17. 488, 30). This is the soul’s beauty: that it be well ordered. The soul should be ordered with the lowest powers under the highest, and with the highest under God; the outer senses under the inner senses, these under the **intellect** <note>original: *Verstand*.</note>; the intellect under **reason** <note>original: *Vernunft*.</note>, reason under the **will** <note>original: *Willen*.</note>, and the will into **unity** <note>The highest point of the soul where it is one with God.</note>, so that the soul may be alone and nothing else may enter it but the **Godhead** <note>original: *Gottheit*; the essential nature of God beyond specific persons or attributes.</note> (514, 12). The highest powers should be raised into God, entirely given over and dedicated to him. But all suffering should be left to the body, the lowest powers, and the senses; the spirit, on the other hand, should rise with its whole strength and simply sink itself into its God. The suffering of the senses and of the lower powers, and their temptations, do not concern the spirit (567, 15).

Thus, the moral person has, to a certain extent, a dou-

This coexistence of the two natures was present in no one more perfectly than in Christ. Therefore, Christ is the highest realization of the moral ideal, and every virtuous life appears from the perspective of an **imitation of Christ** (567, 9).

### 7. The Imitation of Christ.

What Eckhart taught regarding the Christ of revelation we shall consider later. Here we are concerned only with the fact that Eckhart linked his ideal of the **perfectly moralized human** <note>original: *ganz versittlichten Menschen*; a person whose entire being has been transformed by ethical and spiritual principles.</note> to the biblical conception of Christ, though certainly not without reshaping the image of Christ found in Holy Scripture in essential ways. The person in whom the entire divine essence dwells without any subtraction, who is himself entirely elevated and entered into the divine essence, and who now perfectly proves this divine principle in earthly life—this person Eckhart calls "Christ." He is identical with the **eternal Word** <note>The *Logos*, or the Second Person of the Trinity.</note> which God has birthed, with the second person in the Trinity. Such a person has existed once and has represented the absolute Divine in joy and sorrow, in the highest bliss and the heaviest torments, in interaction with God and with men. To follow the tracks of this holy life, to become Christ’s disciple and follower, that is our moral task. Through this, each of us becomes precisely that same Christ and exactly as he is. The abstract principle of morality becomes a concrete vision in the image of Christ.

Christ alone—the saints are explicitly excluded from this dignity—is our end, whom we follow, and our goal, toward which we should strive and with which we should be united in the equality of all his honors, according to the measure that the union belongs to us (295, 7). The true confessors of God take the life and the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ as a model for all their lives, in order to...

The spirit increases and receives God's nature by following the person of Christ and his human nature (515, 12). But the highest rule is this: one should pursue Christ's humanity until one grasps the divinity and becomes free of humanity with its painful and pleasurable perceptions (636, 29) <note>Eckhart suggests that the physical life of Christ is a "ladder" to be climbed and then eventually transcended to reach the pure Godhead.</note>. The soul should practice with constant diligence in the model of Christ's humanity. For thus, God first becomes familiar to her and comes to her as a King of friendship (348, 17).

There are two traits in particular that *Eckhart*, influenced by the way of thinking of his time, emphasizes in the *Image of Christ*: first, that the absolutely holy one was also the one most heavily burdened with suffering and bore this suffering joyfully and willingly; second, that he was poor and desired to be absolutely poor. In suffering, the perfect surrender of self-will and unity with the divine will was proven; in poverty, the renunciation of the world, of all things, and of all pleasure in selfhood <note>original: *Eigenheit*; refers to the "own-ness" or ego-driven attachment to oneself.</note> was revealed. These now are the two main characteristics of the true followers of Christ: willing *suffering* and perfect *poverty*.

### 8. *Suffering.*

In Christ, nothing was present in such high measure as *suffering*. Therefore, next to God, there is nothing more glorious than *suffering*. When Christ was born, *suffering* also appeared and did not leave him as long as he was human on earth. And had Christ been only human without divinity, his *suffering* would nonetheless have elevated him above the entire human race. For he who suffers most is the most glorious. If there were anything more glorious than *suffering*, we would have been redeemed by it. *Right suffering* is the mother of all virtue; for it wards off pride and makes one humble and chaste; it kills all vice and erases all sin (337, 26 ff.). What can be too difficult for a person to suffer when he considers the *suffering* of him who was in divine form? The good soldier does not complain of his wounds when he looks upon the king who is wounded with him. He offers us a drink that he himself has previously

In the deepest suffering lies the highest blessing. Without suffering, man cannot reach his salvation <term>Heil: a term encompassing both spiritual health and eternal salvation</term>. Only in the darkness of suffering and hardship does the light reach us. The darkness of suffering is to be transformed into bright light; yet our intention should not be focused on this reward; we should find sufficiency in the suffering as such (334, 27). Nothing is more bitter than suffering, nothing sweeter than having suffered. Joy brings sorrow and sorrow brings joy (492, 23). The greater the suffering, the lesser it is, like two buckets at a well: the heavier one is, the lighter the other becomes <note>Eckhart suggests that as the "weight" of divine grace increases, the subjective "burden" of the suffering decreases.</note>. If you suffer for your own sake, the suffering hurts you and becomes heavy for you to bear. If you suffer for God's sake, and for God's sake alone, the suffering does not hurt you and is not heavy for you; for God bears the burden (45, 22). A good person should have such trust in God that it is impossible for God to allow suffering to happen to a person unless God intended to spare the person much greater suffering, or provide much richer comfort, or offer a much better good (425, 27). More truly, one receives God in lack than in receiving. For if a person receives, the gift itself contains what makes the person happy and comforted. But if one receives nothing, one has nothing, and finds and knows nothing to rejoice in except God and God's will alone (427, 4). How then can suffering cause me sorrow, if suffering becomes free from sorrow when held within God? Anyone who would take away from a friend a few days of suffering—knowing it would bring that friend great benefit, honor, and well-being for a long time—would not truly be a friend and would not love him. Therefore, God would not permit His friends to ever be without suffering, provided they were willing to suffer and were able to suffer without [feeling] the distress of suffering (443, 29. 444, 2).

### 9. Poverty.

Christ, the absolute model, was not only the one who suffered most; he was also the poorest of all. And just as his suffering is to be our model—to suffer as willingly and joyfully as he did—so his poverty should drive us to find our greatest wealth in the most extreme poverty.

Poverty is another expression for the highest degree of detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit: the state of being "cut off" or "released" from worldly attachments to allow God to act within the soul</term>. But while detachment refers more to the internal relationship of the spirit toward God and created things—forming the foundation and prerequisite for sanctification—poverty is a specific element of the virtuous life itself. It repeats the theme of detachment in its practical application regarding the treatment of all earthly and finite things.

### 9. Poverty.

This [poverty] is good and very much to be praised in a person who takes it upon himself joyfully out of love for Christ; for Christ himself possessed it while on earth. But there is another kind: inward poverty. It is in this sense that the Lord’s word is to be understood: "Blessed are the poor in spirit." <note>Matthew 5:3. In Eckhart's theology, this is the highest virtue.</note> A poor person is one who wants nothing, knows nothing, and has nothing. As long as a person still has the will to fulfill God’s will, he is not yet truly poor. If a person wishes to be truly poor, he must be as free of his created <term>will</term> <note>The "created will" refers to our individual human desires, which must be set aside to make room for God.</note> as he was when he did not yet exist. Furthermore, he must be poor in all his own knowledge, so that he knows nothing—neither God, nor the <term>creature</term> <note>original: "Créatur"; in medieval philosophy, this refers to any created thing (animals, people, objects) as opposed to the uncreated God.</note>, nor himself. Finally, the poor person has nothing; he does not even have a place within himself where God could act. All distinction and all separation cease there; we are free of God himself as a being distinct from us, and when God acts in the person, He acts in Himself (280–282. 417–418). Whoever truly desires poverty has such a need for it that he does not begrudge anyone else having less of it than he does. <note>Essentially, the virtuous person is so devoted to poverty that he wishes for everyone to attain the same high level of spiritual detachment.</note> And so it is with all virtues; he wants to reach the highest point, to always occupy the highest stage that can be reached here below, and does not tolerate anyone being above him (276, 4).

Poverty encompasses all essential requirements for the moral person. It describes that state in which a person, free and unencumbered by everything finite, has turned toward the Absolutely Simple <note>The "Absolutely Simple" refers to the unified, uncomplicated essence of God.</note> in the innermost part of his being. Those who are willingly poor give up friends, possessions, and the world's honor; they plunge themselves into the valley of <term>humility</term> and bear the shame and hatred of the world. They keep themselves free from guilt and all faults; they cling to nothing that is finite; they desire no reward; they forget all individuality and flow with everything they are into the <term>bottomless abyss</term> <note>original: "grundlosen Abgrund"; a central term in German mysticism describing the infinite depth of God where the soul loses its individual identity.</note> of their origin. Without this willing poverty, no one can reach their highest destiny in knowledge and life (393, 4; ibid., 17 and 38). The poor in spirit are those who have left all things to God, just as He had them when we did not yet exist (533, 20).

Along with the <term>imitation of Christ</term> in willing suffering and in poverty, a state is described—not so much of the soul's powers, but rather of the <term>ground of the soul</term>. <note>original: "Seelengrund"; the deepest, spark-like essence of the human soul that Eckhart believed was identical to God's own essence.</note> The task now is to [bring] this state into real life and the world of finite things...

## 10. The Contemplative and the Active Life.

1. The state of perfect poverty is the state of perfect immersion in the Absolute. Insofar as a person wants nothing, knows nothing, and has nothing, there remains only an immediate relationship to the absolutely indeterminate, which can only be understood by analogy to the purely theoretical activity of reason: it is the state of pure intuition. The first requirement for one who wishes to follow Christ is thus that he always have the Godhead present within the <term>spark of the soul</term> <note>original: "Fünklein des Geistes"; in Eckhart's thought, this is the uncreated core of the human spirit that is capable of direct union with God.</note>, and that he lead a <term>contemplative life</term> <note>The "contemplative life" (vita contemplativa) refers to a life focused on prayer and internal reflection rather than external work.</note>.

Contemplation is the state of perfect rest. It belongs to the contemplative life that all individual powers of the soul fall silent as such, all being gathered into the one center of the soul; that all particular soul-activities cease and that the entire energy of the soul be turned toward only one thing: the resting, timeless contemplation of the absolute Being. It is the characteristic essence of reason only to act inwardly upon itself. The Godhead acts only within itself and all its acting flows back into itself; what goes out from it remains, rather, within it. In this way, reason should act. It must not go out from itself; it must be closed off against everything external. It should not allow itself to be pulled out of itself by clinging to any specific ideas or desires; and when it relates everything to itself, it should relate it to itself not as a characteristically determined being, but insofar as it is the Absolute itself.

But <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "Contemplation"</note> would not be of the right kind if it sought to place itself in hostile opposition to the <term>active life</term> <note>original: "wirkenden Leben"; the life of external work, service, and duty.</note>. Earthly life has its unavoidable demands that seek to be fulfilled. So long as the soul is in this body, the needs of finite existence approach it with the full justification of divine obligation; it must place itself with active love into the conditions of its own life and into the interests of its brothers. Contemplation and this...

Earlier and later mystics have assumed such a contrast between the contemplative and the practicing or active life, as if the two excluded one another—as if <term>contemplation</term> <note>The practice of deep, silent prayer and focus on the divine.</note> could not endure earthly activity, nor the busyness of action endure the rest of contemplation. Thus, contemplation was regarded as the higher state, as the only condition perfectly corresponding to the divine will, and a monastic life of withdrawal from all worldly occupations and needs was seen as the life of true holiness. It is the merit especially of **Saint Bernard** <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic who balanced a life of intense prayer with significant political and ecclesiastical activity.</note> to have emphatically countered such a one-sided view. However, even he does not move beyond the ideal of monastic holiness. **Eckhart** treats the same question much more thoroughly and, by virtue of the richer premises of his teaching, much more deeply; the result he achieves is far more satisfying.

2. To describe pure contemplation, no expression is too bold or too high for the Master. It is from grace that one reaches the goal. Grace excites desire and draws the soul out of itself, so that with grace and in grace it goes beyond grace into God and arrives at its first origin. There, all senses fall silent; the will of the soul and the will of God flow into one another and embrace each other lovingly in perfect union. There, the soul can perform nothing more and nothing less than divine works, because nothing lives within it anymore but God. There, an arrow is shot without anger, and one feels it without pain; there, the pure and clear fountain of the **medicine of grace** is opened, which illuminates the inner eye so that it perceives, in blissful intuition, the delight of divine visitation. In this state, one finds spiritual treasures of things never heard, which have never been heard nor preached and never recorded in a book (401, 22). God raises the soul above all conceptions of material and transitory things. In this blessed union with God, the soul has no coming or going, nor pleasure or sorrow from any thing; there, it possesses all things in the eternal, unchangeable <term>Now</term> <note>original: "Nu"; in Eckhart’s philosophy, the "Now" refers to the "Eternal Present," a state where past and future vanish in the presence of God.</note>, in the eternity that is God Himself.
