# IV. On the Moral Life.

...lifts the soul even above every duty of internal or external action (375, 37).

But this insensitivity and immobility cannot rule in the soul alone and exclusively. If it did, the connection between the soul and the body would cease, and earthly life would be destroyed before its time. Rather, this quiet <term>contemplation</term> <note>The practice of deep, silent spiritual focus on the divine.</note> must be able to exist within the turbulence of feeling, willing, and desiring. And this is indeed the case. Contemplation must not be one state existing alongside others; instead, it must permeate all human states equally. The task is for this contemplative <term>union with God</term> <note>A mystical state where the human soul feels one with the divine presence.</note> to become the very essence of the person, not a mere passing state. It should be ever-present, even when it does not fill the foreground of conscious thought. Like the fundamental tone of the entire spiritual life, it should resonate through all the diverse activities of the spirit, neither disturbing nor thwarting them, but rather directing them all toward a single goal: that this immersion in God may restore itself with ever greater strength and vitality. Contemplation belongs to the <term>ground of the soul</term> <note>German: "Seelengrund"—a central concept in German mysticism referring to the deepest, most essential part of the human being where God dwells.</note>, while the active life belongs to the "powers" or faculties of the mind. The two do not contradict one another; rather, one is supported and sustained by the other.

If a person were to remain uninterrupted in a state of unity with God, that would by no means be the best thing. For in such a state, a person could perform no work other than a single divine work. However, man is called to perform many works, and for this reason, it is necessary that the highest power of the soul keep its gaze fixed firmly on salvation in God, but that it also communicates what it beholds to the lower powers. It must grant these lower powers a <term>discursive knowledge</term> <note>Logical, step-by-step reasoning, as opposed to the direct, intuitive "seeing" of contemplation.</note> of good and evil (496, 29). Contemplation, therefore, demands a living activity of all powers. **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Italian Dominican friar and philosopher who sought to synthesize Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology.</note> teaches that the active life is better than the contemplative life in those instances where one’s activity flows out in love, giving to others what was drawn into oneself during contemplation. In such a case, there is still only one thing; for one grasps the divine nowhere better than in that very ground of contemplation, and then allows it to become fruitful in one's activity, thereby fulfilling the purpose of contemplation. And even if movement is associated with this, it is still only one thing; it comes from a single starting point and returns to the same. ### 10. The Contemplative and the Active Life.

...indeed movement and yet it would be only one in one. Thus, in this activity, one possesses nothing lower and nothing higher than that contemplation within oneself. The one rests upon the other and fulfills the other. For God intends the fruitfulness of action within the unity of contemplation; for in contemplation you serve yourself alone, but in the practice of virtue you serve the many. Christ exhorts us to this through his entire life and the lives of all his saints, all of whom he has driven to serve the many. Therefore Timothy is instructed to preach the word <note>Reference to 2 Timothy 4:2: "Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season."</note>, not the outward word that strikes the air, but the inward word hidden in the soul. He was to preach this word so that it would become known to the [soul’s] powers and they might feed upon it, and so that the person might enter into all outward life where a neighbor might have need, so that all of this might be found in you as you accomplish it according to your strength. It should be within you in thought, in reason, in will, and radiate forth in works. In this sense Christ spoke: "Let your light shine before men." <note>Matthew 5:16. The author uses this to argue that spiritual depth must result in visible good deeds.</note> This is spoken against those who only cultivate contemplativeness, but renounce the practice of virtue and say they have no need of it, for they have moved beyond it.

Of course, many finite mental images <note>original: "Vorstellungen"—the concepts or mental pictures the mind uses to process the world.</note> belong to this acting. Every work arises from a specific mental image—inner as well as outer works, such as teaching and comforting and ordering. In this, that rest and concentration seem to cease. But rather: everything that the <term>active intellect</term> <note>German: *wirkende Vernunft*. In medieval philosophy, this is the part of the mind that takes in raw sensory data and turns it into abstract thoughts or "images."</note> does in a natural person, God does the same and far more in a <term>detached</term> <note>German: *abgeschiedenen*. A central concept in German mysticism referring to a soul that has "cut itself off" from worldly desires and self-will to be totally open to God.</note> person. He takes the <term>active intellect</term> away from him and sets Himself in its place, and there He performs everything that the <term>active intellect</term> was supposed to perform. Indeed, when the person empties himself completely and the <term>active intellect</term> is silent within him, then God must undertake the work and be the master craftsman Himself and be born into the <term>passive intellect</term> <note>German: *leidende Vernunft*. Also known as the "potential" or "receptive" intellect; the part of the soul that receives knowledge or divine illumination.</note>. The <term>active intellect</term> can only ever have one mental image after another. But when God takes its place, He generates a fullness of images all at once and as one. When God thus drives you toward a good work, immediately all your powers stand ready for all good things; your mind is immediately directed toward everything good. Whatever good you are capable of expresses itself and stands ready, all at once in one vision and in

...a single moment. Active reason <note>original: "wirkende Vernunft"—the "agent intellect," a concept in medieval philosophy describing the part of the mind that makes thinking possible by processing sensory data into abstract concepts.</note> would not be capable of that; thus it is clearly God’s work, who carries all mental images within himself as one. Therefore, those images are also not yours and do not belong to nature, but to the Master Craftsman of nature, who works them and has imprinted his image within them. Do not credit it to yourself, for it is his and not yours. Even if you receive it in a temporal form, it is nonetheless begotten and given by God beyond time and in eternity, beyond all pictorial form. — Now, of course, all spiritual powers must always have a specific, finite object for their activity. For this very reason, reason never rests in this life; rather, an unquenchable longing fills it, driving it ever further beyond everything specific into pure being. Everything that God reveals to us of himself in this life is as nothing compared to what he is in himself. Even if truth is present in the ground of the soul, it is nonetheless covered and hidden from reason. Therefore, reason strives ever higher with unsatisfied longing. But this longing does not disturb the inner stillness and recollection. If you have completely emptied yourself of yourself and surrendered <note>The German "gelassen" refers to *Gelassenheit*, a central concept in Eckhart’s mysticism meaning "releasement" or a state of letting go of one's own will to let God act.</note> to God: whatever then emerges within you and takes hold of you, that is not yours—it is your God's, to whom you have surrendered, just as the word does not actually belong to the one who hears it, but to the one who speaks it (18—21).

Throughout, the contrast between the active and the contemplative life is linked to the figures of Mary and Martha <note>In Luke 10:38–42, Martha works while Mary listens to Jesus. Mary is still in the stage of preparation; Martha has vividly grasped the truth. She has won it as her full possession through living experience and by habituation in all virtue; the highest good has become her very essence, and she can therefore express it in an active life. In contemplation <note>original: "Beschaulichkeit"—the quiet, meditative state of looking upon the divine.</note>, there is the danger that one might remain immersed in devotion out of a sense of pleasure and not progress further to truly perform God’s works. Mary must first become what Martha already was; she is still going to school and learning how to live. Martha had already attained a well-practiced virtue, fortified within itself, and a freedom of the mind that no storm of external things can hinder; Mary should first...

...still to be won. In this mystical tradition—particularly in Meister Eckhart’s thought—Martha represents the more mature stage where contemplation has become so internalized that it can coexist with outward activity.</note>. Some people wish to reach a state where they are free from activity. This cannot be. Only after the disciples had received the Holy Spirit did they begin to practice virtue. Christ himself is the proof. From the beginning—from the moment God became man and man became God—he began to work for our salvation until the very end, when he died on the cross. There was no limb of his body that did not practice virtue in its own specific way (47—53).

It is indeed true that the inner stillness of contemplation surpasses all works of the outer person in glory and inner joy. But even if the inner life is better in itself, the outer is sometimes better when there is a need for physical help; thus, it is better to provide food to the hungry than to indulge in inner contemplation at that moment (328, 37. 330, 30). And were a person in a state of ecstasy <note>original: "Verzückung"—a rapturous spiritual state or trance.</note> like St. Paul, and he knew of a sick person who needed a little bowl of soup from him, it would be much better if you abandoned the ecstasy out of love and served the needy person. In this, one should not imagine that they are being robbed of grace. For whatever a person joyfully lets go of out of love, they receive back much more gloriously (553, 38).

Thus, the whole life of Mary, the mother of Jesus, was a reproach to all imperfect existence. She lived among people for this reason: so that they might be drawn to God through her good example. She comforted the sorrowful, strengthened weak faith, and never refused her counsel to anyone. But now, people who strive for the appearance of holiness flee into monasteries and hermitages <note>original: "Klöster und Klausen"—monasteries and secluded monastic cells or enclosures.</note> to be free from the temptation of earthly things. That may be good if they think only of God in doing so; but it is to be feared that some think more of themselves than of God (340, 26).

If the spirit works according to the likeness of God’s activities, then the outer person must work according to the likeness of the spirit (385, 29). ## 11. The Principle of Moral Action.

Earthly life thus imposes the duty on the moral person to work within earthly matter. The life in God, which constitutes the character of morality, must express itself in works of love. The task at hand is to describe this working of love—to set forth the all-encompassing norms and general laws for the infinite variety of individual actions. This is a demand that *Eckhart* does not fulfill; indeed, he expressly rejects it.

The prerequisite for all moral action is a spirit united with God, a spirit for whom virtue has become its very essence <note>original: "Wesen"</note>, and which has so emptied itself <term>Entäußerung: the process of letting go of one's own ego or "selfness" to make room for God</term> that it is no longer the person themselves who acts, but God acting in them and in their stead. This state is one of absolute freedom; moral action is its immediate consequence. A spirit thus deified can no longer have the laws of its actions outside of itself; whatever it does must necessarily be good, because it is an expression of its purely good essence. For such a person, there are no binding formulas; at this level, the law is transcended. The moral person has only to obey the God within, and they cannot err.

1. The moral person is the truly free person. Insofar as the will remains untouched by all "creatures" <term>Creatures: in medieval theology, this refers to anything created (people, objects, desires) rather than the Creator</term> and all finitude, and turns away from itself back to its origin, the will is free (67, 3; ibid., 12). God leads the spirit into the "wilderness" <note>original: "Oede"—often referring to the 'desert' of the soul where God and the soul are one</note> and into the unity that He Himself is, where He flows out from Himself. In that state, the spirit has no finite goals; otherwise, even pure unity would have to have finite goals. There, the spirit stands in unity and freedom. God does not conquer the will; He sets it free, so that it wills nothing other than what God is and what freedom itself is. The spirit *can* will nothing other than what God wills, and this is not a lack of freedom, but rather its own peculiar free-

This state of "deification" results in a unique form of spiritual freedom where the human will spontaneously aligns with the divine.</summary>

### 11. The Principle of Moral Action. 269

He pays no heed to any thing; he has God, therefore he needs nothing else (178, 31).

Therefore, no kind of external rule or specific formula is sufficient to prescribe a way of acting for the moral person. One must cast down every barrier that separates us from the pure essence, not only scorning the world and possessing virtues: rather, I must also leave virtue itself if I wish to gaze upon God directly; not in the sense that I scorn virtue, but that virtue should be within me as my essence, and I should be beyond virtue. Then there is no longer any barrier between God and the soul, and as far as the soul follows God into the desert <note>original: "Oede," a key term in Eckhart’s mysticism referring to the silent, undifferentiated, and absolute essence of the Godhead</note> of the Godhead, so far does the body follow Christ into the desert of voluntary poverty, and just as the soul is united with the Godhead, so is the body united with Christ in the practice of true virtues (182, 31. 183, 13).

4. At this height, man is now the turning point in which every creature returns to its origin. In the sanctified person, all creation is ennobled. Therefore, he is the unlimited lord of all creation. Why—one might ask—if God raises the soul above itself and all creatures and leads it home into himself, why does he then not ennoble the body so that it no longer requires anything earthly? When the soul attains that unity with God, only then has the body fully reached the point where it can enjoy all things to the honor of God. For it is for the sake of man that all creatures have flowed out from God, and whatever the body can reasonably enjoy of creatures is not a diminishment for the soul, but an increase of its glory. For creation could not flow back into its origin in a more glorious way than through the righteous man who allowed his soul, even for a single moment, to be drawn into the divine unity (182, 40). All things are then man's property; all creatures bow before him and are subject to him, as if they had been created by him (351, 20).

# IV. On the Moral Life.

This, then, is what that perfect poverty, which belongs to the moral life, amounts to. Of such a person it is said: "all things are yours." To the pure soul, all creatures become pure for its enjoyment; for it enjoys all creatures in God and God in all creatures (602, 7). An inwardly poor person should enjoy as much as is possibly allowed to them. For whatever things they enjoy, they raise back into their origin <note>This refers to the idea that humans act as priests of creation, returning the world to God through their conscious use of it</note>. Rather, within the moral person, all virtues should be, as it were, enclosed and flow out from him. He should pass through and beyond all virtue, grasping virtue only at the ground <note>original: "Grund," a central term in Eckhart’s mysticism referring to the shared essence of the soul and God</note> where it is one with the divine nature (71, 2). It is a state of inner harmony; all multiplicity is gathered under the highest power, and this highest power plunges itself into God and remains there in undifferentiated unity (253, 5). This alone is the deciding factor; everything depends on this supreme principle. The right principle naturally results in the right effects. Whoever wishes to begin a good life should act like someone drawing a circle; if they have placed the first point firmly, the circumference will be good. Thus, a person should first learn to adhere constantly with their heart to God, to all virtue, and to all works of virtue; for even if one performs many individual virtuous acts, yet their heart is inconstant, it helps little or not at all (200, 20). A person should simply turn their will toward God in all their doing and keep God alone in view; then they may go calmly on their way and have no fear, and not stop to think whether they are on the right path or doing something wrong. For if a painter wanted to think of every brushstroke while making the first one, he would never finish his work. And if someone wanted to set out on a journey and first pondered at length how to place the first foot, he would never reach his goal. Therefore, one should simply follow the principle <note>The "Principle" here refers to the inner divine source or starting point of action.</note> and go one's own way; in this way, one arrives where one should, and that, after all, was the point (179, 1). The spirit that is rightly disposed in its principle experiences no increase in its wealth through individual virtuous acts. For these are all for the sake of earthly necessity, and that does not make the spirit richer. It is not the virtuous actions themselves, therefore, but rather their fruit that enriches the spirit (681, 14).

Moral action results from the essence of the moral person quite naturally and without any struggle. He does not need to wrestle for each individual action, as he has won the victory once and for all. For the characteristic of the moral...

#### IV. On the Moral Life.

...[it] is that he is capable of everything he perceives; this is granted to him by the light of eternity, which has enlightened him (641, 5). This is called **virtue become essence**: that a person stands at a point where no desire of the heart ever becomes a [sinful] deed, that one perceives what one ought to do and is capable of doing what one perceives, and possesses the full capacity that belongs to the soul in its original glory (648, 3). People who only repeatedly practice individual virtuous acts, and then perhaps also acts of an opposite kind, are like the prophets, who only occasionally and with struggle cease from what they should and do what they ought. When the Holy Spirit, through His grace, uses them as His instruments, they are virtuous; afterward, they return to being as they were before. For this very reason they are called "virtuous" <note>The author distinguishes here between "virtuous" people, who perform good acts occasionally, and "moral" people, whose very nature has become good.</note>; for they practice virtue in a specific form—that is, they practice virtue and occasionally its opposite. Those who are truly moral <note>original: "Die Sittlichen"</note> are more than prophets; for they have a full knowledge of duty and the full capacity to fulfill it in the highest sense, without any struggle, with the joyfulness that is their essence, and out of their essence, which is pure joyfulness (635, 10). The <term>Birth of God: Eckhart’s concept of the divine essence being continuously generated within the human soul</term> in the soul produces such essential morality. It is like a lightning strike, which turns everything it hits toward itself. What was previously an obstacle to you henceforth serves as an advancement. Whatever you see and hear, in everything that birth—in everything God alone—confronts you. Just as when a person looks into the sun for a long time: whatever else they look at afterward, the image of the sun is impressed upon it (28, 30). —

In the circle of ideas presented here, we believe we recognize the profoundest understanding of the nature of moral character. The *form* of moral action has never been described more thoroughly or more truly. Yet something essential is missing. The *content* of moral action is not presented by Eckhart. This content can only be derived from the nature of the moral goods that the moral person must uphold in their actions. Eckhart, however, knows only one moral good, and that is the "highest good," which he strips of all content by virtue of his <term>pantheistic abstraction: the philosophical tendency to view God as everything, which can lead to a loss of specific, individual distinctions</term>. He regards the moral person as a genius whose deeds are bound by no rule and arise with necessity from his essence...

But even from the working of a genius, at least an approximate rule could be abstracted;—one certainly never gets beyond this in the description of subjective morality. Furthermore, the moral person is not immediately—to stay with the image—a virtuoso of the highest perfection. For the moral education of one person by another, of each by oneself, and of all through the moral community of the Church, the rule and the law are indispensable; only the law which permits, commands, and forbids is the adequate form of instruction regarding the present state and the path to the glorious goal. However, Eckhart thinks too little of the importance of the law for moral education; he has perfected holiness almost exclusively in view. And yet, this latter state is impossible on Earth, whereas the need for education is valid for everyone in the same way. He therefore does not recognize an actual <term>Moral Law: A set of objective rules or duties (like the Ten Commandments) that govern behavior</term> at all. The principle of morality is the indwelling of the spirit in the absolute essence: from this, certainly, no principle for individual moral actions can be derived. 

Morality, however, is in fact the agreement of the direction of the will—which has become dominant in a person through faith—with the requirements arising from the nature of moral goods. Eckhart's thought mostly flies unstoppably toward the highest ideals, toward the final blessed state of perfection; he has not turned with equal interest toward the conditions of finite existence. He was unable to follow the "realm of ends" <note>A reference to the Kantian "Kingdom of Ends," where all people are treated as ends in themselves; the author critiques Eckhart for not mapping out how this works in the practical, earthly world.</note> down into its deeper levels and earthly branches. The essential deficiency of his ethics is the lack of a doctrine of moral goods; had he considered the nature of these latter things, his conception of virtue and duty would also have assumed a more concrete character. However, that lay far beyond the horizon of his time. He did not entirely fail to recognize the greatness of the earthly calling; but he does not do it sufficient justice. The striving to find an image of the infinite within the finite is alive in him; but all too quickly he lets the latter merge into the former. He was therefore unable to designate the actual content of moral action. His enthusiasm belongs to "the Good" and the submission of all things to the Good; the shallow morality and the false <term>Doctrine of Recompense: The medieval practice of "settling accounts" with God through external acts, penance, or payments, rather than internal change</term> that circulated under ecclesiastical authority, [he] through-

## 12. Education Toward Morality.

That virtue becomes man's essence, and man himself becomes virtue, is the highest goal; and Eckhart energetically asserts the ideal possibility of reaching this goal for everyone who wills it. He urgently exhorts us to strive toward this highest point and not to cease until it has been reached. Man should not be content with a lower standpoint, as if he could go no further; the state of gradual progress itself is not yet the right one. Whatever can be said of perfection, one can also attain (642, 28). No one should consider anything impossible. To the soul that has God’s grace, nothing is impossible; everything becomes easy for it, whether in doing or in refraining (230, 26). Whoever is still ascending and increasing in grace and enlightenment has not yet arrived in God. In the state of "increasing," one sees nothing of God yet. As long as we are on the way to God, we possess nothing of him (140, 10. 80, 20). 

But this does not prevent Eckhart from acknowledging the actual imperfection of all earthly morality alongside the ideal possibility of the highest perfection. This is not a contradiction. According to Eckhart, all true morality begins with the <term>Birth of God: A central concept in Eckhart's mysticism where the Divine Word is born within the individual soul</term> in the soul. There, God unites with the <term>little spark: (*vünkelîn*) the highest, most pure part of the human soul that Eckhart believed was uncreated and remained in constant contact with the Divine</term>; but the powers of the soul are not yet seized by it. Only now does the process of sanctification begin. That union of the soul with God establishes itself in a timeless moment in the form of ecstasy into eternity (652, 26); this highest contemplation passes by the soul as quickly as a lightning bolt (329, 12). Morality, however, as perfect virtue, is meant to be realized in a temporal process lasting throughout one's whole life; the powers of the soul should attain the same union with God as the "little spark," and the Divine should be present in them not just once or temporarily, but forevermore. And only then, when this is achieved, is the sanc- <note>The word "sanctification" (*Heiligung*) is interrupted here by the page break.</note>

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from "sancti-" on the previous page</note>fication is completed; only then can earthly actions no longer hinder the spirit. At that point, the whole person is transfigured, and the natural side of the human disposition is perfectly spiritualized. The "birth" <note>Eckhart’s concept of the "Birth of God in the Soul," where the divine essence enters the human spirit</note> is the beginning and the prerequisite for this development; but this development, in turn, reacts upon the ground of the soul and grants it the possibility of perfect and constant <term>essential unity: the state of being one in substance or nature with God</term>. Just as true virtue is only made possible through rebirth, the perfection of one’s being is only made possible through the practice of virtue. A person can reach a point, even in this earthly life, where they are no longer even capable of sinning. This is then a fruit of practice and habituation, which ensures that no evil inclination can arise in the heart (460, 11). Those pagans <note>Likely referring to ancient philosophers like Socrates, Plato, or the Stoics, whom Eckhart often admired</note> who are famous for their knowledge of right virtue or for their high works of virtue were more firmly established in virtue than Paul was after his first ecstasy. The practice of virtue purifies the spirit (264, 21). Therefore, Eckhart distinguishes between practiced and unpracticed people. <term>Reason: in this context, the higher intellectual faculty capable of perceiving divine truth</term> must be educated and habituated with great diligence. If a person who is not yet habituated and practiced in the good were to try to carry themselves and act in the same way as a practiced person, they would completely ruin themselves and nothing would ever come of them. Once a person has first broken the habit of all things and rid themselves of their self, then they walk a sure path in their actions, and then they can enjoy things or do without them without being hindered by them. But for a person to enjoy whatever they have a desire for, be it in eating or drinking or in whatever else, would be very dubious in an unpracticed person (569, 10).

It is an infinite task to habituate and educate all spiritual powers to the point that they can perform nothing other than what is divine, and to transform the entire natural disposition into an obedient instrument for the principle of holiness that has become alive in the ground of the soul. For this reason, even the highest saints here below always still lack something of perfection; therefore, in this earthly life, we are never free from temptation and affliction, from weaknesses and faults. # IV. On the Moral Life.

<note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "Surely" or "Essentially"</note>ly, one in whom God is born cannot fall into any mortal sin; they cannot even commit minor sins with intent and knowledge. They can no longer turn away from the Divine (10, 14). The capacity for all unseemly action is taken away from them. But this is initially only a gift of grace, not the outflow of their innermost essence. The soul is surrounded by the radiance of divine light; God’s glory sustains it, so that goodness—the very essence of the Holy Spirit—is reflected within it. If it were an outflow of the soul’s own essence, then all effort would be superfluous, and that is not the case (667, 14; ibid., 24). Even after their enlightenment, the saints still commit minor sins; indeed, they sometimes incline toward them more easily than other people. They are so focused with their inner disposition upon the One <note>In Eckhart’s mysticism, the "One" is the simple, undifferentiated essence of God</note> that it vexes them to pay close attention to every individual mental image. But as soon as they begin to direct their attention to it, it is as if it never happened, and they are rid of it without a struggle, simply by virtue of their essence. St. Paul, after his conversion, was not sinless; our Lord Christ himself still had to overcome, for the thought of his future torment <note>Referring to the Agony in the Garden and the Passion</note> filled him with deepest agony; St. Peter still committed sin after the outpouring of the Spirit (645, 24. 654, 19. 653, 3). The righteous man falls seven times a day <note>A common medieval reference to Proverbs 24:16, emphasizing human frailty even in the holy</note>; his "fall" consists in his sinking down from the highest standpoint of sublimity above all creatures (647, 21). Temptation, which approaches the soul from the outside, never ceases; and even if the temptation itself were far away, the possibility of temptation would remain. This must not be seen as an imperfection. Rather, it serves to make the soul bow humbly beneath God and recognize that it is sustained by grace and not by the power of its own essence; on the other hand, it has the blessing that the soul, by resisting such temptations, earns a reward (663, 19). In this sense, Eckhart can also speak of a reward for the practice of virtue, in that it advances the person and brings them to the goal of salvation. This reward for good works consists in the spirit attaining the <term>vision of God: the direct, unmediated experience of the divine essence</term>, while the body, along with the soul, is transfigured on the Last Day (645, 8).

# 12. Education in Morality.

...glory that awaits us, we must not forget the path that leads there. Only perfect virtue does not need to fight or struggle; until we have reached that ultimate perfection, all our virtue presents itself in the form of a struggle. At all times and without ceasing, one can increase and progress; we can never come to an end with this (573, 20). <note>Citations such as (573, 20) refer to specific page and line numbers in 19th-century editions of Meister Eckhart’s works, likely those by Franz Pfeiffer.</note> Never should we be satisfied with what we have achieved, nor should we ever stand still. In this life, there is no such thing as standing still. No human being has ever been allowed to be content with themselves, no matter how far they had advanced. Initially, the will is only an accidental, insubstantial will; however, it must become a firm, reliable, and practiced will. It is not enough for a person’s inner disposition to be detached in a given moment; rather, one must possess a well-practiced <term>detachment (Abgeschiedenheit)</term> <note>original: "Abgeschiedenheit." This is a central concept for Eckhart, meaning a state of being "cut off" from worldly distractions and self-will to be fully open to God.</note> that lasts before and after. It is not enough for us to give ourselves and all that we have and are capable of just once; rather, we should frequently renew ourselves and continually collect ourselves and make ourselves free (570, 6; ibid. 14 and 34).

This spiritual growth is threefold: first, the overcoming of all natural impulses, so that a "holy aversion" to all temptation toward evil arises like a second nature. Next, a person should become so spiritualized that, even without being consciously aware of it, their word, their conduct, and their very being illuminate others like a light in which they recognize their own imperfection. And finally, a conscious growth in divine enlightenment takes place, so that the person merges ever more intimately with their love into God’s love (639, 25).

And precisely for this reason, virtue at this stage of preparation appears as something that is fulfilled in struggle, in ever-new decisions of the will, and in nothing but individual acts, mediated by specific ideas of the situation at hand and the resulting duty. But where there is a struggle, there is also the honor of that struggle and a reward for victory. The fact that inclination is not the determining factor of the will is declared to be the very hallmark of true virtue. To refrain from something simply because one feels no inclination toward it is the effect of mere nature. True spiritual virtue, by contrast, consists in recognizing what one should do or leave undone and fulfilling it, whether one has an inclination for it or not (656, 10). ### IV. On the Moral Life.

**Virtue of temperament.** Some people are tempted little, others are tempted more intensely. Through the relationship to the world of things, the outer person is moved to anger, to vain ambition, or to sensuality. This is initially only a defect of nature, not of the will, just as many a person has an angry or proud temperament. If he resists now and does not fall into sin, then his reward is much greater and his virtue much more glorious than that of one who is not tempted. For the perfection of virtue comes from the struggle (551, 18). <note>Meister Eckhart frequently argues that the presence of "inclination" to sin is not a sin in itself, but rather the "material" or opportunity for the soul to prove its strength.</note> No one becomes a master all at once; no one may sit idle <note>original: "die Hände in den Schooss legen," literally "to lay one's hands in one's lap."</note> as if he had overcome once and for all. It would be wrong to cease with self-observation and self-reproach, or with the specific consideration of each moral task. As long as there is still anything left to overcome, one should never be satisfied. No one can be entirely without any defects. But one should resist them, so that one overcomes whatever is at hand in each instance. One must guard oneself closely against the false wisdom of committing errors yet failing to hold oneself accountable for them. One should never be free from this self-reproach so long as one is not free from all faults. 

And for this very reason, one requires an exact knowledge of each respective duty. In one's **essence** <term>essence (Wesen)</term> <note>In Eckhart’s philosophy, the "essence" is the innermost core of the human being, where one is united with God, while the "understanding" or "intellect" (Verstand) is the active faculty of the mind.</note> one should be beyond this notion of the finite, but not in one's understanding. For if one lacks this awareness in the understanding, then one commits faults without recognizing them and without reproaching oneself; thus, one is never freed from them and never loses the notion of the finite even in one's essence. Only through clear intellectual knowledge can and should one gradually attain that freedom of essence from all determination by the finite; only then, when all imperfection ceases, has virtue become essence (663, 40). 

This growth into a morality that has become essence should fill the entirety of earthly life, and only with death does it reach its conclusion. It is for this reason that the pious love this earthly life, because it allows them an unlimited progression in <term>sanctification (Heiligung)</term> <note>original: "Heiligung." This refers to the ongoing process of becoming holy through the cooperation of the human will with divine grace.</note> (470, 5). All temporal knowing and loving here below is limited and veiled; but through the practice of virtue, the barrier is expanded into the infinite; man becomes <term>godlike (Gottähnlichkeit)</term> <note>original: "Gottähnlichkeit." This is the central mystical goal: becoming like God so that the soul may be united with Him.</note> and through this godlikeness, he is united with God (677, 2).

# 12. Education in Morality. 279

In this sense, the moral life is the **imitation of Christ**, especially regarding his human side. One must not seek this imitation in external busyness, in being moved while contemplating Christ’s suffering, or in emotional excitements of pleasure and pain. One need only test people who follow Christ in such a way with words, and one finds how little serenity <note>original: "gelassen," referring to *Gelassenheit*, a cornerstone of Eckhart’s philosophy meaning a state of detached equanimity and "letting-be."</note> they possess. To overcome all naturalness—that is the true imitation of Christ; through this, one moves beyond the Lord’s humanity toward his divinity. For this, one does not need many external works or such agitated feelings. 

But the true and essential imitation of the Lord lasts until death. Following Christ fully and perfectly is, of course, impossible for a creature; for God’s works are, like God himself, infinite and incomprehensible, while the creature is finite and limited, and so is its work. Therefore, man should follow Christ as far as is possible for a creature. To bear poverty, misery, shame, and hatred patiently—and not just patiently, but willingly, even joyfully—and to long for it, to be raised above pleasure and pain, to be empty of oneself and all things, to desire nothing for oneself, and to cling to no thing with one's inclination: that is what it means to follow the example of Christ (636, 29). And if imperfection is inseparable from all earthly action, then the hallmark of a pious and holy mind is that one makes a great matter of conscience out of a small misstep (647, 13).

How Eckhart describes this education in virtue more closely does not need further explanation; it follows naturally from what has been said so far. True practice consists of renunciation, in poverty, patience, detachment <term>Abgeschiedenheit: the state of being "cut off" or withdrawn from the world to be fully present to God</term>, and immovability. He recognizes no practice in positive, creative action. The practitioner desires suffering most of all, because suffering is the most beneficial; indeed, he seeks it out voluntarily, though only spiritual suffering. The deprivation of inner focus and refreshment, of joy in God, and of the sensation of God's presence is, for him, a sign of special grace; to be free from suffering means, to him, to be abandoned by God. It is not surprising that among Eckhart’s students, such as **Suso** <note>Henry Suso (c. 1295–1366), a German Dominican friar and a leading author of the Rhineland school of mysticism.</note>, and among people more distantly connected with the Master, such as the **Friends of God** <term>Gottesfreunde: a 14th-century mystical lay movement in the Rhineland that sought a deep, personal union with God</term>, an inventive self-mortification emerged, which in its coarse physical manner was certainly entirely foreign to the Master—

# IV. On the Moral Life.

Otherwise, Eckhart emphasizes above all the commandment of universal and unrestricted love, which relates to everyone in the same way. Man never attains true peace with God unless he keeps peace with his neighbor. That one keeps peace with those who are like him is a small thing; but that one keeps peace with those who are unlike us, who are our adversaries, that is far more glorious; for there, it is clearly only the love of God that is the cause of peace (381, 24). Hence follows the commandment of <term>gentleness<gloss>German: *Sanftmuth*</gloss></term>—even when we must point out a neighbor's sin—as well as joyful service, submissiveness, and patience in the face of external injustice and false accusations. How little Eckhart is inclined to stop at a mere external legality, and how strictly he maintains moral requirements, is proven by his explanation of the seven deadly sins. He places **Pride** <note>original: *Hoffahrt*</note> at the front; it is the most dangerous vice. The self-deception of pride is that through which one robs oneself of one's own <term>blessedness<gloss>German: *Seligkeit*</gloss></term>. Pride reveals itself wherever one wishes to please oneself or other people through one's actions. **Sloth** <note>original: *Trägheit*</note>, furthermore, shows itself whenever one does something in place of which one could have done something better. **Greed** <note>original: *Geiz*</note> refers to every desire directed toward that which is not God. **Envy** and **Hatred** consist of doing to another what one would not want done to oneself; but it appears especially in words where we attack the honor of another, for the loss we cause him thereby is irreplaceable. We commit the deadly sin of **Wrath** <note>original: *Zorn*</note> even through harsh words toward our neighbor, and it is most destructive when we rebuke someone for their sin in a harsh manner. **Gluttony** <note>original: *Unmässigkeit*, or intemperance</note> is committed by whoever eats multiple courses while a fellow Christian hungers and thirsts—one who, by virtue of his poverty, is actually closer and more similar to God. **Unchastity** appears in all words and works that go beyond measure, beyond necessity (449—451).

### 13. Instruction for a Blessed Life.

Eckhart is prevented by the nature of his fundamental view of morality from surrendering to a [particular] life <note>The text likely refers here to a life based on external works or legalistic piety</note>. Nevertheless, a number of statements from him exist regarding how the moral person should arrange their conduct, partly scattered here and there, and partly in a more connected form. These expressions are all the more important because they show how the Master maintained that **prudence** and **moderation** to a high degree in the field of ethical conduct—qualities he so often abandons in his usual style of <term>speculation<gloss>Deep, abstract philosophical or mystical theorizing</gloss></term>. To be sure, the image of the truly moral person he designs is not so much furnished with a rich abundance of positive traits; rather, he is primarily concerned with weeding out all those characteristics that are foreign to it and are only held to be attributes of morality through misuse or prejudice. What he does give as positive remains solely the abstract principle of immersion into the **Absolute** <note>In Eckhart's thought, the "Absolute" refers to God in His purest essence, beyond all names or descriptions</note>, a principle incapable of a richer development. He therefore describes the figure of the moral person almost exclusively in negations. We are most interested in those points where he placed himself in decided opposition to the prevailing worldview of his time in order to present a truly <term>evangelical conception<gloss>A view based on the Gospels rather than church tradition</gloss></term> of the task of life.

1. The entire Middle Ages did not know how to grasp the positive moral content of earthly powers of life. True piety and the sanctification of the will were simply opposed to everything belonging to this world. The external world as such—not thought of as "worldliness of the heart"—was the enemy of the Kingdom of God. Every striving for the earthly was considered "worldly" in itself, regardless of the heart's position toward Christ or the spirit from which that striving arose. Therefore, among those who were most serious about their sanctification, external poverty, the renunciation of all earthly goods, and the flight from all striving and concern for earthly purposes were considered conditions for a pious life. In the <term>flight from the world<gloss>German: *Weltflucht*</gloss></term> found in monasticism, a higher degree of holiness could be achieved exclusively; through external exercises, through self-imposed deprivations and tortures, people believed they could earn heaven. The sharp contrast between the holy and

# IV. On the Moral Life.

The distinction between the **sacred** and the **profane** permeates the entirety of ethics within the Catholic Church, even among its most liberal minds.

Eckhart, however, is compelled toward an opposing view by the supreme principles of his teaching on morality. Everything external is utterly indifferent; morality is purely an inner state of the spirit. No single action can be called moral or immoral in itself; rather, it is only the spirit that reveals itself through the action. Thus, nothing is holy or profane by its own nature; it only becomes so through the state of the spirit active within it. By this principle, all <term>work-holiness<gloss>The belief that external religious deeds, rituals, or legalistic observances can earn spiritual merit</gloss></term> is fundamentally cut away. The true opposition to the kingdom of God is not the external world, but rather the worldly disposition of the heart. A sanctified spirit can take possession of every thing and every relationship; it stands above every particular form of action, every external rule, and every commanding law.

There is no contrast between the sacred and the profane. It is not enough that external things simply do not hinder us in our inner life; rather, we should use all things for our salvation, no matter how foreign or inappropriate they may seem. In this "art," we should constantly increase and never reach an end. In all things and activities, we should pay the highest attention only to the state of our heart, grasping God in the highest sense in everything. We must apply the greatest diligence and all our strength to this; in doing so, we find God in the same way in all things. To be sure, activities are different in themselves; but if our heart’s position is the same in all of them, they all have equal value, and God shines out toward us in the most worldly business just as much as in the holiest. It is one of two things: either we grasp God in all our doing, or we must refrain from all doing. The latter is not possible in this life, so our striving must be directed toward the former (550) <note>Reference to a specific passage in Eckhart's Middle High German works, likely the *Reden der Unterweisung* (Talks of Instruction)</note>. The essence of all morality is that the human <term>soul<gloss>German: *Gemüth*; refers to the deep seat of disposition, will, and inner feeling</gloss></term> be entirely turned toward God. Let all your effort aim for that. The more you achieve this, the better your actions are, regardless of their nature. If you cling to God, He will attach everything good to you. Seek God, and you will find God and all good things. In such a disposition, you could step upon a stone, and it would be a holy work in a higher sense than if—

### 13. Instruction for a Blessed Life.

...you were taking the body of the Lord <note>original: "Leib des Herrn"; a reference to receiving the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> and were thinking more of yourself during it. What you previously sought, now seeks you; what you previously hunted, now hunts you; what you previously had to flee, now flees you (546, 33). Anyone who believes they can obtain more from God in inner stillness, devotion, gentle stirring, and especially close union than they can at the fireside or in the stable <note>Eckhart frequently uses the "stable" or "fireside" to represent the most mundane, lowly household chores</note>, does nothing differently than if they were to wrap a cloak around God’s head and hide him under a bench. For whoever seeks God in a specific external form captures the form but lets God go, who is hidden within that form (66, 10).

Do not seek peace by fleeing the world. Whoever stands internally as they should, stands rightly in all places and among all people; and whoever does not stand internally as they should, stands wrongly in all places and among all people. Whoever truly carries God within themselves has him on the street and among people just as well as in the church, or in the wilderness, or in the <term>cell<gloss>The small, private room of a monk or nun</gloss></term>. Their actions are not so much performed by themselves, but rather by God within them. Just as little as God himself, such a person cannot be distracted by the clamor and the restless bustle of the world. That same <term>disposition<gloss>German: "Gemüth"; the inner state of mind, soul, and emotion</gloss></term> with which you are in the church or in your cell, you should preserve and carry among the people and into the clamor.

To regard all occupations, places, and people as equal would be wrong; certainly, in itself, praying is a better work than spinning <note>Refers to spinning wool, a common domestic task of the era</note>, and the church is a better place than the street. But you should maintain the same posture of the heart everywhere and grasp your God with the same earnestness everywhere. Then no one can hinder you from having God always present. But for someone in whom God does not truly dwell, who must only take him in from the outside through specific external things—whether they be actions, people, or places—it may well be that something hinders that person; and therefore, they are hindered not only by bad company but also by good company, and not only by the street but also by the church, and not only by bad words and works but also by good ones. For the hindrance lies within themselves.

That one carries God so truly within oneself does not mean that one must constantly think of God in the exact same way; for that would be impossible for human nature and not even the best thing. A person should not be satisfied with a "thought-God." If the thought passes away, then the God also passes away. Rather, one...

## IV. On the Moral Life.

...should have an essentially indwelling God. Whoever is intensely thirsty may well do things other than drinking and think of things other than water; but whatever they do or pursue, think or intend, the idea of the drink never leaves them as long as the thirst lasts, and the more intense the thirst, the more effective and vivid the idea of the drink becomes. Or whoever loves something ardently, wherever they may be and whatever they begin, they find the image of the beloved object everywhere. So it is here as well. Such a person does not search for peace, for no unrest hinders them. A person is worthy of God when they grasp all things in the highest sense. This requires diligence, love, and constant attention to oneself. A person does not learn this by fleeing the world and going into external solitude; rather, they must learn to have an internal solitude, wherever and with whomever they may be. They must learn to master things and to grasp their God within them (547, 14).

2. Just as little as fleeing the world, so too is external self-mortification, external poverty and deprivation, misery and shame—which one imposes upon oneself—the way to true peace. No matter how great and difficult such things may be, they are worth nothing and are unable to give peace. Those who seek it there are seeking in the wrong place; the further they go, the less they find what they seek, like someone who has lost their way: the further they walk, the more they go astray. One should leave oneself first; in doing so, one has left all things. If a person were to leave a kingdom, even the whole world, but kept themselves, they would have left nothing. Conversely, if a person leaves themselves, they may keep whatever they wish—wealth and honor and whatever else—and yet they have still left all things. St. Peter <note>The Apostle Peter, often cited by Eckhart as an example of "leaving all" despite only owning a few tools.</note> had left nothing but a meager net and a small boat, and yet he was permitted to say:

> “Behold, Lord, we have left all things.” <note>original Latin: "Ecce nos reliquimus omnia," quoting Matthew 19:27.</note>

Whoever joyfully leaves the small things does not leave these alone; rather, they leave everything that people with worldly hearts gain, indeed, everything they could possibly desire. Everything that you are willing not to desire for God's sake, you have left for God's sake. This is the <term>spiritual poverty<gloss>German: "geistliche Armuth"; a state of being detached from one's own will and possessions to be filled by God.</gloss></term> which the Lord calls blessed. Also, from the perspective of the <term>Imitation of Christ<note>original: Nachfolge Christi; the medieval devotional practice of modeling one's life after the life of Jesus.</note></term>, one should not impose suffering upon oneself; indeed, one should not hold to a specific rule or an external, literal guideline. True imitation of Christ consists of each person paying attention to and holding fast to that which they specifically are most urged toward by God. For all people are by no means directed onto a single path to God. If you find that for you, the nearest path to the goal does not consist of many external works, great toil, and deprivation—which, in any case, do not matter much unless a person feels particularly driven to them by God and has the power to do them without disrupting their inner life—if you do not find this within yourself, then be completely at peace and do not concern yourself much with it. One should respect everyone’s custom and despise no one’s custom. Let each person hold fast to their own good custom and draw all good and every custom into it. What is life for one is often death for another (565, 22). ...you would want to accept it just as gladly and joyfully. So it is with food and drink, with friends and relatives, with everything that God gives you or takes from you. The best thing is to surrender oneself entirely to God; to accept what he imposes on us—shame, hardship, suffering—with joy and gratitude, and to let oneself be led by God, rather than imposing such things upon oneself. Then one can accept honor and prosperity; but should dishonor and distress befall one, one can bear them, and bear them just as gladly. God is satisfied with a good and righteous will; otherwise, he would spare his friends no form of suffering, since such infinite <term>salvation<note>original: Heil; can also mean "healing" or "blessedness" in a spiritual sense.</note></term> lies in suffering. In particular, however, you should flee all <term>peculiarity<note>original: Absonderlichkeit; refers to the practice of making oneself appear "different" or "special" through outward signs of piety to gain attention.</note></term> in clothing as well as in food and in your words; there is no benefit in it. Yet, not all peculiarity is forbidden to you. There is some singularity that one must maintain at certain times and before certain people. For he who is truly set apart must also at times appear unusual in various ways (563, 12). It would often be a special joy for pious people to practice great and difficult works. But they would place their confidence in these works, and therefore the Lord takes the opportunity away from them, so that he alone may be their support and their confidence. Our works do not deserve that God should give us or do for us anything; the Lord wants to remove this opinion from us, for he wants to bestow his gifts upon us for no other reason than his own free goodness (564, 22).

Also, the inclination of the heart is not to be entirely mistrusted. People often worry whether their inclination is from God or not. For this, there is a simple sign: If one finds in oneself the disposition that, if one knew or recognized God's will, one would want to follow it above all things, then one can know that what one feels the greatest inclination and urge toward is from God (685, 17).

...consecrated life is to be sought not in a special, distinguishing form of specific <term>piety<note>original: Frömmigkeit</note></term>, but solely in the devotion of the heart to God. Divine service, devotion, prayer, the use of the sacraments: all of this is good and irreproachable; however, one should not find sufficient satisfaction in them, nor bind oneself to them, nor cling to the *formula*. The greatest gifts are bestowed upon us only through prayer and sacrament; but prayer requires no specific formula; the whole of life should be an uninterrupted prayer; instead of the external sacrament, the internal sacramental disposition of the spirit serves just as well, without which the former means nothing.

Yet we shall speak later of *Eckhart’s* conception of the Word, the Sacrament, and prayer. We will only mention here what he says regarding the external gestures of piety. A common Christian life, he teaches, is best; one should not be aimed at extraordinary deeds (177, 33). One should strive beyond every specific external form; it is not the stormy resolution to constantly do or refrain from this or that, but rather *humble equanimity* <note>original: *Gelassenheit*; a central term in Eckhart’s mysticism, referring to a state of being "let go" or released from self-will and worldly attachments.</note>, which accepts everything from God with equal gladness, that advances you toward the highest goal. If a person prescribes a rule for themselves—"I will do this or that, whatever the cost"—that is wrong, for then the person is holding fast to their *self-will* <note>original: *Eigenwillen*; refers to the ego-driven desire to control one's own spiritual progress rather than surrendering to God.</note>. And if he feels annoyance or unrest over what God assigns to him, that is equally wrong.

A person cannot tell if they are progressing in the <term>moral life<note>original: sittlichen Leben</note></term> by whether they fast much and perform many external works; rather, there is *one sure sign* of progress, namely when the *eternal* becomes dearer to them and the *transient* becomes more burdensome. If a person had a hundred marks and gave them for God’s sake and built a monastery, that would be something great. But it would be greater still if a person despised and annihilated just as much within themselves for God’s sake (178, 9). That our whole life should become *God-like* <note>original: *gottähnlich*</note> does not depend on us having sweet words and spiritual gestures, or spreading a particular scent of holiness around us, so that our name is carried far and wide and pious people feel a true quickening through us. Nor does it depend on us being pampered and spoiled by God in the emotional pleasure of prayerful stirring, nor on our thinking that whatever we desire from God must be granted to us on the spot. See, it is then that we should hide ourselves in his divine nature and seek help alone in the word that Christ spoke: "Father, let your whole will be accomplished in me" <note>original: „Vater, all dein Wille werde an mir vollbracht“ (182, 1); a German rendering of the prayer in Gethsemane.</note>. It is a mistake to see a special holiness in states of <term>ecstasy<note>original: Verzücktheit</note></term>, in visions in which one believes they receive direct communications from God, in the excitements of religious feeling, or in the gentler refreshment or stormy jubilation of the soul. Such things are often the effect of mere sensuality, a false impetuosity, or the desire to distinguish oneself before other people; these do not increase with the growth of genuine love, but rather decrease, and an activity performed in love is worth far more than all ecstasy (553, 21). On the other hand, Eckhart warns against unjustified timidity and anxiety in one’s actions and dealings. If only the heart is otherwise in the right position, then one can never, ever lack God in any activity. And should it happen that a person somehow makes a mistake, speaks an improper word, or that something wrong occurs to them: if the work was only begun with God, then God must take the damage upon himself, and you should not cease your work because of it. One is never rid of such temptations in this life. Just because rats occasionally get into the grain, one should not throw away the noble grain (556, 21). Eckhart advises that order and moderation should prevail everywhere, constantly utilizing everything that belongs to God’s praise and the benefit of Christendom and one's neighbor, within the <term>vocation<note>original: Berufe; the specific station or professional calling a person occupies in society.</note></term> in which the person is placed. Order and moderation in all things yield inner and outer peace (381, 38).

Eckhart’s <term>Antinomianism<note>The theological view that the "inner light" or grace exempts a person from the obligations of moral law; a point of great controversy in medieval mysticism.</note></term> might perhaps rightly appear questionable, and the polemic of his students against extreme consequences drawn from Eckhart’s teachings—against the "wild ones," as they are called in <term>Suso<note>Henry Suso (c. 1295–1366), a prominent student of Eckhart and a key figure in the Friends of God movement.</note></term>—proves that in reality, this teaching resulted in a distorted moral attitude for many. What was then considered the foundation and prerequisite of all genuine piety could easily deceive even a deeper spirit through its heroic character. In fact, anyone at that time who contested the preference and merit of external poverty had to appear as if he wanted to seduce people into fleshly comfort and security; no further reason was then needed to prove wickedness and hostility toward everything Christian and divine. 

Therefore, when Eckhart describes his ideal of moral sanctification in a "God-become" woman <note>Eckhart frequently used the figure of a "God-become" or "deified" person to illustrate the soul's union with the Divine.</note>, he allows her the trait of preferring—even after reaching perfect <term>deification<note>original: Vergottung; the mystical process of the soul becoming one with God.</note></term>—to continue on the path that led her so far: the path of renunciation and self-denial. This is despite her confessor explaining to her that everything is now permitted to her and that she may enjoy everything, since she indeed possesses the power to carry all things up into God with her. She, however, wishes to be miserable and poor, although she has now pressed beyond the humanity of Christ up to his divinity; she certainly no longer wishes it for the sake of the practice or to come to God, but rather out of <term>piety<note>original: Pietät; here used in the sense of a devoted imitation of Christ's life.</note></term>. Just as Christ "practiced" until his death, she wishes to do the same. 

Thus, Eckhart's <term>antinomianism<note>The theological idea that the "perfect" or those under grace are no longer bound by moral laws.</note></term> is only an ideal principle, which he advises even the most perfect to soften in practice. In principle, it is true that for the pure soul, all <term>creatures<note>original: Creaturen; meaning all created things in the world.</note></term> become pure. Or as the fictional confessor says to the fictional saint:

> You shall eat when you are hungry and drink when you are thirsty; you shall wear soft clothing, you shall sleep and let yourself be well, and you shall take for yourself everything your heart desires in food and pleasure, and live for no one but yourself. If you saw everything God ever created sinking away before your eyes, you should not want to turn it away with a <term>Hail Mary<note>original: Ave Maria</note></term>; you shall command all creatures to serve you for the glory of God (473, 31).

But Eckhart gives in to experience and the reality of life far enough that, even at the standpoint of the highest sanctification, he still advises an active and practicing life as at least the more pious one. A grand one-sidedness may indeed prevail in the presented ethical teachings of the Master <note>The "Master" refers to Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328), the influential German mystic and philosopher.</note>; though the separation of that deepest ground, in which the soul acts as a totality, from the individual powers and their finite activity upon <term>empirical matter<note>original: empirischen Stoffe; the physical, observable world of the senses.</note></term> may be overstated and unsustainable in such sharpness; and though the Master may finally be turned away too much from the diversity of finite goods and finite duties and tasks: nonetheless, he rises in his conception of moral questions like a giant above all thinkers of the Middle Ages, and the principles of his ethics are still today a subject of the most serious consideration for us. Similar ideas are found only sporadically among the men who were more or less inspired by him, and if, for example, ***Nicolaus of Basel*** <note>A legendary figure associated with the "Friends of God" movement; historically, his identity and existence have been a subject of scholarly debate.</note> meets with ***Eckhart*** here and there, it is only a sign of how far the man’s teachings were carried abroad—teachings whose deeper inner core and connection no one in the times immediately following him was able to grasp. No wonder, then, if those who followed were able to become unfaithful to these teachings once again in a fantastic superficiality. By no means has everything that is undoubtedly authentic and true yet become common property, even among the best, which ***Eckhart*** recognized and taught. To be sure, he presented it in a time little receptive to his most unique ideas, and later generations no longer had direct access to him. Even his very closest students grasped and disseminated only isolated points of his circle of thought in a one-sided manner, and the subsequent ages up until ***Kant*** took hold of religious and ethical questions with interests of quite a different kind. Under ***Tauler’s*** and ***Ruusbroec’s*** names, those very writings were partially distributed in a more or less fragmentary form, from which we can most clearly perceive ***Eckhart’s*** ethical teachings. But these writings were processed almost into caricatures; in many decisive passages, the meaning was turned into its direct opposite in Latin or modern German translations, and through omissions and additions, a completely different doctrine—more closely related to the ecclesiastical and prevailing views—was corrected into them. ### 14. The Perfectly Sanctified.

When Eckhart admits the imperfection of all things earthly, it is proof that he has not entirely lost his prudence and a healthy gaze for the reality of life; however, even if he makes this concession—compelled by rational clarity and moral moderation—he does so only with half a heart. Rather, his heart clings to the highest ideal; he wishes to call us to its contemplation, to pull us away from all satisfaction in lesser things, and to inspire a striving for perfection. For this reason, he depicts the state of final perfection with such great warmth and dreams himself into the realization of the ideal. One must, therefore, regard his description of the perfectly sanctified state not as absolute and sober earnestness, but partly as a rhetorical device. He himself makes the necessary <insert>qualifying</insert> deductions in other places. Nonetheless, it is our task to conclude the presentation of the Master’s ethics with his conception of that state, which he represents as the final result of all moral striving—an ideal of perfected sanctification realized on earth.

The conclusion of Eckhart’s doctrine of salvation was the perfect union of man with God. This, however, was still conceived as a super-temporal moment; it took place essentially and

The task of morality was to take that which had initially been won through sanctification only for the <term>ground of the soul<note>The "Seelengrund" is the inner essence of the person, deeper than the faculties of memory, will, or intellect.</note></term> and to form it into all the individual, finite powers of the soul and even into corporeality. Through habituation and practice, the goal was to make dwelling in the highest good the constant and essential state of the entire human nature. This demand is realized in those who are perfectly sanctified. Let us see how these people appear according to the Master’s depiction.

When the soul has regained its true essence and stands in its original innocence—once reason and all finite things have been left behind and the soul is taken up into pure unity—then God works within the soul that which it had previously worked with its own highest power. Of a person who has attained this, one may well say: this person is God and man. He has attained through grace everything that Christ possessed by nature. The body is so permeated by that essential glory which the soul has received from God and through the infusion of the divine light, that one might well say: this is a divine human being. Ah, dear children, have mercy on such people; for they are something strange and incomprehensible to everyone else. No one can truly recognize them except for those who have shared in that same light, and perhaps also those who are on the path to this highest good but have not yet won it. Know this: if I knew of such a person, and I possessed a cathedral full of gold and precious stones, I would give it all for a single chicken that such a person consumed. Even more: were everything mine that God ever created, I would give it all to that person at once for them to consume; and I would do so with good reason, for everything is theirs. God is theirs with all that He is capable of. And were all those who live in sin and suffer from hunger to stand before me, I would not wish to take away even the wing of a chicken from that sanctified person's <term>necessity<note>Original German: "Nothdurft." This refers to the basic physical requirements for life.</note></term> in order to feed all those people. For what the sinner eats and drinks, he draws down and makes a part of his sinful nature. But what the good man eats and drinks, he carries up in Christ to the Father. Where body and soul are united in a perfect way, there the person has become the absolute master of all things. In this mystical context, true "possession" refers not to material goods, but to that which is unified with the soul's essence.</note></term>. I may call that my possession which shall remain mine eternally and which no one can take from me. The work of these people brings the highest <term>salvation<note>German: "Heil." This term carries a dual meaning of both spiritual salvation and a state of holistic well-being or blessedness.</note></term>; yet their work happens inwardly, in the <term>ground of the soul<note>The "Seelengrund" is a core concept in German mysticism, referring to the deepest, most hidden part of the human soul where it is one with God.</note></term>. We can content ourselves with this rendering of the description. So great is the value of the righteous person that all other people do not even come into consideration compared to him; so great is his freedom that nothing may restrict him in his external actions or enjoyments. The sanctified person is the final purpose of <term>creation<note>German: "Schöpfung."</note></term>; he leads all creatures back into God. He is most often portrayed in beggar’s robes, in the appearance of the utmost misery, while he is in possession of the highest bliss. This beggar is the true king; his kingdom is within him, in his heart; he is the one who is absolutely without need; his individual personality is now only a semblance; at the foundation of his being, he is no longer anything specific, but rather the <term>absolute essence<note>German: "absolute Wesen." This refers to the state where the individual self has been shed to reveal the divine essence underneath.</note></term> itself (623—625). Thus, the sanctified human being is the end of the <term>absolute process<note>A philosophical term describing the cycle of the Godhead flowing out into creation and returning back to itself.</note></term>; in him, and through him, the <term>Godhead<note>German: "Gottheit." In mysticism, the Godhead is the "essence" of God, often distinguished from God as a "Person."</note></term> returns from its revelation back into itself.

## V. Revelation and Church.

The teachings of *Eckhart*, as we have presented them thus far, develop from their own internal motives without any clear connection to a prevailing church conviction; they do not unfold in the forms of rigorous science, yet they do so in such a way that a strict intellectual coherence connects all the individual parts of the doctrine with one another. But even if *Eckhart* almost never made himself dependent on an established doctrine, nor weakened or otherwise changed the <term>conclusions<note>original: "Consequenz." This refers to the logical outcomes or necessary implications that follow from his philosophical and mystical premises.</note></term> resulting from his principles in favor of a dominant opinion, he nevertheless held his propositions to be identical to <term>church doctrine<note>original: "kirchliche Lehre." The body of official teachings and dogmas upheld by the medieval Catholic Church.</note></term> in good faith. He linked his ideas to that doctrine and intended to reveal its deeper meaning. For him, the content of the church's faith is a material with which he deals freely, inserting it into the whole of his own teaching wherever appropriate—though certainly not without often altering it in its deepest essence.

A presentation of *Eckhart’s* teaching would be incomplete if it did not also intend to take into closer consideration the relationship he established toward <term>revelation<note>original: "Offenbarung." In a theological sense, the disclosure of divine truth to humanity, usually through scripture or mystical experience.</note></term>, toward the church, and toward its institutions and <term>dogmas<note>original: "Dogmen." The authoritative principles or core beliefs of the church that were considered incontrovertible truths.</note></term>. It is this task that we undertake to accomplish in the following pages. Only in this way will the peculiar position of the man in relation to his time and the powers ruling within it, as well as his significance for the later developments of the <term>Christian spirit<note>original: "christlicher Geist." This refers to the overarching intellectual and spiritual evolution of Christianity throughout history.</note></term>, become perfectly clear to us.

<summary>This page introduces a new chapter examining the relationship between Meister Eckhart’s independent mystical philosophy and the formal doctrines of the Catholic Church. It argues that while Eckhart believed he was clarifying church teachings, he often fundamentally altered their meaning to fit his internal logical system.</summary>
