# 1. Holy Scripture.

Eckhart likes to refer to Holy Scripture as the highest authority and is most fond of appealing to the agreement of his teachings with its pronouncements precisely where his views appear the boldest and most daring (32, 17). God himself, he teaches, speaks to us in the prophets; one must surely believe the sayings of Christ recorded in Scripture, for Christ is the truth itself. The holy writers were inspired and driven by the Holy Spirit to communicate what they had recognized to us for our salvation (307, 20). Every created thing, angel and saint, must be silent when the eternal wisdom of the Father speaks, and this wisdom speaks to us in Scripture (280, 4).

Nevertheless, Eckhart does not have a completely definitive relationship with Scripture. As often as he appeals to it—citing particularly the sayings of <term>Paul<note>Referencing the Apostle Paul, whose letters provided the theological foundation for much of Eckhart's view on the nature of the human spirit.</note></term> for his doctrine of man and those of <term>John<note>The Gospel of John, known for its high Christology and philosophical themes, was a primary source for Eckhart's focus on the "Logos" or Word.</note></term> for his doctrine of God—he nevertheless has little hesitation in reinterpreting the simple literal sense of Scripture in his own way. For this is his supreme principle: Scripture indeed contains the truth, but one must first uncover it and expose its deeper meaning (146, 8). Thus, historical accounts are understood entirely through <term>allegory<note>The practice of interpreting texts as having a hidden spiritual or moral meaning beyond the literal words.</note></term>, with an allegedly deeper meaning read into everything. If Scripture contains the truth, then it must contain what appears to Eckhart as the truth; to be able to find any meaning in any given passage, no means is too adventurous. Eckhart is quite <term>naive<note>The author here suggests Eckhart was "naive" not in lack of intelligence, but in his uncritical adoption of the medieval style of interpretation where the text's original context was secondary to its spiritual utility.</note></term> in this regard and artlessly follows the manner customary in his time. In allegorical interpretation, he proceeds as boldly and with as much arbitrariness as any of his predecessors—indeed, with more, because his speculation is that much more abstract and removed from sensory parables. Examples are found everywhere. The biblical texts that he uses as the basis for his sermons are claimed for mystical doctrines as isolated individual sentences, without any regard for the natural context of the passage. He takes his favorite passages primarily from the <term>Book of Wisdom<note>A book in the Catholic Bible (part of the Apocrypha in Protestant bibles) that focuses on the personified Wisdom of God.</note></term> or the <term>Song of Songs<note>Also called the Song of Solomon; a book of love poetry traditionally interpreted by mystics as an allegory for the union between the soul and God.</note></term>; but every other biblical book serves in a similar way. In Eckhart’s mysticism, this refers to the "soul-spark" or the indestructible, divine core of the human spirit that remains in direct contact with God.</note></term>, the supreme reason, the head of the soul. This terminology—which is encountered in a similar fashion as early as <term>Peter Lombard<note>A 12th-century theologian whose "Sentences" became the standard textbook for medieval theology.</note></term>, where the man and woman within the soul are distinguished as higher and lower spiritual faculties—is then standard. It is precisely to this that the Lord's conversation with the Samaritan woman is applied. Her five husbands are then the five senses, and so forth (109). The rich man in the story of poor Lazarus is even God Himself (313); five yoke of oxen signify, once again, the five senses (114). The city of Nain is the soul; the disciples are the divine light that flows into the soul; the crowd accompanying the Lord are the virtues; the gate he enters is love; the widow's son is the will (123). The arbitrary nature in all of this is so great that one must believe it was not practiced unconsciously, and that Eckhart deliberately used these scriptural passages—torn from all natural context—merely as a convenient starting point for his own train of thought, without any intention of saying anything about the actual meaning of the Scripture itself.

It cannot, therefore, seem strange to us that Eckhart admires nothing so much in Scripture as its multiplicity of meaning. It applies to everyone according to the measure of their ability. For this, he refers especially to the sayings of <term>Saint Augustine<note>The influential 4th-5th century Bishop of Hippo. Eckhart frequently cites him to justify finding deeper, non-literal meanings in the biblical text.</note></term>. Where a lamb reaches the bottom, there the ox or the cow swims, and where the cow swims, there the elephant loses his footing and it goes over his head. Here, Scripture is called a deep sea in which the humble, simple person finds firm ground; the coarse, unenlightened person at least takes from it what satisfies him; but people of proud reason and high arts rummage through the Scripture and lose themselves in its labyrinths. It is an ancient doctrine that one cannot interpret Scripture as straightforwardly as it reads; the sensory expressions must first be unlocked through allegorical interpretation. For one it reaches to the ankles, for another to the knees, for a third to the belt, for a fourth it goes over the head and he sinks entirely. Scripture smiles enticingly at young children, and in the end, it mocks the wise. No one is so simple that he does not find in it what...

...is precisely suited to him, and no one is so wise that they would not find it even deeper and richer when seeking to fathom it. Everything in it carries a hidden meaning within itself; all our understanding does not reach the truth of the matter (331, 16).

To understand the Scripture, a higher knowledge originating directly from God is therefore required. For this reason, the <term>Scripture scholars<note>Refers to the university-trained Scholastic theologians whom Eckhart, himself a Master of Theology, often criticized for their dry, intellectualized approach to faith.</note></term> do not necessarily understand it best. There are many among us masters of the Holy Scripture who have occupied themselves with the Scripture for thirty years and more, and yet understand its meaning as little as a senseless beast; for there are enough and too many of them; if the Scripture were to testify to them of their vain conduct like a loud herald before an entire congregation, they would not have so much desire and diligence for sinning as they do now, where the word of the Scripture remains hidden from them, although their punishment ought to bring their sinful state to their recognition (353, 26). Scripture has its origin in God, who wishes to work through it in the soul. Only one in whose heart the Spirit from God, the Spirit of Love, has become powerful can understand and fulfill the Scripture (436, 37).

But for this very reason, the Scripture is not the highest and ultimate stage in the knowledge of God. For this knowledge disdains all definite forms, parables, and intellectual concepts. To believe what the Holy Scripture teaches and to do what it commands is indeed counted among the gifts of the Holy Spirit (369, 24), and Eckhart once asserts that he believes the Scripture more than himself (4, 19). Nevertheless, he is not very firm in this belief. Thus, for example, he believes like <term>Johannes Erigena<note>Johannes Scotus Eriugena (c. 815–877), a Neoplatonic philosopher whose works influenced medieval mysticism by suggesting that biblical language is often metaphorical.</note></term> that Moses's account of the creation is not to be taken literally as the absolute truth; rather, the prophet accommodated himself to the understanding of the multitude and presented the timeless in a temporal form (7, 35). Given his entire standpoint, Eckhart cannot be fully serious about allowing the Scripture to stand as the highest authority. He strives beyond every definite concept, beyond all contemplation in images and parables, toward the adequate knowledge of the Absolute. At that point, every finite form of expression ceases to be justified. Thus, he says explicitly that one [must seek] God out of the

...cannot recognize Scripture. The reason we do not find God is precisely because we seek Him through <term>parables<note>German: *Gleichnisse*. In this context, it refers to any symbolic or metaphorical language used to describe the divine, which Eckhart believed could never truly capture God's essence.</note></term>, for whom there is absolutely no likeness. Therefore, the highest level to which Holy Scripture can guide us is a knowledge that is far more unlike God than like Him (513, 38). <term>Augustine<note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian whose views on the limitations of language in describing God influenced medieval mysticism.</note></term> says: all Scripture is in vain. God's essence cannot be expressed in words (91, 31). Because every external form of communicating the truth is inadequate, the holy writers resorted to sensory matter; they wished to teach us to know God through images taken from lowly, created things (307, 36).

In this way, Eckhart agrees with the <term>Pseudo-Dionysius<note>An anonymous 5th-century author whose "Negative Theology" argued that because God transcends all understanding, we can only describe Him by what He is NOT.</note></term>. Naturally, anyone who wishes to free themselves from all parables and all figurative speech—indeed, from all speech whatsoever—cannot find satisfaction in Holy Scripture. Therefore, Holy Scripture is only a preliminary stage. A wise man says that God reveals Himself in Scripture and in His creatures; but <term>Paul<note>The Apostle Paul. Eckhart often contrasts Paul’s direct encounter with the "third heaven" against the indirect knowledge found in books.</note></term> says: God has revealed Himself in His only-begotten Son, and in him I am meant to recognize everything, from the lowest to the highest, thoroughly and purely in God Himself. To achieve this, we must outgrow everything that is not God (317, 28).

The mystic would thus be directed to a higher and more immediate source of knowledge: the "inner light," the revelation of God within one’s own soul. But it would be wrong to attribute to Eckhart the view that a <term>fanatical<note>German: *schwärmerisch*. This refers to an overly emotional or "enthusiastic" form of religiosity that relies on feelings and imaginative visions rather than intellectual or spiritual clarity.</note></term> interaction with the divine persons, perceived through the senses, could take the place of this revelation. He finds this revelation in a super-rational way of thinking, which he is nevertheless only able to describe as the highest abstraction, devoid of any positive content. To him, visions—the pictorial beholding of the divine in a state of ecstasy—and the receiving of special revelations are rather reprehensible things, because they are mediated through the senses; they are a beholding of sensory forms (381, 7). Indulging in visions is actually a sign of alienation from God; the agitation of the emotions still proves the power of the sensory within the human being (240, 19. 655, 36). Such supposed revelations from God spring instead from the soul itself, which has accustomed itself to standing in a closer relationship with God; as a result of the familiarity of its interaction with God, it imagines...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Master Eckhart’s relationship with Scripture. <header>V. Revelation and the Church.</header>

...regards its inner processes as something perceived externally. When God has completely seized the soul, so that it stands naked and free from all sensuality, it transcends everything finite so entirely that it has no object other than its own <term>Reason<note>German: *Vernunft*. In Eckhart’s thought, this is not mere logic, but the highest faculty of the soul—the "spark" where the human mind meets the Divine mind.</note></term>, which has thoroughly become its essence. There, the knower and the known become one; the soul draws from its own light what it desires, and because it is embraced by the rays of divine light streaming into it by virtue of the glory of the Reason that has become its essence, it draws divine truth from within itself. Therefore, where there is still a reflective, distinguishing understanding, there God does not speak; God's speaking is an immediate presentation of divine truth, by virtue of which the spirit is transported above itself and above all finite understanding into pure Reason. There the soul understands without "understanding" in the <term>Absolute<note>A term for God or ultimate reality as it exists beyond all human categories and limitations.</note></term>. For this reason, those sensory revelations <note>Referring to visions or audible voices perceived by the physical senses.</note> are not to be believed further than they correspond to this essence of the soul and receive their confirmation through it (634, 3).

One sees that Eckhart's mysticism is not specifically biblical. He stands in relation to the revealed Word more like the <term>Scholastics<note>The "schoolmen" of medieval universities who used logic and philosophy to explain Christian doctrine.</note></term> than like those pious men nourished by the spirit of the Bible, such as <term>Bernard of Clairvaux<note>A 12th-century abbot known for his deeply emotional and Christ-centered devotion.</note></term> or <term>Thomas à Kempis<note>The 15th-century author of *The Imitation of Christ*, whose work emphasizes humble, practical piety over intellectual study.</note></term>, whose mysticism is not a high, soaring speculation, but rather a deep glow of prayerful love for God. For Eckhart, Scripture is not a true source of knowledge. He draws upon it, so to speak, only after the fact, in order to attach the speculative views—which resulted from his personal spiritual disposition, the religious and scientific education of his contemporaries, and his study of the science of past ages—to it, and to strengthen them by leaning on such a high authority. Here lies the center of what is <term>enthusiastic<note>German: *schwärmerisch*. In a theological context, this refers to a type of "visionary excess" or "religious enthusiasm" that relies on subjective inner experiences rather than objective, external foundations.</note></term> in his mysticism. For his speculating had to become enthusiastic because, according to the measure of the education of his time and the disposition of his personality, a gradual and sober progression to the heights of knowledge from a secure foundation of individual factual truths was not possible for him; yet he rejected finding satisfaction in what had always been recognized as the secure foundation of Christian knowledge.

<header>2. Sin.</header>

## 2. Sin.

A second point we must consider in this context is Eckhart's teaching on sin. He does not arrive at the inclusion of this concept in his doctrine through a purely speculative route; rather, he carries it over from <term>Revelation<note>In a theological sense, "Revelation" refers to truths revealed by God through Scripture or the Church, rather than through human logic or observation.</note></term>. He could have contented himself with the categories of finitude and naturalness. But while he bases his more speculative doctrine on this latter concept, it is the fact that he views our <term>Created Nature<note>German: *Creatürlichkeit*. This refers to the state of being a "creature" (a created being) as opposed to the Creator.</note></term> through the lens of sin that first gives his thinking a truly religious character.

1. Regarding evil in general, Eckhart’s view aligns with the concept inherited from Greek philosophy and dominant throughout the entire Middle Ages: that evil is nothing positive <note>Here, "positive" means having its own independent, "real" substance or existence.</note>, but rather a deprivation, a lack of the good, or an imperfect good. The <term>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite<note>A highly influential Christian philosopher of the late 5th century whose writings blended Christian theology with Neoplatonic philosophy.</note></term> treated few questions as extensively as the possibility of evil, given that God—as absolute goodness—is all in all. His answer, based on <term>Neoplatonic<note>A school of mystical philosophy that views all of existence as a series of "emanations" (flowings-out) from a single, perfect source called "the One."</note></term> teachings, is as follows: there is no such thing as "evil" in the sense of an independent existence; rather, all that exists is good. However, there are degrees of goodness—a hierarchy that coincides with the various <term>Emanations<note>The process by which everything in the universe flows out from the divine source.</note></term> from the one highest Good and their relative distance from it. Since everything is connected to this source, everything is good; it is "evil" only insofar as it is different from Him. Consequently, evil itself participates in the Good; it is a means toward the Good. Each thing is evil only to the degree that it is deprived of the good proper to its own nature. There is nothing evil that is evil absolutely or for everyone. Evil is a partial deprivation and possesses power and efficacy not because it is a deprivation, but because it is not *entirely* a deprivation <note>original: *De div. nom. Cap. 4.* - A reference to Chapter 4 of Pseudo-Dionysius's treatise *On the Divine Names*.</note>. We must assume this line of thought was a given for all medieval thinkers, not just the mystics, and Eckhart holds no different view (613, 6. 327, 15). Despite all internal kinship and external dependence on Pseudo-

<summary>This page explores Meister Eckhart's definition of sin and evil, arguing that he follows the medieval tradition of viewing evil not as a substance, but as a "privation" or lack of the Good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Master Eckhart’s departure from his predecessors, specifically moving from the Neoplatonic view of evil as a metaphysical lack to a theological view of sin as an act of the human will. It connects the previous discussion of "pure Reason" to the practical ethics of the soul's return to God.</meta>

<page-num>302</page-num>
<header>V. Revelation and Church.</header>

Dionysius's world of thought was expanded by Eckhart with a completely different, essentially ethical interest than that which had prevailed in the model of the <term>Doctrine of the All-One<note>German: *Alleinslehre*. A term for Pantheism or Neoplatonic monism, where all reality is seen as a single, divine substance.</note></term>. This is shown by the fact that those investigations into evil <note>Referring to the previous page's discussion of evil as a mere "lack" of good.</note> were not taken up again by Eckhart. Instead of evil being treated as a quality of things, the concept of sin as a quality of the will prevails for him.

For Eckhart, there is nothing evil except the evil will, the outward form of which is sin. The essence of this evil will is clinging to the finite, to <term>Selfhood<note>German: *Eigenheit*. In Eckhart's mysticism, this is the egoistic attachment to one's own individual existence as something separate from God.</note></term>. That finite things exist is also God's will, but it is not His will that they should make themselves independent. Rather, the finite should constantly surrender itself and flow back into the divine, absolute essence. The being that is meant to mediate this return of all things to God is the human soul. By surrendering its created will to God, the soul simultaneously leads the "All" of things—both the sensory and spiritual worlds—back into God. If, however, a person does not make themselves a servant to this divine plan for the world, but instead strives to maintain themselves in their own selfhood (that is, in their finite form of existence), and if their desire clings with pleasure to finite, created things, then this resistance against the divine will results in the concept of sin.

In this, Eckhart acknowledges the fact that the natural will of all people we encounter in experience is evil. He believes that the longing for the good and the receptiveness to the good are indelibly present in the soul, but they lie dormant in the <term>Ground of the Soul<note>German: *Seelengrund*. The deepest, innermost part of a person where they remain eternally connected to God.</note></term> until they are enabled to gain mastery over the soul through the action of divine grace. It is now a matter of explaining this fact through its causes. The perfectly explanatory cause would seem to be the free will that God granted to humanity. But with that same free will, a person was just as capable of turning toward the divine as toward the finite. How then does it happen that, with unbreakable necessity, every new human individual naturally turns their will toward the finite and falls into sin? This remains a problem, given that the essence of a human is not sin but the good, and free will should provide the possibility to turn away from finite things and remain in God.

<summary>Eckhart redefines evil not as a metaphysical lack, but as 'sin'—a deliberate choice of the human will to cling to individual selfhood rather than returning to God. He struggles to explain why human nature seems to fall into this sin by necessity despite having free will and an essentially good soul.</summary>
<keywords>Meister Eckhart, Sin, Free Will, Selfhood, Divine Grace, Soul's Ground, Ethics, Return to God</keywords>

To this question, Eckhart does not answer with the logical consequences of his <term>speculation<note>In this context, "speculation" refers to philosophical or theological reasoning rather than mere guessing.</note></term>; even less does he develop mythologizing ideas after the manner of certain medieval sects. Here, in this essential point, his mysticism distinguishes itself from every Gnostic or Manichaean conception. There is no trace in Eckhart’s work of him independently pursuing the problem of sinfulness as a theoretical puzzle. Sin is a fact which he recognizes as such, but he does not undertake to derive its necessity from a conceptual framework.

2. On this point, Eckhart holds fast to the Christian doctrine as it had developed by his time. All sin is to be derived from an original <term>Fall<note>German: *Sündenfall*. The biblical event where Adam and Eve first disobeyed God.</note></term>, which has been inherited by the entire human race. When God created the first human, He formed him in such a way that he was not susceptible to any suffering; for, like a golden chain, a well-ordered harmony proceeded from the Trinity into the highest powers of the soul and permeated even the lowest ones, so that they were obedient to the higher powers; therefore, no illness or suffering of body or soul could find entry until he transgressed the commandment (397, 26). When Adam was created, his body was of a similar constitution to his soul, so that it could not feel pain; his lowest powers stood in right order beneath the higher ones in their natural glory, unhindered by materiality and sensuality, and he possessed this through the very design of his nature. Had he remained within the <term>nobility<note>German: *Adel*. A recurring term in Eckhart’s work describing the divine dignity and original high status of the human soul.</note></term> of his nature, he would have held fast to it in its Creator. He recognized that God had created him and that divine nature was to be united with human nature; he recognized in clear concepts all creatures, each in its natural glory as it had proceeded from God's hand, and that was his delight (651, 33). Had Adam gazed upon God in His absolute essence, he could not have fallen. He recognized that God had created him and for what purpose He had created him, and his gaze clung to *that* <note>meaning: his own created purpose and status</note> with delight. That was his fall and nothing else (658, 2. 652, 12). — In this manner, Eckhart interprets the story of the Fall not as an outward deed, but spiritually as an internal direction of the will. The original glory of man, however, is in Eckhart's view—

...[unhindered by any defect, his original state was] not understood as a *superadded gift* <note>original: *donum superadditum*; in Scholastic theology, this referred to a grace added to human nature by God, rather than being part of human nature itself. Eckhart argues here that this grace was intrinsic to man’s original substance.</note>, but as the genuine condition of his nature belonging to the very substance of man—a view that became dominant in the dogmatics of the Reformation. Only his finitude prevented Adam from an adequate vision of the divine essence; through this alone was the Fall made possible.

Just as he speaks of the Fall of man, Eckhart also speaks of the Fall of Lucifer, the highest angel; however, he does not mention a connection between the two events. Lucifer is brought into a closer relationship with Christ. His soul and Christ’s soul were of the same rank when they were created. But while Christ’s soul turned toward its Creator, Lucifer turned toward the finite; therefore he fell and will fall eternally, and so fall all those who turn away from God toward the transitory (674, 12. 476, 19.)

The consequences of the Fall are now described as follows. Had Adam remained in his natural glory, he would have been capable of all he willed, and all <term>creatures<note>In medieval theology, "creatures" refers to all created things, including animals, plants, and physical elements.</note></term> would have been obedient to him. But with his Fall, his own body and all creatures ceased to be obedient to him; they were no longer faithful to him because he had become unfaithful to God. Thus, mortality is also a consequence of the Fall; without it, Adam would have remained in the same condition in which God created him on the first day until the <term>Last Day<note>The day of final judgment.</note></term> (657, 32). From this arises the fear of natural things, which entered into human nature not as a means of salvation, but as a disturbance caused by the Fall (368, 10). Furthermore, all the powers of the soul were corrupted. In Adam, all powers worked together harmoniously, and as long as this harmony lasted, he had gathered the power of all creatures into his highest power. A magnet shares its power with a needle and attracts it; the needle in turn can share its power with another and attract it, and so on. If one pulls the top needle away, the others all fall as well. So it happened to Adam; when he was separated from God in his highest power, all his powers fell. Because of this, separation also entered into the creatures; they have become divided against one another, and strife has broken out among them (496, 36).

## 2. Sin.

Eckhart does not investigate exactly how this original sin is transmitted to all people. He is a Creationist <note>Creationism (or Creatianism) in this historical context refers to the theological belief that God creates a new, individual soul for every human body at the time of conception or birth, rather than the soul being inherited from the parents.</note> entirely in the manner of *Thomas* [Aquinas] and distinguishes between the *sensitive soul* <note>original: *anima sensitiva*; the part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement</note> and the *intellectual soul* <note>original: *anima intellectiva*; the higher, rational part of the soul</note>. On the fortieth day after conception, God creates the soul much faster than in a single moment, after all the natural organs have already been formed. The activity of mere nature then ceases, and the entire bodily organization becomes a tool of the rational soul (260, 40. 366, 27). Despite this, the reproduction of sin remains unclear. However, the fact is acknowledged that the sin of the first humans deprived their descendants of the freedom to decide for the Divine. Bodily birth, according to the order of nature, makes man a sinner. Man enters the world as a child of the evil enemy <note>The devil.</note>. Of himself, man has nothing but malice and infirmity. God has only "loaned" him everything good, not "given" it <note>This implies that man does not own his virtues as his own property, but holds them only by God's continuous favor.</note>. Whatever you have in yourself—heart and senses, body and soul and every faculty—is corrupted by sin. Without grace, the soul is like a dead tree that is unable to bring forth any living fruit (369, 37. 433, 4. 561, 9. 366, 31).

The carrier of sin in man is the body. Because the soul originates from heaven—that is, from God—but the body originates from the earth, they are always at odds with one another (396, 29). Body and flesh stand forever in hostile opposition to the spirit (29, 17). Therefore, as long as the soul is burdened with the mortal body, it must suffer misery and distress in a continuous struggle against its enemies. On the other hand, the assumption that evil is merely a byproduct of our nature is erroneous; rather, it stems just as much from habit. We must not be overcome by our enemies, as some believe; for while they certainly inflame the evil within us, they are not its cause. Within man is a hidden fire that the devil may well stoke and ignite; but we can resist him (357, 13). Thus the soul has three powerful enemies: the flesh, the world, and the devil, which hang together like "three cherries on one stem," and among these the body is the worst, into which the soul is banished as if into a prison—not so that it may fulfill the body's evil desires, but so that it may resist them, and thereby daily [earn] the eternal reward in heaven and the love poured into it here below...

3. Sin is extremely repugnant to God, and nothing is as foreign to God as sin. But in the whole of the divine plan for the world, sin also occupies a positive position. God brings his will into reality by means of sin and beyond sin. God is more powerful than sin, and even sin must serve his purposes. Man intervenes disturbingly in the activity of God insofar as his intention is evil (529, 26). Nevertheless, there would never have been a true finitude and a multiplicity of soul-activities without sin, and this multiplicity is indeed meant to exist, though only to be resolved <note>original: *aufgehoben*; a term meaning both to abolish and to preserve at a higher level</note> within unity. Not the original unity, but the unity restored from the rupture is the true purpose of creation (496, 29). Sin is first of all man's greatest misery. For it blocks the paths upon which the divine light should shine into the soul (12, 3). But on the other hand, sin is also again the point of passage for man's greatest salvation. Indeed, sometimes sin is placed under the same point of view as other physical evils and sufferings, and God is regarded as the one who directly imposes sin upon man, in order to prepare him thereby for an even greater bliss. If nothing can happen without God's will, then neither can sin; but if sin belongs as a means and point of passage into the system of the absolute purpose, then one can also imagine God not merely as permitting sin, but as the actual author of sin. We will miss clear decisiveness here in Eckhart's statements; but this much is obvious: that at least at times, the prevailing tendency—to trace everything back to God in the last instance in a pantheistic <note>Pantheism: the belief that God and the universe are identical, or that everything is part of an all-encompassing God.</note> manner—pushes aside every opposing consideration. Sin, once it is present, is not entirely and in every respect that which "ought not to be." Least of all is it so in a subjective sense as an act of man. Sin belongs to man as a condition of redemption; in this respect it is a *<term>fortunate fault</term>* <note>original: *felix culpa*; the theological concept that the Fall of Man was a "happy fault" because it resulted in the even greater good of the Incarnation and Redemption.</note>, as the expression has long been voiced in the Church—

Therefore, the angels do not grieve when a person commits sin; for they have insight into the justice of God and perceive all things in him just as they are in God (111, 8). God, who carries the ideas of all things within himself, also beholds evil and sin, but not as such; rather, he sees them in the form of the good that is opposed to them. For example, he beholds the lie in the image of truth (327, 20).

And if it seems at times that he is angry with the sinner, it is not anger, but love. His wrath stems from love, for he feels wrath without suffering (42, 5). 

God also does not punish sin; sin is itself its own heaviest punishment. That very fact—that you do evil—that is your entire harm and is woe enough for you. Be certain of this by the eternal truth: it is such a heavy wrath of God that he could do nothing worse to the sinner, neither with hell nor with anything else, than he does by allowing it to happen to him, or ordaining it upon him, that he is a sinner, and by not imposing heavy suffering upon him to break his sinful will. Even if God gave him all the woe of the world, he could not strike him harder than he is already struck by the fact that he sins (277, 10).

### 3. Christ.

Twice in the course of our presentation, we have touched upon Eckhart’s Christology. In the doctrine of the Trinity, we encountered the second person in the triad of the manifest God—the object of divine self-reflection <term>self-reflection: "Sichselbstdenken," the process by which God the Father contemplates His own nature, thereby generating the Son</term>, which united with the subject in oneness: the Son or the Word of the Father, in whom all things are spoken. We then saw how Eckhart presents the moral ideal in a personality that unites divine and human nature within itself, and whose imitation is an essential characteristic of moral life. Eckhart links both concepts—that of the eternal Son of God and that of the perfectly sanctified human personality—to the God-man <term>God-man: "Gottmensch," a theological term for Jesus Christ, who is fully God and fully man</term>, Jesus Christ, of the Revelation. In this single historical personality, the second person of the Trinity took on the form of human individuality, and the moral ideal found its fully valid representative. In this, Eckhart essentially adheres to the dogmatic view of the Church, although he certainly attempts to define the concept of this God-man in detail in his own peculiar way, making it more conceptually precise and intelligible.

1. The task of Christology as Eckhart defines it is to understand how the eternal Son—the immanent member of the essential Trinity <term>essential Trinity: "Wesenstrinität," referring to the internal relationship of the Persons within the Godhead</term>—could nonetheless appear in time in the form of a specific historical personality. For, first and foremost, he does not intend to discard any essential part of Christ’s full human reality. He carefully distinguishes between this historical person—who came into being at a specific moment in time and is a creature in body and soul, a man like us—and what this person was according to his eternal essence. In himself, Christ is an individual man; in his essence, he is humanity itself. From...

By nature, the souls of Christ and Mary are the same as my soul or the soul of any other human being. Christ’s soul never fully fathomed the Godhead, because it is a creature and was created in time. As a child, Christ was so simple <note>original: "einfältig," here meaning innocent, humble, or lacking complex worldly knowledge</note> that he did not recognize his father and mother. Even in heaven, he sees nothing with physical eyes except what is in front of him; if he wished to see something behind him, he would have to turn around. Christ’s soul participates in the divine nature through grace, just as God possesses it by nature (501, 19. 397, 19. 535, 13). If God were to withdraw what is His from the soul of Christ, Christ would remain a mere creature (51, 37). Jesus Christ’s human will was as powerless against the divine will as nothing is against something, or as the created is against the eternal (659, 9). Christ’s body was mortal and susceptible to suffering; his soul was bound to the body, senses, and intellect, and held fast in this union which was unworthy of it. The mere connection of his soul with a mortal body was a humiliation for it; to this was added his suffering within that body. His soul was deprived of the full vision <term>vision: "Anschauung," the direct, intuitive contemplation of God's essence</term> of God, his will was limited, and his lower faculties were filled with the deepest suffering. To progress in the vision of God, he required grace (292, 29).

2. What is it, then, that distinguishes this man—who in all other respects is so like the rest of us—so fundamentally from all others before and after him? First, it was the miracle of his physical birth. In heaven, Christ has a Father and no mother; on earth, he has a mother but no father. The will of the Father and the obediently subordinate will of the Son, through the power of the Spirit common to them both, took the purest drop of blood <note>This reflects a medieval biological belief that the embryo was formed from the mother’s purest blood</note> in the "pure chamber" of the virginal heart of Mary—who had been chosen as the instrument for this from the beginning—and from it fashioned a flawless human being with all its limbs and infused into it a soul with all its powers; and this occurred by the power of the Godhead. The soul was created by God at a specific moment in time out of the nothingness in which it had hovered from eternity (660, 6. 292, 2). The other thing that most distinguishes Christ, however, is the effect of grace, unique in its magnitude, which was bestowed upon him at the very moment of his birth. 3. The inseparability of this union, which was never disturbed for a single moment in Christ’s temporal existence, appears—when viewed from the perspective of divine causality <note>God acting as the primary cause of all things</note>—as an effect of divine grace, granted in a degree never to be bestowed again. But when viewed from the perspective of the free decision of the man Jesus, it presents itself as Christ’s free act and a virtue equally incomparable and unique in its degree. The soul of Christ never insisted on its own particularity <note>his individual, separate existence as a human person</note>. In the first moment when Christ’s body and soul were united with the Godhead, his soul gazed upon the Godhead just as it does today. But with the lower powers of his soul, which were active in the body—those with which he preached, taught, and performed other works—the enjoyment of this vision was perhaps diminished, but not the vision itself. For the highest powers—and it was in those that the union took place—stood at all times in pure contemplation. Only his bodily nature, not his soulish nature, stood in a mediated relationship to God. Nevertheless, he did not cease for a single moment to accomplish all the works for which his heavenly Father had sent him, and through this he earned reward and honor. His reward is that his body, together with his soul, was glorified in his resurrection; the honor, however, which he earned with his holy life, consists in his being called the Head of holy Christendom (644, 22). Therefore, Christ could not increase in the divine light dwelling within him; but in every individual thing in which he was active, he gained new and ever greater blessedness (643, 16). Christ’s soul was the wisest that ever existed; in the creature, it turned toward the Creator, and therefore the Father clothed it with a divine garment and shared His nature with it (674, 12). 5. In order for Christ’s mission and activity to become fruitful for us, it is necessary that we follow him (293, 21). Neither what Christ was nor what he attained belongs exclusively to him. Christ was the first human being who completely regained the unity with God that was lost in Adam, just as we can now regain it through him. Therefore, we rightly praise and exalt Christ as our Lord and God, even though according to my general nature, I possess everything just as much as Christ is able to achieve according to his humanity (64, 34). For Christ’s nature is our nature (678, 29). Christ’s uniqueness consists entirely in the perfection of his virtue. For if we were as holy as he, then the eternal Word would unite with us in exactly the same way as it did with Christ. Therefore, in Eckhart’s view, Christ is by no means the **substitute** <note>original: "Stellvertreter." In traditional theology, this refers to Christ acting as a legal proxy for humanity; Eckhart shifts the focus to Christ as an internal transformation of the self</note> who covers our nakedness through the perfection of his merit; rather, he is the **model** <note>original: "Vorbild," meaning an exemplar or archetype to be realized within the believer</note>. To the extent that we follow him, we also participate in his essence and his divinity. He shows us what we could be and should be. Where a clod of earth falls, it indicates where the earth's true resting place is; and where a spark flies, it indicates where the fire belongs. Now we have sent a **spark** <term>Spark: "Funke," often called the "Seelenfünklein" or little spark of the soul; the highest, most divine part of the human spirit that remains eternally one with God</term> to heaven, namely the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ; this shows us that the resting place of all souls is nowhere but in heaven. In Christ’s body, however, we have sent a clod of earth toward heaven, and therefore every earthly body also belongs in heaven (237, 1). We are only blessed, however, insofar as he is in us and we are in him. Indeed, God bears his Son unceasingly; but if this birth does not occur within me, what does it profit me? Rather, everything depends on it happening within me (3, 7). A master says: because God became man, the entire human race has been exalted and honored; we may well rejoice that Christ our brother, by his own power, has ascended above all the choirs of angels and sits at the right hand of the Father. This master spoke well; but truly, I would not give much for it—

# V. Revelation and the Church.

What would it help me if I had a brother who was a rich man, while I remained poor, or a brother who was wise, while I remained a fool (64, 22)? What would it help me if Mary were "full of grace," unless I too were full of grace (274, 33)? If a rich king gave his beautiful daughter to a poor man's son, everyone belonging to that family would be elevated and honored by the union. Christ has taken on human nature; thus, everything that Christ has won is my own, provided that I rise to this same nature (64, 18 and 30). Therefore, the fact that Christ is blessed does not make me blessed, unless I myself become Christ <note>Eckhart’s radical "mysticism of identity" suggests that the believer must psychologically and spiritually unify with the divine nature just as Christ did</note>, and am myself born as the Son of God. This is something I can achieve, for Christ has opened the way and the access to it through his teaching and his example.

Eckhart expresses this latter thought through a parable as follows. For five thousand and two hundred years <note>A common medieval calculation of the time elapsed from the creation of the world to the birth of Christ</note>, God struggled to draw humanity up to Himself without accomplishing anything. Then, Christ offered to step in for Him; he took on human nature and all our physical misery, excluding only the sin and irrationality that stems from Adam. All his words, his works, and his very limbs were a rope by which he pulled us toward him for thirty-three years, until bloody sweat broke out from his holy body. Even then, he saw no success; yet he saw that all things were beginning to move in order to follow him. Therefore, he allowed himself to be lifted up on the cross and laid aside all his glory and everything that could hinder him from pulling. And only then did he pull with real strength, accomplishing more in a few hours than he had in many years before. He drew the Father to himself through his equality with Him, so that He might set aside His anger for the sake of this unheard-of sacrifice; and his blood extinguished the fiery sword with which the Cherub <note>A reference to the angel guarding the Garden of Eden after the Fall of Man</note> had closed off Paradise. By pouring out his blood, Christ, with the "power of a vacuum" <note>original: "Kraft des leeren Raumes." Eckhart uses a physical metaphor here: just as nature abhors a vacuum and rushes to fill it, God's mercy is drawn into the "emptiness" created by Christ’s total self-sacrifice</note>, drew God’s mercy and grace into himself so abundantly that it sufficed for the entire world. And just as the warmth of the sun draws the vapor of the earth toward itself, so the fervor of love that Christ proved on the cross drew all the world after him, so that those who take his death and his martyrdom to heart will be eternally blessed with him. And since then, the Holy Spirit also pulls, driving out from us all evil works of the flesh and birthing his gifts within us,

### 3. Christ.
<page-num>319</page-num>

...through which the reward of eternal life is bestowed upon us (218—220).

Eckhart does not entirely lack turns of phrase that align with the Church's traditional teaching of a <term>Savior</term> <note>German: *Heiland*</note> who cancels our sins through his sacrificial death and intercedes on our behalf. Christ is called the Redeemer; he has washed us clean with his blood and redeemed us from original sin (452, 37); he has "killed our death" (242, 18). Christ calls our sin his sin and his works our works; for he has made satisfaction for our sins as if he had committed them himself, and we obtain the merit of his works just as if we had performed them (184, 8). However, the actual <term>Doctrine of Satisfaction</term> <note>The theological theory, popularized by Anselm of Canterbury, that Christ's death was a necessary legal payment to satisfy God's justice on behalf of humanity</note> itself is not present. Even in the act of redemption, Christ appears only as an archetype or model. That Christ suffered is intended to make our own tribulations light. The brave warrior does not complain about his wounds when he looks upon the King who is wounded alongside him. He offers us a drink that he himself has already tasted. He commands nothing of us that he did not first do or suffer himself (184, 11). If God was the common redeemer of all the world, then I too should be a redeemer for every other person and, through my own sanctification, atone for the sins of all (561, 5). In this sense, Christ has freed us from everything that came upon us through Adam’s transgression—from the bonds of being a mere <term>creature</term> <note>In this context, a "creature" refers to anything created, which in mystical thought is seen as limited or "nothing" compared to the Creator</note>—and in his knowledge has ascended to the One who sent him, in order to lead us directly to Him (244, 13). And because suffering is the most direct path to salvation, Christ appears above all as the one who has suffered the most (501, 40; 183, 21; 337, 30).

But what is truly exemplary about Christ is essentially his divinity. By virtue of his humanity, he was originally a creature, a man like any other. Therefore, we must not let our devotion remain fixed upon the image of his humanity. Rather, it is the God within him toward whom we should strive. We have already encountered the formula: we should pursue the humanity of Christ until we find the divinity. For this reason, Eckhart finds the sentimental, emotional contemplation of the suffering and death of Jesus to be a hindrance rather than a help to true devotion. The body of the Lord, apart from his divinity and his soul, is nothing compared to the <term>inner birth</term> <note>A cornerstone of Eckhart’s teaching: the "Eternal Birth" of the Son of God within the human soul</note> of God in the soul. For every blessed soul is something more noble than the dy[ing]—

Let us briefly survey Eckhart's <term>Christology</term> <note>The theological study of the person and work of Jesus</note>. While Eckhart maintains the supernatural birth of Jesus, it remains without essential influence on the image of Christ that the Master sketches. Christ attained an advantage over all other people through the grace granted to him, as well as through perfect sanctification and sinlessness, by which he becomes the model for all. The union of his human nature with the divine in such a way that he is absorbed into the person of the Son of God is nothing other than the consequence of his holiness; by giving up his finite individuality, he immediately entered into the second person of the <term>Trinity</term> <note>The Christian doctrine of God as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>. In this, he is not to remain the only one; rather, all who are truly sanctified attain exactly what he attained by following his example. Christ is everywhere different from us not in kind, but only in degree. There is no talk of Christ interceding for us; rather, we are to become Christ ourselves through moral perfection, and without this, Christ's suffering and death can be of no help to us. While most mystics tend to indulge in the touching portrayal of Christ's sufferings <note>Late medieval piety often focused intensely on the "Passion," using graphic imagery of Christ’s wounds to evoke emotional responses</note>, *Eckhart* actually warns against this and mentions these sufferings only to call for the joyful endurance of one's own suffering and for devotion to God. In all this, the **metaphysician** reveals himself more than the **religious man**, and in no other point does *Eckhart* stand in such sharp contrast to church doctrine. But his intention was obviously not to dispute the Church's teaching here either. He knows very well that the common view might rebel against his; but his comfort remains that the pronouncements of Holy Scripture speak in his favor (289, 6). With the best of intentions, he only wants to spiritualize the doctrine of Christ, not abolish it; yet, unconsciously to himself, the actual dogmatic-religious content of the doctrine is lost in the process. In how many points his <term>Christology</term> <note>The theological study of the nature and work of Jesus Christ</note> echoes more modern interpretations of the doctrine, we do not need to remind ourselves of in detail.

## 4. The Church.

1. The mystic as such behaves indifferently toward the Church, and in many cases, dismissively; few mystics have succeeded in moving with a secure footing on the ground of the Church. In *Eckhart's* circle of thought, the Church plays only a subordinate role; yet he never fights against it and never speaks of the Church and its institutions with anything other than reverence. He knows only the one Roman Church; he honors it from a sincere heart as the bearer of salvation and the possessor of truth. However, she possesses the truth in an imperfect, finite form; the mystical standpoint strives beyond her. God, he says, is our Father, and Christendom (the Church) is our mother. But however beautiful and glorious she may be, and however useful with her statutes, everything is still imperfect—a mixture of light and darkness. Without hesitation, *Eckhart* counts the Church among those things which partly belong to this world (91, 2). On the other hand, he still considers following the laws of holy Christendom to be a sign of receptivity to salvation (638, 1). —

# V. Revelation and the Church.

He also accepts the external institutions of the Church as a given; he disputes neither the *papacy* nor the *priesthood* in general. Admittedly, he only mentions the *Pope* in a context that is not suited to showing excessive reverence (446, 24). Neither the *Pope* nor a *Bishop* can release one from vows taken, because through these one has pledged oneself directly to *God* (23, 11). *Human nature* is worth just as much in the poorest and most despised person as it is in the *Pope* or the *Emperor* (57, 7 and 9). That the *Pope* is the *Pope* costs him much worry (62, 1). One should honor the *clergy* (332, 9). In the *sermon*, one should pay attention to the divine word that flows to us through the *preacher* like *water* through a *pipe* <note>original: "Kanal." Eckhart often uses the image of a conduit to explain that the spiritual quality of the person delivering the message does not diminish the truth of the message itself</note>, and not whether the *preacher* is stained with any sin (76, 35). The high clergy are not exactly models of *devotion*; since their office often entangles them in worldly affairs, they rarely receive special *consolation* from *God* (348, 22). Elsewhere, he emphasizes the privilege and the resulting higher obligation of the *priesthood*, which, because it is constantly occupied with spiritual things, must all the more direct its thoughts toward divine *mysteries* (481, 32). Against the dogmatic view of some priests, he defends his own perspective as the deeper one (233, 29. 234, 37). *Monastic vows* otherwise appear to him quite worthless because the holy life is not bound to any specific external forms, and often an unholy disposition is hidden behind them (340, 30); but he does place special value on the vow of *obedience* (544, 2), just as he does not absolutely reject external *poverty* as a means to salvation. — *Eckhart* knows and teaches a closer path to God than the ecclesiastical one; but the Church does not prevent one from taking this path. On the other hand, those for whom the "better way" is too high may content themselves with the Church’s mediation of *salvation*. Many people reach the *Kingdom of Heaven* who, on earth, enjoy no more of mystical intimacy with God than one enjoys the bright sun in a dark forest (77, 39). Everyone can, and everyone should, become their own *confessor*; but the right and honorable *confessor* <note>original: "Beichtiger." In the medieval context, a priest who hears confession and grants absolution</note> can become the guide who helps the seeker toward this goal. The ecclesiastical exercises and regulations are not the highest thing; but they have

2. **Eckhart** praises the saints as patterns of piety and virtue; but he knows nothing—or wishes to know nothing—of their worship by humans or of their intercession for humans (454, 13), and to consider them as the highest models for the moral life seems to him mistaken. For this dignity belongs only to **Christ**. All human virtue and holiness, except for that of Christ, is finite and limited, and we ought to strive beyond everything finite toward the perfect. **Christ** calls **John the Baptist** the greatest among all those born of women. But neither **John** nor anyone else among all the saints is a supreme model whom we should follow, or a specific boundary behind which we must remain. No saint in heaven is so holy and perfect that their virtue was not bound within certain limits, and the degree of their bliss corresponds to these limits. No saint in heaven is so perfect—you can break through the limit of their holiness and attain a place in heaven beyond them and remain there eternally (295, 5). For the lowliest person, who might eternally lack God, **Christ** has performed more works of love than all the saints ever performed for Christ's sake (404, 16). Many thousands have become saints who were lesser than they should have been, and many are saints who never received the highest communication of grace (650, 11).

But from another perspective as well, we should move beyond the concept of saints. Even with Christ, we should look beyond the <term>creaturely-human</term> <note>Eckhart distinguishes between Christ’s human nature (the "creature") and his divine nature (the "Godhead").</note> and hold to his pure Godhead. Everything belonging to the <term>creature</term> <note>In mystical theology, a "creature" (Creatur) is any created thing—including humans and saints—which is distinct from the uncreated God.</note> is like a splinter in the eye of the soul and hinders union with God. Therefore, the soul should cast out all saints and "Our Lady" <note>The Virgin Mary.</note>, because they are all creatures (241, 35). > “People, what do you seek in the dead bones? Why do you not seek the living salvation that can give you eternal life? For the dead have nothing to give nor to take” (599, 26).

The Virgin **Mary** also occupies the highest place among humans next to **Christ** in **Eckhart’s** view; but he is far from raising her to an object of adoration. **Mary** serves him in particular as a model for the proof of virtue throughout the entire course of earthly life. One honors her correctly when one follows her example. Not that she was the physical mother of **Christ** grants her such great preference, but that she was free from all sin. Before she became the mother of **Christ**, she had already born God spiritually within herself. To speak of the miracles of **Mary** means little; one should speak of her holiness and perfection. Only the overflowing fullness of the Divine, which dwelt within her and which also shaped her body accordingly, made her also physically the mother of God. When **Mary** bore God spiritually, that was more pleasing to God than when he was born of her physically. ### 4. The Church.

Regarding the *Sacraments*, *Eckhart* teaches mostly in the spirit of the <term>church-scholastic</term> <note>Scholasticism was the dominant medieval school of philosophy and theology that sought to use logic and reason to understand Christian revelation.</note> view. The mystery of the <term>communication of grace</term> <note>German: "Gnadenmittheilung"</note> through physical-material mediation, particularly <term>transubstantiation</term> <note>German: "Substanzverwandlung"; the doctrine that the substance of bread and wine is changed into the actual body and blood of Christ during Mass</note>, finds an easy connection in the Master's mind, as he views the sensory world as essentially without being in itself, but as something becoming spiritual. On several occasions, he himself discusses the mystery of the <term>Eucharist</term> <note>German: "Abendmahl"; literally "Evening Meal," referring to the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion</note> in particular, using the dialectical skills common in that era. Yet, he nevertheless places the highest value not on the external process or the physical means, but on the *greatness of devotion* with which the gift is received.

*Eckhart* names the seven-fold number of the *Sacraments*; however, besides the Eucharist and Baptism, he only mentions Confession and Marriage. In the seven Sacraments, the soul is sanctified and transported into a divine life; they are established so that the soul may continually prove and realize itself anew in grace. They receive their sanctifying power from the eternal Idea, the form in which they have existed in God from eternity (328, 12). The highest means of grace is the Sacrament of the Eucharist. God draws the soul up to Himself through the great gift of His holy body. Therefore, this noble Sacrament is a great joy to all the devout. The person is blessed who often receives our Lord’s body with a pure heart and a quiet conscience. However high the heavens and however wide the firmament: you are yet higher and wider; in our Lord’s body, you receive a height above all height and a width above all width, which heaven and earth are unable to encompass. All creatures in truth could not give or offer for a single moment the great and unthinkable perfection and the wonderful joy that the soul possesses through the blessed presence of God in the holy Sacrament (378—382).

For in the Sacrament, in reality only the appearance of the bread remains—only those properties which are perceived by the senses and are therefore also capable of nourishing the physical body. In truth, however, a completely new essence has been added through <term>consecration</term> <note>original: "Consecration"; the ritual act where the priest blesses the bread and wine</note>, the essence of the immortal, glorified body of Christ (678—680). # V. Revelation and the Church.

...taken in one form and returned in another form, as if in a concealing vessel. One does not like to see or touch a precious jewel without its covering. The garment in which He has clothed Himself is the parable <note>German: "Gleichniss"; can also be translated as "likeness" or "image."</note> of the bread (112, 18). This elevation of the sensory to the bearer of the spiritual should not be surprising. He honors God rightly who honors Him equally in all things. All things change their form in order to rise to a higher form; they ennoble themselves, they strive back toward their original purity, they enter into man as nourishment. Thus, the food I eat is transformed into my soul. In nature, there is a power that separates and expels everything sensory, and the spiritual communicates itself to the lower nature down to its smallest parts. Why should God not also be able to make the Body of Christ out of bread? (112, 20. 334, 12). All grace and the bliss of all good works, all the bliss of the saints and of the Son of God Himself according to His humanity—all of this is encompassed in the Body of God; for there the soul receives the end, the ultimate purpose of all things, which spring from it and end in it again (355, 40).

The effect of the <term>Eucharist</term> <note>German: "Abendmahl"; literally "Evening Meal," referring to Holy Communion.</note> is union with God. Christ was God and man. He has given us His most holy body; whoever receives it worthily receives the person of the Son and the divine nature all at once—specifically, he receives the human nature in its union with the divine nature. Where He is worthily received, there He is certainly present (389, 36). Whoever receives this food rightly becomes as one with it as flesh and blood are one with my soul (112, 22). On earth, the soul is not more closely united with God than through the sacrament of the Body of Christ, and this union is then perfected in the imitation of His glorious example (638, 13). It is especially the <term>spark of the spirit</term> <note>German: "Fünklein des Geistes"; in Eckhart’s theology, this is the innermost, uncreated part of the human soul that is capable of direct union with God.</note> that enjoys this food and in which its effect is revealed (111—115).

Whoever goes to the Eucharist should not pay so much attention to his moods and feelings, but rather consider what he is receiving and what he intends by it. Married life does not consist of a man and a woman joining together and following their outward senses and living according to their desires, but in a pious way of life. Marriage is an image of the union of divine and human nature and of the unity between God and the soul (239, 9).

# 4. The Church.

...holding fast to the **communication of grace** <note>German: *Gnadenmittheilung*; the transmission of God's favor through ritual.</note>. For this reason, he teaches that many people are hindered from the immediate and highest contemplation of the absolute Being by clinging to the **outwardness** <note>German: *Aeüsserlichkeit*; the external, material aspect of a rite as opposed to its spirit.</note> of the sacraments. For the sacrament is something external, but the truth is something internal. "Sacrament" means "sign." Whoever clings to the sign does not reach the inner truth to which the sign merely points (239, 26). 

This also applies to the Body of the Lord. The soul’s **bliss** <note>German: *Seligkeit*; a state of supreme spiritual happiness or salvation.</note> is greater in that God gives birth to himself within it without physical union, than is the body of Christ considered apart from his divinity and his soul (396, 39). Only those people truly enjoy the sacrament who are rightly called "Christ" themselves, and these receive it in a **supra-sacramental** <note>German: *übersacramentlich*; a state where the believer is so unified with God that the external ritual is transcended.</note> way. Therefore, Eckhart dares to say: anyone who possessed the same inner state when eating ordinary food as they do when receiving the sacrament would receive God just as well as in the sacrament. As bold as this statement may seem to many, it is nevertheless true. My right inner disposition must bestow upon the gift its right quality; in this way, I would be the "right state" for that which is intended to bring me into the right state (592, 26).

# V. Revelation and the Church.

...connects with a personal interaction with a personal Father in heaven, who is just as much the absolutely Wise and absolutely Good as He is the Almighty. Therefore, prayer first requires the consciousness of the infinite distance between every **creature** <note>German: *Creatur*; in this context, it refers to any created being, emphasizing the distinction between the finite human and the infinite Creator.</note>—and the soul itself—and their Creator; then, the consciousness that God is accessible to the plea and the heart's concern of the creature. Furthermore, it requires that there be a specific object of the request, which is recommended to God as something morally justified and pleasing to Him. **Eckhart's** standpoint abolishes all these requirements of actual prayer from the outset. The separation between God and man, which lies in the latter's mere status as a creature, is for him something that should not be and something that can be purely and completely abolished at every moment. Furthermore, God's activity is conceived so thoroughly as **supra-temporal** <note>German: *überzeitliches*; existing outside or above the flow of time.</note> and timeless, so far from all change and so much as a simple rational consequence of God's essence, that there can be no talk of a real change of will in God, or of an actual answering of prayer. Finally, the heart becomes unholy and ungodly precisely because it still clings to something specific, be it a virtue, a duty, or an external good. No single thing, no specific idea or desire, no particular concept is worthy at all of filling a human heart; thus, there is no heart's concern that could rightfully be presented to God. In all these respects, prayer from the mystic’s standpoint is an impossibility.

Nevertheless, **Eckhart** can speak to a certain extent about the significance of the life of prayer for the development of the inner person—not because of its influence on God, but because of its effect on the person praying. Prayer, and even specific prayer formulas and times, are ordained by the Church as a useful exercise to gather the scattered senses and direct them toward the "one thing that is necessary" (240, 8); it is a privilege of pious people, and especially of the **priestly class**, upon whom these exercises are imposed through external regulations, that they are thereby led more frequently to **recollection** <note>German: *Sammlung*; a spiritual practice of withdrawing the mind from external distractions to focus entirely on God.</note> in God. **Christ** asks the Father for transfiguration; he could just as well have prayed in secret,

## 5. The Last Things.

We conclude our presentation of Eckhart’s doctrine with a compilation of his statements regarding what lies beyond this earthly life. Eckhart’s entire temperament pulls the holy and eternal so deeply into the development of life in this world <note>original: *Diesseits*; referring to our current earthly existence.</note> that little remains that is unique to a "hereafter" <note>original: *Jenseits*.</note> as distinct from the "here and now." It is only by exception, therefore, that he includes the afterlife within the scope of his treatment at all, and then with the explicit intention of correcting—that is, spiritualizing—the prevailing ideas circulating about it.

1. We saw that Eckhart assumes the possibility of constant progress in knowledge and sanctification for life in this world. Physical death, however, is an absolute conclusion. When the soul departs from the body, that is its last day, and it will never reach a higher standpoint of the **knowledge of God** than it had attained at that moment (639, 18). The task of earthly life is to gradually permeate all the powers of the soul and body with the divine principle through practice and habituation. After this earthly life, however, the soul flows back into its natural origin from which it flowed, and the more it has kept itself free from temporal concepts and **created things** <note>original: *Creaturen*; in mystical thought, this refers to anything that is not God, which can distract the soul from its divine source.</note>, the more God-like it flows back into God (413, 32). **Blessedness** <note>original: *Seligkeit*; a state of supreme spiritual joy and union with the divine.</note> is nothing other than the enjoyment of this **God-likeness**; it consists especially in the pure and adequate vision of God. To the soul that persists in God-likeness and in its glorious disposition, and which progresses from one good to another, eternal life is opened at the moment it departs from the body. There, it is embraced by a divine light, transplanted into God, and formed into Him. Each power of the soul then receives the **likeness** of the Divine Persons: the will receives the likeness of the Holy Spirit, the reason that of the...

# V. Revelation and Church.

...of the Son, the memory that of the Father and the divine nature, and yet at the same time it remains an undivided whole (386, 28). There the soul is beyond time and space and every form of finitude. In heaven, a thousand souls have room on the point of a needle, and yet the space allotted to the soul is much larger than heaven and earth and everything God ever created. Indeed, however many heavens and earths, however many worlds and creatures God could have created, all that would still be less than a needle’s point in proportion to the space occupied by a soul that is united with God (474, 32).

Eckhart strives most earnestly to exclude every hint of sensory satisfaction from the concept of bliss <note>original: *Seligkeit*; also translated as "beatitude," referring to the ultimate state of spiritual fulfillment in God.</note>. The Absolute, by revealing itself, draws the spirit out of itself into the hidden origin that remains within itself. Then the spirit loses every particular knowledge; it loses the light, which is a definite form and not knowledge of the Absolute; but it also loses the darkness, which is the knowledge of the Absolute without a definite form. For now the spirit no longer knows with its **created faculty** <note>original: *creatürlichen Vermögen*; the natural, finite cognitive abilities of a human being.</note>, but the knowing of the Absolute, which belongs to the blessed spirits, is a knowing by means of the entire power of another than they themselves are (518, 22). Bliss consists in having all that has being and is worth being desired and brings joy; furthermore, that one has it undivided with the whole soul and that one has received it in God in the purest and highest form, unveiled in the final <term>primordial ground<gloss>original: *Urgrund*; Eckhart's term for the absolute, undifferentiated essence of God where the soul and God are one.</gloss></term> of all being, precisely where God himself receives it (106, 23). Neither love nor knowledge constitutes the essence of bliss. Man has the vision of God when he is born in God. But once he is born, he no longer looks at God as something else; for there he lives where the Father lives, in the absolutely simple and in pure being (191, 31). If God gave my soul everything he ever created or could still create and God were not there, and if there were only a hair’s breadth missing, my soul would have no satisfaction and would not be blessed. If I am blessed, then all things are in me and God too; where I am, there is God, and where God is, there am I (32, 9).

# V. Revelation and the Church.

...has forfeited his life, in that he has robbed him and his friends of their honor and attacked his life, even though the Lord has shown him nothing but good and has constantly hoped for his improvement and grieves over the lack thereof. The King takes possession of the man by means of a **just judgment**, but does not kill him, so that he may atone for the disgrace he has inflicted upon him. First, they bind his hands and feet and throw him into the lowest tower among toads and snakes. Then they take him out and place him in a **place of shame**, so that all people may see his open disgrace and he may see the joy of all people. Thus his pain is all the greater. So one adds one disgrace upon another, the greatest that can be devised; he is thrown back into prison again and again, and he expects at any moment that they wish to destroy him. There one can say: the man is in the King’s castle; for the tower is just as much in the King's castle as the banquet hall where the King is with his beloved friends, and yet you well understand that their condition is different. And this misery must last eternally (471, 8). The pain of Hell consists essentially in the fact that the damned see the joy of the blessed with envy (455, 33), and that they are conscious of their own worthlessness while they must be deprived of the <term>beatifitc vision</term> <note>original: *Anschauung Gottes*; the direct perception of God's essence.</note> of God (522, 18). To the question of what burns in Hell, the usual answer is: it is <term>self-will</term> <note>original: *Eigenwille*; the stubborn insistence on one's own desires apart from God.</note>. But it is rather <term>the Nothing</term> <note>original: *das Nicht*; a central Eckhartian concept referring to the absence of being or the lack of divine likeness.</note> that burns in Hell. If I lay a glowing coal upon my hand, it is not so much the coal that burns me, but rather it is **the Nothing**; namely, that the coal has something in itself which my hand does *not* have. For if my hand were of a fiery nature like the coal is, then all the fire in the world could not harm it. It is exactly the same with the damned. Because God, and all who are before God’s face in true bliss, have something in themselves which those who are separated from God do not have, it is this **Nothing** that torments the souls in Hell more than self-will or any fire (65, 20). By necessity, all creatures must be in God. Whoever falls out of the hand of God’s **mercy**, falls instead into the hand of **justice**. Eckhart also speaks of <term>Purgatory</term> <note>original: *Fegefeuer*; literally "cleansing fire."</note>; however, he regards the word as a sensory and metaphorical expression for a spiritual state. For it is through divine mercy that the sinner—after suffering unspeakable torment—finds grace on the Last Day, if not sooner (453, 36). When the soul departs from the body in faithful love and with the firm will to do all things for God’s sake and to leave all sin behind, the soul bears great sorrow that it can no longer act, and it waits for the day when God takes pity on it. Eckhart corrects the popular conception of the <term>Last Day</term> <note>original: *jüngster Tag*; the Day of Judgment.</note> and the Judgment by saying that every human being passes judgment upon themselves there. People falsely say that St. John and other friends of our Lord ascended to heaven with body and soul. In God, nothing can exist but God; there is neither mouth nor nose, hand nor foot, nor anything created that belongs to the body. They cannot, therefore, have arrived there with the physical body. The body, which was meant to decay in the earth, was consumed in the air, so that only the essence of the body reached God—that essence which would have followed the soul anyway on the Last Day <note>original: *jüngster Tag*; the Day of Judgment at the end of time.</note>. So it also happened with Mary and all those of whom it is said that they ascended to God with their bodies. One can also see this in the <term>Ascension of Christ</term> <note>The event where Jesus ascended into heaven forty days after his resurrection.</note>. He ate as he journeyed toward heaven. Naturally, the food had to dissolve during the ascension, and everything that Christ had taken on here below also remained behind here below. Into the Father, he could bring back nothing except what had flowed forth from the Father. The essence of Christ’s soul drew the essence of our Lord Jesus Christ’s noble humanity up with it in a divine state of being. Thus the person stands in the Father, so that he is one with the Father; and thus stand all those in the Father who attain through grace what Christ possesses by nature—not in such a way that they take the life of the body up with them when they depart from here; rather, it must remain behind until the Last Day. Only on that day, when all things come to nothing, will the essence of the body be granted to the soul according to the usual rule. But whomever God wished to grant special grace, He did for them exactly what He did for John (472, 5). This bodily <term>transfiguration</term> <note>original: *Verklärung*; a spiritual transformation into a glorified, radiant state.</note> after the resurrection is compared by <term>Eckhart</term> to the Transfiguration in which Christ appeared to the disciples on the mountain (17, 23).
