# Conclusion.

Eckhart’s doctrine, as we have attempted to portray it in the preceding pages, will prove itself to any impartial judgment as a deeply conceived and grandly executed **structure of thought**. One must conclude that Eckhart’s endeavor was directed toward the highest aims, and that in him, an admirable power of thought was combined with the most inward devotion and a childlike **purity of soul**. To prove his fundamental **metaphysical** outlook in all areas of religious life—this is the task he set for himself and solved in a singular manner. In this, he is entirely original, however much he may owe to others in specific details. All the thoughts he adopted from foreign systems of doctrine take on a new meaning through the new context in which he places them. Indeed, the mere fact that he strove for such an inextricable connection, and that in the bold consistency of his thought he did not shrink from any prevailing opinion, would alone make him a **phenomenon** without equal in that era <note>original: *Weltalter*; referring to the medieval period in which Eckhart lived.</note>. He wants, as we might express it, to raise all mental representations to clear concepts, to trace every parable back to its deeper meaning, to interpret all mysteries, and to spiritualize everything sensory. And in this, he stops before no barrier, whether self-imposed or established by authority. But for this very reason, his thinking ends in an **abstraction** in which no definite concept can be grasped any longer; and the world of the individual and the finite has sunk so far into the bottomless nothingness of pure essence <note>original: *reinen Wesens*; for Eckhart, "essence" often refers to the Godhead beyond all distinctions, which can seem like a "nothingness" to human logic.</note> that he no longer knows how to find the way back to it.

<summary>This concluding section evaluates Meister Eckhart's work as a grand, original synthesis of logic and devotion. It highlights his radical consistency in spiritualizing all aspects of life, which ultimately led to a metaphysical abstraction where the physical world is lost in the "nothingness" of God.</summary>
<keywords>Meister Eckhart, metaphysics, structure of thought, purity of soul, abstraction, pure essence, medieval philosophy, religious life</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the concluding section of the work. # Conclusion.

Eckhart essentially views himself as a teacher of Christian truth. He absorbed the scholarly education <term>Scholasticism: the dominant medieval method of learning that combined Christian theology with Aristotelian philosophy</term> of his time and was a student of the most distinguished thought systems of that era. As a highly renowned teacher at the **University of Paris**, he defended and formally presented the teachings of his school. However, he only truly found his calling in a more **pastoral** capacity <note>original: *seelsorgerischen Thätigkeit*</note> as a clergyman in high offices and dignities. Now, the learned master no longer addresses his professional colleagues, but rather the poor monastic folk and laypeople. Now he no longer wishes merely to impart knowledge, but to pave and illuminate the path to the kingdom of heaven. Now he is concerned with the intellectual advancement of his listeners only insofar as it is the precondition for a **moral rebirth**.

The school from which he emerged was an idealistic one, which ascribed true being only to God and the Ideas within God. But this school bowed before the authority of the Church and became an important tool—not only to establish and bring the pure doctrine of the Church to consciousness, but also to support and theoretically justify the Church's practice itself, even in its glaring abuses. This was accomplished with the richest display of ingenuity, by allowing the standpoint of the "Idea" to shift into finite intellectual concepts and frolicking in the most subtle **dialectic** <note>The art of logical argument and investigation of truth through discussion.</note> with an untiring passion for argumentation. That was sufficient for the service of a Church increasingly calcifying in external forms, and for a domineering **priesthood** that proudly separated itself from the unlearned common people. But it was not enough as soon as one wanted to take seriously the idea that every individual Christian must seek salvation from within themselves and in their own person, through personal communion with God; it was not enough as soon as one thought not so much of the promotion of the Church as a hierarchical institution, but rather of the revitalization of the need for salvation and the powers of salvation in the hearts of the simple and lowly <note>original: *Unmündigen und Geringen*; referring to those without formal status or education.</note>.

This latter aim, however, was Eckhart’s goal when he began to teach and preach independently. He was not alone in this endeavor. Even the great luminaries of Church science did not disdain to preach to the Christian people; but it was absolutely necessary that in doing so, the actual

# Conclusion.

The foundations of their fame—the subtle and artificial theological solutions to problems that should never have been posed in the first place—retreated behind a simpler, heart-stirring exhortation to piety, to repentance, and to a turning away from the world. But "lesser" people also stepped into this same task—laypeople and clergy who were either ignorant of or had turned away from the high training of academic science <term>Schulwissenschaft: literally "school-science," referring to the rigorous, systematic theology taught in medieval universities</term>. They were full of pity for the poor, ignorant masses who, with their deep spiritual needs, were reliant on insufficient "soul-food" <note>original: *Seelenspeise*</note>, and for whom the priest—in possession of the Church's treasury of grace <term>Treasury of Grace: In Catholic theology, the infinite merit of Christ and the saints, which the Church believed it could dispense to the faithful</term>—was expected to do everything. These folk-teachers had the advantage of being able to practice their work on souls single-mindedly, without falling into conflict with their other activities, and could thus purely draw out the consequences of a Christian doctrine of grace. But the concern was that they lacked a firm and secure foundation of teaching; their knowledge was deficient and poorly developed. Consequently, fanaticism <note>original: *Schwärmerei*; a term used to describe over-enthusiastic, "wild," or ungrounded religious fervor</note>, which so often pairs with an overstrained piety where firm and clear concepts are missing, was the inevitable result.

Eckhart wished to teach like the latter, yet he possessed the scientific education of the former. Certainly, he never entered into direct fellowship with the heretics with whom the Church lumped him together. Without doubt, he became acquainted with the heretical sentiments so widespread at the time and likely recognized how much of his own strivings and teachings shared a common nature with them. Yet, even though he was not by nature a polemicist <term>Polemicist: a person who engages in aggressive verbal or written attacks against the opinions or principles of others</term>, he rejected their exaggerations and errors and sought to refute them. However, no matter how far his personal contacts may have gone, if the path he took eventually led him to a goal very similar in nature to the heresies then in vogue <note>the author refers here to groups like the Brethren of the Free Spirit</note>, he was nonetheless originally worlds apart from them in both education and character. Indeed, precisely what distinguishes Eckhart's teaching from the common heresies constitutes his essential significance.

Eckhart is a religious teacher of the Christian people; but from the start, he is a professionally trained philosopher, and

# Conclusion.

...[Certainly, he was what] was defined in those times as a theologian. For him, science and religious doctrine coincide, and in every single point he strives just as much for clear concepts as for Christian edification. And yet, that unity of scientific concept and religious dogma in him is not to be understood in the same way as with the great teachers of his Church. These others subject thought to the already fixed church dogma and, if necessary, bend their teaching to accommodate authority. **Eckhart’s** highest authority is the human heart's need for salvation <note>original: *Heilsbedürfniss*</note>. He needs no other foundation for his world of thought; he disdains any other interest. The soul wants to go to God to become one with him: this religious interest determines his circle of thought, conditions the basic layout, and guides every detail in the further execution of his doctrine.

From the school to which he belongs, **Eckhart** possesses that high estimation of human reason and its knowledge. "In knowing lies blessedness," **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Dominican philosopher who emphasized the role of reason in understanding God</note> had taught. **Eckhart** defends this sentence with zeal against the **Scotists** <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), who prioritized the "will" over "reason," sparking a long-running theological debate with the Dominicans</note>, having already defended it once in Paris. Reason <term>Vernunft: in this context, it refers to the highest faculty of the human mind capable of grasping divine truths</term> has the primacy among the powers of the human soul; all salvation rests on rational knowledge. But in this, he goes further than anyone since **Johannes Erigena** <note>Johannes Scotus Eriugena (c. 815–877), an early medieval philosopher who famously argued that true religion and true philosophy are identical</note> had dared: there can be no other or higher authority alongside reason; there can be no doctrine that, being inaccessible to reason, would only be communicated through revelation. And if there were one, it would be worthless. For a revelation that remains foreign to me, that is only held up to me from the outside—how can it help me? My salvation can only come from what I experience or undergo inwardly within myself, what sprouts for me from my own interior through divine grace. And how else should the originally external and foreign truth gain life in me, become the center of my personal life, than through reason? It cannot be an authority upon which my salvation depends, but only my own true essence, and that is reason.

**Eckhart** is forced to teach this way. For he wants to guide Christians to seek salvation not through the foreign mediation of the priest, but through themselves. Salvation must therefore be able to come from within them. A doctrine that

# Conclusion.

[...the reason that] proceeds from this knows no external authority, and it is enough for it to be in harmony with the nature of reason itself. *Eckhart's* theology does not differ from a metaphysics grown out of purely philosophical impulses. From the nature of reason, he generates his world of thought, and only afterward does he link it back to the fundamental concepts of revealed and traditional Christian teaching—naturally, not without these being modified in essential points so as not to fall into contradiction with his metaphysical principles. For while among the great theologians of the time, church dogma was the primary fixed point to which everything else had to conform, in *Eckhart’s* case, the principle of his speculation <term>Speculation: here, the practice of philosophical contemplation or abstract reasoning to understand the divine</term> occupies this position instead.

In *Eckhart’s* teaching, the fundamental aim is edification; all his writings arise from the purpose of clarifying the basic questions of religion and leading people onto the path of a holy life. But one would be mistaken to forget his scientific <note>original: *wissenschaftliche*. In this 19th-century context, "scientific" refers to systematic, academic rigor and logical inquiry rather than modern laboratory science.</note> tendency in favor of his religious enthusiasm. Because of his peculiar position, these two are not separated at all in this remarkable man. The passionate preacher is just as much—indeed, by nature much more—a thinker. Religious knowledge and a pious life do not fall apart for him; they are one and the same. He understands "knowing" in the most profound sense; at least for himself, he seeks to think through the series of concepts to their very end, and he communicates his thoughts directly as the best and most powerful stimulus for infinite satisfaction and a holy life. He often directly and explicitly equates the pleasure of knowing with the joy of the pious in the contemplation of God. According to the principles of the school from which he emerged <note>The Dominican Order, which emphasized intellectual study as a form of worship</note>, systematic knowledge is a supreme good for him which, insofar as its object is God, is no different from the blessedness of the pious. From this standpoint, the work on the soul's salvation completely and entirely coincides with the work of intellectually penetrating the sacred. And thus, a standpoint emerges that is not so essentially different from that of modern thinkers. The realm of thought must be expanded independently in all directions; an external authority cannot restrict this striving. And if the moderns carry out the work of thinking for the sake of the...

<meta>This page continues the comparison between Meister Eckhart’s medieval mysticism and 19th-century German philosophy (likely Hegelianism). # Conclusion.

...knowledge for the sake of science <note>original: *Wissenschaft*. In this 19th-century context, this refers to systematic academic scholarship and rigorous logical inquiry rather than just "natural science."</note>, which is its own highest purpose, whereas *Eckhart* pursues it for the sake of the soul's salvation; yet this salvation consists in nothing other than right knowing, and so thinking for the sake of thinking exists in both instances. While the *moderns* <note>Likely referring to 19th-century German Idealists who claimed their philosophy was "presuppositionless."</note> boast of the lack of presuppositions in their pure thinking, they nonetheless have one presupposition: the essence of the human soul. In this, they share common ground with the old Master, who likewise allows no other presupposition. The universality of scientific interest is not actually lacking in the latter because he focuses so purely and exclusively on the soul's salvation and what can serve it, but rather due to the theological and dialectical character of the science of his time. At the very least, it was a natural step to develop this teleological <term>Teleological: an approach that explains things by the purpose or "end" they serve rather than just their physical causes.</term> system so that the significance of every detail of finite appearance for the whole was demonstrated. Indeed, this is the very interest from which modern systems of thought shaped a philosophy of the universe, in which the phenomena of nature and history were equally claimed as expressions of the eternal essence of the Idea. In this sense, modern German speculation is a further development of the Master’s teaching, possessing a more multifaceted interest, a purified scientific form, and a richer basis of intuition and knowledge.

To be sure, the form in which the Master communicated his teachings is not that of a scientific system. He did not produce manuals or textbooks of philosophy, but rather sermons and devotional writings. He attaches his instruction—his spiritual reinterpretation of religious concepts—to allegorically understood biblical passages as if to a coincidental occasion. A strict and simple progression of thought is often missed in these works. And yet, how infinitely superior is *Eckhart* even in this regard to his students and contemporaries! One need only look at how, in the works of *Tauler* or *Rusbroek* <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361) and Jan van Ruusbroec (1293–1381) were influential mystics who were deeply influenced by Eckhart but often wrote in more practical or less strictly philosophical terms.</note>, thought winds along laboriously and without a plan; how a random word becomes the occasion for a long-winded explanation; how subdivisions are created without any real distinction; and how viewpoints are listed and numbered that are essentially the same and differ only in expression. In contrast to this

# Conclusion.

...the development of thought in Eckhart is at least a far more rigorous one; we are dealing here with a thinker who, even if at times in a looser manner than we are accustomed to demanding, communicates thoughts rather than mere intuitions and seeks to prove them strictly. He would believe himself to be making a futile effort <note>original: *einen Schlag in's Wasser zu thun*, literally "striking the water."</note> if he did not explain and prove his propositions. Where the connection of his thoughts does not appear outwardly, it was nonetheless present inwardly; his teaching, though presented unsystematically, is internally a well-structured system strictly developed from a consistently applied principle. This is proven by the unwavering certainty and precision with which he gives identical answers to the most difficult questions across the most diverse contexts. He himself remains very well aware of the highest unity that drives all his individual thoughts out of itself, and he returns to this "One" again and again where—admittedly in ever-new attempts—he sets himself the task of clarifying his propositions or developing them further into detail.

This "One" thing, which forms the animating soul of this remarkable world of thought, is the conviction that man is of a divine nature and always remains so. Therefore, to him, all people are equally called to the highest unity with God; therefore, the nobility of the soul is inalienable, and finite individuality and sin are merely an accident <term>Accident (Latin: *accidens*): In philosophy, a non-essential attribute that does not affect the core essence of a thing.</term> which cannot impair the essence of the soul. For this reason, man need only turn back to himself—to his true essence, his original nobility—to partake in the Highest. And even if this divine predisposition of the soul is hidden in temporal life, this possibility of elevation remains constantly present in the ground of the soul <term>Ground of the soul (German: *Seelengrund*): Eckhart’s term for the deepest, innermost part of the human being where the soul meets God directly.</term>. The doctrine of the inalienable godlikeness of the soul thus takes shape as the doctrine of the godlike "ground of the soul" as the unity of all soulful powers—of the "little spark" <note>original: *Fünklein*. This is one of Eckhart's most famous concepts, referring to the "spark of reason" or the divine element within the human spirit.</note> in contrast to the individual powers that have entered into the multiplicity of activities and perceptions.

A remnant of godlikeness in man had also been taught by Scholastics <note>The mainstream medieval academics who combined Christian theology with Aristotelian logic.</note> and Mystics before Eckhart. Indeed, the absolute inability of man to even receive the gift of salvation would be the consequence if one were to [regard] man as...

<meta>This page concludes the study by contrasting Eckhart’s "spark of the soul" with the views of his predecessors and later theologians. # Conclusion.

...as *Flacius* <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer who held a very pessimistic view of human nature as totally corrupted by sin.</note> wanted to see man as entirely forsaken by God, essentially as a finite devil of flesh and blood. The word "little spark" <note>original: *Fünklein*; Latin: *scintilla*</note> is found in similar usage before *Eckhart*. A related concept existed in the idea of "Synteresis" <term>Synteresis: In medieval theology, the innate spark of conscience that remains even in a sinful person.</term> in the works of *Alexander of Hales*, *Bonaventure*, *Albertus Magnus*, and *Thomas Aquinas*. However, the essential difference is that for these earlier thinkers, this likeness to God appears merely as a remnant, whereas for *Eckhart*, it appears as the true essence of the soul. Furthermore, while they understood it as a quality of a single power of the soul—such as the conscience—he understood it as the deepest ground of the soul, the very essence of its totality.

This collective power of the soul takes the form of "resting contemplation" <note>original: *ruhender Betrachtung*</note> in *Eckhart’s* thought, an unswerving turning toward the Absolute. Elevated above all finite concepts and all the restlessness of specific desires, the "little spark" remains in pure intellectual intuition. The guidance for such a conception of the soul's essence is provided by the philosophy of *Plato* and *Aristotle*; the further development of these elements was carried out by the *Neoplantists* as well as by *Augustine*. The "soul-center" <note>original: *Seelencentrum*</note> of *Plotinus* is the closest precursor to *Eckhart’s* doctrine of the "little spark" of the soul. 

However, *Eckhart’s* merit lies partly in having consistently developed the relationship between this highest unity of the soul and its various powers, and partly in having carried that supreme distinction in the functions of the soul through the doctrines of knowing and willing. He made it the conditioning principle of his entire vision of divine and human things; in this regard, he presents new problems even for the scholarship of our own day. The doctrine of the "soul-ground" <note>original: *Seelengrund*</note> enabled *Eckhart* to speak movingly to the moral consciousness, to develop the conditions of salvation from the soul's own innermost essence, and to cast aside all the shackles of blind authority through a free, spiritual understanding. The soul-ground is pure reason <note>original: *reine Vernunft*</note>, no longer thought of as a "creature" or a property of a creature, but as one with the Absolute itself.

The doctrine of the soul-ground has a closer relationship to the Averroist <note>Followers of the philosopher Averroës, known for their focus on the shared nature of human intellect.</note> conception of the "active intellect" <note>original: *νοῦς ποιητικός* (nous poietikos)</note> as a rational element that is identical in all human persons and devoid of individuality...

<summary>This page defines Eckhart’s "spark of the soul" (Fünklein) as the core essence of humanity rather than a mere remnant of conscience, linking his thought to Neoplatonism and the Averroist active intellect.</summary>

# Conclusion.

Principles. While the Averroists <note>Followers of the medieval Islamic philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), who believed that the individual human intellect was temporary and only the universal "active intellect" was eternal.</note> view personality as something transitory—merely an accidental stage for the activity of the active intellect—for Eckhart, the Eternal is so essentially immanent <note>Immanence refers to the idea of the divine being present within the material world or the human soul.</note> within the personality that the personality itself participates in eternity. This single Absolute is always present in the soul, not so much as a specific power to act or through particular expressions, but as an absolute possibility and receptivity for the Eternal. You have all truth essentially within you; do not seek it outside: this is the supreme principle of Eckhart. You yourselves are the truth, as soon as you desire it; your personality is the vessel of absolute reason, as soon as you cast off all individual limitations and restore this pure rational relationship of yourself to your true essence. The doctrine of the <term>soul-ground</term> <note>original: *Seelengrund*; Eckhart’s term for the deepest, uncreated center of the soul where man is one with God.</note> leads to the doctrine of the inextinguishable immanence of God in the soul.

And the distinction established by Eckhart between the most abstract, "over-absolute" Being <note>original: *überabsolutes Wesen*</note> and the single divine nature as the principle of the divine persons has this deep meaning: that between the world of finite individuals and pure Being, the "Person" stands in the middle, mediating and relating to both. What was merely a helpful concept for <term>Gilbert de la Porrée</term> <note>A 12th-century scholastic theologian who distinguished between the "Godhead" (the divine essence) and "God" (the person of the Trinity).</note> to make the Trinity comprehensible—the distinction between Godhead and God—is here, in Eckhart’s thought, most intimately connected with the deepest principle of his thinking. The concept of the "Person" becomes the center of the system. If one strips away from human individuality everything that disfigures it and hides its essence, what remains is the pure relationship of knowledge to itself—a self-knowledge as a "Person" that coincides with the divine personality. The individual shall become a Person; that is the moral requirement. The individual becomes a Person; that is the process of pure thought. The Person is the eternal fundamental form of all true being, insofar as it is determined by unity with the absolute Being. You are already a Person as soon as you are able to grasp yourself in your essence, and as a Person, you are not distinct from the Son of God. As pure Being, God is immanent within us and is the former of our personality.

With such principles, Eckhart stood very close to pantheism <note>The belief that God and the universe are identical, or that God is everything.</note>. God is not a specific being alongside others,

<meta>This page continues the concluding analysis of Eckhart’s mysticism. It follows from the previous page's discussion of the "Person" as a mediator between finite individuals and the "over-absolute" Being, transitioning here into how God realizes His nature through the soul and the Trinity.</meta>

# Conclusion.

He is all Being, and thus everything that truly exists. He is in all things, and all things are in Him. *Eckhart* is unable to soften this conviction through any kind of figurative or metaphorical representations. He draws the final and most extreme consequence from this proposition, which can no longer be surpassed. God, as pure Being, is pure Reason, which only becomes conscious of itself by entering into the process of <term>person-formation</term> <note>original: *Personbildung*; the philosophical concept of the divine essence manifesting as distinct persons, specifically the Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>. Although this process is given within the pure essence itself, the latter must nevertheless be thought of as existing without any specific determinations—and thus not yet as a "person." In the work of *Hegel* <note>Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770–1831), a German philosopher who, centuries after Eckhart, similarly explored how the Absolute realizes itself through a logical process.</note>, this thought returns, though for him the process of person-formation is not actually conceived as an inner-divine one, but rather as the process of world history. The Trinity, eternally proceeding from the one divine nature—which for him constitutes the true center of all "becoming"—places *Eckhart’s* doctrine at least closer to the fundamental concepts of *Christianity*.

The idea of world history as the realization of the divine personality is foreign to him; but in the eternal Son, all human personalities are potentially included. Indeed, according to *Eckhart's* view, God thinks Himself and loves Himself in our souls just as He thinks and loves Himself in His Son. Furthermore, as a rational being, God stands under the laws of reason; He must act according to the reason of His essence and cannot do otherwise. This is not because He suffers compulsion from something lying outside of Himself, but because it is the law of His own essence that drives Him. There is no arbitrariness in God, but His freedom—that is, the indestructible harmony of His will and His rational essence—is the model of the freedom that we too should achieve: namely, that we cannot act otherwise than in accordance with our rational essence.

Furthermore, if God is all Being, then everything that later emerges into specific reality was established in Him from the very beginning. Thus, the soul was eternally included as an integrating moment in the divine essence and helped to perform all the works of God. God is not complete without the world—indeed, not without every single creature. Never has the standpoint of the immanence <note>The philosophical idea that the divine is manifested in and through the material world and human souls, rather than being purely external to them.</note> of God in all things expressed itself more boldly and ruthlessly. That crude pantheism, of course, which conceives of God merely as the sum of the forces of the universe, remains foreign to the refined and noble Master.

<summary>This concluding page explains Eckhart's radical view of divine immanence, arguing that God realizes His self-consciousness through the soul and that the world is an essential expression of God's rational nature.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the analysis of Meister Eckhart’s philosophical system. It transitions from the previous discussion of the Trinity and the "Person" to how Eckhart views the physical world and his structural opposition to the organized Church of his time.</meta>

# Conclusion.

In the world of the <term>creature</term> <note>In medieval theology, a "creature" refers to any created thing—animate or inanimate—distinguished from the Creator.</note>, he sees nothing but the negation of true Being; yet it remains unclear how he was nevertheless able to perceive in them a participation in the Essence, an indwelling of God, and a reflection of divine glory.

Eckhart developed his system of thought in an obvious, yet to himself hidden, opposition to the Roman Church, its doctrine, and its practice. He believed that it is not dogmatic rules that bring salvation, nor good works, nor the Church or its sacraments, nor the priest or any external authority. Whoever wishes to be saved must experience and live God within themselves. Zealously opposing all <term>justification by works</term> <note>The belief that religious rituals and "good deeds" are the primary way to earn salvation.</note>, all <term>service for reward</term> <note>original: *Lohndienst*; the idea of performing religious duties specifically to receive a reward in the afterlife.</note>, and all belief in external authority, he does not merely abolish the Roman Church, but in principle, the concept of "Church" entirely. Indeed, in the audacity of his formulation of the moral task—exaggerating the principle to the extreme and mocking all finite boundaries—he essentially makes moral action itself impossible. For in truth, the human essence cannot be so dualistically divided that the pure essence of the spirit remains unchangeably immersed in God without any finite purpose, while the active powers work in the world of creatures with specific interests, without the latter canceling out the former. This contradiction against the Roman system drives him to the opposite extreme, and with such conviction, he stands just as foreign to <term>Protestant dogma</term> as he does to Catholic dogma.

Between his metaphysical doctrine and Revelation, between his world of concepts and <term>Holy History</term> <note>The narrative of the Bible viewed as a sequence of historical, providential events.</note>—which alone mediates a living faith that is more than mere conceptual speculation—there exists only a loose and external connection. This medieval thinker is far from doubting Holy History from a rationalistic perspective based on its supernatural character or its miracles; he has no awareness yet of the strictness of mechanical laws of nature. However, history itself is a matter of indifference to him; he seeks the "concept" in its place. When he wishes to reconcile his doctrine with Christian consciousness, he is forced to reinterpret into spiritual terms not just individual biblical passages, but the entire context of the sacred text, in order to bring it into harmony with his teaching. Thus he reinterprets the Creation, thus the <term>Fall of Man</term>, and thus the tradition of Christ himself, which...

# Conclusion.

...the latter is drawn into his speculations almost exclusively as a fertilizing seed from the history of the Kingdom of God.

Eckhart is far removed from the aristocratic mindset of many earlier mystics, who carefully separated the ignorant masses from the initiated, believing that parables and pictorial representations were good enough for the former, while adequate spiritual knowledge was reserved for the latter alone. Eckhart believes that salvation lies only in knowledge, and salvation is for everyone. Therefore, the highest truth must be made accessible to all. Eckhart clearly strives for a popular style of presentation in order to be clear to everyone. We know that he presented his teachings mostly to the "poor in spirit." <note>A reference to the Beatitudes: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 5:3). Here, it also refers to the uneducated or simple-hearted commoners.</note> And yet, he certainly admits that those who cannot grasp the highest truths must be content with the lesser things, and he is inconsistent enough to see the possibility of <term>salvation</term> <note>original: *Erlösung*; literally "redemption" or "deliverance" from sin or the material world.</note> even in these lesser things. In this way, he reconciles himself with the Church. Her way is sufficient for those who are unable to penetrate higher. Why should he dispute it? He lacks any desire for polemics—at least when it comes to fighting against the worldly powers. For he himself hints that he has engaged in scholarly battles. Immersed in the mysteries of the divine essence, he disdains conflict with men. He does not see error in the Church, but rather only half-truth. If one cannot attain salvation *through* the Church, one can nonetheless be saved *despite* the Church—and indeed, even with the help of the Church. And if the <term>practiced person</term> <note>original: *durchgeübte Mensch*; referring to a person advanced in spiritual discipline or "mystical practice."</note> does not need the Church, the unpracticed person and the beginner certainly do. What is permitted to the former is not fitting for the latter, and external matters—harmful to the <term>enlightened</term> <note>original: *Erleuchtete*; those who have attained direct spiritual insight or union with God.</note>—are indispensable for the coarse person, sunken in sensuality, who must first work his way out. But every "coarse" person can and should become an enlightened one; therefore, Eckhart does not haughtily distance himself from the crowd with his preaching but attempts to reach every individual.

Admittedly, it makes a strange impression when one reads these sermons and writings that were intended for the uneducated masses. Even assuming a far deeper understanding of Christian mysteries and a far more heartfelt need for Christian enlightenment among the people of that time: how

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Meister Eckhart’s legacy, specifically addressing how his complex ideas were received by his successors and how they shaped the "German spirit" of theology and philosophy despite his condemnation by the Church.</meta>

# Conclusion.

Few were likely capable of following the Master’s soaring thoughts! Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a German philosopher, theologian, and astronomer who was deeply influenced by Eckhart’s mystical thought.</note> was right to want these writings—which contain much that is good for those who understand—withheld from the hands of the masses. A poor monk of the 15th century, "a sinner, God help him," translated a treatise into Latin that popularized the Master's teaching and presented it in figurative form. It is not fitting, he believes, to throw pearls before swine. <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6; the monk believed Eckhart's deep truths were too precious for the uneducated or unspiritual public.</note> Ecstatic enthusiasm and a fanatical curiosity regarding the secrets of religion were frequent occurrences in the 14th century. It is Eckhart’s peculiar fate that his teaching mostly catered to and promoted these moods, which he fundamentally rejected. In the works of Suso, <note>Henry Suso (c. 1295–1366), a student of Eckhart and a popular mystical writer.</note> who speaks of the Master with the highest reverence, Eckhart’s <term>speculation</term> <note>original: *Speculation*; here meaning deep, abstract philosophical or theological contemplation.</note> becomes a vehicle for those visionary states and that horrific self-torture through which this sensitive, imaginative, and affectionate man appears so strange to us. It was not <term>Christian science</term> <note>original: *christliche Wissenschaft*; in this context, it refers to systematic theology and scholarly study rather than the modern Christian Science denomination.</note> that gained directly from Eckhart; rather, he planted new seeds for a renewal of Christian life. Those who followed him, instead of carrying his doctrine further, tended to weaken it or allow it to wither in principle, but in return, they gained a wide-reaching influence in the realm of practical Christian living.

One must not underestimate Eckhart's effectiveness for posterity, either. To be sure, the writings of the man condemned by the Church were not generally accessible; but they lived on in secret, and there was no shortage of those who openly confessed him as their master. Through Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous Dominican preacher and mystic.</note> and through that precious writing which essentially bears the stamp of the Eckhartian spirit—the *German Theology*—the tradition continued through all following centuries. Eckhart's thoughts are not the accidental ideas of an individual. In all these eccentric propositions, there lives as their soul that form of spirit which is the specific gift of the German people: bold speculation, which leaps over the finite concepts of the intellect and seeks to immerse itself in the heart of things, and a high ethical enthusiasm which lives in the ideal, free from all considerations of utility.
